en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Root Commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
Commentary on the Twenty Verses:

1. In this commentary on the Dhamma, the act of paying homage to the Teacher is for the purpose of generating confidence in the Teacher by way of the Dhamma’s being well-expounded, and for the purpose of generating confidence in the Dhamma by way of making manifest the Teacher’s state of teaching that which is not otherwise.
For it is through faith in both of these that the correct practice of the Dhamma occurs and the accomplishment of great benefit follows.

Alternatively, the words of salutation to the Triple Gem are for the purpose of making known one's own faith in the Triple Gem; that, in turn, is for the purpose of winning over the hearts of the wise;
that is for the purpose of causing them to grasp the commentary; and that is for the purpose of bringing about every form of excellence.
This, however, is the purpose intended by the Teacher: the dispelling of obstacles. For he will say: "Of this act of prostration...

[and so on]... without remainder. Indeed, the performance of homage to the Triple Gem is capable of dispelling obstacles because it constitutes a specific merit that destroys the demerit which creates obstacles, because it is itself an auspicious state, and because it wards off calamities such as fear. How so?

Should it not be understood that this [recollection] possesses the nature of destroying demerit and so forth? For it is said: "Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not overwhelmed by lust," and so on; and:
"Worship of those worthy of worship—this is the supreme blessing"; and: "For those who thus recollect the Buddha and the Dhamma..."
"And for the Saṅgha, O monks, there will be no fear, nor trembling, nor horripilation"—because of this statement.
In that context, he said "as if with compassion" and so forth in order to show the specific qualities of the Teacher to whom he wishes to pay homage.
For one who possesses specific qualities is worthy of homage, and homage paid to one worthy of homage indeed accomplishes the stated purpose.
...it is so. Furthermore, the Blessed One’s teaching in the Vinaya Piṭaka is dominated by compassion (*karuṇā*), while in the Sutta Piṭaka it is dominated by both wisdom (*paññā*) and compassion.
For that very reason, when composing the commentary on the Vinaya Piṭaka, the praise of the Blessed One was made with an emphasis on compassion;
and when composing the commentary on the Āgamas, it was made with an emphasis on both. However, as for the Abhidhamma teaching...
Considering that wisdom is the primary factor, he praises wisdom itself by taking compassion as a simile in the phrase "as [compassion] toward beings," thereby extolling wisdom.
In this context, "as compassion" is an illustrative expression; just as compassion has proceeded toward all beings, so too does wisdom.
The meaning is: "In this way, wisdom also proceeded with respect to all knowable phenomena (*ñeyya-dhamma*). "Among beings" (*sattesu*) is an indication of the object (*visaya*).

"Wisdom" (*paññā*) is an indication of the phenomenon to be indicated. "Of whom" (*yassa*) is an indication of the person who is the basis for that [wisdom]. "Great Seers" (*mahesi*) is its qualification.
"With respect to knowable phenomena" (*ñeyya-dhammesu*) is an indication of the object of wisdom. "All" (*sabbesu*) is its qualification. "Proceeded" (*pavatti*) means it occurred.
This is the demonstration of its function (*kiriyā*). "According to one's wish" (*yathāruci*) is the demonstration of mastery (*vasībhāva*).

In this context, it "scatters" (*kirati*), thus it is *karuṇā*; the meaning is that it scatters away and removes the suffering of others. Beings are called *sattā* because they are attached (*visatta*) to form and so forth.

Furthermore, because that designation (*paññatti*) is established in reference to the continuity of the aggregates (*khandhasantāna*), even those who are free from desire and lust are called "beings" (*sattā*).
They are called [thus]. "Pajānāti" (he understands) means *paññā* (wisdom); the meaning is that he penetrates by way of various modes according to the true nature [of things].

"Yassa" (of whom) is indefinite; by the phrase "having bowed at his feet," it should be understood as definite. "Mahesī" means one who seeks (*esi*) or searches for (*gavesī*) the great aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth;
thus, he is a Great Seer (*mahesi*). "Ñātabbā" means those to be known (*ñeyyā*), in the sense of being maintained as their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and so forth.

“Phenomena” (*dhammā*). Therein, by the word “knowable” (*ñeyyā*), he rejects the unknowability of phenomena. By the word “phenomena,” he rejects the status of a self, a soul, and so forth, in those things that are knowable.
“Knowable phenomena” (*ñeyyadhammā*) means those things which are both knowable and phenomena. “In all” (*sabbesu*) is an expression of exhaustive inclusion;
by this, he shows their state of being unknown [by others]. “Have occurred” (*pavattittha*) means they have arisen. “According to one’s preference” (*yathārucīti*)...

"Whatever inclination" (*yā yā ruci*) means according to one's inclination; "inclination" (*ruci*) is desire, that is, the wish to act. "Whatever has occurred" (*yā yā pavattā*) refers to its various manifestations, or "according to inclination" (*yathā vā ruci*), meaning it has occurred in accordance with that inclination;
thus it is said, "it has occurred according to inclination" (*yathāruci pavattitthā*).

Alternatively, wisdom (*paññā*) that has occurred in whatever way the inclination occurred—that is, it has occurred in exactly that manner—is called "wisdom that has occurred according to inclination."
In this context, it should be understood that compassion (karuṇā) as it occurs in the Blessed One is the illustration of the Blessed One’s wisdom (paññā).
For that is the uncommon Great Compassion, and not any other. The phrase "of whom" (yassa) indicates the person who is the substratum for both compassion and wisdom.
Since there is no compassion without a substratum, when "compassion" is mentioned, the person who serves as its substratum must be indicated.

Since there is no other person mentioned here who could be that [person], and since there is no purpose in abandoning what is near to grasp what is distant, the very individual indicated by the word "yassā" (of whom) is the basis for compassion. Therefore, this is what is meant:
"In whom wisdom also proceeded just as his own compassion did. But how did compassion proceed toward sentient beings?

In what manner does wisdom also proceed with respect to phenomena? It proceeds exhaustively and according to inclination. For the Blessed One’s compassion proceeds toward all sentient beings without exception, leaving no being out;
and while proceeding, it operates according to his own inclination—toward one or toward many—and is not shared by others. Indeed, for others who are plunging into the great flood...
"To those who perceive that 'among beings, there is no one other than me who has emerged from the flood,' compassion arises just as it did for the Blessed One.
The wisdom of the Blessed One operates regarding all phenomena without exception;
and as it operates, it functions unobstructed and unique by way of knowing the intrinsic nature, function, and so forth, both in regard to a single phenomenon and to many phenomena.

According to his inclination, and according to how compassion arises in the Blessed One as he contemplates, all that should be understood through the analysis of Great Compassion-knowledge (*mahākaruṇāñāṇa*) in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*;
and the way wisdom (*paññā*) functions according to his inclination should be understood through the analysis of the unique knowledge not shared with others, and so forth.
By the mention of "wisdom," one should understand the unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times and the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths.

The knowledge of the four analytical insights (*catu-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*)—excluding that [knowledge] because the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti-ñāṇa*) is included under the mention of "compassion"—and other unique knowledges such as the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), the ten powers (*bala*), the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the forty-four bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*), and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge:
these and many other classifications of wisdom (*paññā*) are thus comprised. Therefore, of that...
The manner in which that wisdom functions according to one’s inclination should be understood. Therefore he said: “…like compassion… according to one’s inclination.
Therein, by the mention of compassion, he shows the root of Great Enlightenment (mahābodhi).
For, having seen the multitude of beings beset by great suffering, [one thinks]: “There is no other refuge for them; being myself liberated, I shall liberate them”—thus it is through compassion.
Having stirred his mind and made his aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, and having accumulated the requisites for enlightenment, he gradually attained perfect awakening;
thus, compassion is the root of great enlightenment. By the phrase "toward sentient beings," he shows the purpose of great enlightenment.
For sentient beings are the ones who provide the purpose for great enlightenment; indeed, omniscience exists for the sake of ferrying sentient beings across [to liberation].
It was thus aspired:
"What need have I for this one man who has crossed over and perceives strength?
Having attained omniscience, I shall ferry across the world together with its devas."

By the mention of "wisdom" (paññā), he indicates Great Enlightenment (mahābodhi). For the knowledge of the path (maggañāṇa), which is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for omniscience, and the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa), which is the proximate cause for the knowledge of the path, is called "Great Enlightenment.

By the phrase "in all knowable phenomena," he refers to the aggregates, bases, elements, truths, faculties, dependent origination, foundations of mindfulness, and so forth—the various categories that must be directly known, fully understood, abandoned, developed, and realized by the beings who are to be saved.

And he shows all phenomena (dhammas) distinguished as wholesome and so forth. By the phrase "it proceeded according to his wish," he demonstrates the fulfillment of the purpose through the manifestation of the knowledge of teaching preceded by the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha) and the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa).

For the knowledge of penetration regarding all phenomena occurred at the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka); indeed, it was the knowledge of the Path (maggañāṇa) itself that was the continuum (tantrī).
And the knowledge of reviewing specifically occurred during the seven days in the Jewel House (Ratanaghara). Thus, for those who have penetrated and reviewed [the truths]...
The knowledge of teaching arose regarding the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma and other such events, and specifically regarding the teaching of the Seven Treatises on the Paṇḍukambala stone.
By teaching with the knowledge of teaching, the Blessed One practices for the welfare of sentient beings.
By all of this, he demonstrates both the practice for his own welfare and the practice for the welfare of others. Through the manifestation of Great Enlightenment—
For by the first [phrase], the practice for one's own benefit is shown; by the others as well, the practice for the benefit of others is demonstrated.
By this, he shows that among the four types of persons—those practicing for their own benefit and so forth—the Blessed One is the fourth type of person.

And by that, he demonstrates his own status as the unsurpassed recipient of offerings (*anuttara-dakṣiṇeyya*), his fitness to receive unsurpassed salutation, and, through his activity, his status as having become a field of merit (*khettaṅgata*).

And here, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), the Blessed One’s perfection of all mundane qualities is shown, because it illustrates his uncommon qualities that have attained the state of loftiness among mundane things;

and by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), his perfection of all supramundane qualities is shown, because it illustrates the knowledge of the path which has the knowledge of omniscience as its proximate cause.
Furthermore, by the word "compassion," his approach is shown to be free from defilement; and by the word "wisdom,"...
It shows his departure. By showing his approach, he demonstrates that he was born and raised in the world; by showing his departure, he demonstrates that he is unsullied by the world.

Furthermore, the phrase "toward beings as if with compassion" shows the Blessed One’s conduct in accordance with worldly convention, while the phrase "wisdom functioned toward all knowable phenomena according to his wish" shows it through technical terminology (*samaññā*).

Non-transgression. For when there is a lack of comprehension regarding the true nature of all phenomena, one transcends conventional designations and clings to the view that "a being" or "a soul exists.
Furthermore, among all the qualities of a Buddha, compassion is the beginning because it is the primary cause;
wisdom is the end because there is nothing further to be done beyond it. And by showing this beginning and end, all the qualities of a Buddha [are encompassed].
They are indeed shown. By the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*)—preceded by the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*)—is shown;
for virtue has compassion as its source, since it proceeds from the abstention from killing and so forth, and because it is associated with the first three meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).

By the word "wisdom" (*paññā*), the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*) is indicated. Furthermore, virtue is the beginning of all the qualities of a Buddha, concentration is the middle, and wisdom is the end.
"Conclusion" (*pariyosāna*): in this way, all the qualities of a Buddha are shown to be excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.

Having thus praised the Blessed One in brief by means of all his Buddha-qualities, he spoke the words beginning with "By that compassion" (*dayāya tāyā*) in order to praise, through that specific teaching of the Abhidhamma which is not shared by others, the one whose commentary he intends to compose. Of that...
However, in order to show both the occasion (*nidāna*) and the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) of the teaching, it was said: "By that compassion," and so forth.
The occasion is twofold: internal and external. The internal is compassion; the external consists of the place, time, and other such factors.
The origin is the wisdom of the teaching. Therein, showing the internal occasion, he says: "By that compassion toward beings, my mind was stirred up."
He said: "In this context, 'dayā' (compassion) is intended as *karuṇā* (pity). For it was by being inspired by that [compassion] that he set forth the path of the Abhidhamma discourse.
Regarding the word "tāya" (by that), this pronoun *ta*-suffix is a reference back to what was stated previously.
In the preceding verse, wisdom (*paññā*) was indicated as the primary factor, while compassion (*karuṇā*) was indicated as its qualification; for that [compassion]—
The subordinate [compassion], being merely an illustration of it, has been excluded by way of distinguishing it from that; therefore, it does not deserve the reference "by that" (*tāya*).
And as for the wisdom (*paññā*) which is the predominant factor—that is the source of the teaching, not its instigator—so too, a reference to it is not appropriate.
It is well said that a reference to wisdom is first of all inappropriate; however, regarding compassion (*karuṇā*)...
However, the specific designation [of "compassion"] is not inappropriate, because the two words "dayāya" and "tāyā" stand in a relationship of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

For when two words are coreferential, there exists a relationship between the qualifier (*visesana*) and the qualified (*visisitabba*), as in the case of the form-aggregate (*rūpakkhandha*) and so forth.
Indeed, the word "form" (*rūpa*), being spoken for the purpose of excluding other aggregates, serves as the qualifier; the word "aggregate" (*khandha*)...
And [the relationship] must be specified because of the common status of the words as that which is to be excluded and that which is to be included;

likewise here too, because the two words "dayāya" and "tāyā," being joined by a single case-ending, stand in a state of grammatical coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇa), there exists a relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.
In that context, "dayā" (compassion) is the primary [term], and this [phrase] is a word common to both that which is to be excluded and that which is to be included.
Therefore, this is a term that must be qualified as "of compassion" (*dayāya*).
And just as it is qualified by the word "by that" (*tāya*), so too its status as a correlative reference (*paṭiniddesa*) must be applied.

For the pronoun *ta-* does not function as a qualifier of compassion when it serves as a correlative reference to wisdom (*paññā*), but it does so when it serves as a correlative reference to compassion (*karuṇā*). Furthermore, having set aside wisdom, which is the primary factor, [the text says] "of compassion."
Being connected with this [word], the pronoun *tāya* (“by that”) ought to be a reference to compassion (*karuṇā*) as the subordinate factor.

This is the meaning here: it is not just any compassion by which he was impelled, but rather the Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which serves as the illustration for omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*); by that he was impelled.

But how is compassion (*karuṇā*) to be understood as "pity" (*dayā*)? Is it not stated in the commentary on the phrase "one who has entered into pity" (*dayāpanna*) that "he has entered into a mind of loving-kindness" (*mettacittatam*)?
Therefore, would it not be more appropriate for pity to be loving-kindness (*mettā*), rather than compassion?

If that were so, since it is stated in the commentary on the phrase "one who has not entered into pity" (*adayāpanna*) that "he has entered into a state of lack of compassion" (*nikkaruṇatam*), then it would also be inappropriate for pity to be loving-kindness.
Therefore, wherever the word *dayā* occurs, it should be applied according to the intended meaning (*adhippāya*).
For it is not incorrect to say that when the word *dayā* functions by incorporating the sense of "protecting" within itself, it applies to both loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*).
In this way, there is no contradiction with the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). And as for compassion (*karuṇā*), in the teaching...
It is stated as being by way of a cause, not loving-kindness (*mettā*), as in such passages as, "At that very time, the Blessed One dwelt in the abiding of compassion" (*karuṇāvihāra*).
Therefore, it should be understood that here compassion itself is taken by the word "pity" (*dayā*).
For that [compassion] is uplifting, whereas loving-kindness proceeds in accordance with wisdom (*paññā*).
Why was it stated thus as “among beings”? Is it not the case that by the word “by that [compassion],” compassion having beings as its object is already included?

It is not that it is not included; however, in the preceding verse, all forms of compassion—both those directed toward limited beings and those directed toward unlimited beings—were described in the phrase “compassion toward beings proceeded according to his wish.
Here, however, in order to grasp the aspect of being directed toward unlimited beings, it is said “among beings.”

[The compassion] shown has beings without exception as its object. Therefore, incited by compassion whose object is all beings, he set forth the path of the Abhidhamma discourse for the gods, and not merely for those whose object is the gods alone.

Thus, it is clearly shown that he set forth the path of the Abhidhamma discourse for the gods for the sake of the welfare of all beings, and not solely for the sake of the gods themselves. Alternatively, [the meaning is as follows:]...
“Among beings”: this is not an indication of the object of compassion; rather, by this, the sphere of his exhortation is shown.
For it was not only among the devas that the Blessed One was exhorted by compassion for the purpose of setting forth the path of discourse on the Abhidhamma;
rather, he was exhorted among all beings who are capable of being enlightened, because [his teaching] proceeds for the benefit of all. Therefore, among beings...
“With an uplifted mind” means that his mind was uplifted toward sentient beings, whether as objects or as signs; it should be understood as having an incited heart.

Having thus shown the internal cause (*abbhantaranidāna*), he spoke the words beginning with “at the conclusion of the miracles” (*pāṭihīrāvasānamhi*) in order to show the external cause (*bāhiranidāna*).
Therein, in order to show the time at which the path of Abhidhamma discourse was set in motion by the Blessed One, [he says]: “at the conclusion of the miracles.”

It is said, "dwelling. From the statement, "Dwelling at the end [of his life] in the abode of the Thirty-three," it is understood that the Twin Miracle performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree—which was performed at the end of his life in the abode of the Thirty-three—is what is meant here by "the miracle" (pāṭihīra), and not the miracles performed at the foot of the Bodhi tree and so forth, nor the miracles of mind-reading (ādesanā) and instruction (anusāsani).
This is because [this miracle] is both manifest and proximate.
That very thing should be understood as "grasped. Regarding the etymological meaning of the word *pāṭihāriya*, they say:

"It is called a miracle (*pāṭihāriya*) because it removes its opposite, that is, because it takes away the defilements such as lust. However, the Blessed One has no opposites such as lust that need to be removed.

For even in the case of ordinary worldlings, when the mind is free from secondary defilements, endowed with the eight qualities, and its opposites have been destroyed, the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) arise.
It occurs [there], therefore it cannot be called a "pāṭihāriya" here by way of the conventional usage current there.
However, if the defilements residing in those to be converted are the adversaries of the Blessed One, the Great Compassionate One, and because he removes them, it is called a "pāṭihāriya";
this being so, it is appropriate. Alternatively, [it refers to] the adversaries of both the Blessed One and his Dispensation.
Regarding the *titthiyas*: it is a "manifestation" (*pāṭihāriya*) because of its taking away (*harana*) of them.

For they are taken away and removed by means of supernormal power (*iddhi*), mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsanī*), owing to their inability to display their own views and because their views have been taken away.
Alternatively, this word *paṭi* conveys the meaning of "afterwards," as in such passages as: "When he had entered therein, another brahmin arrived."
Therefore, "patihāriya" (the miraculous) refers to that which is to be performed and set in motion after the mind has become concentrated, free from defilements, and has accomplished its task;
or, it is the subsequent removal [of defilements] once one's own defilements have been removed by the paths of the fourth jhāna.

Furthermore, the miracles of psychic power (*iddhi*), mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsani*) are for the benefit of beings by one who is free from defilements and has accomplished his task.
Furthermore, they must be performed again; and because they remove the defilements of other beings from one's own defilements—which are like green grass—they are called *paṭihāriya*.

Indeed, *pāṭihāriya* is simply *paṭihāriya*. Alternatively, each individual member of the collection consisting of psychic power (*iddhi*), mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsanī*) is called a *pāṭihāriya* because it exists within that collection of *paṭihāriyas*.
Or else, the fourth jhāna and the Path are *paṭihāriya* because they remove opposing factors.
*Pāṭihāriya* means that which is born therein, or that which has that as its sign, or that which has come from that; thus it is a marvel (*pāṭihāriya*).
Here, the word *pāṭihīra* is used as a synonym for *pāṭihāriya*. By the phrases "dwelling at the end" and "in the abode of the Thirty-three," he indicates the time.

For the time for setting forth the path of the Abhidhamma discourse is delimited by the dwelling in the abode of the Thirty-three at the conclusion of the performance of the marvels. Regarding "in the abode of the Thirty-three":
He indicates the location. For that is the place where the discourse on the Abhidhamma and the Path is set forth, because it was delivered by one dwelling there.
3. Furthermore, in order to show the specific location within that, it is said: "At the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree," and so forth. Regarding Yugandhara:
among the Snowy Mountains (Himavat), there is one [peak] forty-two thousand yojanas in height; and the sun travels along a path at that same height.
The meaning is that he sat shining in such a way that, were it possible, he would have outshone Mount Yugandhara.
4–5. Now, pointing to individuals who receive the Dhamma, he says, "From thousands of world-systems," and so forth.
"From all sides" means from all directions having come together from every quarter, or by way of their arrangement, seated all around.
The intended meaning is "by ten thousand world-systems," not "by ten times ten thousand world-systems.
If that were the case, it would imply an arrival by more than forty thousand world-systems, yet this is not what was intended.
Alternatively, it should be construed as "seated all around" (*samantato sannisinnena*); that is, by one who is seated evenly or properly (*samaṃ*, *sammā*), thus "seated."
The meaning is: having sat down without harming one another, having shown reverence for the Blessed One, having lent an ear, and having avoided the faults of sitting;

or alternatively, the construction should be made as: "surrounded by a host of deities who were seated with their mother at their head," or "having placed his mother at the head, he set forth the path of the Abhidhamma discourse."
Now, showing the origin of the teaching, he said: "By the power of that wisdom.

This refers to that wisdom which was compared at the outset to compassion—wisdom capable of knowing all knowable phenomena according to their true nature, capable of knowing the various types of things to be taught, and capable of discerning the inclinations, dispositions, and so forth of the individuals to be awakened; and it is by means of the aforementioned strength of that wisdom.

This is the meaning. By this, he shows the unique (asādhāraṇa) nature of the Abhidhamma discourse, demonstrating that only omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) is capable of being the source (samuṭṭhāna) for the Abhidhamma discourse, and nothing else. "Path" (magga) means the means (upāya).

Because it serves as the means for the realization of the aggregates, bases, and so forth, as well as for the wholesome states and so forth—or specifically for the penetration of the Truths—it is called the "path of the Abhidhamma discourse."

It is called a discourse (*pabandha*). Or rather, a "discourse" (*magga*) is so called because it is like a path (*magga*) due to its length; therefore, this continuous discourse on the Abhidhamma is called the "Path of the Abhidhamma Discourse.
Having said "surrounded by a host of deities," the repetition of the word "deities" indicates their capacity to comprehend [the teaching].
For the Blessed One does not teach those who lack such capacity.

6. Thus, having shown that the Blessed One is worthy of the highest homage through his qualities—namely, compassion and wisdom—and through his setting forth the path of the Abhidhamma discourse as well as his practice for the welfare of others, he now utters the intended homage, saying: "Having paid homage at his feet.
By means of this very praise of the Blessed One, the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma and the state of being well-practiced by the Saṅgha are also demonstrated.

It exists because there is no other state for that which originates from it; therefore, while bowing to that pair of jewels who are worthy of homage, he said: "And his True Dhamma... [and] with palms joined.

In this context, because the Buddha is described as "the Tathāgata, worthy of veneration in the world with its devas," and the Saṅgha is described as "well-practiced... [and] worthy of reverential salutation with palms joined," he says: "At his feet..."
It is said: "Having paid homage, having made the añjali-gesture toward the Saṅgha.

Furthermore, the Dhamma—endowed with qualities such as being well-expounded—is to be honored by recollecting it in that way, according to the statement: "One should dwell having honored, revered, and relied upon that very Dhamma.
It is to be honored in every way through body, speech, and mind; therefore, it is said: "And having honored the True Dhamma."
Regarding the term *Sirīmato*: here they say that *siri* (glory) is a designation for wisdom (*paññā*) and merit (*puñña*).
Alternatively, the excellence of physical beauty and so forth produced by merit—which rests upon those who have performed merit, or which issues from those who have performed merit—is called *siri*.
Since the Blessed One possesses this glory in an eminent degree, he is *Sirīmā*; [the phrase means] "of that glorious one."
7. *Nipaccakārassa* means of the act of prostration. *Ānubhāvena* means by power. *Sosetvā*—having dried up; the connection is:
"I shall explain the meaning after having made it disappear. *Antarāye* means in that which obstructs the explanation of the meaning. *Aseṣato* means without remainder, in its entirety. 8.
Now, in order to illustrate the difficulty of explaining the meaning because the Abhidhamma possesses a profound meaning, [the author] says: "By one of purified conduct and virtue," and so forth.
This shows the act of requesting. One who is "pure in conduct" (*visuddhācāra*) is so through purification from grave offenses (*thullaccaya*) and the like;

one who is "pure in virtue" (*visuddhasīla*) is so through purification from offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*) and formal meetings of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*). Alternatively, one who is "pure in conduct and virtue" is so through purification regarding proper behavior and prohibitions.

By that [term], he shows that it is impossible to show disrespect in the exposition of the meaning. "Carefully" (*sakkaccaṃ*) means having made it a matter of importance. "Requested" (*abhiyācita*) means requested in person. By that, he shows that it is impossible to show disregard in the elucidation of the meaning.
9. Now, in order to show that which he intends to explain, he says: “That which the God of Gods,” and so forth. Therein, “that which” (*yam*) refers to the Abhidhamma.
“God of Gods” (*devadevo*) means the God among the gods of purification, conventional designation, and rebirth.
For in the world, those who are to be gone to as “refuge and ultimate resort,” having become the goal, are called “gods” (*devā*); and the Blessed One has become the goal for all gods.
"Guides" (*nayati*) is said in brief. "Expounds" (*samācikkhi*) means he expounds correctly so that the Elder may understand.

He "leads" (*vineti*) those beings who are to be trained; thus he is a "guide" (*vināyaka*). Alternatively, it means he is a "Self-Become One" (*sayambhu*) because he is devoid of a leader (*nāyaka-virahita*). 10–12.
"And what" (*yañca*) refers to the connection with the phrase "and whatever Abhidhamma he recited to the bhikkhus" (*payirudāhāsi*). "Recited" (*payirudāhāsi*)...
He spoke. By the word "iti," it means "in this sequence. Regarding the phrase "yo dhārito" (that which was borne):

the pronoun *yaṃ*, used here in the accusative case, when connected with the word *dhārito* (borne) in the nominative case, undergoes a shift to the nominative case. Therefore, the construction should be made thus:
"I shall explain the meaning of that which was borne and that which was rehearsed. One who strives (*īhati*) by means of wisdom (*vedena*) through understanding (*paññāya*) is so called.
"By the sage of Videha" means by that ascetic. "Repeatedly" (*abhiṇhaso*) means many times. "Of the Abhidhamma" (*abhidhammassa*) should be connected with the phrase "I shall explain the meaning.
Now, in order to show the basis for this explanation of the meaning, he said "from the beginning" (*ādito*), and so forth.
Therein, "from the beginning" (*ādito*) means at the beginning, in the first council.
13. As for this commentary that has been rehearsed (*saṅgītā*), whose commentary is it?
Since there is no other [work] spoken of [here], it is stated, "whose meaning I shall elucidate. By virtue of the context, it is understood as "of that Abhidhamma.

It is called "rehearsed" because, in the appropriate places for elucidating the meaning, [the meanings] have been collected together, stating, "this is the meaning of this," and "this is the meaning of that."
[The Dhamma] was spoken [by the Buddha], and it was subsequently recited again at the second and third councils.
14–16. *Abhisaṅkhatā* means composed. *Tato* means from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). *Tantinayānugaṃ* means following the course of the tradition (*tantigatiṃ*).
*Bhāsaṃ* means the Māgadhī language. *Nikāyantaraladdhīhi* means by those inserted here and there [from other schools]. *Asammissaṃ* means unmixed.
"Uncorrupted" (*avokiṇṇaṃ*). "Unconfused" (*anākulaṃ*): even within its own collection, it is untroubled and well-defined.

By saying, "I shall clarify the meaning by illuminating that determination of meaning belonging to the residents of the Mahāvihāra, which is unmixed and unconfused," the Theravāda as expounded by the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga and others is thereby included.
Alternatively, having set aside the language of Tambapaṇṇi and [adopted] the Māgadha language...
Having set forth [this work], I shall explain the meaning of the Abhidhamma— meaning which is unmixed and unconfused,
and which constitutes the definitive judgment of the Mahāvihāravāsins— as I illuminate it, showing that "this is the judgment of the Mahāvihāravāsins.
For by that very illumination, it is thus made manifest.
17. Regarding the phrase *tosayanto vicakkhaṇe*: they explain the meaning as "pleasing" by construing it thus:

"having grasped what is to be grasped, pleasing the wise one. If this were so, it would follow that the act of pleasing is accomplished solely by the grasping of what is to be grasped, and not by any other exposition of the meaning.
If the construction is "I shall explain the meaning so as to please," then by that very fact, the grasping of what is to be grasped and all other elucidations of the meaning are accomplished;
thus, through all of that, pleasing is effected. Therefore, the phrase "pleasing, I shall explain the meaning" is appropriate.
18–20. Now, wishing to provide an exposition of the meaning, he says "the meditation subjects" (*kammaṭṭhānāni*) and so forth, in order to avoid the charge of prolixity.
"Commentary on the meaning" (*atthavaṇṇanā*): here, "commentary" (*vaṇṇanā*) means speaking by way of opening up and expanding. "In this way" (*iti*):
in the manner shown by such passages as "having removed from there the [Pali] speech," and so on. This is the reason for generating enthusiasm in the listeners.
He shows [this]. "Abhidhamma-kathā" means the commentary on the Abhidhamma. "Nisāmetha" means listen.
Now, encouraging him firmly by saying that this must certainly be heard, he says: "For this discourse is difficult to obtain.
The commentary on the twenty verses is finished.
In explaining the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the teachers must first clarify its arrangement (*sannivesa*). Therefore, this is said:
“The meaning of the words, the divisions, and the arrangement of the text;”
The reflection by the Sāgaras, the profundity of the teachings,
the grasping of the continuity of the teaching-body,
as well as the Elder’s method of recitation and its cultivation.
“First, through realization and the words of the Buddha and so forth,
there is the accomplishment of the state of an Abhidhammika for the All-Seeing One.
Then, by means of the Vinaya and the Gosiṅga Sutta spoken by the Great Sage,”
The successful accomplishment of what has been spoken is illuminated by means of the introduction.
Having explained all this, the discourse on what was admitted (paṭiññātakathā) has been made;
one should discern this arrangement within the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
Thinking, "When the Abhidhamma discourse is being expounded, it will shine for one who has understood the general meaning of the Abhidhamma through knowing the meaning of the words;
therefore, a thorough mastery of the Abhidhamma itself is appropriate at the outset," he asks for that purpose: "In this context, in what sense is it 'Abhidhamma'?
Therein, the phrase "in this context" refers to what was stated: "I shall elucidate the meaning of the Abhidhamma."
In that [context]: the meaning is, "In what sense is that Abhidhamma—which was promised by the words 'I shall explain its meaning'—called Abhidhamma?
Or alternatively: the meaning is, "In what sense is that which is called 'Abhidhamma-kathā' (Discourse on Abhidhamma) the Abhidhamma mentioned therein?
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of being a dhamma that exceeds and is distinguished from [ordinary] dhamma": here, "dhamma" plus "atireka" (exceeding) constitutes "dhammātireka."
The meaning is: "the Pāḷi that has the Suttantas as its subject matter. *Dhammavisesa* means a distinction of the Dhamma, an excellence of the Dhamma;
the meaning is "variegated Pāḷi. *Dhammātirekadhammavisesattha* means the meaning consisting of the distinction of the Dhamma that exceeds [ordinary] Dhamma.
A singular designation is made for both meanings because they are common to the word *Abhidhamma* in its capacity as a meaning. Therefore...

Since the prefix *abhi*—as in such expressions as “they advance” (*abhikkamanti*) and “of surpassing beauty” (*abhikkantavaṇṇā*)—indicates a sense of exceeding or distinction, therefore this Dhamma is also called “Abhidhamma” in the sense of being a Dhamma that exceeds and distinguishes itself from other Dhammas; this is the connection [of the passage].
Herein, it might be asked: in the case of “they advance” and “of surpassing beauty,” when the prefix is employed before a verbal root...
The prefix *abhi* indicates an exceeding distinction in the action because it functions as a preverb (*upasagga*), which is appropriate;
however, since the word *dhamma* is not a verbal root (*dhātu*), the prefix *abhi* is simply not applicable before it.
Even if it were applied, prefixes qualify actions, and since *dhamma* is not an action, [the prefix] could not indicate an exceeding distinction for *dhamma*.

Is it not appropriate? It is not inappropriate. For it is shown that even when another prefix is employed before a non-verbal root, it indicates an exceeding or a specific distinction, even in the absence of an action.

To clarify this point, he says "just as" and so forth, providing examples such as *aticchatta* (an extra umbrella). "In the same way" means that just as *aticchatta* and so on signify meanings such as an umbrella that exceeds [the ordinary] or a specific type of umbrella.
Just as the prefix *ati*, even when used before a non-verbal root (*adhātu*), indicates the state of being [excessive] in relation to an action that is not actually occurring,
so too this Dhamma is called "Abhidhamma" in the sense of being a specific distinction of Dhamma that exceeds [ordinary] Dhamma;
for the prefix *abhi*, even when used before a non-verbal root, indicates the state of being [pre-eminent] in relation to an action that is not actually occurring.
And the intention is that it illuminates their existence.
They are analyzed by way of a single part [only]: “And what, monks, are the five aggregates? The aggregate of form... pe... the aggregate of consciousness.
And what, monks, is the aggregate of form? Whatever form, whether past... pe... or near, this is called...”
It is analyzed merely by way of a summary and a detailed exposition through such passages as "the aggregate of form," and so on;
however, because it lacks the *abhidhammabhājanīya*, the *pañhapucchaka*, and the *paṭiniddesa*—such as "therein, what is past form? and so forth—it is not analyzed exhaustively.
But when it reaches the Abhidhamma, it is analyzed exhaustively... therefore, this Dhamma also [is distinguished] in the sense of being a specific Dhamma that exceeds other Dhammas.
“Abhidhamma” is said because it possesses the status of an *atireka-pāḷi* (supplementary canon) and the status of a *visesa-pāḷi* (special canon) for all three methods (*naya*) without exception;
this is the intended meaning. Because the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) do not appear together in the Suttanta, there is no Suttanta-bhājaniya in the Indriya-vibhaṅga.
Regarding dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), [the Suttanta-bhājaniya is absent] from such passages as “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,” and so forth.

The conditionality of the conditioning states for the conditioned states has been stated; and having asked [questions] regarding the wholesome and other qualities of those stated states, the answers must be given.
However, since there is no such statement in the form of a summary as "ignorance and volitional formations" here, there is no section consisting of questions on the subject.
In the Sutta, the five training rules beginning with abstaining from the taking of life have been stated.

[The terms] beginning with "veramaṇī" (abstinence). Now, if that abstinence were analyzed by way of its intrinsic nature, function, and so forth, it would be precisely the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya [section], starting with "dislike, abstention," and so on.
Or, if it were analyzed by way of the arising of consciousness, it would likewise be precisely the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya. Furthermore, there is no other way to analyze abstinences.
In whatever manner the Suttanta-bhājaniya ought to be stated [for each rule], there is therefore no Suttanta-bhājaniya in the Vibhaṅga of the training rules (sikkhāpada).

Having explained the meaning of the words in the Abhidhamma, he says "by way of the divisions of the treatise" (*pakaraṇa-paricchedato*) and so forth, in order to make it known by way of its structural limits.
Only a few sections of questions remain; having not been included in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*, they appear in the *Mahādhammahadaya*.
The meaning is that only a few remaining sections of questions have come down by way of the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga* exposition;

it is said that "there is nothing new" because they are included right here. The phrase "only a small portion of the tradition remains" refers to the fact that if the detailed discussion of earth and the other elements—which did not appear in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga* but did appear in the *Mahādhammahadaya*—is the *Mahādhātukathā*, [then this is what remains].
In the *Rūpakaṇḍa*, the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*, and so forth, the detailed exposition of the *Dhātukathā*—
which does not appear in the *Dhātukathā* itself but has come down through the *Mahādhātukathā*— is intended to be considered of minor importance.
As for what was said, "Since it was spoken by disciples, you should discard it," that [objection] is refuted by demonstrating its status as having been spoken by the Buddha.
In order to refute [this], he said, "For he is a Perfectly Enlightened One," and so forth. Regarding the four questions:

when the admission "it is found" or "it is not found" has been taken, the phrase "that which is the ultimate reality" (*saccikaṭṭha*) was stated for the purpose of taking a negation by relying upon that ultimate reality as a basis;

thus, even though there are two sets of five [questions] occurring based on that, they constitute one question. As for "in all places" (*sabbattha*), it refers either to the entire body or to every location.
One [instance] occurs by depending on a single [thing]; one [occurs] by depending on time, namely "always";
and one [occurs] by depending on all [things], namely "in all," provided that aggregates, bases, and so forth are taken.

However, if it is [meant] that "no true reality (saccikaṭṭha) whatsoever—whether place or time—is left ungrasped" by these [terms] "everywhere" and "always," then the investigation proceeds by taking those [terms] in their general sense.

"Done, not by way of division"—this refers to the four [positions] among which it is said "in all," taken with respect to the divisions of truth, reality, place, time, and location, and occurring as "one" in relation to them. Regarding the phrase "of two sets of five":
here, one is "The person is apprehended... [etc. ...is wrong," another is "The person is not apprehended... [etc. ...is wrong," and [the third is] "If you think... [etc.]"
"This of yours is wrong"—this is one; "If these two are difficult to restrain... [as before] ...this of yours is wrong"—this is one;
"They should not be restrained in this way; therefore, as for that which you have restrained... [as before] ...the counter-argument is well-executed"—this is one.

Thus there is the making of a refutation, the making of a counter-argument, and the wrapping up with a counter-argument by establishing an admission from one who desires the refutation to be a valid refutation.
For one who desires the difficulty of counteracting a counteraction, there is the "untying of the refutation" by showing that it is difficult to refute through the demonstration of that [difficulty];
and there is the "cutting off" by means of attributing the state of being unrefuted and so forth— this is one pentad, which is designated in the Commentary as the *anuloma-pañcaka*,
the *paṭikamma-catukka*, the *niggaha-catukka*, the *upanayana-catukka*, and the *nigamana-catukka*.

Regarding one's own position (*sakavāda-pubbapakkha*), it is called the "fivefold sequence-and-contrary" (*anuloma-paccanīka-pañcaka*); regarding the opponent's position (*paravāda-pubbapakkha*), it is likewise called the "fivefold contrary-and-sequence" (*paccanīya-anuloma-pañcaka*).
Thus, two fivefold sets are to be understood. This applies to the remaining questions as well;
thus, eight fivefold sets, or eight modes, are called the "method of debate" (*vādayutti*). "Method" (*yutti*) means a means (*upāya*); the method of debate is "debate-method" (*vādayutti*).
The meaning is: "the means for setting forth a debate.

Having shown the initial defeat in the fivefold sequence of the direct-and-indirect (anuloma-paccanīka), and having likewise shown the initial defeat in the fivefold sequence of the indirect-and-direct (paccanīya-anuloma), he said, "But this...
and so forth, in order to illustrate the matrix (mātikā). "Person" (puggala) refers to the self, the being, the soul (jīva). "Is found" (upalabbhati) means...

"It is obtained by approaching through wisdom. By the phrase "in the sense of the ultimate reality" (*saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena*), he asks: is it not found in the manner of an unreal appearance like an illusion or a mirage;

nor is it to be grasped through hearsay and the like as if it were merely a state of supreme excellence; rather, is it apprehended as a real and supreme state of being? The other, desiring such [an answer], assents.
Again, [he asks] regarding that which is in the sense of the ultimate reality...

He investigates: "Does that which is apprehended as the ultimate reality (*saccikaṭṭha*) and the supreme reality (*paramattha*) exist as something other than its basis, or apart from them, or as their basis;
or does it exist as non-different from them, whether by way of having the nature of being afflicted (*ruppanādi-sabhāva*) or by way of having the nature of being conditioned (*sappaccayādi-sabhāva*)?
He asks this regarding "that which is the ultimate reality... [etc.]... the supreme reality. The other [responds] regarding the person (*puggala*) and the aggregates such as form (*rūpa*), etc.
Not desiring either difference or non-difference, he rejects [the proposition] by saying, "Certainly not.
Then the proponent, having established that what has been admitted as a unity should not be rejected, yet rejects it, raises a censure and says, "Understand the censure.
When asked, "Is a person not apprehended? the proponent, while negating the view of a person, [proceeds].

“He asserts, ‘Yes. Then the other pursues him: ‘The person who is not found in the sense of ultimate reality—is that [person] found to be either different from or non-different from the sense of ultimate reality and the supreme reality?’—for there is no other mode [of being]. He pursues this with the words, “The person who...
in the sense of ultimate reality and the supreme reality. However, since the person is not found at all in any way whatsoever, [the opponent’s position falls away].
Therefore, for one who rejects the doctrine of a person (puggalavāda), the pursuit of otherness and non-otherness is not a pursuit;

because [the opponent] does not incur [a fault], [the respondent] rejects it with "Certainly not. The other, seeing only the appearance of incurring [a fault] despite his admission, and failing to understand the unerring meaning, levels the charge of defeat, saying: "Understand the defeat!"
The word *iti* refers to that by which the matrix (*mātikā*) was established; the intended meaning is "because it was taught in this way.

The phrase *yathā kiṃ* means "in what manner," referring to the illustration of how that which is called "spoken by the Buddha" came to be. The phrase *yatonidānaṃ* means "having whatever as its source," the sense being "having the six internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) and so forth as its cause.
The term *papañcasaññāsaṅkhā* refers to categories of perception associated with the conceptual proliferations (*papañca*) of craving, conceit, and views. *Samudācaranti* means "they operate."

"They overstep. Herein, "if there is nothing" means that among these bases (*āyatana*) and so forth, there is nothing to be delighted in, nothing to be approved of, and nothing to be clung to by way of craving, conceit, and views.
[Objection: Is it not already the case that there is nothing? Why then is it said, "if there is nothing"? [Response: It is true that there is nothing.
However, for worldlings (*puthujjana*) who have not abandoned delighting, approving, and clinging, there are various modes such as "to be delighted in" and so forth.
Since the sense bases and so forth do exist, it is not possible to say of them that "they do not exist";
however, for those who have abandoned delight and so forth, [delight] is entirely non-existent, and thus it is said, "If it does not exist.

"Eseva anto" means that the path which effects the non-existence of delight and so forth, or the fruit which consists in their subsiding, is the end or limit of the underlying tendencies such as lust; the meaning is that they no longer occur.

"Knowing, he knows" means that by means of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), he knows whatever is to be known. For one who possesses only partial knowledge does not know everything that is to be known.

"Seeing, he sees" means that by means of the five eyes—namely, the divine eye, the eye of wisdom, the eye of Dhamma, the Buddha-eye, and the universal eye—he sees whatever is to be seen. Alternatively, "knowing, he knows" means that unlike others who possess distortions (*savipallāsā*), [he knows things as they truly are].
Those who maintain that there is full understanding of sense-desire and form know through the influence of perversion even while they know; the Blessed One is not so.
Rather, because he has abandoned perversion, the Blessed One knows simply by knowing, and because there is an absence of the seeing of views, he sees simply by seeing—this is the meaning.
"Become the eye" means that because he consists of the eye of wisdom and because he produces it among beings, he has become the eye of the world.
The meaning of "Ñāṇabhūta" (Become Wisdom) should be understood in exactly this same way. "Dhammas" refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya*). "Brahmā" is the Path;
because the world arises through them and because they cause its arising, he is "become of that" (*tabbhūta*). He is a "speaker" (*vattā*) because he speaks on the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
He is a "proclaimer" (*pavattā*) because he proclaims while causing the penetration of the Truths to endure for a long time. He is a "guide to the goal" (*atthassa ninnetā*).
One who, having extracted the meaning, shows it; or one who leads others to the ultimate goal, which is Nibbāna.
"Giver of the Deathless" means one who gives the Deathless by generating the realization of the Deathless among sentient beings.

He is the Lord of Dhamma because the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhammā) are dependent upon him. "Embraced by a golden armlet" refers to a small golden armlet or bracelet. It is like a hundred-petaled lotus in full bloom.
"Resplendent and beautiful, as resplendent as a hundred fully blossomed lotuses.

From the moment it was offered with appreciation... [etc] ... "that which is called 'spoken by the Buddha' has arisen"—by this, it appears as if the meaning is being stated that appreciation (*anumodanā*) is the cause for the state of being spoken by the Buddha;
and this being the case, the state of the *kathāvatthu* (the subject of discourse) being spoken by the Buddha [is established].
It would not be so because it was not formally approved; therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows:

having seen that "Mahākaccāyana will analyze this in such a way," the Blessed One laid down the matrix (mātikā) and entered his dwelling. Then, in exactly that manner, the Elder analyzed the matrix established by the Blessed One according to the method given.
Thus it came to be known as "spoken by the Buddha" (buddhabhāsita), for that is made manifest through approval.
With reference to this meaning of "arisen" (*jāta*), it was said: "Thus by the Teacher... [and so on]... such a name has arisen.
Now, in order to show the arrangement of the text, he says: "In that regard, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* treatise," and so forth.
"Eight from the sense-sphere wholesome" means that, taking the four aggregates within the sense-sphere wholesome, one extracts eight consciousnesses from them. First.
Some also say it means "analysis" (*vibhatti*). Regarding the phrase "eighty-nine states of consciousness":

those passages in the Canon where these states of consciousness are analyzed are called "the eighty-nine states of consciousness. The collection of those [passages] is the "Analysis of Consciousness" (*cittavibhatti*);
therefore, it is appropriate to say, "The eighty-nine states of consciousness are the Analysis of Consciousness. Having thus recited the matrix (*mātikā*), one extracts each individual term therein.
Since the consciousnesses have been analyzed, the matrix (mātikā) is also included within that analysis of consciousness;
thus, this statement—that the "Section on the Arising of Consciousness" is twofold by way of the analysis of the matrix words—is also appropriate.
"From the root" means speaking by way of summarizing the wholesome and so forth through their roots, such as "the three wholesome roots," and so on. "The aggregate of feeling," and so forth...

[The classification] is by way of aggregates (*khandha*). By way of doors (*dvāra*), it is as in "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*) and so forth. By way of planes (*bhūmi*), it is as in "in the plane of happiness, in the sense-sphere" (*sukhabhūmiyaṃ kāmāvacare*) and so forth.

Meaning (*attha*) is cause-and-effect. Phenomenon (*dhamma*) is the cause. Classification by way of phenomena (*dhammato nikkhepa*) according to cause is as in "the three roots of the wholesome, the three roots of the unwholesome," and so forth. "Associated with that, originated by that, and belonging to the same category as that..."
The summary by way of cause and fruit is the "exposition of meaning" (atthanikkhepa) through such passages as "the defilements," and so forth.

Alternatively, "dhamma" refers to what is spoken; "meaning" (attha) refers to the meaning of what was spoken. "The three wholesome roots" is the *dhamma*; "In this regard, which are the three wholesome roots?
Non-greed," and so forth, is the *attha*, and that too is *dhamma*. "In this regard, what is non-greed? and so forth is the *attha*. Thus, there is an exposition by way of both *attha* and *dhamma*.

It should be understood. By way of name: this refers to the presentation of the phenomena mentioned as "the three roots of the wholesome" by way of their names, such as non-greed and so forth. By way of gender:
this refers to the presentation of even a single enumerated phenomenon by way of masculine and other genders, such as "non-greed, the state of not being greedy, the state of having no greed.
By way of numerical application: this refers to the occurrence of enumeration. "They bring together" means they make equal or complete; likewise, that which is to be brought together.

"Even here": regarding such passages as "those who partake of true knowledge (vijjābhāgin) and those who partake of ignorance (avijjābhāgin)," when these are understood, the Abhidhamma masters do not become weary while listening to or reflecting upon the Suttas, because they have already understood the meaning of terms such as "vijjābhāgin" as they appear in the Suttas.
It is with reference to this fact that it was said: "They were established for the Abhidhamma masters... so that they would not become weary."
"Without a known beginning" (*anamatagga*) means its beginning is unknown. "The diversity of aggregates" (*khandhantara*) refers either to the variety of aggregates or to the aggregates themselves.
It is "subtle" (*saṇha*) because it is impossible to grasp, and "subtle" (*sukhuma*) because it must be grasped by subtle wisdom; thus, it is the "subtle-subtle phenomenon" (*saṇhasukhumadhamma*).
It is "powerful" (*balava*) because it proceeds with the force of powerful knowledge and because it serves as the sign for that powerful force of knowledge. It is precisely "profound" (*gambhīra*).

“Deeply penetrated” (*gambhīragataṃ*): it is called “deeply penetrated” because it has gone into the depths, or because it possesses deep modes of progression. “In due order” (*yathānupubbaṃ*): according to the proper sequence. “In its entirety” (*nikhilena*):
taught without remainder, or taught by the Blessed One who is free from the five obstructions (*khila*).
“As if it were a form in hand” (*rūpagatamiva*): like a form held in the palm of the hand [is seen] by the eye. “The *Samantapāsādikā* [is so called] because of the knowledge of penetration.”
"He who sees [it] truly exists, not that it does not exist"— thus the Elder speaks with reference to the self (*attā*).
Among the one hundred and eight defilements (*kilesa*) mentioned in the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga*, excluding the one hundred and eight modes of craving (*taṇhāvicarita*),
the remaining sixty-two views (*diṭṭhi*), when doubled by way of their arisen and unarisen states, constitute one thousand five hundred defilements.
They amount to more than ten; however, because a small excess or deficiency does not affect the count, it is stated as "one thousand five hundred defilements.
The non-inclusion of the others—due to their being past and so forth—should be understood as a rejection based on their lack of actual existence.
"Black cloth" refers to cloths that appear dark blue. "Color-elements originated by mind" means those originated by the conditions of mind and temperature.
The meaning to be understood is "the element of color" (*vaṇṇadhātu*). Why? Because matter originated by mind does not go outside;
however, it is stated thus because it has come down through a succession of matter originated by mind.
Alternatively, in the phrase "the element of color originated by mind," having elided the words for condition and temperature, the very same meaning previously stated is [expressed as] "goldenness."
It is like the quality of having a pleasant voice. For here, although "having a pleasant voice" is mentioned in the context of derived matter (*upādinnaka*), there is no sound that is itself derived;
therefore, it is spoken of in this way because it depends upon derived material bases such as the lips and palate.
Likewise, here too, with reference to that which is produced by mind and temperature, he says: "the color-elements are mind-produced."

*Kāyasakkhin* means "one who has direct personal experience. *Dantāvaraṇa* means the two lips. *Mukhādāna* means the opening of the mouth. *Siliṭṭha* means joined together and well-formed. "Having grasped the sign in the sound" means having grasped the sign by way of the sound of the Dhamma, thinking "this is called Dhamma," and not by way of the secondary characteristics of the defilements. Regarding the phrase *ekappahārena*: [...]* In this context, it refers to the simultaneous occurrence of the three factors: the sound, the sign, and the Dhamma. Just as when one says, "This is a bowl," the sound, the sign, and the bowl itself occur simultaneously, so too here the sound, the sign, and the Dhamma occur simultaneously. Therefore, it is said that one should grasp the sign in the sound. One should not grasp the sign by way of the secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*) of the defilements, such as the mark of a woman or a man. One should grasp the sign by way of the sound of the Dhamma, thinking, "This is called Dhamma. This is what is meant by "having grasped the sign in the sound. By means of this method, one should develop concentration. When concentration is developed, the hindrances are abandoned; when the hindrances are abandoned, the jhāna factors arise. Thus, one attains the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion, and which possesses the five factors. Having attained this first jhāna, one should emerge from it and reflect upon it. How? One should reflect thus: "This first jhāna is peaceful and sublime, having transcended the five hindrances and possessing the five factors. Having reflected thus, one should again enter the first jhāna. Emerging from the first jhāna, one should reflect upon it once more. Having reflected, one should again enter the first jhāna. In this manner, one should develop the first jhāna until it becomes familiar and well-mastered. Once the first jhāna is well-developed, one should proceed to the second jhāna. How? One should abandon applied and sustained thought, and attain the second jhāna, which is inward composure, unification of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of concentration. Having attained the second jhāna, one should emerge from it and reflect upon it. How? One should reflect thus: "This second jhāna is peaceful and sublime, having transcended applied and sustained thought, and possessing the three factors. Having reflected thus, one should again enter the second jhāna. Emerging from the second jhāna, one should reflect upon it once more. Having reflected, one should again enter the second jhāna. In this manner, one should develop the second jhāna until it becomes familiar and well-mastered. Once the second jhāna is well-developed, one should proceed to the third jhāna. How? One should abandon rapture, dwell in equanimity, and with mindfulness and full awareness, experience happiness with the body; one should attain the third jhāna, which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindful, and happy. Having attained the third jhāna, one should emerge from it and reflect upon it. How? One should reflect thus: "This third jhāna is peaceful and sublime, having transcended rapture, and possessing the two factors. Having reflected thus, one should again enter the third jhāna. Emerging from the third jhāna, one should reflect upon it once more. Having reflected, one should again enter the third jhāna. In this manner, one should develop the third jhāna until it becomes familiar and well-mastered. Once the third jhāna is well-developed, one should proceed to the fourth jhāna. How? One should abandon pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, one should attain the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity. Having attained the fourth jhāna, one should emerge from it and reflect upon it. How? One should reflect thus: "This fourth jhāna is peaceful and sublime, having transcended pleasure and pain, and possessing the two factors. Having reflected thus, one should again enter the fourth jhāna. Emerging from the fourth jhāna, one should reflect upon it once more. Having reflected, one should again enter the fourth jhāna. In this manner, one should develop the fourth jhāna until it becomes familiar and well-mastered. Once the fourth jhāna is well-developed, one should apply it to the higher knowledges. How? With the mind concentrated, purified, and cleansed, free from blemish, rid of defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, one should apply it to the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. One should recollect one's manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-dissolution, many eons of world-evolution, and many eons of both dissolution and evolution: "There I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, and such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; there too I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, and such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared here. Thus one recollects one's manifold past lives in their modes and details. Having attained this knowledge, one should emerge from it and reflect upon it. How? One should reflect thus: "This knowledge of the recollection of past lives is a super-knowledge, a state of distinction, and a noble attainment. Having reflected thus, one should again apply the mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, one should see beings passing away and reappearing—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and understand how beings fare according to their deeds: "These beings, on account of misconduct in body, speech, and mind, or due to holding wrong views, have arisen in states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell; these beings, on account of good conduct in body, speech, and mind, or due to holding right views, have arisen in a happy destination, even in the heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, one sees beings passing away and reappearing, understanding how they fare according to their deeds. Having attained this knowledge, one should emerge from it and reflect upon it. How? One should reflect thus: "This knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings is a super-knowledge, a state of distinction, and a noble attainment. Having reflected thus, one should again apply the mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. One should understand as it really is: "This is suffering"; one should understand as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; one should understand as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; one should understand as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. One should understand as it really is: "These are the taints"; one should understand as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints"; one should understand as it really is: "This is the cessation of the taints"; one should understand as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. When one knows and sees this as it really is, one becomes disenchanted with suffering, disenchanted with its origin, disenchanted with its cessation, and disenchanted with the way leading to its cessation. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: "It is liberated. One understands: "Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. Having attained this knowledge, one should emerge from it and reflect upon it. How? One should reflect thus: "This knowledge of the destruction of the taints is a super-knowledge, a state of distinction, and a noble attainment. Having reflected thus, one should again apply the mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. One should understand as it really is: "This is suffering"; one should understand as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; one should understand as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; one should understand as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. One should understand as it really is: "These are the taints"; one should understand as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints"; one should understand as it really is:

"pahāra" refers to the third part of the day. "Evaṃ sante" (this being so) means that, having disregarded what was stated previously, he challenges [the opponent] by taking only the statement that the path of recitation originates from the Elder, thereby rejecting the preceding statement.
"Tenetametassa" means of this Vinaya. "In its divisions such as one's own welfare and the welfare of others" refers to the person who recites or hears that Sutta.
It causes one to speak, it causes one to reflect, and it causes one to teach;

thus, the meaning consisting of virtue and so forth is included within that sutta for oneself, and because it must be accomplished by another, it also exists for another—therefore, that sutta "indicates" (sūceti) and "illuminates" (dīpeti) both of those. Likewise, by the word "etc.
(*ādi*), it includes other types of meanings such as those pertaining to the present life and the future life, or mundane and supramundane meanings. And this word "meaning" (*attha*)...

It is a statement employing a beneficial method, not a statement whose meaning is merely what was spoken. If it were so, then the sutta would indicate its own spoken meaning as well as that of another sutta;
thus this [proposed] meaning would follow. Furthermore, since the meaning revealed by a sutta belongs only to that [sutta] itself, the meaning of another is not indicated by it.
And therefore, the other meaning which ought to be indicated or established by it is precluded.
Since there is no self, the mention of "self" should not be made;

and since there is no meaning of speech that is divorced from one's own welfare and the welfare of others, the mention of "beginning" (ādi) should also not be made. Therefore, because the aforementioned meaning is impossible within the Sutta itself, the welfare of oneself and others is spoken of by way of the person who is the locus of the Sutta.
Alternatively, disregarding the Sutta, those classifications of meaning such as one’s own welfare and so forth, which were stated in the Niddesa—namely:
"one’s own welfare, another’s welfare, the welfare of both; the welfare pertaining to the present life, the welfare pertaining to future lives;

the obvious meaning, the profound meaning; the hidden meaning, the concealed meaning; the meaning that must be inferred, the meaning that has been drawn out; the blameless meaning, the stainless meaning..."
The meaning is that it indicates the meaning, the purified meaning, the ultimate meaning, and the purpose; thus, it is called a *sutta* because it "indicates" (*sūceti*) these.

Alternatively, it indicates its own benefit (*attattha*) by the words "he himself is of few desires," and it indicates the benefit of others (*parattha*) by the words "he is one who speaks to others about having few desires.
In this same way, *sutta* passages such as "he himself abstains from taking life" and so forth should be applied. [This applies] to both the *Vinaya* and the *Abhidhamma*.
And having distinguished [the meaning], the meaning of the word *sutta* must be stated;

therefore, it is through a teaching that proceeds according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*) that self-benefit, benefit for others, and so forth, are most eminently manifested, rather than through one that proceeds merely by way of the nature of commands or the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*).
For this very reason, it is said: "It is called *sutta* because it indicates meanings (*atthānaṃ sūcanato*)."

In the Sutta, the nature of the teaching and the Dhamma conforms to the disposition of those to be trained (*veneyya*), whereas in the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, the disposition of those to be trained does not conform to the nature of the teaching and the Dhamma.
Therefore, the teaching of the Suttanta leads to the attainment of absolute welfare for those to be trained;
thus it was said: "And herein, the meanings are well-spoken," and so forth. "It brings forth" means it bears fruit. "Suttāṇā" [means]...

To explain its meaning, it is said: "It protects them well. Furthermore, one should connect the fact that the Sutta serves as the authoritative standard (*pamāṇa*) in the determination of one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and so forth, with its role as their compendium;

and because the Sutta is primary in the elucidation of those meanings, it is distinguished from the others. "This" refers to the statement of the meaning beginning with "Because it indicates the meanings. "Of this" refers to the Sutta.
Regarding "approaching" (*abhikkamanti*): here, the prefix *abhi-* indicates the state of increase, the excessiveness of the act of going. Regarding "by means of the approach" (*abhikkantena*):
here, it is appropriate that the prefix signifies the superiority or distinctness of the beauty, because the prefix functions as a qualifier of the action.

In the cases of "well-known" (*abhiññāta*), "eminent king" (*abhirāja*), and "well-disciplined" (*abhivinaya*), the prefix *abhi-* [is used] with respect to night and so forth, which are characterized, honored, or delimited.

How is it appropriate that they "occur"? Because they indicate the performance of defining characteristics, knowledge, honoring, delimitation, and so forth, and because the night, kingship, and discipline are connected with those respective functions.
They possess growth through development, pervasion, and increase. "By way of objects, etc.
means by way of objects, associated states, kamma, doors, paths of practice, and so forth. "Undifferentiated" refers to [states] among those that are mutually differentiated.
The meaning is that the word *piṭaka* is common and undifferentiated across the Vinaya, Suttanta, and Abhidhamma.
"In the manner already stated" refers to the method beginning with "in this way, by means of the twofold sense.
*Desanā* (teaching) is the imparting or awakening of the meanings to be explained, according to the method of instruction such as commands and so forth, which depends upon the teacher.

*Desanābhedam*, *sāsanabhedam*, and *kathābhedam*: Teaching (*anusāsana*) is the act of instructing and disciplining (*vinayana*) individuals who are to be trained, according to their respective offenses and so forth.
Discourse (*kathā*) is the speaking of the meaning—such as restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)—which is to be explained, consisting in the formulation of words.
The word "division" (*bheda*) should be applied separately to each: [namely] "the division of teaching, the division of the dispensation, and the division of discourse," as appropriate.
"Paridīpaye" means to illuminate. "Bheda" means diversity; the sense is "making a distinction. "Sikkhāpahānagambhīrabhāvaṃ" refers to the profundity of the trainings and the abandonments;
that he should illuminate. "Yaṃ" refers to the scriptures and so forth. "Yathā" means by way of various methods such as thorough mastery, for the purpose of refutation and so on.
Regarding the phrase "In all three of these, there are the Dhamma, the meaning, the teaching, and the penetration":

here, since the *tanti* (the text), the meaning of the *tanti*, and the penetration of the meaning of the *tanti* constitute the domain of the *tanti*, it is logical that they serve as the basis for the meaning, the teaching, and the penetration of the Vinaya Piṭaka and so forth.

However, since the Piṭakas themselves are the *tantis*, how could they logically be the basis for the Dhamma? [The answer is: because the *tanti* as a collection [serves as the basis] for its constituent parts, the *tanti*.
Because they serve as the basis [for the teachings] and because phenomena (*dhamma*) and so forth are difficult to fathom, the Vinaya and the other [teachings] are profound;

thus, the fourfold profundity of the Vinaya and the rest has been stated. Therefore, one should not raise the objection: "Only phenomena and the like are profound because they are difficult to fathom, but the Vinaya and the rest are not.
In that regard, because penetration (*paṭivedha*) is difficult to achieve, [the profundity of] the phenomena and their meanings...
The profundity of the teaching should be understood from the difficulty of its exposition and from the fact that it is difficult to fathom.

Furthermore, its profundity should be understood from the impossibility of producing full penetration (*paṭivedha*) and from the difficulty of the arising of the knowledge that has that [penetration] as its object.

According to the meaning of the statement, "The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*) is knowledge regarding the cause," how is the state of being the cause of phenomena [to be understood]?
Is it to be known? It is so because, in demonstrating the meaning of the component words of the compound term "dhamma-paṭisambhidā," it is stated as "knowledge regarding the cause" (*hetumhi ñāṇa*).

For in the phrase "analytical knowledge of the dhamma" (*dhamme paṭisambhidā*), the word "dhamma" is explained by "regarding the cause" (*hetumhi*), and the word "analytical knowledge" (*paṭisambhidā*) is explained by "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*).

Therefore, by demonstrating that the words *hetu* (cause) and *dhamma* (phenomenon) have the same meaning, as do the words *ñāṇa* (knowledge) and *paṭisambhidā* (analytical insight), the fact that a phenomenon is the cause [of its fruit] is established.
The relationship between the cause and the fruit of the meaning (*attha*) should be understood in exactly the same way.
