In the phrase *yathādhammaṃ*, the word *dhamma* includes both the cause and the entire range of causes and fruits. For this term denotes intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), not merely the state of being a cause for the scriptures (*pariyatti*).

Therefore, "in accordance with the Dhamma" means: in regard to each respective phenomenon (dhamma), such as ignorance (avijjā) or volitional formations (saṅkhāra). "Expression of the Dhamma" (dhammābhilāpa) refers to an unerring expression that reveals both the meaning and the phrasing.

By this, he shows the "expression of the linguistic designation of phenomena" (dhammanirutti) mentioned in the passage: "Knowledge regarding that expression of the linguistic designation of phenomena is the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā).
Alternatively, by the phrase "explaining by way of the direct order (anuloma) and so forth," he [shows] that very linguistic designation of phenomena.
“Expression” (abhilāpa) indicates the speaking and the occurrence of that speech. By the word “intention” (adhippāya),
it is shown that the statement “teaching is a designation” (paññatti) was spoken with reference to the expression of the linguistic formula for phenomena (dhammaniruttābhilāpa),
and not with reference to a designation abstracted from that.
Regarding what was stated as "it is both mundane and supramundane," in order to make clear by way of the manner in which one realizes, that which is realized, and its intrinsic nature, he said:
"It is the understanding of phenomena and so forth, according to their meaning and so on, through their objects and through non-delusion.

For therein, "understanding of phenomena and so forth, according to their meaning and so on, through their objects" has for its objective support the phenomena such as ignorance, the formations and so forth, the meaning of both, and the designation thereof.
Worldly clear comprehension (*lokiyo abhisamayo*). Worldly clear comprehension is the understanding of phenomena and so forth, in accordance with their meaning and so on, through non-delusion;
it has Nibbāna as its object, is associated with the Path, and destroys delusion regarding the aforementioned phenomena, meanings, and designations.
To show another sense of penetration (*paṭivedha*) other than "clear comprehension," he says: "Of this or that," and so forth. "Penetration..."
By the verbal meaning "realization" (*abhisamaya*), it is [the path]; by the verbal meaning "that which is penetrated," it is "penetration" (*paṭivedha*).
Thus, it is appropriate that penetration is the non-erroneous intrinsic nature of each respective phenomenon, such as form and so forth.
In order to show the profound nature of the Piṭakas through the aforementioned phenomena and so on, he said: "Now, because in these Piṭakas... and so forth.
"Whosoever herein": among these various teachings contained in the respective Piṭakas, "whosoever" refers to the penetration (paṭivedha) [of them];

and "herein" in these Piṭakas, it should be construed as "whosoever is the unerring nature (aviparītasabhāva) of those respective teachings. And its "depth of difficulty" (dukkhogāhatā) is to be understood in the manner already stated.
However, this is the distinction here: "The penetration, which consists of the unerring nature, is difficult to fathom precisely because it is hard to understand."
This was said with reference to a wrong grasp of the scriptures (*pariyatti*). "The meaning" (*attha*) refers to both the literal meaning of what was spoken and the purposeful meaning.
"They do not examine" means they do not investigate. "They do not find satisfaction in contemplation" means they do not find satisfaction in the wisdom of contemplation;
the intention is that, having contemplated, they are not to be accepted after being seen and approved by wisdom. "Thus" (*iti*) means in this way, by means of this...

They master the Dhamma for the purpose of gaining release from debate; that is, with the aim of escaping the censure or defeat of a position imposed upon themselves by others. Alternatively, "release from debate" means release from blame.
"For the sake of which" means for the sake of fulfilling virtue and so forth, or for the sake of liberation through non-clinging. "They master the Dhamma" means according to the proper method.
The intended meaning is "they master. "Assa" means "of this Dhamma. "They do not experience" means they do not find [the benefit].
Because those teachings have been wrongly grasped by them, they lead to their harm and suffering for a long time, by way of being causes for criticism, conceit, arrogance, malice, and spite.
One appointed to a storehouse is a "storekeeper"; one who is like a storekeeper is a "storekeeper" (bhaṇḍāgāriko).

A protector of the jewel of the Dhamma. Without regard for any other purpose, it is like that of a storekeeper; thus, "the learning of a storekeeper" (*bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti*) refers to the learning [of the texts].

The restriction "of those very [teachings]" serves to indicate the absence of detailed explanations regarding the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) and the four analytical insights (*catupaṭisambhidā*) within the Vinaya.
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). For in the Verañjakaṇḍa, only the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*) are analyzed.
In the second [case], the restriction “of those very same” is made in relation to the four analytical knowledges (*catasso paṭisambhidā*), not in relation to the three types of higher knowledge;

for those are already analyzed in the Sutta as being included within the six direct knowledges (*chalu abhiññā*). The construction is: “having known, it is being compiled. “Of them” means “of those Piṭakas. “All” means...

The entire word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*) is "conformable" (*anulomika*) by virtue of its conformity with the meaning. To clarify this very state of being conformable, the passage beginning with "But why? was stated.
"Even a single *nikāya*" means even a single collection. The Poṇikas and the Cikkhallikas are [classes of] Khattiyas; their dwelling place is the Poṇika *nikāya*.
And the Cikkhallika-nikāya. Thus, having concluded the eighty-four thousand divisions of the Dhamma from the perspective of the aggregates of Dhamma—
namely the Piṭakas of the Buddha’s word and so forth— all that has been described above, beginning with the first recitation of the Buddha’s word,
as well as other classifications such as the compendia of summaries (uddāna-saṅgaha), were established through the First Council, which was adorned by the manifestation of many wonders.
The passage beginning with "Thus all this is so" was commenced for the purpose of demonstrating that [the Abhidhamma] is known.

It should be understood that by the very demonstration of its status as a Piṭaka— through such expressions as "this Abhidhamma is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka"— the status of the Buddha’s word as being of the Middle [Length] and the Tathāgata’s status as being primarily an Abhidhammika from the outset are likewise shown.

Here it might be argued: "If the status of the Abhidhamma as spoken by the Tathāgata were established, and its status as the word of the Buddha from the Majjhima Nikāya were also established, then that would indeed be proven; however, that very point is not yet proven.

To demonstrate the basis for proving its status as spoken by the Buddha through the Vinaya and other sources, he said: "Among the monks who preserve it," and so forth. "Of all the assemblies" means of all the monastic orders (nikāyas).
"Even while mastering the five Nikāyas": he says this because the entire Vinaya Piṭaka has not been mastered. "The mere Vinaya has been mastered":
he says this because the two Vibhaṅgas have been mastered. There is no offense for one who says, "Master the Abhidhamma," out of a desire not to disparage the Vinaya;
[and likewise for] a monk who has not made room for the Abhidhamma.

By the Blessed One’s statement that there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for one who asks a question while another is speaking, the fact that the Abhidhamma was spoken by the Buddha is illuminated;
for such speech occurs together with the Suttas and other discourses spoken by the Buddha, whereas it is absent among those spoken by outsiders.
Even more compelling is the fact that by granting his approval (*sādhukāra*) to the Abhidhamma, he severed [the Elder’s] doubt.

"Another action than [the first] action is 'another action' (*kammantara*); by describing that—such as a sense-sphere action—as being a fine-material-sphere action, or a black-resultant action as being a white-resultant action, one confuses it.
'In the Conqueror’s Wheel' means in the Conqueror’s Dispensation. 'He deceives' means he misleads. Regarding 'one of the grounds for schism'..."
"It is thus that one is seen to declare: 'This was spoken, this was uttered by the Tathāgata; this was not spoken, this was not uttered by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, he should be addressed as follows... [and so on] ... "It is not the domain of others"... [and so on] ...

"There is no such thing as the function of a nidāna"—[this is said] for the purpose of making clear those things—such as the time, the place, the teacher, and the assembly—that were previously obscure, by means of a nidāna accompanied by instruction therein.
It must be so; for because it is not within the scope of others, the teacher is well-known; because the *okkantika* (introductory) and other [sections] are well-known, the time is well-known;
and because the fact that it was taught in the world of the gods is well-known, the place and the assembly are also well-known—so what need would there be for a "source" (*nidāna*)?
That wherein the aggregates and so forth are analyzed without exception is called the Abhidhamma; therefore, by means of its source...
With the intention that the place where the aggregates and so forth have been penetrated must be without exception, the Elder shows that "the Abhidhamma has the Great Enlightenment as its source.
By means of the method beginning with, "I understand thus:
feeling also has right view as its condition," he examines feeling through its conditions and so forth, by way of the categories of the aggregates and so on, such as the aggregate of feeling.
He dwelt. Regarding "the Dhamma," it refers to the range beginning with the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth.
"Turning over the Dhamma" means turning over the Pāḷi together with its commentary (*sāṭṭhakathā*);

having encountered this challenge from an opponent, he said, "This is the opponent," and so forth. While there exist those like us who know the origin (*nidāna*) and who can serve as a refuge, [he was] without a refuge.
It is as if one were crying out in the wilderness; even though we exist as witnesses to the presence of the cause (*nidāna*), he acts as if making a claim without witnesses.
He does not even know that the cause exists, yet while speaking, he says, "Is this not the cause?

He says "only one" because it was taught solely as the cause of the teaching (*desanā-nidāna*), since it was taught in accordance with the intention (*ajjhāsaya*). He says "two causes" in accordance with the phenomena (*dhamma*) to be realized and those to be taught.
Because it has been taught. It points to the realization as the root of the realization of the Abhidhamma; thus, it is the "source of realization" (*adhigamanidāna*).

"By means of the faith of the aspiration for enlightenment" (*bodhi-abhinīhāra-saddhāya*) refers to that faith by which he directed his mind toward enlightenment and made his vow in the presence of the Fortunate One Dīpaṅkara.
*Sumedhakathāvaṇṇanā* (The Commentary on the Story of Sumedha)
And having transcended the four incalculable [aeons] by way of ascending upwards, there was a city named Amara;

this is how the remainder of the statement should be construed. "With ten" means with the tenth sound, namely: elephants, horses, chariots, kettledrums, conchs, drums, lutes, singing, and clapping, [accompanied by the call] "Eat!
Drink! Feast! To show these by way of illustration, it says "the sound of elephants," and so forth.
It has been said. In the phrase "elephant-sound" (*hatthisadda*), the instrumental case should be understood in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇatthe upayogo*).

Alternatively, one should construe it as "not devoid of the sounds of drums, conchs, and chariots," or "resounding" (*ghosita*). Or else, "elephant-sound" refers to a city possessing the sound of elephants.
In the phrase "Eat and drink indeed," the particle *iti* should be seen as unconnected because its meaning is that of what is well-known (*ñātattha*).
"Endowed with all limbs" means being possessed of gardens, lotus ponds, and so forth. "In characteristics" refers to the characteristics of women and the characteristics of men.
"In ancient lore" refers to the past. "In his own Dhamma" refers to his own threefold knowledge (tevijjā) and the procedures for sacrifice and so forth.

"Reached the further shore" means he has gone to the attainment of the further shore through transcendent knowledge (pāraññāṇa). "I pondered" means "I, having become Sumedha, pondered," says the Teacher.
"He will exist" means that being present, he will come to be. "Not without cause" means not to cease to exist. "In this very way" means exactly thus.
"He does not seek" means he does not strive to go, he does not desire, or he does not pursue.

"He washes" means while washing. "Independent" means having mastery over oneself. "Self-governed" means having one's own power. "Like a great thief" refers to [the state of] misconduct through the influence of greed for the body.

"Cutting off the goods of the wholesome. "Having a protector" means possessing a protector. Since the meaning of such passages as "free from the five faults" is written in certain commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), we shall not explain it here. Regarding the word "in the Dispensation" (*sāsane*):

here, the Dispensation refers to the ascetic training (*tāpasa-sāsana*) and the meditative absorptions and direct knowledges (*jhāna-abhiññā*). "While I am one who has attained mastery"—while I am thus situated, Dīpaṅkara...
The Conqueror has arisen. People purify themselves. By means of synonymous expressions such as "the straight path" and "the way of the journey," he speaks of the path itself.
In the phrase "mā naṃ akkamittha," the word *naṃ* is a particle used merely for the completion of the meter.
In the phrase "ghātiyāma haṃ," both *a* and *haṃ* are particles; alternatively, there is a single particle *ahaṃ* with a nasalized vowel. "Āhutīnaṃ" refers to the sacrificial offerings.

“Manti mama, maṃ vā abrūvi. Even though this was said after the kappa had passed, he spoke the words beginning with “The Bodhi of that Blessed One” in order to include it within the enumeration of the Mother and so forth.
“With ease” means with supreme happiness. “Unequaled” means unequaled by ascetics. Such [happiness] is even more distinguished than the happiness of the higher knowledges (abhiññā).
I obtained the bliss born from the prophecy of my future Buddhahood. Regarding the signs that appear: "it turns back" (*ābhujati*) means it revolves.

"They cry out" (*abhiravanti*) means they make a sound. "Cast out" (*chuddhā*) means expelled. "It does not rise up" (*nuddhaṃsati*) means it does not go upward. "Both" (*ubhaya*) is a dual expression.
"Permanent and eternal" (*dhuvasassataṃ*) means absolute eternity; the meaning is that it is precisely non-perverted. "Of those who have entered a womb" (*āpannasattānaṃ*).
Of pregnant women. As far as the ten directions extend, therein. "In the element of phenomena" (*dhammadhātuyā*) means in the element of phenomena; the meaning is: "I investigate among all phenomena.
That which is full vomits out its water entirely. "These" (*ete*) is expressed in the plural because even a single perfection of giving has many modes.
"It protects what is fastened" is the ellipsis of the sentence; or it is used in the locative sense.
"In the four planes" means in the planes of restraint, such as the *pātimokkha* and so forth.

"With an undivided mind" means having a mind that has not fallen into a state of duality—such as being patient at one time and impatient at another, or patient toward some and impatient toward others.
The "path of truth" (*saccassa vīthi*) refers to the actual object, whether seen or unseen, exactly as it is. "Resolution" (*adhiṭṭhāna*)...

The commitment to the undertaking of wholesome states (*kusalasamādānādhiṭṭhāna*) means that once wholesome states have been undertaken, remaining unshakable is what is called "commitment" (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

"Equanimity toward the earth" (*pathaviyā upekkhanā*) means not undergoing transformation. "Other than" (*aññatra*) means "another. Regarding the phrase "in its own-nature, essence, and characteristic" (*sabhāvarasalakkhaṇe*):

here, "nature" (*bhāva*) refers to non-perversion and actual existence; "own-nature" (*sabhāva*) is that which is together with nature—that is, the non-perverted [state] characterized by one's own function of maturing for enlightenment.
"Flavor" (raso) refers to the characteristic consisting of the relinquishing of the basis for blamelessness and so forth;

it is the characteristic of the flavor of intrinsic nature. "From that, by means of comprehension. "By the splendor of the Dhamma" means by the splendor of knowledge. "Because of trembling" means because of shaking or quivering.
"The remainder" means what was left over. "Do not fear" means do not be afraid. "All calamities" means may all misfortunes and afflictions avoid him.
The commentary on the Sumedha story is finished. "He bestows" means he gives. "By means of yoga" means by way of skillful means (*upāya*). "They gathered together" means they assembled.

"Those whose minds have not reached [the goal]" refers to monks who have not attained *arahantship* and are thus subject to reproach. "Empty" means void or vanished. A *sālakalyāṇī* is the name of a certain tree.
It is said that this arises in a single day only during the time of a Buddha-Cakkavatti.

"Perfection of gender" (*liṅgasampatti*) means being male. "Causes" (*hetu*) means possessing a rebirth-linking consciousness with three roots (*tihetuka*). "Perfection of qualities" (*guṇasampatti*) means attaining the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
"Duty" (*adhikāra*) means performing service for the Buddhas. "Zeal" (*chandata*) means the application of desire for the attainment of Buddhahood.

“Endowed with all limbs” means having made a vow by bringing together the eight factors. “Pakkhika” refers to those who are cripples (pīṭhasappikas). “Paṇḍaka” refers to those devoid of both sexual organs.

To show that Bodhisattvas—during the times of the first aeons following rebirth in the Brahma-world—are indeed devoid of both sexual organs, yet are not included among the category of *paṇḍakas*, [the text says] “included... [and so forth].
It is said that they "do not exist"; or, among the aforementioned faults, they do not exist as being included within them;

or, they are included among or contained within the Bodhisattvas; or, because their cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is limited, the Bodhisattvas who are so included do not become those with dual sexual organs or eunuchs—this is the meaning.
Because they always have a pure range of activity (*śuddhagocara*), they therefore do not cultivate wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
"Wrong view" (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) refers to the views of nihilism, lack of cause, and non-action. "Existence and non-existence" (*bhava-abhava*) refers to both small and great states of existence.
"Bhojaputta" refers to hunters. "Lagana" means attachment. "Aññathā" means dejection. "Gāmaṇḍala" refers to village children. "Rūpa" means a distorted appearance.
This, then, is the introductory narrative (*nidāna-kathā*) by which the fact that the Abhidhamma was spoken by the Buddha is established.
The application of meaning (atthayojanā) should be made.
The commentary on the Introduction (Nidānakathā) is finished. 1.
The Section on the Arising of Consciousness (Cittuppādakaṇḍa).
Commentary on the Words of the Tikamātikā:
Now, in order to provide the discourse on what was promised, he said: “Now, thus for me... [etc. ...the opportunity for speaking has arrived,” and so forth.

“From here onwards” means from the word *kusala-dhamma* (wholesome phenomena) onwards. 1. “Named after all the words”: because the term *vedanā* (feeling) exists in all three sections, it is named after that.

It receives its name from all the words. Is it not the case that there are four phrases—“states associated with pleasant feeling,” and so on—and likewise for the others, making twelve such phrases rather than three?

Therefore, one might object that the expression “from all the words” (*sabbapadehi*) would have to refer to the fact that the word *vedanā* (feeling) is a constituent part of those three phrases, and thus [your statement] is not tenable.
For the word “of feeling” (*vedanāya*) is a separate phrase and does not belong to anyone [else].

It is not a part of a word, nor does it possess the status of being a word such as "pleasure" (sukha) and so forth; therefore, how could that which has received its name [from a single member] be called by the name of all the words?

Because the collection of words that conveys the intended specific meaning is itself a "word" (pada). For a "word" is so called because one goes to (pajjati) or understands (avabujjhīyati) by means of it;
and by this collection of words, namely, "states associated with pleasant feeling" (sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā dhammā), [the meaning is understood].
Since the intended meaning is fully understood when complete, that collection of words is called a "phrase" (*pada*). The others should be understood in the same way.
Therefore, it is appropriate that the name derived from a part of those three collections is also derived from all the words.
Regarding the phrase "both by way of the text and by way of the meaning": here, because of the connection with causal phrases, phrases accompanied by causes, and so forth, it is "by way of the text."
Because they are connected through the meanings of "cause" (*hetu*), "having a cause" (*sahetuka*), and so forth, their mutual relationship should be understood according to their meaning.

For the "Duo of Having a Cause" (*sahetuka*) and the "Duo of Being Associated with a Cause" (*hetusampayutta*) are connected to the "Duo of Causes" (*hetuduka*) because they are linked by causes; thus, the "Duo of Having a Cause and Causes" is connected to both the "Duo of Causes" and the "Duo of Having a Cause" by way of each being a single term. Likewise, the "Duo of Causes and Being Associated with Causes" is connected to the "Duo of Causes" and the "Duo of Being Associated with Causes."

The "pair of the causeless and the caused" (nahetu-sahetuka-duka) is connected to the "pair of causes" (hetu-duka) and the "pair of the caused" (sahetuka-duka) by way of being the first and second members [respectively].
"Like a central whorl" means like a flower-made central whorl. "Like a cluster" means like a collection of flowers and so forth in a bouquet of flowers and the like.
For in the case of a central whorl, a cluster, and so on, the flowers and other elements are mutually connected by means of their stalks and so forth; thus it is a state of such mutual connection.

These have been explained as dyads. "By way of the commonality of dyads" means by virtue of being identical to other dyads, such as those concerning causes (*hetu-duka*), etc. "By others" refers to dyads such as those concerning having an object (*sārammaṇa-duka*), etc.
Those which possess a portion that is not included [in other categories] are "with portions" (*sappadesa*); however, those which do not possess such a portion are "without portions" (*nippadesa*).
Having made clear the very matter thus asked—"Is it well with you, sir?"—it was said, "Is it free from affliction, sir?
Therefore, the word *kusala* has the meaning of being free from affliction (*anāmaya*).
In the *Bāhitika-sutta*, while the steward of the Dhamma was extolling the Blessed One’s bodily conduct and so forth, he said: "That bodily conduct, O Great King..."
"Blameless" refers to wholesome bodily conduct. For there is no action for the Blessed One that results in a pleasant ripening; thus, all blameless bodily conduct and so forth are called "wholesome.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in wholesome states," the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) are called "wholesome.
And these, being associated with insight, the path, and the fruit, do not exclusively result in a pleasant ripening.

The word *kusala* has the sense of "blameless. In the phrase "of the limbs and members" (*aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the locative due to its connection with the word *kusala*;

or alternatively, the meaning is "in the naming, activity, application, and so forth, of the limbs and members. In the phrase "of dancing and singing" (*nacca-gītassa*), the genitive case is also used in the sense of the locative;
or it should be construed as "in the specific instances of dancing and singing. [It is] "by reason of undertaking wholesome states" (*kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samādāna-hetu*).
Thus, this merit increases; therefore, the kamma that produces the ripening of merit is called "wholesome" (*kusala*).

"They are phenomena" (*dhammā honti*) means they exist as mere phenomena—that is, as mere intrinsic nature due to their emptiness. In the phrase "thus contemplating phenomena among phenomena," the word *dhamma* should also be understood here in the sense of emptiness.
Regarding the phrases "they move" (*salayanti*)... [and so on] ... "they shatter" (*viddhaṃsenti*): here, each subsequent term is a synonym for the preceding one.

Alternatively, the three terms beginning with "moving" (*calana*), which illustrate the meaning of "shifting" (*salana*), should be connected respectively with "abandonment by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgappahāna*) and the others.

Unwholesome states, lying within the continuum because they have not been abandoned, are called "vile" (*kucchita*) due to their association with the impurities of lust and so forth, and because they are the cause of manifold suffering.

They lie down according to their form. Since even for those states dissociated from knowledge, knowledge serves as a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), all wholesome states are called "wholesome" (*kusala*) because they are to be set in motion by wholesome knowledge.

Because they are included among both the arisen and the unarisen portions, they cut off the side of defilement belonging to both portions—just like the two right efforts—by means of abandoning and non-arising.
When investigated by wisdom, they are not devoid of intrinsic nature (nissabhāva), but rather they bear their own specific nature;
thus they are called *dhammas*. There is no such thing as a *dhamma* other than the nature that is being borne.
For there are no *rūpa*-elements, etc., other than the qualities of deformation (*ruppana*), etc., nor are there *pathavī*-elements, etc., other than hardness (*kakkhaḷa*), etc.

"Vijjanti" means they exist. However, since it is not possible to make them understood otherwise, the phrase "they bear their own intrinsic nature" (attano sabhāvaṃ dhārenti) is stated by treating the known and unknown phenomena—which possess an intrinsic nature—by way of name as if they were something else.
Showing the distinction among conditioned phenomena (sappaccaya-dhamma), he said:
"Or they are borne by conditions" (dhārīyanti vā paccayehi). "Dhārīyanti" means they are closely borne; the sense is that they are characterized.
"Unwholesome" (*akusala*) is not merely a negation of the wholesome, nor a statement of the mere absence of the wholesome, nor a statement of something other than that;
rather, it is a term for its opposite. To show this, it was said: "Just as non-friends (*amitta*) are the opposites of friends," and so forth.
That it is a term for its opposite is understood by its being classified within the third group, the indeterminate (*abyākata*). For if it were a statement of the mere absence of the wholesome...
The term *akusala* [would be redundant], because no dhamma has been mentioned by it; and by the very expression "indeterminate" (*abyākata*), the third group would not have been stated.
This would result in a dyad—namely, "dhammas that are both wholesome and indeterminate"—rather than a triad.

And this being the case, there would be no purpose for the mention of the term *akusala*. If it were argued that the word "indeterminate" should instead be stated as "non-indeterminate" (*anabyākata*) [to exclude the wholesome], [the same fault would apply].

Since [the indeterminate] arises merely from the absence of both [the wholesome and the unwholesome], then, just as the mere state of being indeterminate exists when speaking of mere absence, the unwholesome would not be a distinct category consisting of the mere absence of the wholesome; thus, there would be no third category called "indeterminate.
Furthermore, since the indeterminate is spoken of as a third category, it is understood that the unwholesome is one [separate] category. Therefore, it is not a term for non-existence.
Because the word *akusala* stands in grammatical apposition with the word *dhamma*— in the sense of "that which possesses its own intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvadhāraṇa*),
and so forth— it does not signify merely the absence of the wholesome (*kusala*), nor does it signify something other than that, precisely because it refers to a third category.

For if unwholesome states were distinct from the wholesome, just as non-mental factors are distinct from mental factors, then by the mention of both "wholesome" and "unwholesome," all phenomena (*dhammas*) would already be included.

Since there is no third category consisting of those not included [in the first two], this dyad might have been stated as "wholesome states" and "unwholesome states," just like the dyad of mental factors (*cetasika-duka*), rather than a third category called "indeterminate" (*abyākata*) being stated; yet it was indeed stated.

Therefore, the word "unwholesome" (*akusala*) does not merely denote "other than that" (i.e., other than wholesome), because the application of the negative prefix *a-* is seen in its usage toward their opposites by way of elimination (*pārisesa*).
In the world they are called "enemies" (amittā), and in the Dispensation they are called "non-greed" (alobha);
here too, the fact that the term *akusala* denotes their opposite is established, and because it is conventionally fixed in that sense, it does not denote anything else.

Furthermore, their state of being opposites should be understood from their contradictory natures and from the fact that they are to be abandoned by them, not from the destruction of the wholesome (*kusala*) by the unwholesome. For the wholesome are not to be abandoned by the unwholesome, owing to the latter's great strength.

However, it is precisely the wholesome [states], accomplished through application, that abandon the ever-latent unwholesome states by means of abandonment through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), and eradication (*samuccheda*).

"Not indeterminate" (*abyākata*) means they have not been so described. But how are these not described? Are they not indeed described by the terms of the triplets and dyads such as "associated with pleasant feeling," and by the terms for eye-consciousness and so forth, as well as the terms for contact and so forth? It is not that they are not described.
However, those [previous] statements are not intended here, because they were not explicitly stated and do not follow through.

For it was not said that "states associated with pleasant feeling" and so forth are "indeterminate"; therefore, since those do not follow through here, there is no lack of being stated as something to be defined by those terms.
But the terms "wholesome" and "unwholesome" do follow through here, because they were explicitly stated.
Since the state of being "unspoken" is understood through the fact that it is not something to be explicitly defined, he said: "The meaning is 'not spoken of as being either wholesome or unwholesome.
Alternatively, "unexpounded" (*abyākata*) means "without result" (*avipāka*); and by the very term "unexpounded," the sense of being without result is understood.

For the word of the Blessed One does not require a logical proof to be understood; rather, it was for the sake of awakening those [beings] whom the Blessed One—being skilled in their dispositions, latent tendencies, conduct, and so forth—intended to instruct.
The phenomena (*dhammā*) have been stated; immediately following their utterance, there is the penetration of their meaning.

However, regarding how the Blessed One spoke those various words for the sake of their awakening by means of the subsequent [words], and how they penetrated that meaning—all of this must be understood by attending upon and listening to a teacher.
Therefore, without stating the reason, [it is said]: "By way of being wholesome or unwholesome..."
The meaning is "because it was not mentioned. And as for one who might say, "Because it was not mentioned by way of being an unwholesome result, wholesome states would follow as being indeterminate;

and because it was not mentioned by way of being a wholesome result, they would also follow as being unwholesome," he too must be refuted on the grounds that "the Blessed One’s speech is established by what is implied" (aññāpakasādhanīyavacano), since even that which is not explicitly mentioned is understood through the nature of the words that follow [the context], and because that which is not mentioned [in this case] possesses the state of being indeterminate.
For it is not the case that the statement "without result" was spoken while the statement "wholesome" was left unsaid,

such that the former would be the subject under discussion and the latter would remain unmentioned as something to be defined by that term; therefore, there is no indeterminate nature for the wholesome,
and in this same way, the application regarding the non-indeterminate nature of the unwholesome should be understood.
Alternatively, the prefix *vi-* signifies opposition (*virodha*), while the prefix *ā-* indicates the state of being directed toward (*abhimukhabhāva*).

Therefore, they are called "indeterminate" (*abyākata*) because they have been explained as being made to face mutual opposition by their own conditions, due to the opposition of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*)—that is, the relationship between the destroyer and the destroyed—just as the wholesome and unwholesome states are opposed.
They are thus "indeterminate. For they are indeed opposed by way of their characteristics, just like the wholesome and unwholesome.

They do not exist. For non-resultantness does not conflict with either painful resultantness—as painful resultantness conflicts with pleasant resultantness—or with pleasant resultantness—as pleasant resultantness conflicts with painful resultantness;
nor do they abandon anything, nor are they to be abandoned by anyone. This is my own opinion on this matter.

Regarding the phrase "characterized by the ripening of blameless happiness" (*anavajja-sukha-vipāka-lakkhaṇa*): here, "blameless" (*anavajja*) means that there is no blame (*avajja*) in these [states];
the sense is that they are faultless, being devoid of the state of being censurable. By this, he shows their state of being beyond censure, not merely their lack of being censurable.

Since there are other faultless states that are indeterminate (*abyākata*), seeing the flaw that those too would incur the status of being wholesome (*kusala*) through the mere term "blameless," he [specifies further].
He spoke the words "resulting in happiness" in order to exclude [other possibilities]. Or rather, here "blameless" (*anavajja*) is stated as the opposite of "blameworthy" (*avajja*);

it is not, as in the *Bāhitika-sutta*, "blameless" in the sense of being tranquilized (*paṭippassaddha*), nor merely "devoid of blame. Therefore, by the term "blameless," the state of destroying blameworthiness is shown.
Furthermore, [this quality] distinguishes [the wholesome] from the indeterminate (*abyākata*) while being common to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
The phrase "having the characteristic of having a result" (savipāka-tālakkhaṇa) was stated in order to show a specific distinction within that characteristic;

for the distinction between wholesome states and unwholesome or indeterminate states is already established by the former [term]. Those which have a pleasant result are "pleasant-resulting" (sukhavipāka).
By this, he shows that while wholesome and unwholesome states share the commonality of being phenomena that possess results, they differ in their specific nature of ripening as a pleasant result.
It is not merely that they possess a pleasant ripening (*sukhavipāka*). Because they are both blameless (*anavajja*) and possess a pleasant ripening, they are called "blameless and pleasant-ripening.

That by which the wholesome (*kusala*) are characterized is a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*); those for whom this blameless and pleasant ripening is the characteristic are "those whose characteristic is blameless and pleasant ripening.
But surely it is those very wholesome states that are blameless and pleasant-ripening; how can they themselves be their own characteristic?

This is because they possess the relationship of the characteristic and the characterized through the state of being known and unknown by the word "wholesome" (*kusala*). For, by way of the meaning of the word "wholesome," the unwholesome are to be characterized; it is logical that what is known by way of the meaning of the words "blameless" and "pleasant result" (*anavajja-sukha-vipāka*) is the characteristic.
Alternatively, that which is characterized is the characteristic, namely, the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). [The wholesome] are blameless and have pleasant results.

And the phrase "and they are characteristics" means that their characteristic is a blameless and pleasant result; thus, the meaning is that those intrinsic natures which, being blameless and having a pleasant result, are perceived as such, are called "wholesome" (*kusala*).
Alternatively, by the word "blameless" he expresses the state of being blameless, and by the words "pleasant result" he expresses the state of having a pleasant result; therefore—

"Blameless and having a pleasant result" is *anavajja-sukha-vipāka*. That [result] is their characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*)—since the word "characteristic" can have both the sense of an instrument and the sense of an object—and it is their very nature (*sabhāva*).

Thus, they are "characterized by blameless and pleasant results" (*anavajja-sukha-vipāka-lakkhaṇā*); that is to say, being characterized by the nature of blameless and pleasant results, they possess that nature, and are therefore called "wholesome" (*kusala*).
In this context, by the term "blameless," the state of being pleasant during its occurrence (*pavatti-sukhatā*) is indicated.
By the expression "resulting in happiness," it shows that wholesome states have happiness as their result.
For the former statement is a description of the characteristic by way of the nature of its own occurrence, while the latter is by way of its capacity to produce a result at a later time.
Likewise, by the former he shows the self-purification of wholesome states, and by the latter, their purity of result. And by the former, the wholesome state...
It turns [the mind] away from the nature of the unwholesome; by the latter [term], it indicates the nature of the indeterminate because of its having a result.

Or alternatively, by the former, through the function of showing the state of being the opposite of faults, it illustrates the quality of destroying the unwholesome in the sense of its "function" (*rasa*);
by the latter, through the sense of attainment, it illustrates the quality of desirable fruition as its "function. And by the former, in the sense of the mode of appearance...
By the first [term], he shows that purification is its manifestation; by the latter, in the sense of being a fruit, he shows that it has a pleasant ripening as its manifestation.
Furthermore, by the first, he clarifies that wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) of wholesome states, for it is from that that they arise blameless.
By the latter, he shows that they are the proximate cause of other wholesome states, for they lead to a pleasant ripening.
"Are they causes? Here, in the phrase "resulting in pleasant ripening" (*sukha-vipāka*), the word "pleasant" (*sukha*) should be understood as a synonym for "desirable.

For wholesome states result in the four desirable aggregates, not merely in the ripening of pleasant feeling. Furthermore, there is no possibility of [wholesome states] resulting in the ripening of the pleasure that consists in the subsiding of the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkha*);
for that is not their ripening. However, if the word "ripening" (*vipāka*) is used in the sense of "fruit," [then it is appropriate].
The state of having a pleasant ripening (*sukhavipākatā*) should also be connected with desirable form by way of its outflow-ripening (*nissandavipāka*).
Regarding the phrase "characterized by blameful painful ripening," both the meaning and the construction should be understood according to the possible application following the stated method.
The state of being fit for ripening is stated as a characteristic of wholesome and unwholesome states; it is not, however, stated as being [the characteristic] of those states themselves.
Since the indeterminate (abyākata) states have the nature of not being subject to ripening (avipāka), it is said: "The indeterminate are characterized by non-ripening.

For just as the wholesome and unwholesome states are described as having the characteristic of being subject to the ripening of pleasure and pain because they are capable of such ripening, so too here the indeterminate states are described as having the characteristic of being non-ripening because they are incapable of ripening. Therefore: "There was action; it did not exist..."

For those who hold views such as "there will be no result of kamma," "there is no result of kamma," "the result of kamma does not exist," "there is kamma but there is no result of kamma," "there will be kamma but there will be no result of kamma," or "there will be kamma and there will be no result of kamma"—

for such types of wholesome and unwholesome states, there is no lapse from their status as wholesome or unwholesome, nor do they incur the status of being indeterminate (*avyākata*). For it is not the case that...

They do not "possess the result of pleasure or pain" because they are of a nature that possesses results (*vipākadhamma*); nor do they "not possess the result" because they lack the state of being of a nature that does not possess results (*avipākadhamma*).
The phrases "wholesome" (*kusala*) or "states" (*dhammā*), and so forth, refer to two pairs of wholesome-state terms, two pairs of unwholesome-state terms, and two pairs of indeterminate-state terms.
These are "synonymous yet distinct in meaning," as each pair within the respective categories is mutually dependent upon the other.
He challenges [the opponent] regarding the identity and difference of meaning, not regarding the concealed [meaning].
Knowing that the challenger asks here because he wishes to state a fault, the teacher says, "What is there [to be said]?

This means: "Since your challenge regarding this identity and difference of meaning is incomplete, first explain what remains. If [the words] were identical in meaning, like the words *Inda* and *Sakka*...
The distinction lies only in the words themselves, not in the meaning; this is the case with the terms *kusala* and *dhamma*.
Just as when "Indo Sakko" is said, it is equivalent to saying "Indo, Indo," so too the expression "kusala dhammā" is equivalent to saying "kusala, kusala.
Likewise, in the other cases, [the expressions] "akusala, akusala" and "abyākata, abyākata" are similar.
And one should apply the similarity of what was stated [in the case of] "indeterminate" (*abyākata*).

Now, if they have different meanings, then just as with the words *Inda* and *Kuvera*, there is a distinction between the wholesome dhamma-terms both phonetically and semantically; likewise for the unwholesome dhamma-terms and so forth.

Thus, by means of six and four phrases respectively, six and four distinct meanings are stated, which constitutes the state of being a "wholesome triad" (*kusala-ttika*) and so on, up to a "wholesome hexad" (*kusala-chakka*) and so forth.
And it would follow that the triads and dyads, etc., would themselves become the tetrad-groups of causes, and so forth.
[Objection: But surely, just as with three instances of the word *dhamma* or three instances of the word *inda*, there is no difference in meaning because there is no difference in form;
thus, they will not constitute a group of six. Therefore, this should instead be stated thus: "It follows that the triads and dyads become the tetrad-triads."

It should not be said that, because there is no purpose in stating three words for "dhamma" as if they were synonymous like three words for "Inda," a difference in meaning can arise even for those words of identical form— just as in the case of the three words for "māsa.
For just as a single word "māsa," though identical in form, denotes time, a specific type of grain, and a gold coin, so too [is it here].

One might argue that since the single word *dhamma* is capable of denoting distinct meanings—just as the word *māsa* (month) serves as the referent for time and so forth—the category of "fourfold" or "threefold" would necessarily follow due to the non-difference in its being the referent (*padattha*) for those distinct meanings it expresses.
However, this does not follow, because a single word does not denote things distinguished by genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*kiriyā*).
For the single word *māsa* [does not denote] time and so forth, which are distinguished by their genus.
In the interim, it functions as a denotative term through the grammatical operation of *sarūpa-ekasesa* (retention of one among similar forms).
And here, if *sarūpa-ekasesa* were applied, the second and third instances of the word *dhamma* could not have been uttered; yet they have been uttered.

Therefore, like words such as *kusala*, these three and two instances of the word *dhamma*—despite their common form (*rūpasāmañña*) regarding the undifferentiated classes of *kusala* and so forth—function by excluding other classes, just as the word *māsa* [denotes specific months] despite its common form.
"Entailing" means that the triads and dyads themselves result in being sixfold and fourfold.

And "the lack of connection between the terms" means that there results a lack of mutual connection between the terms for wholesome phenomena (*kusaladhamma*), as well as between the terms for unwholesome phenomena (*akusaladhamma*) and indeterminate phenomena (*abyākatadhamma*). For it is the connection between pairs [of terms] that is intended.
"It is not [the case] that for all [terms], or for four [of them], there is no mutual [connection]. But why does he raise this objection?

Is it not the case that when words denoting "dhammas" are spoken for the purpose of showing a difference in meaning while their referents are distinct, a lack of connection—as in the case of the words *kusala*, *akusala*, and *abyākata*—is indeed appropriate?
True, this is so; however, having established that lack of connection, the previous objection [remains].

It was stated [previously] that "the state of being a group of six and a group of four would result from the triads and dyads"; however, it should be understood that this objection is raised here in order to establish that [the former position] is irrelevant to the present context.
Alternatively, the construction here should be made as follows:

if, on the other hand, you do not accept the state of being a group of six and a group of four, then there must be a connection between the words according to the method already described; and that [connection] occurs only between those [words] that possess identical case-endings.

The connection between each pair [of words] would be appropriate if they possessed a single meaning; however, since you assert that they have different meanings, it follows that there is no connection between those words.
[To this, he replies: "It does not follow. The particle *ca* has the sense of restriction.

[This refers to the case where] for one who does not accept the state of being a group of six or four, [the words] become purposeless in their preceding and succeeding [order]; whereas for one who accepts that they have different meanings...

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). To show that a connection must necessarily be established in order to avoid falling into a contradiction between what precedes and what follows, he said, "And as for this...

and so forth. For by means of the transposition of words in the question, it demonstrates the identity of meaning (*ekattha*) of the terms *dhammā* and *kusalā*—which are taught here as "wholesome states" (*kusaladhamma*)—and indicates that they do not have different meanings (*nānattha*), even for one who might claim otherwise. Indeed, the states (*dhammā*)...
If one takes [the term] to mean "wholesome" (*kusala*), a contradiction arises with that very question; yet it is stated that the question is such, so a difference in meaning is not tenable.
Regarding the phrase "another method," he challenges the identity and difference in meaning of the three instances of the word *dhamma* in the pairs "wholesome states" (*kusalā dhammā*) and so forth.
In the passage beginning "the unity of the three states," just as by the three words *inda*...

The meaning is this: since the referents of the word *inda* (lord) are one in their nature as "lordship" (*indabhāva*) and are not other than that, there is a unity among the referents of the words *sakka*, *purindada*, and *sahassakkha*;

likewise, since the referents of the three words for *dhamma* are one in their nature as "phenomenon" (*dhammabhāva*) and are not other than that, there results a unity among the referents of the words *kusala*, *akusala*, and *abyākata*.
Thus, "dhamma" is called a "state" (*bhāva*) in the sense of "bearing its own nature" (*sabhāvadhāraṇa*), and so forth.

He says this with the intention that what has been stated is indeed of the nature of existence (*bhāva*) itself, and not of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*). Let it be existence; what follows from that?

If the three words "dhamma" have different meanings, then whichever one among those three things is existence, whatever is not other than that—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—is each individually existence. But as for that which has become existence...
Since two other things (dhammā) are non-existents (abhāva), any two among the wholesome and so forth that are not different from them are also non-existents.

Furthermore, even that single thing which is apprehended as an existent (bhāva), because there is no restriction that this alone is the meaning of "existent" among the three synonymous uses of the word *dhamma*, becomes a non-existent when another thing possesses the meaning of "existent"; therefore, it is also a non-existent insofar as it is not different from that [other existent].
If it were to follow that [a being] has attained non-existence, then the non-existence of all things, such as the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth, would necessarily follow.
For it is not the case that because Indra is a non-human (*amanussa*), Sakkas and others who are not different from him must therefore be human.
But even so, is it not impossible to assert the non-existence of others without the existence of one? And in that regard—

Is it not the case that, because there is no restriction that "it must exist as only one state," once the statehood of all three is established, the statehood of the wholesome and so forth—which are not other than those three—is also established? No, it is not so; for it has been admitted that the three words "dhamma" have different meanings.
Indeed, there is no difference in meaning when all three possess the statehood [of being dhammas], yet you have admitted that very difference. Is this not so?
"Even in the absence of the three phenomena, would there not be non-difference? "Let there be no non-difference;
however, I say 'this is a fault' to you who claim that there is non-difference, for I have neither admitted non-difference nor admitted identity—so how could there be any contradiction on my part?
Or else, [it means] "not other than the phenomena that have reached the state of non-existence."
The statement, "Even the wholesome and so forth would become non-existent," is said without restriction with reference to the fact that any two phenomena whatsoever having fallen into non-existence,
there would be the non-existence of some two [others] among the wholesome and so forth,
because one exists. As for what was also said, "And there might be a non-existence other than those, which is even wholesome," [it refers to the same].
This was stated for the purpose of showing that [the classification] is not fixed, not for the purpose of proving the non-existence of all [such states]. For this is the meaning here:
if there were a state belonging to the unwholesome or the indeterminate, then there might also be a state belonging to the wholesome that is distinct from them.

"All this is without reason" (akāraṇa); here, "reason" (kāraṇa) means logical justification (*yutti*). It refers to the absolute identity of meaning, as in the case of the words *kusala* and *kusala*.

Having considered the absolute difference in meaning—as in the case of wholesome form, the eye, and sound—the objection raised regarding the fault of redundancy, the occurrence of sixes and fours, and the lack of connection or contradiction, is entirely untenable;
for it has been stated that such [faults] do not exist because there is both identity and difference in meaning.
Whatever is consented to, in whatever way consented to, is established through conventional usage by means of that very consent. By consent.

The meaning is that it is "in accordance" (*anurūpa*) or "according to consent" (*yathānumati*); that is, it functions in a manner consistent with that consent as a means of establishing conventional usage (*vohārasiddhi*).

For consent (*anumati*) occurs—due to the absence of a distinction between qualifier and qualified—to clarify the unopened meaning of a word by means of a specific grasping of certain actions, qualities, and so forth, in cases where things are absolutely non-different, such as "Sakka, Indra, Purindada. In some cases, [it occurs] absolutely...
As in the case of distinct things, such as: "Let the *dhava*, the *khadira*, and the *palāsa* trees be brought.

In some instances, due to the relationship between the qualifier (*visesana*) and the qualified (*visesitabba*), there are things possessing both difference and non-difference, such as "a blue lotus" or "a wise person"; by virtue of each respective consent, those various conventional expressions (*vohāra*) are established accordingly.
Therefore, here too, because of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified among the terms for wholesome phenomena (*kusaladhamma*), [the same applies].

Since the occurrence of distinction and non-distinction is accepted when the meaning is the same through the apprehension of specific and general meanings, this conventional usage is established in accordance with each respective acceptance.
Therefore it was said: "All of this is without reason. [The terms] illuminate their own specific meanings;
thus, they are what is grasped by themselves and what is expressed by themselves.

The intention is that they explain the state of being wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth—such as having the ripening of blameless happiness—as the meaning of the word *dhamma*, by way of illustrating that meaning as being of that nature. For the word *dhamma* itself is not the state of being wholesome and so forth.

"By this very [method]" refers to the method beginning with "the word *dhamma* is seen in the sense of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and so forth," and "they bear their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*)," and so on; for it is the same in all these instances.

Since the word *kusala* is seen in the sense of health and so forth, [the etymological definition] beginning with "it causes one to decay in what is base" (*kucchite salayanti*) and so on—which follows the method of qualification—should be understood as set aside by the statement: "Henceforth, I shall speak only of the specific distinction.
For the qualifications such as "associated with pleasant feeling" and so forth do not function by taking up the specific distinctions of "wholesome" (*kusala*) and the rest.

2. Regarding the phrase "with the abandoning of pleasure" (*sukhassa ca pahānā*): here, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) is called "pleasure" (*sukha*), and since that is indeed a pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*), it is said that "it is seen in the term 'pleasant feeling'.

However, this is not because the word "pleasure" has the same meaning as the compound term "pleasant feeling"—as in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling... and so forth. For this [word "pleasure"] has the specific meaning of the faculty of pleasure.
The word "pleasure" (sukha) occurs by taking up bodily pleasure, bodily support, and a specific kind of gratification;
it does not, however, occur by taking up the generality of gratification as in the case of the word "pleasure" in such passages as, "whatever feeling one feels, whether pleasant...
or "whatever is pleasant, that [he regards] as suffering," and so on. That in which the occurrence of the causes of pleasure exists is the root of pleasure.

When there is the arising of a Buddha and the fading away of desire through the transcendence of sensual pleasures, there occurs the manifestation of the causes of happiness, such as merit and tranquility;
therefore, that [form] is called "the root of happiness" and "happiness. And because it is the object of happiness, form is called "happiness.
As for this expression "merits," it is a designation for happiness and a designation for desirable kamma-result.

The meaning is: "the ripening of desirable results for that purpose. Because they are the place, the occasion, and the delight of desirable things such as forms which are conditions for happiness, it is said:

"Heavenly bliss, the joy of happiness. "In this very life" (*diṭṭhadhamme*) means in this present personal existence. "Abidings in happiness" (*sukhavihārā*) refers to the abiding in the first jhāna and so forth.
They are called "unafflicted" (*abyābajjhā*) because they are free from the afflictions of the hindrances and other such obstacles.
It has been said [that Nibbāna is bliss]. Because it extinguishes the suffering of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), or because it is their cessation, it is called "Nibbāna is bliss.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*): regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling], it is said, "The peaceful state that is neither painful nor pleasant is indeed spoken of as bliss";
and regarding pleasant and equanimous [feelings], it is said, "Ānanda, both feelings have been described by me through a particular method as pleasant feeling and painful feeling."
In such passages as "and desired things" (*ca iṭṭhāsūti*), the occurrence [of suffering] is included.

"Basis of suffering" (*dukkhavatthu*) means the locus of suffering. For even though that suffering arises through its own conditions, it arises having those [bases]—birth and so forth—as its foundation when they are present. "Condition for suffering" (*dukkhapaccaya*) refers to the cause of suffering; of suffering...

The meaning is "Janaka" (the producer). "In the place of conditions for suffering" means in the place of undesirable objects such as forms, which act as auxiliaries to the karma that produces suffering.
For the word *paccaya* (condition) applies both to that which produces and to the auxiliary of that which produces. By the word "etc.

(*ādi*), the occurrence [of suffering] in the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*) and so forth—according to the teaching "whatever is impermanent, that is suffering"—is to be understood. [Furthermore, it occurs] in the associated [mental states], in the physical basis (*vatthu*), and in the body born of karma (*karajakāya*).

It is called *sukhā* because it makes one happy (*sukhayati*) by providing assistance when the enjoyment of what has been obtained is maintained. Regarding the term *sukhā*, its neuter gender was not employed here because, in relation to the word *vedanā* (feeling), it merely indicates the state of being pleasant (*sukhabhāva*) rather than the specific quality itself.

That which is desirable by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and by way of intention (*saṅkappa*), or the experiencing of that, or the experiencing of a desirable mode, is "the experience of the desirable" (*iṭṭhānubhavana*).
"Samam" means "evenly" (*avisamam*). It should be construed as: "joined together as if they had attained a state of unity," or "joined together simultaneously" (*samam vā saha yuttā*).
"Arising together" (*ekuppādā*) means those whose arising is one and the same; the sense is that they arise simultaneously through identical conditions.
Since it might follow that material and immaterial phenomena which arise simultaneously would also be mutually associated, it is stated: "ceasing together" (*ekanirodhā*).
Those things that have a simultaneous arising and a simultaneous cessation are associated; thus, the mutual association between material and immaterial phenomena is precluded.
Even so, it might follow that inseparable material phenomena would be mutually associated;

therefore, it is stated, "having a common basis" (*ekavatthukā*). Those things that have a simultaneous arising, a simultaneous cessation, and a common basis are associated. Even so, regarding inseparable material phenomena...

Since one great primary element (mahābhūta) is the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya) for the remaining great primary elements and the derived matter (upādārūpa), those [derived matters] share the same physical basis (ekavatthuka) because of it;

or alternatively, for one who might conceive that the great primary elements which serve as the supports for the eye and so forth constitute a single basis upon which these [derived matters] depend, and thus they are "ekavatthuka," there would follow the consequence that they are associated (sampayutta). To prevent this, it is stated: "they have the same object" (ekārammaṇā).
Those which arise together... [and so on] ...and have the same object, these are associated.

Or, conversely, if it were said "having the same object," then the five sense-consciousnesses and their receiving consciousnesses—which arise in the same cognitive process (vīthi) but have different bases—along with those arising in different processes within another continuum, would all fall into the state of being associated despite having different bases; therefore, it is said "having the same base."
It was stated: "Those which have the same physical basis (*vatthu*) and the same object (*ārammaṇa*) are associated (*sampayutta*).

However, in this way, it would follow that the [mental states] of reception (*sampaṭicchana*), investigation (*santīraṇa*), and so forth, would also be associated; therefore, it was stated: "having the same cessation (*nirodha*)," meaning:

"those which have the same cessation, the same physical basis, and the same object are associated. But do these three characteristics apply even to those that arise separately, or only to those that arise together?
The term "arising together" (*ekuppādā*) is stated for the purpose of showing that, when analyzed, these [mental states] possess these three characteristics while arising simultaneously.

3. Regarding "of immaterial phenomena that have reached the state of fruition": just as the fruits produced from rice seeds and the like are called "ripened" because they are generated resembling their cause and receive the designation "result" (*vipāka*), whereas the roots, sprouts, leaves, stalks, and stems do not.

Thus, the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome [kamma] receive the designation "vipāka" (resultant) because they are similar to their causes by way of being immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), by way of having an object (*sārammaṇa*), and by way of being white, black, and so forth, having attained the state of having matured;
this is stated to show that material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), even though produced by kamma, are not similar to the kamma itself.
"Having the nature of birth and aging" means having the nature of being born and decaying. "The natural state of resultant" means...

It has the nature of maturing (*vipaccanapakatika*). Its state of having the characteristic of maturing consists in its being active within a continuum where ignorance, craving, and conceit are uninterrupted;

by this, its quality of being subject to maturation (*vipākadhammatā*) is established, even though it does not produce the results of wholesome states such as the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) or the results of unwholesome states that are to be abandoned through cultivation.
Furthermore, in the phrase "the state of having matured" (*vipakkabhāva*), the word *bhāva* denotes precisely the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). This is as previously stated.

Having taken both the state of having already ripened (*vipakkasabhāva*) and the state of being in the process of ripening (*vipaccanasabhāva*) as stated for the second [type of clinging], he said: "by way of the negation of both these states. 4.

That which is grasped by one who is possessed (*upeta*) is "clung-to" (*upādinnā*). But what is that possession? By what is one possessed? How is one possessed? And what is it that is grasped by that [possession]?
[This is] in order to exclude those [states] which, while serving as objects for certain supramundane [consciousnesses], are not [clung-to].
It is "endowed" (*upeta*) by means of craving and views—which constitute the fourfold clinging—as expressed by the word *upaya* (means/endowment) connected with the word *upeta*;
and it is endowed with them by way of being their object (*ārammaṇa*), not by way of possession (*samannāgama*).
And although all phenomena of the three planes can serve as objects of clinging, those [resultant aggregates and kamma-produced matter] are "our fruits" because they have been produced by us.

Those kamma-formations of the three planes, which are brought together into a unity by way of their nature as kamma—as if they were being grasped by those who are taking hold—are here termed "clung-to" (upādinna).
Furthermore, the resultant and kamma-produced material phenomena generated by them are also "clung-to" states.
To show all of this, it is said: "by way of making an object," and so forth. This method of meaning should be applied according to what is possible.

"Not by way of sequence of words. Here it is said: if, by way of making an object, things belonging to all three planes are "clung to" (*upādinnā*) by craving and views when one is "endowed with" (*upeta*) them—and since the word "endowed with" (*upeta*) is not established solely in the sense of the object (kamma), there is no reason for taking only kamma—therefore, [this applies] to those things arisen through conditions that belong to all three planes.

It follows that the formations and other effects produced by causes such as ignorance would themselves be "clung-to" (*upādinnatā*), because they too are apprehended by those [causes] as being effects.
Furthermore, by the prefix *upa-*, only the state of being approached is indicated, not the act of making them an object, nor does it exclude their possession;

and by the word *ādinna*, only the state of being taken is expressed, not the specific quality of being originated by kamma. Therefore, [this definition would apply] to all things arisen from conditions.
Does it fall into the state of being "clung-to" (upādinnatta)? It does not so fall, because the teaching proceeds according to the inclinations of those to be enlightened.
For those for whose sake this was said—"clung-to"—they understood the phenomena in the manner described through that very statement.
But now, by one who is unable to understand by that much alone, the meaning should be known upon hearing [the full explanation]. This is the point.
The analysis of the meaning has been made thus: "by kamma.
However, this other meaning should also be seen: the prefix *upa-* signifies "approached" (*upeta*).

For when this prefix *upa-* is employed in a compound, like the word *ati-* in such examples as *atimālā*, it denotes an approach together with its means, as well as a transcending together with its means.
It speaks; and approaching (*upagamana*) is the means (*upāya*) for grasping (*upādāna*); therefore, that which has been approached is "endowed" (*upeta*).

But what is it? That which does not exist when grasping is absent—that is, the karma of the three planes spoken of as "existence conditioned by grasping"—is called "endowed" because it has been approached by the preceding birth's grasping acting as its condition. For nothing whatsoever exists without having been approached.
"One performs karma without desiring it. By means of that karma thus undertaken, there is the grasping for renewed existence (*punabbhava*).
For it is by means of tainted (*sāsava*) karma that beings grasp at renewed existence; therefore, renewed existence is manifest as that which is to be grasped.
And that "existence" (*upapattibhava*), comprising the resultant states of the three planes and kamma-produced matter, is what is referred to here in the phrase "with existence as condition, birth."
Regarding the statement "included within the term 'birth'": by the expression "clung-to" (*upādinna*), the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) is meant;
and it has been declared in the *Dhātukathā* that the state of rebirth consists of the resultant and functional materiality of the three planes.

Therefore, since those very phenomena are called "clung-to" because they are taken up (*ādinnā*), this meaning is established. Having thus explained the meaning of the word "clung-to" (*upādinna*), he concludes that section.
In order to state the meaning of the term *upādāniya* independently, without reference to the term *upādinna*, he said, "having approached the state of being an object," and so forth.
For that very reason, it was stated without distinction: "This is a designation for those things that have become the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for clinging.
Furthermore, that which is subject to clinging (*upādāniya*) is twofold: clung-to (*upādinna*) and not-clung-to (*anupādinna*). Therefore, showing this by means of a qualification:
He said, “They are both acquired (*upādinnā*) and subject to clinging (*upādāniyā*),” and so forth.
5. *Saṃkileso* (defilement) refers to the ten bases of defilement (*kilesavatthu*). *Saṃkiliṭṭhā* (defiled) means being afflicted and tormented by them.

Furthermore, because they are associated with defilement and are non-different from them through such factors as simultaneous arising (*ekuppāda*), they have, as it were, reached a state of identity with them, just as [poisons like] *visa* and the like do.
Just as ghee and other substances become defiled, soiled, afflicted, and tormented, they are said to be "defiled" (saṃkiliṭṭhā) because they are possessed of defilement (saṃkilesa).

The meaning of "they deserve defilement" is that they are fit to receive it by way of being the objective support (ārammaṇa) for defilement. By the phrase "because of not transcending the state of being an objective support," it is precisely the non-transcendence of defilement that is indicated.
The occurrence of the word *saṃkilesika* (defiled) should be understood as being like the words *vatthayugika*, *suṅka*, and *sālika*.

6. The phrase "they exist together with applied thought" (*saha vitakkena*) should be connected as an ellipsis (*vacanaseso*), because the meaning is understood even though it is not explicitly stated.
Taking the single word *mattā* as signifying "measure," the meaning is stated as: "Vicāra alone is the measure (*mattā*) of these."
In other cases where applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are inseparable, *vicāra* alone is their measure;
the meaning is that they do not associate with applied thought beyond that point. This is another interpretation: the word *matta* has the sense of excluding a qualification.

For phenomena accompanied by both applied and sustained thought (*savitakkasavicārā dhammā*) are "with sustained thought" (*savicārā*) because of a *vicāra* distinguished by applied thought; these [latter], however, are [only] by means of *vicāra* alone.
Because they are devoid of the specific quality designated as "applied thought" (vitakka), they are therefore called "accompanied by sustained thought only" (*vicāramattā*);

the meaning is that they possess sustained thought only. Since the state of being without applied thought is established by the term "sustained thought only," the term "without applied thought" (*avitakkā*) is used for the purpose of indicating the existence of others who are likewise without applied thought. For there are those who are without applied thought but possess sustained thought, and there are those who are without sustained thought; thus, [the former] are to be excluded and [the latter] are to be included.

Furthermore, if those [states] were not mentioned, since it would not be shown what among them is to be excluded or included, one would fall into the position that they are merely "without applied thought" (*avitakka*) simply by virtue of being "with sustained thought" (*savicāra*).
However, since the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified can occur as desired, the sequence of the term "without applied thought,

with sustained thought only" (*avitakkavicāramattā*) was established to show the state of qualifying phenomena by means of "having sustained thought only" together with the general quality of being "without applied thought."
Alternatively, those with vicāra are of two kinds: with vitakka and without vitakka. Of these, the first term was stated in order to exclude those without vitakka.
Those without vicāra are also of two kinds: with vitakka and without vitakka. Of these, the third term was stated in order to exclude those with vitakka.
As for those excluded by both [terms]—those without vitakka and with vitakka, as well as those with vicāra and without vicāra—among them:
Either a separate demonstration must be made, or a combined demonstration.

If a combined demonstration were made, if it were said "with applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakkasavicārā*), it would result in being the meaning of the initial term. If it were said "without applied thought and without sustained thought" (*avitakka-avicārā*), it would result in being the meaning of the final term.

But if it were said "without applied thought but with sustained thought" (*avitakkasavicārā*) or "with applied thought but without sustained thought" (*savitakka-avicārā*), [the same fault would follow].

Otherwise, there would result either the non-existence of distinct entities— as if they were internal and external— or the fault of confusion, or else the contradiction of a single [state] being both with thought and without thought,
and both without investigation and without analysis. Therefore, in order to indicate the other by means of seeing one,

and to exclude the "with thought and without investigation" state among the two types that must be mentioned by the term "without thought," he says "without thought and with only investigation" (*avitakkavicāramattā*) while demonstrating the "without thought and with investigation" state.

Alternatively, by the term "without applied thought" (*avitakka*), they are specified as being "with sustained thought only" (*vicāramatta*) in order to show that, due to the absence of applied thought, these states consist of sustained thought alone, and that there is no other phenomenon apart from sustained thought. 7.
"He is equanimous" (*upekkhati*): even while experiencing [feeling], the neutral feeling remains indifferent toward both the mode of pleasure and the mode of pain.
This is the meaning. Alternatively, *upekkhā* is the seeing (*ikkhā*) that is approached (*upetā*), joined (*yuttā*), and not opposed to pleasure and pain; it is experiencing.

"By way of seeing distinction" means by way of seeing diversity. For if those accompanied by rapture were necessarily accompanied by pleasure, then since they would already be established by the term "accompanied by rapture" alone, the term "accompanied by pleasure" would not need to be stated; or [conversely], if they were "accompanied by pleasure," [the same would follow].

If it were stated [only as] "accompanied by rapture" (*pītisahagatā*), one could not say that; therefore, in order to complete the triad, the phrase "accompanied by pain" (*dukkhasahagata*) would have to be mentioned.
And if that were the case, it would lead to the conclusion of the statement: "This is merely the triad of feeling.

Consequently, by saying "accompanied by rapture" and then saying "accompanied by pleasure" (*sukhasahagatā*), one implies that there is also pleasure dissociated from rapture—that which is associated with the body-consciousness of the third jhāna.

The intention is that it shows pleasure as distinct from rapturous pleasure (*sappītika-sukha*). Alternatively, this triad was stated for the purpose of showing the difference between rapture (*pīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*), whose differences are difficult to discern.
For in the phrase "accompanied by rapture" (*pītisahagatā*), only a portion of pleasure is included, not rapture;

whereas in the phrase "accompanied by pleasure" (*sukhasahagatā*), rapture is included, not pleasure. [The third type is] "accompanied by pleasure dissociated from rapture" (*pītivippayutta-sukhasahagatā*).
And since those [states] not included by the former are included by the latter, the distinction between rapture (*pīti*) and happiness (*sukha*) is established.
8. "By way of seeing Nibbāna": this is said with reference to having Nibbāna as its object.

Alternatively, "seeing" refers to that which has not yet reached the state of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) because it arises repeatedly; and the Dhamma-eye (*dhammacakkhu*) performs its function through full understanding (*pariññā*) and so forth.
