The respective illuminations for that should be made.
Regarding "of that man": "Just as if, monks, there were four strong-bowed archers, well-trained, skilled of hand, and practiced, standing in the four directions;
then a man might come and say: 'I [shall... regarding those who are well-trained, skilled of hand, and practiced."
"Taking it from the stalk, I shall bring it even though it is not firmly rooted in the ground"—thus spoke the swift man.

"So very brief" refers to a period of time even shorter than that required for the sons of the gods, who delight in traveling, to run toward one another face-to-face in alternating positions, during which the sharp edges of their hooves meet upon their heads and feet. This is the "time" (samaya) reckoned as a duration.
When it is spoken of as delimited by consciousness, it demonstrates its own limitedness by means of that very delimiting consciousness, saying, "I am thus limited.
And just as I am, so too is the entire duration of the occurrence of wholesome consciousness; thus it demonstrates its limitedness.
The demonstration of sound should be understood according to the method already stated.

Just as for the proponents of substantial entities (*pakativādīnaṃ*) [the production of a single entity] is like that of a great mass, so too for the proponents of atoms (*aṇuvādīnaṃ*), it is like that of a dyad (*dviaṇuka*).

Because it demonstrates the state of being dependent on conditions—since it illuminates the fact that existence is contingent upon conditions—the quality of having its existence dependent on another, which is designated as "cause" (*hetu*), is stated.
However, when there is this state of dependence on conditions, the dependence upon the totality of conditions (*paccayasāmaggī*) is demonstrated by what is designated as "conjunction" (*samavāya*).

Because it is not the primary state [of the Blessed One], its function as an illuminator of that [state] was not mentioned. The meaning is: "The Blessed One prohibited [it] by being the agent (*kattubhūta*) at this time, or by being the instrument (*karaṇabhūta*) at this time.
This same method applies to the previous explanations. "By way of the locus" (*adhikaraṇavasena*) means by way of the support (*ādhāra*).
"In this" (*ettha*) means when the time, which is reckoned as a collection of moments, is taken.
For time (*kāla*) too, though it is delimited by consciousness and non-existent by its own nature, is designated as a "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) precisely because it serves as a support;

this is because of the absence [of the action] before and after that moment when the action occurs at that very instant. "State" (*bhāva*) means action (*kiriyā*). The definition of one action by another action is "the characterization of a state by a state.
For example: "He went while the cows were being milked; he returned when they had been milked"—here, the action of milking [characterizes the other actions].

Just as "going" is the characteristic of the action of moving, so too here, when it is said "at whatever time," the meaning "mindfulness" is understood precisely because there is an absence of connection with any other action and because the state of the word-meaning lacks an absence of existence; thus,
in both cases, the action of the arising of consciousness and the action of the manifestation of contact and so forth are characterized by the action of existence (*sattā*).
In the word *samaye*, the locative case ending is employed because it is connected with a state that serves as a characteristic (*lakkhaṇabhūtabhāva*).
"From the summary" (*uddānato*) means from the enumeration (*uddesa*), that is, in brief.

The defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*), by partaking in the nature of the object-desire (*vatthukāma*), partakes of it by way of being desirable (*kāmanīya-vasena*), not by way of being desired (*kāmana-vasena*); thus, by way of being desired, it is only defilement-desire and not object-desire. It is of two kinds.
By this statement, he includes the sphere of activity for both types of the "conjoined" (sahita).

By that, the two realms—the fine-material and immaterial—have been excluded as the locus of occurrence for sense-desire objects (*vatthukāma*). But is it not the case that both types of the conjoined also occur in the fine-material and immaterial realms?
For the phenomena belonging to those realms are themselves sense-desire objects, and the lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms has those very phenomena as its objective support.

Is it because of the establishment of the state of defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*)? No, because here [in this context] sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), which is characterized by abundant defilements, is included under the category of "defilement-desire" (*kilesakāma*).
And having done so, attachment to sense-sphere phenomena (*kāmāvacaradhamma*) occurring within the form and formless realms is not included here, due to its subtlety.
Even though all types of desire have been indicated by the summary statement, "In brief, there are two kinds of desire."

For here, in the phrase "this is twofold," it is precisely those states which have the basis of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) as their foundation—being delimited by their mutual association—that are included as a portion of that [twofold division].

Alternatively, since the entire defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*), consisting of the divisions of sensual craving (*kāmatanha*), form-craving (*rūpatanha*), formless-craving (*arūpatanha*), and craving for cessation (*nirodhatanha*), occurs here [in this context], the statement "this is twofold" was said with reference to its occurrence in its entirety; and thus, even the object-desire (*vatthukāma*) [is included].
And here, even a small amount—merely the ripening-result (vipāka) of the fine-material and immaterial spheres—is not sufficient;

nevertheless, because they possess the complete set of bases (vatthu), only the phenomena of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) are taken here. By doing so, the simile of the "range of the weapon" becomes appropriate.

In the phrase "he develops the path for rebirth in the fine-material sphere," the word "fine-material existence" (rūpabhava) is stated as simply "fine-material" (rūpa) by eliding the latter member of the compound; likewise here as well.
A deletion of the latter member of the compound is to be understood; otherwise, it would have been called "cittaṃ kāmāvacarāvacaraṃ" (consciousness belonging to the sphere of sense-desire).

In the passage beginning with "by way of making an object," the word "kāma" refers to all craving; therefore, the phrase "if this [craving]... and so forth was stated. Furthermore, while one might expect the form "kāmāvacāraṃ" (belonging to the sphere of sense-desire) from the analysis "it causes one to move within sense-desires (kāme)," the vowel of the suffix "-ca-" has been shortened.

"By conventional usage" means by a word that has become conventional (*ruḷha*) among those associated with knowledge; or else, by a word that has become conventional among those dissociated from knowledge—because they resemble those [associated states] in their having faultless and pleasant results after having occurred among those associated with knowledge.

Alternatively, it refers to the case where, having grasped some sign (*nimitta*), even when other factors associated with that sign are present, one applies a designation (*sammuti*) to a particular object due to the long-standing habituation of that convention, even in the absence of the actual sign.
Conventional usage (*ruḷhi*) refers to such expressions as "it lies on the earth, thus it is a buffalo" (*mahiṃsa*) or "they go, thus they are cows" (*gāvo*);
in the same way, the conventional nature of the word *kusala* should be understood. In the *Paññāniddesa*, it is stated in the Abhidhamma that it means "skill" (*kosalla*);

and since the application of the word *kusala* occurs through its state [of being skill], the expression "it is *kusala* because of its connection with skill" (*kosallayogā kusalan*) is the method of the Abhidhamma. By saying "it is *kusala*," it expresses the state of being *kusala*.

Since fruition (*vipāka*) and the other [types of wholesome states] lack the quality of being the opposite of faultiness, only the wholesome (*kusala*) is stated to have the characteristic of faultlessness (*anavajja*).
The restriction "only the characteristic of faultlessness" is made in order to preclude the status of being a characteristic for that which has the nature of a pleasant fruition (*sukhavipāka*);

and that preclusion is made because its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*) consists in the desire for sense objects (*vatthukāmatā*). Its essence (*rasa*) is the state of purification (*vodānabhāva*), in the sense of excellence (*sampatti*).
In terms of its fruit and its manifestation, it has a desirable ripening as its manifestation. Its specific nature (*sabhāva*) is the unique quality of hardness, contact, and so forth;
its general nature (*sāmañña*) is the common characteristic of impermanence and so forth.

And here, the characteristic of the wholesome should be understood as the "general nature" because it is common to all wholesome states, or as the "specific nature" because it is not shared with the unwholesome and other categories. Its "mode of appearance" is by way of being something to be grasped.

It is the mode of presentation of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). As for the fruit (*phala*), it is called "counter-presentation" (*paccupaṭṭhāna*) because it presents itself either as a reflection of its own cause or by facing toward it.

By the term "it cognizes" (*vijānāti*), he refers to the grasping of an object that is distinguished from the functions of perception (*saññā*) and wisdom (*paññā*). Because it is common to all consciousness, wherever...
"Wherever and in whatever way a meaning can be obtained, it should be understood in that very place and in that very way.
That which accumulates by way of being a condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*), and that which is accumulated because it is conditioned by kamma—this is called "mind" (*citta*) in that sense.

However, that which does not function in that way—the two types of limited functional consciousness (*parittakiriya*) and the final impulsion (*antimajavana*)—is [called mind] by way of its possessing the diversity of thinking (*cintana-vicitratā*) and so forth as they occur.
It should be understood that this refers to "consciousness" (*citta*). As for the "arising of laughter," however, it belongs to the same category as other types of impulsion (*javana*).

Regarding the phrase "of consciousnesses," the meaning is "of various [types]. For, because they are included within that [category], even a single constituent part is called "consciousness" by way of the designation for the whole;

just as when a portion of a mountain, a river, or the ocean is seen, one says "the mountain" and so forth have been seen. "Conduct" (*caraṇa*) refers to the canvas of the mind upon which conduct is to be performed. "Forms" (*rūpa*) means images.
“Internal” (ajjhattika) refers to that which is bound to the sense faculties. “Consisting of mind alone” is said with reference to the mind being the fundamental cause;
for the mind is the cause of kamma. To clarify this meaning, he says, “divided into bodily action and so forth,” and so on.
“Difference in gender” (liṅganānatta) means difference in shape, or the diversity of the body possessing limbs and members of diverse shapes.
Through the medium of conventional usage (*vohāra*), specific aspirations arise toward those things to be designated by way of being "woman," "man," and so forth; from these, specific kamma arises.
Thus, this diversity of kamma results from the diversity of conventional usage. In such passages as "the distinction in the lower realms... etc.," the word "etc.
(*ādi*) includes the various distinctions found in the Suttas regarding destiny (*gati*), rebirth (*upapatti*), individual existence (*attabhāva*), and worldly phenomena (*lokadhamma*).
Regarding the phrase "by way of the diversity of kamma, etc.": here, the diversity of kamma should be understood by way of the wholesome and the unwholesome.

For "diversity" (*nānatta*) means having a dissimilar nature. The multiplicity of wholesome kamma should be understood through its various modes such as giving and so forth, and through its state as bodily good conduct and so on;

likewise, the multiplicity of unwholesome kamma should be understood through stinginess and so forth, and through bodily misconduct and so on. For "multiplicity" (*puthutta*) means having many varieties.

The classification of giving and the other perfections should be understood by way of the gift of food and so forth; the classification of bodily good conduct and the like by way of abstaining from taking life and so forth;

the classification of stinginess and the like by way of envy regarding dwellings and so forth; and the classification of bodily misconduct and the like by way of taking life and so forth. For the "classification" (*pabheda*) of each individual type is its differentiation. The "determination" (*vavatthāna*) of diversity and the rest is their being determined and ascertained in such and such a manner.
By this method, the diversity of gender and so forth should be understood; for these are produced by the diversity of kamma and other factors.

Having shown the occurrence of the present gender from kamma and, in due order, the accomplishment of present kamma, he then connects the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) by demonstrating the production of the future diversity of gender and so forth, [stating]: "The differentiation of kamma..."
He said, “Dependent upon,” and so forth. Therein, it should be understood that by the first mention of "kamma," ignorance (avijjā) and volitional formations (saṅkhārā) are included;

by the mention of "gender" and so forth, consciousness (viññāṇa) and the factors ending with existence (bhava) are included; and by the mention of "destiny" and so forth, birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa) are included.
Therein, "destiny" refers to the five destinies beginning with hell; their differentiation consists in being without feet and so forth. These...
For they are thus distinguished. "Rebirth" refers to rebirths such as those of cattle, buffaloes, kṣatriyas, and the Cātumahārājika devas;
their differentiation consists in being high and so forth. For one who is a kṣatriya may be high by virtue of lineage, wealth, power, and so on, while another is low.
By virtue of those same factors, one is low through inferiority, refined through being led to a state of excellence, well-gone through wealth, or poor through poverty.

"Misfortune" (*duggata*): Based on family, there is high or low status; based on power, there is inferiority or excellence; and based on wealth, there is prosperity or misfortune—these should be correlated accordingly.
"Beauty or ugliness" is stated by way of the purity or impurity of complexions such as white, dark, and so forth.

"Well-born or ill-born" refers either to the physical characteristics of height and girth, such as being well-proportioned like a banyan tree, or to whether one's personal existence (*attabhāva*) has been born complete or incomplete.
"Whether well-proportioned or ill-proportioned" refers to the configuration of the limbs and members.
Furthermore, there is another sutta cited to establish that the aforementioned internal consciousness is "made by mind," beginning with the words "from kamma.
For kamma is produced from consciousness; thus, everything resulting from it is indeed "made by mind."

He establishes [this]. Because it arises from the sign produced by karma, and because it proceeds from the sign based on its root cause—namely, karma—and from its proximate cause—namely, the sign—he says:
"It proceeds from karma... and from the sign. Alternatively, "sign-and-perception" (*liṅgasaññā*) refers to both the sign and the perception;
the meaning is that these two proceed respectively from karma and from the sign. [He states this] to distinguish it from perception.
"They go" means that these phenomena proceed from the perception of the signs of "woman," "man," and so forth, toward the differentiation of conventional designations such as "woman" and "man";
the meaning is that they are to be designated in such and such ways. By this verse, the mind-made mind is shown by way of dependent origination throughout the past and present periods.
The world itself, because it has been born, is "the born" (*pajāti*); this should be understood as the latter line being the explanation for the former line.
Just as an axle-pin is the fastening for a chariot, so too is karma the fastening for the chariot of the world of sentient beings—this is how the application of the simile is to be understood.
Furthermore, by means of this verse, the fact that consciousness is produced by karma is shown through two stages of existence. "Fame" (*kitti*) refers to [praise] in the absence of one's face.
*Kit-tanaṃ* means praise; *patthaṭayasaṃ* means extensive. They "praise" (*pasaṃsanti*) means they offer commendation or eulogy in one's presence.

"Difference in action" (*kamma-nānākaraṇaṃ*) means the difference in production resulting from action, which is inferred by means of those things born of action, or it is the very difference of the action itself.

"Owners of their actions" (*kammassakā*) means having mastery over their own action. "Heirs to their actions" (*kammadāyādā*) means they take up the inheritance of action—that which is to be given by it. And [this applies] to those born from eggs, etc.
Because they are produced from karma among the various modes of birth (*yoni*), karma itself is their mode of birth; thus, they are "born of karma" (*kammayoni*).
Karma is their "bond" (*bandhu*) in the sense of binding them; thus, they are "bound by karma" (*kammabandhu*).
"Of the mind" (*cittassa*) refers to karmic consciousness (*kammaviññāṇa*). Its failure to obtain an opportunity [for rebirth], however, is due to its being obstructed by another karma.
It should be understood that this is because the person is produced in a place where there is no ripening of that [kamma].

Even though kamma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparāpariya-vedanīya*) exists, it should be seen as lacking the remaining conditions due to the absence of auxiliary conditions such as the time of death or the specific application [of effort].
"A certain kind of consciousness" (*ekacca-citta*) refers to a particular state produced by consciousness; he speaks of the variety that is to be produced by that consciousness.
"Having experienced and having become," [means] "removed from what has been experienced" (*apagataṃ bhūtāpagataṃ*).

For the state of having been experienced (*anubhūtabhūtatā*) is expressed by the word *bhūta* through its commonality (*sāmaññena*) with the word *bhūta*. Indeed, it is the commonality itself that is specified by the prefix (*upasaggena*). And the word *anubhūta*, because it lacks the sense of being an object of action (*kammavacanī*), should be understood as denoting the experiencer (*anubhavaka*).
By way of grasping various alternatives (*vikappa*), unwholesome states [arise] through lust and so forth, as well as their opposites.
It experiences the flavor of the object as wholesome (kusala), but not as fruition (vipāka) because it is projected by the force of karma,

nor as functional (kiriya) because those without roots are extremely weak and those with roots arise in one whose defilements are exhausted as being exceedingly tranquil due to the sixfold equanimity.
And here, in the first method, although only the wholesome and unwholesome were intended to be spoken of, it is called "departed from the elements" (bhūtāpagata) by way of the underlying intention.

In the passage, "For the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states and for the stabilization of arisen wholesome states," the term "arisen" is taken to refer to the abandoning and growth of those [states] similar to what has arisen.
However, in the latter method, by means of the word "and" (*ca*), both the wholesome and the unwholesome are drawn in,
so that all conditioned phenomena are stated with the intention of expressing their nature as having come into being and then passed away.
Past kamma that has arisen by way of making room for maturation, and future result that has begun to arise from it, is called "arisen by making room.
With reference to that which is understood as "arisen" even without the word *uppanna*, it was said:
"Bhikkhus, of intentional deeds... and so forth. "In those various planes" means:

[It exists] within the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha), which are designated as the personal existence of humans, devas, and so forth. It is "uneradicated" (asamūhata) because it has not been brought about [to cease] or produced [as such] within this or that continuity (santāna).
And here, that which has obtained a plane is called "plane-obtained" (bhūmiladdha), just like one who has taken hold of fire.

Furthermore, regarding the words "space-maker" (okāsakara) and "arisen in space" (okāsa-utpanna), even though there are two types of meaning—namely, "by whom space was made" and "for whom space was made"—the word *kata* functions in exactly the same way.
The grammatical construction should be understood as follows.
Although the mind intent on going does not actually turn back at all times, it is described as "arisen" because it has not been suppressed by the contemplation of its opposite.
"It causes to disappear" means that mindfulness of breathing suppresses [the opposing state]. "Right there" refers to what has already been attained on the path.
"On the ground" means that which has not been interrupted, having been cut off [previously].

That which is arising—even if it has entered only a portion of the three moments—and is neither past nor future, is said to be "having entered the three moments. The meaning grasped as the primary focus of the teaching is called the "head.
For when one reaches a mundane phenomenon (*lokiyadhamma*) to be taught, the mind becomes the precursor to the teaching; such is the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*).

Or this was said with a specific intention. "Unwholesome" refers to all unwholesome states (*dhammas*). "Volition" refers to some of them. "Partaking of the unwholesome" refers to greed and so forth, which are exclusively unwholesome.
"Belonging to the side of the unwholesome" includes contact (*phassa*) and the rest as well, since they belong to that same side.
"Mind arises before those states" means that even though mind is co-nascent (*sahajāta*), it functions by way of predominance (*adhipati-bhāva*) by including the associated states within itself.
It is said to be "as if it were the first to arise. Even though the associated states follow along with it, they are called "unwholesome states" because they conform to it;
or rather, the quality of being "preceded by mind" is stated with reference to the condition of immediate proximity (*anantara-paccaya*).
"Led by the mind" is said with reference to the formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*), or that which is associated with craving. "Luminous" (*pabhassara*)...
This was said with reference to their natural purity. "Unprotected" means not guarded by mindfulness against attraction, aversion, and so forth; being overwhelmed by lust and the like;
and being made leaky by those very same defilements. Regarding the establishment of the mind's primacy:

the protection of the sutta should be understood here as occurring through mutual reinforcement, or as the prolonged persistence of those [states] brought together which are recognized by the Abhidhamma masters.
The passage beginning with "Katarapaññaṃ tu" has not been included in the canonical text (pāḷi); rather, it is stated in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) that "the Blessed One asks thus.

Furthermore, the question "For what purpose is wisdom? is also one sutta, and its answer is: "It is for the sake of direct knowledge (*abhiññatthā*), for the sake of full understanding (*pariññatthā*), and for the sake of abandoning (*pahānatthā*").
"Sāta" is stated by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāvavasena*), while "madhura" is by way of a simile, meaning "like something sweet. "Ponobbhavikā" means...

They have the nature of producing renewed existence. "Delight" (*nandī*) arises from finding pleasure here and there; lust that has become delight is "lust-delight" (*nandirāga*). Because they are accompanied by the state of lust-delight, they are called "accompanied by lust-delight.
Here, the sense of being "accompanied" does not exist by way of association (*sampayoga*);

rather, the word "accompanied" illuminates the state of lust-delight within craving (*taṇhā*). Its meaning is "having become lust-delight. "In dependence" means upon a basis. "Of those having form and formless objects" [is the phrase].
“Of those having the earth-kasiṇa and so forth, or space and so forth, as their object. *Saṃsaṭṭha* means mixed together like milk and water, having reached a state of oneness.
*Sahajātā* refers to the conjoined and co-nascent, not merely the co-nascent. “In this case too” means that in this word as well, this very meaning is intended;
thus, according to the commentary as shown, the word *saṃsaṭṭha* is intended here in the sense of being co-nascent (*sahajāta*).

"By means of form, the formless" refers to the basis (vatthu) at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "An exalted description" (*ukkaṭṭhaniddesa*) is a description made by way of an exhaustive inclusion; it is an exaggerated statement.

"Precisely because it is not brought forward" (*anābhaṭṭhatāyeva*): "not being brought forward" (*anābhaṭṭhatā*) means that it should not be spoken of [in this context], just as "seen-ness" and so forth are not mentioned in such phrases as "the seen and the heard.
By stating that the second consciousness—which is similar in every respect—is "prompted" (*sasaṅkhārika*), the unprompted nature (*asaṅkhārikatā*) of this [first consciousness] is established.
It is understood; therefore, the sense that it was not included because it was not spoken [by the Buddha] is appropriate.
However, the intention is that because it was not spoken in the Pāḷi, it was not included or collected there as something to be taught, nor is its meaning absent.
Alternatively, precisely because it was not brought into the Pāḷi, it was not included in the Aṭṭhakathā, nor was its meaning stated. "Having determined" means...

Since elsewhere such [consciousness] is described as being "prompted" (*sasaṅkhārika*), here, by not mentioning that, its state of being "unprompted" (*asaṅkhārika*) is established. Regarding the term "mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*):
here, either the "door" (*dvāra*) is called the "basis" (*vatthu*), or else the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*)—which acts as the companion to that door—is meant.
"By way of its own nature" means by way of its own functional capacity (*sakicca*). For ignorance has the function of being the condition for the formative forces (*saṅkhāra*).

The state that is to be tasted and understood as unique to each [condition] is its specific nature (*sarasabhāva*); for example, the specific nature of ignorance (*avijjāsabhāva*), the specific nature of volitional formations (*saṅkhārasabhāva*), and so forth.

There is also a reading, “by way of specific nature” (*sarasasabhāvena*), which has the same meaning. Alternatively, [the phrase] “with ignorance as condition” (*avijjāpaccayā*) is by way of its specific nature, while “volitional formations” (*saṅkhārā*) is by way of their specific nature.
The state of having a single origination and so forth should be applied only to material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), because among them that designation is most prevalent.

The status of being past and so forth applies to both material and immaterial phenomena; or rather, for mind, mental factors, and Nibbāna as well, their respective states of having one, two, or some other number of origins should be applied according to their own nature.
"Not come within range" means not having entered the domain of the eye and the other [senses], like subtle dust and such matter, due to the extreme minuteness of the physical basis (*vatthu*).
[The mind] is [unstable] due to the brevity of the moment, extreme distance, being too near, and because of the past and future states, like a drop of water fallen upon a red-hot iron ball.
The "object" (*visaya*) is stated as such by virtue of its not being anything other [than the object], and the "range" (*gocara*) is stated as such because of moving within it;

the "refuge" (*paṭisaraṇa*) is the mind by virtue of its determination regarding that object. This meaning is established; otherwise, because those [mental factors] have the phenomena as their objects, [the distinction between them] would not hold.
This is because the statement, “he experiences the range and domain of his sense-spheres,” would otherwise be untenable.

Furthermore, nowhere is it stated that visible forms and so forth—which have not come within the range [of perception] according to the method already described—are being taken as objects by the divine eye, the divine ear, or the knowledge of supernormal power;
on the contrary, they are seen to be so stated in such passages as, “he sees a form with the divine eye.”
"It comes into the range" means by way of becoming an object to be grasped by the mind and the fivefold sense-consciousnesses.

"Having struck against" means having gone into the range of the face-to-face encounter. For the reciter or the restorer [of the text], there is the coming into range by way of being seen and so forth;

and for one who is healthy due to food-digestion, the particularity of the season, or specific foods, or due to exertion and so forth, or for one whose body is afflicted by wind and so forth when sick, or for one who is awake following the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

This should be understood by way of the conditions for bodily pleasure, pain, weather, food, and so forth, which depend on movement; the conditions such as the seeing of similar or dissimilar connections and the mental aspiration that resemble [the actual experience];
and the conditions such as the disturbance of the elements (dhātu) that occur when one sees dreams while asleep.

Furthermore, it occurs through a connection with what has been seen or heard—termed "similarity"—regarding the future form of a Buddha or the like, which has not yet been seen or heard, and which serves as the basis for the desire to give faith.
The relationship between the two is not merely through similarity; rather, it should be understood as including opposition to that, being a part of that, association with that, and so forth.
Faith (*saddhā*) is the act of believing in something heard from someone else without investigation; liking (*ruci*) is the finding of pleasure after having investigated it oneself;
and reflection on the mode (*ākāraparivitakka*) is the investigation of the manner [of occurrence], thinking, "It will be thus or thus."
The acceptance of contemplation regarding a view while one is investigating is "acceptance through contemplation of a view" (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*).
Among the elements such as red arsenic, green vitriol, and collyrium, the sign of beauty (*subhanimitta*) is the cause for the apprehension of beauty.

Because it is a sign of beauty and because it is provocative of passion, it is the basis for greed. By way of the restricted mind—that is, by way of restriction—in the same manner regarding the others.

In two cases: *ābhoga* is the act of attending; *ābhujitaṃ* is that which has been attended to. "Persons of coarse nature" are those abounding in hatred (*dosa*). "Persons of gentle nature" are those abounding in non-hatred (*adosa*). "Devoted thereto" means having a mind inclined toward joy (*pīti*).
The intention [of the author] is that this [joy] is to be understood through these [factors], because joy cannot possibly be dissociated from mental happiness (*somanassa*).

Because it serves as a basis for the maintenance of life, the craft itself—such as elephant-riding and so forth—is the "basis of craft" (*sippāyatana*). Likewise, occupations such as agriculture and trade are themselves the "basis of action" (*kammāyatana*).
The sphere of action (*kammāyatana*). The "bases of knowledge" (*vijjāṭṭhāna*) are indeed the sciences such as the science of longevity (*āyuveda*), etc.

"Without affliction" (*abyāpajja*) means in the form-sphere existence (*rūpabhava*) which is free from mental distress and ill-will. "Dhamma-padas" are portions of the Dhamma. "Flow forth" (*pilavanti*) means they appear or become manifest.

"Yokes" (*yoga*) refers to the application of cultivation (*bhāvanābhiyoga*) through concentration. "Making the basis pure" (*vatthuvisadakiriyā*) is the act of making internal and external bases stainless.
The balancing of the faculties is the state of establishing the equilibrium of the faculties, such as faith and the rest, so that they do not exceed one another.

The "reviewing of the practice of profound knowledge" is the reviewing of those discourses (*suttanta*) that must be traversed by means of profound knowledge, or which must be traversed by means of profound knowledge.
"Lineage" (*vaṃsa*) means sequence; "continuity" (*tantī*) means succession; "tradition" (*paveṇī*) means connection. All of this refers to the continuity of conduct and activity.
It is speech. Because it consists of conduct and virtue, it is "consisting of virtue" (*sīlamaya*). Through the utterance of the words "I shall give," the object is transformed;
from that point onward, the giving is said to have commenced, which is why one incurs an offense regarding its dedication and so forth.
When the object exists, from the moment of intending it, the giving has commenced; therein lies the merit consisting of giving (*dānamaya-kusala*).
This is the intended meaning. For it is not the case that there is no merit for one who prepares an object for giving even when it does not yet exist.

However, since that [preparation] is a preliminary stage to the gift itself, it would fall under that same category; so it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā. "By way of family lineage and so forth" is merely an illustration.
It refers to the observance of vows undertaken by oneself, as well as the observances of noble persons, village customs, national laws, and so on.
And the nature of virtuous conduct is to be understood.
"With its basis" means having included the basis such as the drum and so forth. "The existing basis" refers to the basis such as the drum and so forth.

And in the case of the sounding of the proclamation for hearing the Dhamma and the like, it is the giving of sound by making it have a basis, [namely] the places and articulations of the bases of sound.
"Causing it to proceed with sound" should be understood as his reflection on the relinquishing of an existing object.

The Dhamma King showed this by dividing [the gift]: here, as being an object such as form (*rūpārammaṇa*); elsewhere, as being "these three bases for making merit, O monks," namely, consisting of giving and so forth; and in another place, as "which states are wholesome? Three... and so on.
By stating, "bodily action originating from that," and so forth, he explains its status as bodily action and the rest.
"And they are not included" means they are not comprised [within the aggregates] because they do not exist in the ultimate sense and because they belong to another sphere (āyatana).
"The flavor of enjoyment" refers to the joy and mental happiness conditioned by enjoyment. This, however, is a designation based on their similarity in flavor.
It is called "having taste as its object" by way of dependence (*upādāya*), not by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

However, because the apprehension [of it] by way of intrinsic nature is dependent upon joy and mental pleasure, that joy and mental pleasure have only mental phenomena (*dhamma*) as their object; thus it is said, "pleasant feeling has mental phenomena as its object.

It is stated having fixed the object itself, determining it thus: "it has visible form as its object... [and so on] ...it has mental phenomena as its object. Regarding the phrase "because of the non-fixity of kamma":

Because of the non-fixity of kamma. For just as a consciousness directed toward a single object among visible forms and so forth does not have any other object, it is not the case that kamma performed at a single door, such as the body-door, does not arise at another door;

therefore, because kamma is devoid of a fixed door, and the door is likewise devoid of a fixed kamma, it is not stated here by way of a restriction—as was done for the object—without the object. Without the object...

Regarding the phrase "because it does not arise," its meaning should be understood as follows: "Just as one kamma among bodily actions and so forth may proceed through another door even without that specific door, it is not so with consciousness;
a consciousness directed toward a single object such as visible form does not arise toward another object without that specific object.
For it is not the case that what arises at the door of speech is called "bodily action."
Likewise, that which arises with a sound-object is called "having a visible-form object.
[End of] the Explanation of the Discussion on the Door of Bodily Action regarding Wholesome Consciousness of the Sense-Sphere.
"But for this purpose" means for the sake of explaining, by way of such statements as "kamma-s proceed through the doors," the fact that the doors of kamma are not fixed with respect to one another.
Regarding the phrase "the five consciousnesses": here, the sixth consciousness and its corresponding door are not mentioned because the door and the possessor of the door do not exist simultaneously.
And bodies arising from four sources are mentioned by way of determinate material form. This refers to the word "sound."
And there is no inclusion of the material qualities of change and so forth.

Although the air element originating from the first impulsion is unable at that moment to cause matter to move by way of its arising in another location, nevertheless, it should be understood as being accompanied by intimation and change. For in the ten directions...
When one wishes to go in a certain direction or wishes to move the limbs and members of the body, one fixes and sustains mental objects directed toward that very direction;
thus, it possesses a modification consisting in being oriented toward that [direction].

And since a modification co-existent with intention is what constitutes *viññatti* (intimation), by this reasoning, even the act of adverting (*āvajjana*) has the status of originating intimation, through the production of material form that undergoes modification according to the intention.
It has arisen; for it is stated that thirty-two types of consciousness produce material form, postures, and intimation.
Having gone one *yojana*, it brings about the designation "having gone ten *yojanas*" even though it has arisen many thousands of times.
Regarding the air element... [it acts as] a condition for the air element to exist in support and movement.
There exists a particular mode of the great primary elements (mahābhūta) originated by consciousness that is capable [of making itself known]; this is called "intimation" (viññatti).
Because those [elements] possess that mode, it is said that the air element supports and moves them.

By the phrase "not originated by consciousness," he shows its non-existence in the ultimate sense (paramattha). For there is no material form (rūpa) that is without a condition, nor is there any permanent entity except for Nibbāna.

"By way of intimation" means by way of the modification that is intimation. It should be understood that, just like its status as mind-originated, its status as derived matter (*upādārūpa*) is intended here because it is a modification of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
"Bodily action" (*kāyikakaraṇa*) refers to mental activity proceeding through the door of the body; the meaning is "intention. It causes [the body] to act; thus, one thinks.

By this, he shows that the manifestation (viññatti) apprehended through the apprehension of color possesses the quality of being "cognized" because one cognizes the instrument by which it is to be known.
For there is no cognition of the thought "this person is making [something]" in relation to tree-shaking and so forth, which are devoid of manifestation.
Indeed, the function of eye-consciousness is merely the impingement upon visible form; it does not—
It is the grasping of the movement and transformation that coexist with the underlying intention (*adhippāya*).

However, because of the mind’s rapid turnover, those who lack discernment imagine that even a movement cognized by the mental consciousness immediately following the visual consciousness process is "seen" by the eye, just like what was seen by the eye itself.
Therefore, just as [there is no distinction] for a visual consciousness process proceeding due to the impact of a blue object, so too for a mental consciousness process proceeding as "blue"...
And when no interval is perceived, then— once that [object] has been grasped by the mind-door consciousness occurring without such an interval—
there arises, through the mental concomitants known as bodily rigidity, transformation, and movement, a cognition together with the mind [itself] that "this he is making do,
this is his intention."

Upon seeing forms such as palm leaves, one grasps the mode of recognition—the manner in which the palm leaves and so forth are accompanied by water and other things—through the mental-door process (*manodvāravīthi*) that arises immediately thereafter, even though the intervening moments are not consciously perceived; this is like the apprehension of water itself.
Here, by means of a consciousness that follows the apprehension of the visible form through the mode of associating it with water and so forth, thinking "there will be water here," and so on.
It should be understood that by the cognition of water and so forth—which are to be cognized—the state of having cognized their respective modes is expressed.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the apprehension of the prior established relationship serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for this apprehension of bodily action and the apprehension of water and so forth.
Moreover, even if intimation (*viññatti*) is not taken as an object, it [serves] for the apprehension of bodily action...
And it is a condition by way of the supporting influence (*upanissaya*) of grasping a previously established relationship;

for, immediately after the grasping of color—which has become a modification accompanied by intention—the grasping of the intention occurs, since that [grasping of the intention] would be absent in the absence of the modification co-existent with the intention.

This being so, just as the mode of recognition such as "palmyra leaf" arises through the grasping of water and so forth immediately after the grasping of color, so too [does it arise] immediately after the grasping of color.

Since intimation (*viññatti*) becomes manifest precisely through the grasping of the intention (*adhippāya*), it is said that the state of intimation being known occurs simply by knowing the intention, thinking, "He is apparently making this and that.
By the phrase "this one wishes to strike us," he demonstrates the manifestation of intimation through the knowledge of the intention. For indeed...
When that [intimation] is not manifest, there is the cognition of the intention; thus,

it establishes its own nature as twofold intimation, even though it is not present— as in the case of visible forms and so forth that are not within range due to their non-manifestation— and which consists of a transformation co-arising with the mind,
even in the absence of the performance of approaching and so on, because of the desire to inform another.
It should be understood that *viññatti* (intimation) is twofold: it intimates the intention, and it is itself intimated.
They are "established" (*siddha*) in that door because they are to be known through that door, because they receive their name through that very door, and because they are manifest in that door.
Whether wholesome or unwholesome—this must be set aside. Why? Because:
For the opponent, the status of non-resultant action is not established, whereas for the other [the Theravādin], it is established;
thus, having fulfilled the triad by means of the eleven functional consciousnesses that originate intimation, [the position] should be maintained.
Regarding the statement "kamma-s proceed through the doors," this is the intended meaning: if the doors were to proceed through other doors, [then...]

If there were a confusion of doors, there would also be a confusion of actions; thus, the mutual distinction between bodily action and the door of bodily action would not exist, and the same principle would apply when one action follows upon another action.

However, if there were no confusion of doors within the state of being doors, nor any confusion of actions within the state of being actions, then the distinction between actions and doors would be even more clearly established.
It may be so. However, it is not that actions do not occur in other doors; rather, actions occur in other doors as well as in others.

But because actions do not occur in doors other than their own, therefore, by means of those doors—which serve as the cause—actions, even while occurring in other doors, are determined. It is not only actions that are thus restricted.
Furthermore, these doors of action are thus mutually defined by the principle of definition known as "predominance of occurrence" and "frequency of occurrence.
In this context, because the nature of actions— such as bodily action and so forth— is dependent upon the doors,
their definition is established by those doors through which they do not pass, and not by those doors through which they do pass.
The non-determination of the doors by kamma is because bodily action and the rest— though determined by doors that do not themselves depend on kamma—
are what effect the determination of bodily action and the rest as "doors of bodily action" and so forth. Alternatively, even when they operate through other doors,
they operate only as characterized by the body and so on, because the nature of killing and the rest consists in such things as commands, hand gestures, and so forth.
Because even when it is being spoken of, its nature is to be accomplished by means of the body and so forth;
therefore, one does not give another name to a different door simply because another action is operating within it, nor does the action give a name to the door.
Rather, it is established that each respective door gives its own name to the action, and the action—even while operating through a different door—gives its own name to its own door.
This is the mutual determination [of the doors]. Previously, however, the lack of restriction to specific doors regarding kamma was stated with reference only to its wandering into other doors;
it was not intended as a fixed determination.
"Therein" means among those door-kammas. "The place of arising for bodily kamma" refers to the intimation (viññatti) that is co-nascent with it.
It is so called because, although it is not a condition for that [kamma] in any way whatsoever, nevertheless, as an intimation (*viññatti*) that qualifies the kamma, it arises co-nascent with it;
thus it is described as its "place of origin" according to the aforementioned rule, since—by that very rule—there is no arising of another qualification for a qualifying kamma apart from this.
But "by what has been done by means of the body" means having generated bodily intimation (*kāya-viññatti*).
Because it accomplishes the severing of the life-faculty and so forth through its own production, it is said: "kamma done by way of the body.
For here, "body" refers to the instrument.
As for the phrase "distinguished from one another": herein, the body is distinguished as the door of bodily kamma by means of the kamma; it is not...
"Body" (kāya) alone [is not the meaning]. Just as by means of needle-work one determines "the doing of needle-work," and not "a needle" alone, so too should this be regarded.
"Determined mutually" means "distinguished from one another.
"If this were so" refers to taking only the statement beginning with "karmas move at the door," without grasping the aforementioned rule of determination.

It urges [the reader]. In that context, "thus being" (*evaṃ santa*) means when there is the distinction, the acquisition of names, and the qualification regarding the doors and the performance of kamma, as well as their mutual determination.
The commentary on the discussion of the door of bodily kamma is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Door of Verbal Action:
Regarding the passage, "Endowed with four factors, monks," here, abstaining from slanderous speech is defined as speaking what is well-spoken;
abstaining from idle chatter is defined as speaking the Dhamma; abstaining from harsh speech is defined as speaking kindly; and abstaining from false speech is defined as speaking the truth.
"False speech" (*amusāvāda*) refers here to the volition (*cetanā*) that proceeds in such a manner; this should be understood as such.

As for the phrase "together with sound," it is said because [the speech] arises together with the sound produced by that vocal modification. However, because it conforms to the mind, it should be understood that it does not exist as long as the sound exists;
for, according to the doctrine of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* as it has been handed down, the sound resulting from the expansion of applied thought (*vitakkavipphāra-sadda*) is not cognizable by the ear.
It follows that sound originated by mind (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-sadda*) arises even without the impact of intimation (*viññatti*).
For, from the statement, "That which is the intimation by means of that speech," it is understood that there is no arising of intimation together with a sound cognizable by the ear.
Furthermore, in the phrase "the sound-base originated by mind" (*cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ saddāyatanaṃ*), no sound originated by mind is left uncomprised.
With the intention that "there is [such a thing as] name," he refutes the position of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
For in the sixfold classification of matter and so forth, under the categories of "cognizable by the ear" and "seen and heard," there is no sound whatsoever that is not included under "heard.

However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that [name] consists only of those things arising together with intimation (*viññatti*), produced by vocal thought such as the movement of the tongue, palate, and so forth.

The statement that a subtle sound is "heard by the divine ear and then announced" in the Sutta, and that in the Paṭṭhāna it is said of a gross sound that "it is a condition for ear-consciousness by way of object-condition"—it may be on this intended meaning that its being "not cognizable by the ear" is stated.
However, the objection should be understood as follows: "A sound that is not cognizable by the ear" is a contradiction in terms.
“Contact due to intimation” (*viññattipaccayā ghaṭṭanā*) means contact by way of intimation (*viññattighaṭṭanā*), or simply intimation itself.

For it is the modification of the primary elements occurring in the mode of contact that is called “contact. Sound arises simultaneously with the impact; it does not arise through a sequence of prior and subsequent moments.
“Of the earth element” (*pathavīdhātuyā*) refers to the function of the earth element’s impact, which is like the shaking [caused] by the air element.
This is stated by way of emphasis; furthermore, the fact that the transformation is conditioned by that [body] should be understood in the manner already explained.

For it is the state of mutual conditionality among the primary elements (*bhūta*) that undergo such transformations. All other rules of formation should also be understood as being the same as those for bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*).
Regarding the body arisen from the three origins... [as before] ...it is not obtained. For movement is not the striking of what is clung-to (*upādinnaghaṭṭana*). Indeed, movement—
It is the state of a continuous succession of successive arisings elsewhere; "impact" means the closer arising of groups of primary elements due to a specific condition.
Since there is no function of support either, even that which is originated by the first consciousness proceeds in the manner of impact without support;
thus, there is no purpose for support for the sake of impact, as it occurs through the mind itself once it has acquired habituation.
The intention is that this is because the force of the impact is strong. One should understand this after investigating whether or not there is support (*upatthambhana*).
The commentary on the discussion of the door of verbal action is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of the door of mental action.
The statement that "this volition (cetanā) cannot be said not to be karma" is spoken for the purpose of showing that the mind is its door.
"It fashions" (kappeti) means it proceeds as if fashioning [them], thinking, "You perform the touching; you experience [the feeling]. "Fashioning" (pakappana) is precisely that.
"What does it aggregate?"—this question is asked in the sense of accumulation (āyūhana). [It aggregates] the phenomena such as contact (phassa), etc.
For "accumulation" (*āyūhana*) is the proceeding toward one's own functions without being distracted; "volition" (*cetayana*) is the exertion therein;
and "determination" (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*) is the performing [of that] accordingly. Only the three planes are included because supramundane karma brings about the destruction of karma.
The commentary on the discussion of the door of mental action is finished.
In the commentary on the discussion of kamma, regarding the statement "having intended, one performs kamma":

since one performs the kamma of resolution after having intended by means of a prior volition, kamma is preceded by volition and possesses the very same nature as that volition; therefore, "I say that volition is kamma."
This is the meaning. Alternatively, even though they are simultaneous, it is appropriate to speak of the causal activity as being prior in time, and the resultant activity as being subsequent.

And because one performs the impulsive activity through body and speech after having intended by means of volition (*cetanā*), and performs activities such as covetousness through the mind, therefore I say that the volition which is the agent of that activity is "kamma."
The meaning [of the compound] is as follows: "In the body" means either in the body designated as bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*).

"Being present" means existing, or not having ceased. "Bodily volition" (*kāyasañcetanā*) is the volition that originates the body. Furthermore, there must be a kamma capable of producing pleasure or pain;
and since volition has been stated to be what produces pleasure and pain, its status as kamma is established here. "To be willed" (*sañcetaniya*) means possessing the nature of volition.
The Elder Samiddhi answered that question without analysis, saying: "Intentional action, friend... [etc. ...he experiences it as pleasant with the mind.
However, that question ought to have been answered by analyzing it with the words "to be experienced as pleasant," and so forth; therefore, it was not rightly answered.
The same method applies to the other two cases as well. Just as the Suttas stand, so too [the answer] is based on the activity of the mind.
The doors of body, speech, and mind are the bases for the performance of covetousness and so forth;
however, that volition by which they perform acts such as covetousness through those instruments—the body and so on—just as one performs cutting and so forth with tools like axes, is "kamma.
Thus, even regarding the activity of the doors, both the classification of the doors of kamma and the determination of the doors of kamma are seen.
This being the case, verses such as "Whatever action is performed by the body" and so forth are most appropriately applied.
Although the supramundane path is not intended here in this discussion of mundane action, if it were included, it would still fall under three types of action.
By the phrase "immorality of mind," all unwholesome states—including the faults of bodily and verbal transgression—are subsumed.

Or [wrong view, wrong] thought, [wrong] effort, [wrong] mindfulness, and [wrong] concentration. And this too is stated by way of the opposite of the restraint mentioned in the phrase "Restraint with the mind is good," not by way of a failure in virtue (sīlavipatti). For that [failure] is not mental;
thus, because of its vast scope, it is assigned to the Path alone. For the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) would pertain only to mental action (manokamma), and yet—
It is not possible to understand their classification merely by means of classifying them according to the paths [of action].

Even for those actions that have not reached the stage of a full course of action (*kamma-patha*), the convergence and obstruction at various doors, as well as the breach of the door of one action even when another action arises in a different door, is called "convergence of doors" (*dvāra-saṃsandana*).
"Bhikkhus, there are three kinds of bodily volition that are unwholesome... [and so forth].

By the phrase "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*) and so forth, it is stated that only the concluding volition (*sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*) which has reached the state of a course of action (*kammappatha*) is called "action.

Therefore, it is said that all preceding volitions do not constitute bodily action. Regarding the passage "having ordered... not obtaining [the victim]," this is stated with reference to the fact that those who were ordered did not kill;
the intention is that this constitutes verbal misconduct (*vacīduccarita*), yet it does not possess the status of a full course of action (*akammappathabhāva*). "These beings..."

The terms [“killing,” etc. are either included under volition (cetanā) by way of the malice that has arisen as “Let them be killed,” or they are designated as bodily action because they receive the designation of bodily karma;
or they are not so designated because they lack the designation of mental karma. In this context, water and the other elements within the earth and its constituents serve as examples.
“Of the nest” means of the womb, or of the family itself. Because the three councils have not been authorized since they were already established [in the canon].
"Of your sutta" is what was said. The tenfold supernormal power (iddhi) should be understood from the discourse on iddhi in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
He speaks with reference to the supernormal power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*) as consisting in cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*). The comparison is consistent:

the destruction of another is like the breaking of a jar, and the destruction of the supernormal power is like the loss of the water. "Your question" refers to [the case where] there is destruction of another through that which consists in cultivation.
The word *hoti* is used to indicate the intended meaning that one wishes to make known. The power of sorcery (*āthabbaṇiddhi*) is the power consisting of knowledge (*vijjāmayiddhi*).
"In the seventh step" means in the seventh step from the beginning of the mandala.

That which has its meaning to be understood through another statement is of interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*); that whose meaning is to be understood by itself is of definitive meaning (*nītattha*). From the action...
He asks this with reference to the intentional lying (sampajānamusāvāda) intended [by the Blessed One], not to what is stated in the Uposatha-kkhandhaka.
For there, having taken that ignoble mode of speech (anariyavohāra) which was not actually spoken as having been spoken, he speaks it.
"Speech-sound" (vācāgiraṃ) means a sound consisting of speech, or the utterance of speech.
"Khaṇḍasivādayo seṭṭhā": *Khaṇḍa* refers to youths; *Siva* refers to great lords. It should be understood that this is stated for the purpose of illustrating wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).
For it is only those [actions] such as the view of non-existence (*natthikadiṭṭhi*) that have reached the level of a course of action (*kammapatha*) which constitute "kamma.

However, volition (*cetanā*) here is not subject to such designation; thus, even when arising at the door of body or the door of speech, it is [respectively] bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and verbal action (*vacīkamma*).

And it does not receive the designation [of "kamma"] because covetousness and the rest are its predominant factors. However, because of the statement, “Monks, threefold volition of mind is unwholesome mental kamma,” that [volition] is mental kamma by its very nature, not merely because it belongs to the side of covetousness and the rest;
thus, it is not said to be “on the side of covetousness and the rest. In this context, however, without moving the limbs of the body or the limbs of speech—
At the time of reflection, both volition (*cetanā*) and the mental states associated with volition arise solely at the mind-door (*manodvāra*);
therefore, the intention is that there is no way for volition to be excluded from this classification.
This is because of such statements as: "Monks, threefold is bodily volition; it is wholesome bodily action," which refers to that which is the opposite of killing living beings and so forth.

Since the volitions consisting of the abstinences from killing living beings and so forth are distinguished by their respective [mental] applications, it is said that they "belong to the side of volition" (*cetanāpakkhikā*), and not that they "belong to the side of abstinence" (*viratipakkhikā*).
"He protects" means he speaks without destroying [the meaning]. "He splits" means he speaks having destroyed [the meaning].
The commentary on the discussion of kamma is finished.
“Eye-consciousness-door” means the door for eye-consciousness. Alternatively, it is the eye which is the door for consciousness, thus “eye-consciousness-door.
Or, “eye, consciousness-door” is an analysis of the compound. That, however, is simply the eye. This same method applies to the others as well.
In the verse beginning with “Restraint by the eye is good,” [it refers to] the restraint of the body of clarity and the body of impact.

Having grouped them together, restraint by way of the body was spoken of; here, having analyzed that, eight types of restraint are mentioned, and by way of their opposites, eight types of non-restraint (asaṃvara) are described.

Furthermore, although the five restraints beginning with virtue-restraint (sīlasaṃvara) arise through all doors, immorality (dussīlya) and so forth are called "non-restraints" by way of being their opposites.
Among these, immorality is the volition (cetanā) of killing living beings and so forth.

Lack of mindfulness (*muṭṭhassacca*) refers to unwholesome states that are the opposites of mindfulness; some say it is negligence (*pamāda*). Intolerance (*akkhanti*) is aversion toward cold and other such conditions.
Sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) are idleness (*kosajja*).
The term "purely the bodily door" (*suddha-kāyadvāra*) refers to that which is reckoned as such even when it is observed by means of the vocal door, such as false speech (*musāvāda*) and the like.
It is stated for the purpose of preventing that [unwholesome state] because there is impurity due to its occurrence at the door of the body; for that is not bodily action (*kāyakamma*).
Rather, it is precisely verbal action (*vacīkamma*) characterized by the pure door of speech.

Here, by the term "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*), non-restraint characterized by this pure door of the body is expressed even when it arises at another door. [This refers to that which is] uncharacterized by other doors.
It should be understood that all of this includes the unwholesome [kamma] pertaining to those doors.

By taking it in this way, the statement in the *Kammapathasaṃsandana*—“Non-restraint arising by way of the door of bodily non-restraint of seizing is itself unwholesome bodily kamma”—is not in contradiction with such statements as “Unwholesome bodily kamma arises by way of the door of bodily non-restraint of seizing and by way of verbal non-restraint,” and so forth.
For non-restraint exists through other doors as well.
Even while arising, it is said to arise at the six doors, and it is said to have arisen by way of the six doors;
likewise, karma [arises] at another door and by way of another door—thus there is no contradiction.
Alternatively, "herein" means that without considering whether it is pure or impure, it is stated that "it occurs in this."

This being so, bodily and mental action—characterized by other doors—that has attained the status of a course of action (kamma-patha) and arisen at the door of unwholesome bodily intimation is called "unwholesome bodily non-restraint" (*copanākāyāsaṃvara*).
All the rest, like all other unwholesome states arising at those doors, is likewise called "unwholesome bodily non-restraint.

However, bodily action arising at other doors that has not attained the status of a course of action is not so designated; thus, there is no contradiction with the correlation of the courses of action.

If there should be any contradiction therein, we shall explain it right there. The five types of restraint, beginning with the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara), will be made clear in the Section on the Exposition of Terms (Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa).

In that context, it should be understood that within the restraint of knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃvara) is included virtue dependent on requisites (paccaya-sannissita-sīla), and within the restraint of energy (vīriya-saṃvara) is included purity of livelihood (ājīva-pārisuddhi).
Commentary on the Discussion of the Unwholesome Courses of Action (Akusala-kammapatha-kathā-vaṇṇanā)
And *atipāta* (over-killing) is the excessive killing of a living being whose nature is to fall, even before [the natural time of death];
the meaning is that it is a falling [killed] quickly, without allowing it to fall gradually. Alternatively, *atipāta* is the killing by surpassing [the victim] with weapons and so forth.
The great culpability [of these acts] arises from the magnitude of the effort, the object, and so on; for the volition (*cetanā*) arising through those conditions is [extremely blameworthy].

Due to the strength of its nature. Even in the case of the opposites of the aforementioned conditions, the degree of slight or great faultfulness should be understood precisely by way of the strength or weakness of the volition arising from those respective conditions.

[This includes] that consisting of psychic power (*iddhimaya*) and that consisting of the maturation of karma (*kammavipākaja-iddhimaya*), such as in the case of the fang-tip [of a venomous snake] and so forth.
"Guarded by God" means protected by kinsmen. "Guarded by the Dhamma" means protected by those who share the same Dhamma. "One who has a husband" means one who is protected [by him].

"One for whose approach a punishment has been established by the king" means one who is subject to punishment. "One who destroys welfare" is said with reference to that which has reached the level of a course of action (*kamma-patha*), for this is a discussion of the courses of action.
"Because of the lack of desire to give what belongs to oneself," and so forth, is stated because of its commonality with false speech (*musāvāda*).
It has been said: False speech occurs only when there is an intention to deceive with a motive of amusement.
"The state of being empty" means its hollowness due to the absence of joy. Because it is devoid of meaning, it does not reach the heart.
"Not taking up" means that for one who lacks faith, there is no breach of the path of action. However, any idle chatter whatsoever is accomplished through two factors: one's own application and...
It should be understood as "by the mind alone. "He sees wrongly" means he sees falsely.
"From among the factors" means from among the factors that are members of consciousness, such as those beginning with contact as the fifth; the sense is "from among those which are factors.

But is it not the case that volition is not mentioned among the courses of action? Therefore, is it not improper for the seven [mental factors] to constitute the courses of action in their sequential order?
No; it is not mentioned because its causes are different. For it is not omitted from the category of courses of action (*kamma-patha*) because volition (*cetanā*) itself is not a course of action;
rather, it is sometimes a course of action and not always, and thus it is not mentioned because its status as a course of action is indeterminate.
However, when it does become a course of action, its inclusion within the category of courses of action is not precluded. [The five training rules...]

By the statement, "They have only limited objects," he himself will resolve the contradiction regarding the fact that taking what is not given and other such actions have sentient beings as their object, by explaining:
"They proceed by taking as their object only those formations (saṅkhāra) designated as 'sentient beings'.

Furthermore, the view occurring as "There are no spontaneously born beings" has as its domain the phenomena of the three planes; thus, it is said to have formations as its object. [The following are] the results of fruition and outflow.
In due order, these are the miserable states such as rebirth in hell and so forth, which are the results [of unwholesome deeds].
The commentary on the discussion of the unwholesome courses of action is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion of the wholesome courses of action.

Regarding "the abstentions from killing living beings and so forth": this is stated because it is appropriate that those abstentions—with which volition (cetanā) is associated and which are called "bodily and verbal actions"—possess the status of courses of action (kamma-patha). For he will say later:
"In due order, both the seven types of volition and the abstentions are applicable. "Raw flesh and blood" means the flesh and blood of a living being. "One who has deprived [of life]"...
Having offered [the sacrifice], I do not recognize [any such result]. [The unwholesome states] have immorality as their object and that very object as their support.
To show how the life-faculty and so forth abandon immorality and the like, it is said:

“But just as,” and so on. “Of one who abstains through non-covetousness... etc. means of one who abandons covetousness; for there is no separate abstention from mental misconduct, since that is abandoned precisely by non-covetousness and the other [virtues].
Commentary on the Discourse on the Concordance of the Courses of Action:
Regarding the non-restraints of immorality and so forth that have reached the state of courses of action, as well as the misconducts;

and likewise, regarding the restraints of morality and so forth that have reached the state of courses of action, as well as the good conduct—[these are treated] by means of the unwholesome courses of action and the wholesome courses of action respectively.

This is the demonstration of the absence of diversity in meaning. Alternatively, some say that the "connection with the courses of kamma" is the illumination of those [unwholesome and wholesome states] by way of their non-contradiction with the doors of contact and so forth; however, this must be examined.

For there is no status as a course of kamma for the non-restraints and restraints arising in the five doors of contact, the five doors of non-restraint, or the five doors of restraint, nor for killing and so forth, nor for greed for the property of others, ill-will directed toward other beings, or rootless views and the like.

Because they do not arise at those doors. Furthermore, since the threefold bodily misconduct and so forth are already well-known as courses of action (*kamma-patha*), what is the point of demonstrating their lack of difference from the courses of action?

Nor has the arising of misconduct and good conduct been shown by way of the doors such as contact (*phassa-dvāra*), nor that of non-restraint and restraint, because of their state of non-contradiction with the doors of contact and so forth.

This may be an illustration; however, it is only by way of the doors of contact and so forth that the state of being bodily action and so on for non-restraints and restraints that have arisen is illustrated.
And if this were the entirety of the correlation with the courses of kamma, there would be no correlation with the courses of kamma such as:
"Unwholesome bodily action does not arise by way of the five doors of contact," and so forth. This [correlation] also [occurs] by way of the six doors of contact and so forth.
If it is argued that this is merely an illustration of non-contradiction, then the phrase "or else" (*atha vā*) should not have been stated to show the same point by way of another method.

Furthermore, if the word "or else" is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), then while one might speak of immorality and so forth—which have reached the status of courses of action—by the names of bodily action and so on, it would be improper to say that mental action arises by way of the six doors of contact; for it does not arise by way of the eye-door and the others.

Furthermore, if only those non-restraints (asaṃvara) and so forth that have reached the state of courses of action (kammappatha) were included, then—since there would be no other non-restraints apart from the misconducts (duccarita), and since it has been stated that these [misconducts] themselves constitute those respective courses of action—it would not be possible to say:
"The non-restraint arising by way of the door of bodily non-restraint is itself unwholesome bodily action," and so forth. For if that were asserted...
There would be confusion; for verbal and mental actions also arise at the door of the body, and likewise, other types of action arise at the remaining doors.

Furthermore, even if an action arising at another door were to be considered as belonging solely to that door—just as it is said, "The threefold bodily misconduct is unwholesome bodily action alone," and so forth, [and] "Unwholesome bodily action [is defined] by way of the door of unrestrained physical intimation"—[then such a view would be untenable].

Furthermore, this would contradict such statements as: "And it arises by way of the door of verbal non-restraint," for there is indeed the operation of misconduct through other doors, yet what has arisen in one door does not become a separate kamma in another door.

Therefore, since it was stated below that only those [unwholesome states] which have reached the level of courses of action (kammapatha) constitute bodily action and so forth, and since wholesome and unwholesome states arising in their respective doors—other than those—are merely a convergence of doors.

Because of the state of being associated with each respective door, there is here an indication of bodily action and so forth for those non-restraints and restraints that have not reached the status of a course of action (*kammapatha*) due to the absence of volition (*cetanā*), even though they are classified as courses of action;
and likewise for the threefold bodily misconduct and the threefold bodily good conduct, even when they proceed through other doors.

The demonstration of the non-abandonment of the state of bodily action and so forth, as well as the explanation of the arising of unwholesome and wholesome bodily actions—both those that have attained the status of courses of action (kamma-patha) as they have been explained and those that have not—through the doors of contact and so on, is called the "Integration of Courses of Action" (Kammapathasaṃsandana). Why?
Because it shows how non-courses of action are included within the courses of action, and how courses of action are included within the non-courses of action.
This is because they are here combined by way of having a common name, by way of not losing their common designation as "paths of action" among the paths of action,
and by way of the arising of both within the doors.
In that regard, because the actions arisen through the three doors of action possess the nature of being specific types of karma, there is the state of being this or that particular type of karma.

Because their arising has been described in relation to the doors of action (*kammadvāra*), and because there is no statement regarding the manner of the arising of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) and so forth by way of the five sense-consciousness doors (*pañcaviññāṇadvāra*), [the text] sets aside both the doors of action and the doors of consciousness and states, "arisen by way of the five contact doors," and so on. This is according to the passage beginning:
"And whatever pleasure arises conditioned by eye-contact... and so forth.

By such statements as, “There is a feeling-aggregate conditioned by eye-contact that is wholesome,” the manner in which non-restraint and so forth arise is explained by way of the five doors of contact; yet there is no such statement as, “That which is this [conditioned] by eye-consciousness.
For it has also been said: “Contact co-nascent with eye-consciousness is ‘eye-contact,’ and so forth. Therefore...

For it is shown that non-restraint and restraint do not arise simultaneously with eye-contact and the rest, whereas those arising simultaneously with mind-contact do so by way of the doors of eye-contact and so forth.
Thus, by the passage beginning, “For when one has reached a state of agitation at the body-door,
there is unwholesome bodily kamma,” it is shown that what arises by way of the door of bodily non-restraint through agitation is indeed unwholesome bodily kamma.

Furthermore, by such statements as "it becomes [unwholesome]," when verbal actions and so forth that have reached the status of courses of action (*kamma-patha*) and constitute non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) are reduced to the state of bodily actions and so forth, this must be seen as a refutation by means of the exception: "The fourfold misconduct of speech is itself unwholesome verbal action," and so on.
And having done so, in the second section of the analysis of non-restraint shown previously:

And there is no contradiction here. For it is not the case that unwholesome bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and so forth, which consists of the non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) of the impelling body, is itself the vocal action (*vacīkamma*) and so forth.
However, unwholesome mental action (*manokamma*) arises by way of the six doors of contact;
