when that [unwholesome state] reaches the doors of body and speech as an impulsion, it becomes unwholesome bodily or vocal action. In this context, what is meant by "unwholesome mental action"? [As explained] below...

And by the method already shown, it includes the threefold misconduct of mind that has arisen at the doors of body and speech, as well as all unwholesome states that have not yet reached the stage of "impulsion" (*copana*).

If this is so, does it not follow that because such [unwholesome states] lack the status of bodily or vocal action, the statement "that which has reached impulsion is bodily or vocal action" is untenable?
It is not untenable; for that which has reached impulsion is indeed unwholesome action (*akusala-kamma*) of both body and speech.
"It occurs" means by way of the accomplishment of its purpose. But as for that action which is occurring, what kind of action is it? It is precisely mental action (*manokamma*).
This is what is meant: unwholesome [action] that has reached the point of impulsion occurs as mental action in both the door of the body and the door of speech.
Alternatively, without connecting the word "that" (*taṃ*) with mental action, [it refers to] whatever arises by way of the six doors of contact.
The connection must be made with the "tanti" (the thread) as defined by the mere arising previously mentioned. But what is this "tanti"?

Since it occurs within the discussion of action (*kamma*), it is understood to be "action"; and although that arises at the door of mind-contact (*manosamphassadvāra*), it constitutes a threefold action.
To show how that is so, he said: "The impulsion has reached the doors of body and speech," and so forth.

In this context, because no fixed rule has been established, the state of having reached impulsion (*copanappatti*)—by way of being a characteristic mark—serves only to indicate bodily and verbal action;

however, it is not the case that everything which has reached impulsion is exclusively bodily and verbal action, nor is it the case that on the side of the wholesome (*kusala*), that which has not reached impulsion is not bodily and verbal action. Thus, this meaning is established.

Alternatively, the opponent speaks by taking the entire definition of "mental action" (manokamma)—namely, that which arises by way of the six doors of contact—as referring to all action accomplished by the mind, rather than the specific mental action previously demonstrated.
For his intention is this: "Since it is produced by the mind, everything must be mental action alone; it cannot be otherwise."

Having set aside [the objection] that [it is] "by bodily and verbal action," this was begun—"that which has reached the impulsion in the doors of body and speech"—in order to show the restriction to the threefold nature of action (*kamma*).
And here, the absence of confusion should be understood in the same manner as before.
Alternatively, having established a connection with the mere word "action" (*kamma*) without qualification, [this shows] how the aforementioned classification of action occurs.

He shows that distinction. And the absence of confusion is exactly as stated. As for what they say—that when covetousness and so forth, which are co-nascent with bodily and verbal actions, belong to the side of volition (cetanā), then those mental actions become bodily and verbal actions—that is not correct, because those things belonging to the side of volition lack the status of being mental action.
Furthermore, when they are not classifiable [as either], their status as mental action is even more clearly established.
It does not exist. And this has also been said: "Or it pertains to the whole body. Therefore, it cannot be said that mental action (manokamma) is bodily or verbal action.

Covetousness and the rest are mental action only when associated with volition (cetanā) that performs the act of coveting and so forth, not when performing the acts of killing and so forth belonging to body and speech;
thus, their status as mental action is even more established. Consequently, it cannot be said that those which are mental actions possess the nature of bodily or verbal action.

Thus, because there is no fixed restriction between the doors of action and the actions belonging to those doors, no connection between the doors has been made. Now, even though such a connection between the doors has not been established,

[the author] says "therein, the sense-sphere" and so forth, in order to illustrate— according to the sequence stated in the canonical text— the manner in which this consciousness arises by way of whichever doors it may arise from, and by way of the respective courses of action (kamma-patha) associated with those doors.
The statement "consciousness arises by way of the three doors of kamma" is said with reference to its arising through that specific nature which constitutes the door of mental kamma.
Or rather, it should be understood that just as consciousness is called "the sovereign of consciousness" (*cittādhipateyya*) by way of its associated factors, so it is here as well.
[This applies] to the continuity of mind (*manopabandha*) when it is devoid of the two types of physical contact.
But there is simply nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the discussion correlating the courses of kamma is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the doors is finished.

“This is the connection (*yojanā*): the meaning is that the phrase ‘or whatever else’ is connected with the preceding statement, ‘whether it has a visible form as its object… or a mental phenomenon (*dhamma*) as its object.
But what is this connection? Connection is the purpose for which preceding and succeeding statements are linked together.
And here, the demonstration of the state of having all things as objects begins with: ‘having a visible form as its object…’”
Immediately after the passage, "or... pe... or having taken as object a mental state (dhammārammaṇaṃ)," one should see the purpose and the application of the statement, "whatever [else] it may be.
Therein, having shown the fault incurred by the mere phrase "having taken as object a visible form... pe...
or a mental state," the purpose of the phrase "whatever [else] it may be" is shown in order to exclude that fault.
“He below,” etc., he says. In the second interpretation of the meaning, by the phrase “whatever is sown,” he draws in even non-primary [objects] such as visible forms and so forth;
for it is not the case that the primary consciousness has itself alone as its object. “By the method stated below” means by the method beginning with “having all things as its object.
Having stated, “what was already taken below is indeed taken,” the purpose of saying this is—
It is said that this was stated in order to show how one might say, “Taking this or that form... or this or that [object],” with reference to it.
In this context, the phrase “this or that” should be understood as being spoken with reference to all objects of consciousness and so forth.
The Discussion on the Section on the Enumeration of Phenomena (Dhammuddesavāra).
The commentary on the "five kinds of contact" (phassapañcaka) by the Teacher:

this refers to the teacher Revata. However, this should not be regarded as authoritative. For this was not undertaken for the purpose of showing that contact and the other factors belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and so forth; rather, it was for the purpose of showing their intrinsic nature (sabhāva) at that specific moment.
As for the phrase "the first impact of the mind": all mental concomitants (cetasika) are dependent upon the mind and are thus spoken of as being the activity of the mind.
Contact (*phassa*) is said to be "the first impingement upon the mind.

Granted that it is the person—consisting of the aggregate of mind and mental factors—in whom contact has arisen, who experiences the object through the feeling co-nascent with that contact at the very same time;
nevertheless, contact is described as if it were prior, because it is the specific condition for feeling and the other factors, just as a lamp is for illumination. [The example of] the rafters...

The "wing-noose" (*pakkhapāsa*) is wood placed above and across [the opening]. Even though it does not adhere by way of a single part or a single side—just like two pieces of wood and so forth—it shares a commonality with matter in that it is a mere contact (*saṅghaṭṭana*) without adhering; it is not the state of being an object (*visayabhāva*).
And this contact is simply the state of the convergence of the mind and its objects through the coming together of the base (*vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*).
"It comes together" (*sampajjati*) means contact (*phassa*) as the coming-together through impact. Just as there is a meeting of two hands, so too is there a meeting of consciousness and its object;
contact is the condition for the occurrence of consciousness as it meets with its object. Thus, by way of its function (*rasa*), it has the "taste of impact.
For such a state of being a condition is the function of impact belonging to that contact. Just as...

For just as the clashing of one hand against another consists of material phenomena (rūpadhamma) that are specific to it, so too the clashing of the mind against its object should be understood as a single mental factor (cetasika-dhamma) that is specific to it.

By the phrase "in the mind itself," he shows that feeling is a contact (saṅghaṭṭana) whose intrinsic nature is mental and which is unmingled with the physical bases (vatthu) and objects (ārammaṇa), but not that it has a physical basis (vatthunissaya).
It rejects [the object]. The corresponding attention (*tajjā-samannāhāra*) is the cause of that contact;

it is the state of the faculty being directed toward that [object], the making of the object by adverting, the preparedness and the conditioning of the sense-field, and the making of the object for consciousness—this is the meaning.
The intention is that it is only in pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*) that [craving] finds gratification. "Pervasive mastery" (*vissavitā*) means the state of an *arahant*.

For roots have multiple meanings, and the prefix *vi-* combined with the root *su* has the sense of "worthy one" (*arahant*). Alternatively, pervasive mastery is the state of dwelling as a master over one's own people—that is, acting according to one's will.
"Experiencing only a single portion of the flavor of the object" means that this function of contact and so forth is like experiencing only a partial aspect.

Thus it has been stated. For the very nature of being felt (*vedayita*) is experiencing (*anubhavana*). Alternatively, grasping an object by way of contact and so forth is a partial experience, whereas grasping it by way of being felt is an experience of the whole according to one's desire.

Thus, since those graspings are of such natures, there is no experiencing of a state of ownership through the performance of their respective functions, as there is in the case of feeling (*vedanā*), even for contact (*phassa*) and the others.
It should be urged. By the phrase "herein," he refers to the feeling of mental joy (*somanassavedanā*) intended among the five feelings within this consciousness;
therefore, it should be understood that, having set aside the feeling of non-joy, the quality of enjoying a desirable mode [of experience] is stated in relation to the feeling of joy thus grasped.

Recollection (*paccābhiññāṇa*) has the function of recognizing again by means of a sign, and its essence is the act of recognition. The condition for recognizing again is the "condition for recognizing again" (*puna-sañjānanapaccaya*).
That very sign is again... pe ... the sign; its making is again... pe ... the making.
Or, the making of the sign which serves as the condition for further recognition is "again... pe ... making"; the meaning is that this is its function.

The making of the sign as a condition for further recognition should be understood as common to all perception (saññā), whether it be the making of the sign by one who makes the sign or the perceiving by one who perceives through the sign. It is simply knowledge (ñāṇa).
It conforms; therefore, the intention is that it does not produce dogmatic adherence nor grasp things erroneously.
By this same method, it should be understood that there is no lack of duration when associated with concentration (*samādhi*).
"Abhisandahati" means it binds together, it sets in motion. The state of volition (*cetanā*) is the state of activity. "Twofold exertion" means... [not]...
This was said with reference to a twofold application of energy (*vīriya-yoga*), yet it illustrates the great magnitude of its own specific function.
"By way of exertion" means by way of earnestness. For she herself, being characterized by earnestness, inspires earnestness in the associated mental states.
"Cognizing" (*vijānana*) is the apprehension of the object. "Connecting" (*sandahana*) is the linking of one state of consciousness to the next. By the eye...

"Seen" (*diṭṭha*) means that which is to be seen by the eye. Just as in the expression "seen, heard, sensed, and cognized," the terms "seen" and so forth denote what is to be seen and the rest, so too should it be understood here.
In the phrases beginning with "by the eye," etc., the meaning is: "by the door of the eye... [and so on]... by the door of the mind.
Like a city guard, it is merely the manifestation of the object for the mind, a mere sustaining, a mere apprehension.

The function [of consciousness], such as the penetration of the object and the subsequent direct knowledges (paccābhiññā), should be understood as belonging to wisdom (paññā) and perception (saññā) respectively.

"Previously specified" means specified in the determination of the occasion (samaya-vavatthāna). To show that it does not fail to arise—as if one were merely developing it—but rather that it does indeed arise, it is said:
"consciousness exists" (cittaṃ hoti); this refers to the word *hoti* [as synonymous with] the word *uppajjati*.
And if they were identical in meaning, it would be logical; yet if they were identical in meaning, one could not say that "it has arisen there.

For it is not reasonable to say that "what has already arisen arises. Furthermore, since the state of having arisen for consciousness has already been stated in the determination of time, what is the purpose of showing its arising again? And as for that by which the determination of time was made...
If it is not impossible to provide a detailed exposition (*niddesa*), what is the purpose of that exposition?

Since the distinctness of consciousness from contact and so forth is established by the second section—the summary (*uddesa*)—and indeed by the exposition itself, what is the point of stating it again for that same purpose?

However, the latter mention of "consciousness" was spoken because the former mention of "consciousness" served a different purpose; for the former was intended solely for the purpose of defining the occasion (*samaya*).

It was said for the purpose of showing the phenomena existing at the time of their non-determination, while the other [statement] was said for the purpose of showing the phenomena existing at that [specific] time;
it was not said for the purpose of determining the time, nor does a statement meant for one purpose state something else, nor was it spoken by way of a mere pretext.
Therefore, it cannot be maintained that the Greatly Compassionate One does not make the meaning clear.
The commentary on the heap of the five beginning with contact is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the heap of jhāna factors:
in the phrase "he applies thought" (*vitakketi*), the word "dhamma" is specified as the agent in order to exclude any agent other than the dhamma itself. Of that...

However, the designation "bhā" is used for the purpose of excluding the state of being subject to mastery (*vasavatti*), [implying] "the act of thinking" (*vitakkana*). It has the characteristic of striking, as it is like striking [an object] while thinking, "It is form, it is form," or "It is earth, it is earth.
Striking from the beginning or directly toward something is *āhanana*;
striking all around or after turning [the object] over is *pariyāhanana*. In the sense of being grosser than investigation (*vicāra*), it belongs to investigation itself.
In the sense of being a precursor, initial application (*vitakka*) is coarse because it resounds; it is like the striking of a bell, which serves as its precursor.
Just as the striking of the bell is the first impact, so too is initial application the "first impact" in the sense of directing [the mind] toward the object.
It is called "expansive" (*vipphāra*) because it is associated with movement. In the context of occurrence through continuous succession, this refers to the stage of access (*upacāra*).
Or [it occurs] in absorption (appanā) or in the continuity of the stream (santāna-pavatti). For therein, applied thought (vitakka), having become motionless, enters into the object and proceeds.
"Circle" (maṇḍala) refers to the threshing-floor circle.
"It moistens" (piṇayati) means it satisfies or it expands. "The function of suffusion" (pharaṇa-rasa) is the function of pervading the body with sublime forms.
Elation (*udagga-bhāva*) is rapture (*odagya*). The "momentary" (*khaṇika*) arises frequently, having broken off after producing a slight thrill of the hair standing on end; it does not arise again.
The "access" (*ubbega*) is more refined than that, because of its pervasiveness, its immobility, and its long duration.
Taking hold of the sign of tranquility (*passaddhi*), it conceives within it. Only the rapture associated with absorption fulfills absorption-concentration (*appanā-samādhi*).
Having done so, she was established. The other two—momentary concentration (*khaṇika-samādhi*) and access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*)—are fulfilled by rapture (*pīti*).
"With a concentrated mind" means with a mind accompanied by concentration. Non-distraction (*avisāra*) is the very nature of not wandering away from oneself.
Non-diffusion (*avikkhepa*) is the state of being undistracted in those associated [with it]. That mental factor by which those associated [with it] become undistracted is non-diffusion.

"By way of distinction" means for the most part. For there is indeed concentration even when devoid of happiness. By the illustration of the lamp, he shows that the nature of concentration is the persistence of the continuum.
The commentary on the aggregate of jhāna factors is finished.
The commentary on the aggregate of faculties begins.
"By means of this they have faith" (*saddahanti etāya*): this shows that faith is the condition for those phenomena occurring through the act of believing by virtue of its predominance therein.
For when phenomena possess such a conditional state, there arises the conventional expression, "a person has faith.
In objects worthy of confidence, lack of faith (*assaddhiya*)—which is unwholesome and constitutes the opposite of confidence—is wrong resolve (*micchā-adhimokkha*).

Furthermore, the certainty that has reached its object and consists of serene confidence (pasāda) has the characteristic of resolution (adhimokkha); it is not the resolution that is merely a concomitant factor (yevāpanaka-adhimokkha).
It exercises lordship (indaṭṭha) means that it makes the associated mental states conform to itself, as if saying, "There is no resolving for you apart from me;
have faith through me. The same applies to the remaining [mental factors]. "Leaping forward" (pakkhandana) means sinking into [the object].
Mud (*paṅka*) is that which has become thickened from mire. Slime (*paṇaka*) is slippery water-impurity. Yellow water (*pīta-udaka*).

"Characterized by settling" (*okappana-lakkhaṇā*) means characterized by entering [into an object] and determining it thus: "It is so. Clarity (*akaluṣabhāva*) is the state of being unclouded; the meaning is the state of being undisturbed. The objects such as the Buddha are things to be trusted. [These are: attending upon true persons, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma.

The factors of stream-entry (sotāpattiyaṅgāni) should be regarded as being like a hand for grasping wholesome states, like wealth for producing all forms of prosperity, and like a seed for bearing the fruit of the deathless.
"Heroic state" (vīrabhāva) means that quality by which one is called a hero. Exertion (paggaha) is the providing of supporting strength. This is the path (magga).
There is a journey to be undertaken; the journey has been undertaken. There is work to be done; the work has been done. A slight ailment has arisen;
he has recovered from illness, having recently emerged from that sickness.
While wandering for alms in a village or town, he does not obtain a sufficient quantity of coarse or refined food; [or] he obtains... [and so on]... a sufficient quantity.
These are the eight bases for the arousal of energy accompanied by appropriate reflection, or the reflections rooted therein.
"Establishment" is the arrival at the object such as what was done long ago, or the non-relinquishing of the object;
it is the non-yielding of the object so that it may not float away like a gourd in water, but remains as steady as a stone.

Establishing (*ṭhapana*) is recollecting (*sāraṇa*), making non-forgetfulness, and not letting [the object] slip away (*apilāpana*). One performs the act of not letting slip; thus, one "makes it not slip away" (*apilāpeti*).

"Ways of occurrence" (*gatiyo*) refers to accomplishments by way of their arising and their fruit. "Another method" (*aparo nayo*) is undertaken for the purpose of showing the flavor (*rasa*) and so forth.

Non-forgetfulness (*asammoso*) is the function that is the opposite of forgetfulness; it is not merely the absence of forgetfulness. The body and so forth, which serve as the bases for mindfulness, are the "foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*) of the body and so forth.
Or rather, mindfulness itself is the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for the subsequent [states].

For distraction and restlessness. "He makes known" means he causes them to be known in various ways. "It becomes a single light" is said with reference to the radiance that is a defilement of insight (*vipassanūpakkilesobhāsa*).
It is called "mind" (*mano*) because one thinks or cognizes by means of it; and having defined it thus, [the Sutta says]: "In dependence on the mind and mental objects..."
And by the word “and,” the mind (mano) is mentioned as being the cause. For the entire mind is the cause of the consciousness immediately following it.
"It cognizes" means it knows by way of delimitation and apprehension, not by way of perceiving or penetrating as is the case with perception (saññā) and wisdom (paññā).
When it is said "through association with zest and joy," that through which one becomes "well-minded" (sumana) is called joy (somanassa).

Furthermore, it would follow that joy (*pīti*) itself would possess the nature of mental happiness (*somanassa*); therefore, it should be construed as being associated with pleasant feeling even without the body as its physical basis.
In this way, both joyless happiness and happiness accompanied by joy are included;
or rather, the meaning should be understood as "happiness characterized by joy" being either "with joy" (*sappītika*) or "joyless" (*nippītika*).
"Predominance over the continuity of the process" means being the dominant factor for the continuity known as the process.

For the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), by virtue of its protecting itself during its own moment of existence and serving as the cause for the arising of that protection in the immediate succession, the process becomes long-lasting; it remains undifferentiated until death, being distinguished only by the specific variations of the respective kamma.
Or rather, it continues uninterruptedly until final Nibbāna, being associated with the specific state of being alive;

thus, in order to state the common characteristics and so forth of the material and immaterial life-faculties (*rūpārūpa-jīvitindriya*), he said, "of the phenomena inseparable from itself. [The life-faculty exists] only at the very moment when those things to be sustained exist.
For if there were nothing to be sustained, such as a lotus and so forth, what would water sustain? "Of this and that" refers to the sustaining and so forth.
"By way of accomplishment" means by means of accomplishment. And that accomplishment is due to its being the condition for the specific state of one who is living.
The commentary on the aggregate of the faculties is finished.
The commentary on the aggregate of the path factors.
“Rightly” (*sammā*) means by way of being non-perverted and leading to liberation. Its excellence (*pasatthatā*) should also be understood in this very same way.

In the commentary on the “mass of powers” (*balarāsi*): “Because of lack of faith” (*assaddhiye*) means due to the cause of lack of faith. “By way of both terms” (*ubhayapadavasena*) means by way of pairs of terms such as the term “faith” (*saddhā*) and the term “power” (*bala*).
"Internally originated" means that its origination is from birth and so forth within oneself. "Reverential" (*sappatissava*) means listening with respect when something is said by a venerable person;
the meaning is any kind of reverence, whether it be the act of listening itself, that which is associated with such listening, or that which is similar to it.
It arises through reflecting on the greatness of birth and other such qualities.
And because *hirī* (a sense of moral shame) operates there by way of reverence, it is said to have "the characteristic of having respect.
One who fears what is blameworthy and views it as such is called "one who fears blame and sees danger. *Ottappa* (moral dread) has such a nature.
*Hirī* regards evil states as if they were excrement, while *ottappa* regards them as if they were fire. The inheritance consists of the nine supramundane states and so forth.
The fact that moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*) originate internally and so forth is stated because they are manifest in various contexts;

however, there is never a mutual dissociation between them. For there is no such thing as feeling shame while being devoid of fear, nor is there fear of evil while being devoid of shame. *Commentary on the Root Group* (*Mūlarāsivaṇṇanā*)
Non-covetousness (*anabhijjhā*) is the absence of longing (*anabhikaṅkhanā*). "One whose disposition and intention (*adhippāya*) are not attached" is *anallīnabhāvo*;

it is thus that it accords with the simile. A "concordant friend" (*anukūlamitta*) is one who acts in accordance. "The essence of discipline" (*vinayarasa*) means the essence of training (*vinayana*).

"Non-hatred (*adosa*) [is the antidote] to the stain of immorality"—this is said with reference to the fact that immorality originates from hatred and has hatred as its supporting condition (*upanissaya*).

It has been said: "Non-development (abhāvanā) refers to the non-occurrence of that development consisting of wisdom which has been described as follows: 'Development in the sense of the non-transgression of states arisen therein;
development in the sense of the single flavor of the faculties; development in the sense of the driving of energy toward that [goal]; and development in the sense of repeated practice.
Alternatively, it is the unwholesome states that are the opposites of that [development]."
Grasping at qualities where none exist is over-grasping (*adhikaggaṇaṃ*). Grasping after destroying a quality that actually exists is under-grasping (*ūnaggaṇaṃ*).
Grasping through the four perversions (*catuvipallāsa*) is inverted grasping (*viparītaggaṇaṃ*).
Regarding the true nature (*yāthāvasabhāve*): "This much is his quality, this much is his fault"—this refers to the true nature of qualities and faults. [He is] subject to aging...
Because such reflections as, "It decays; how could it not decay here? are possible [through non-delusion];
and because householders lack disputes over fields, land, and so forth through non-greed; and because renunciants lack disputes over speculative views through non-delusion.
For householders dispute with other householders due to the bondage of attachment to sensual desire, while those bound by attachment to views [dispute]...
"Ascetics [interacting] with ascetics": through passion there is intimacy with friends, and through hatred there is conflict;
by way of these specific qualities, there is approaching and departing, or else, toward objects such as visible forms, there is compliance and resistance.

The occurrence of non-neutrality—consisting of aversion and attachment—is due to delusion. In the transformation of pleasure and in the conjunction with suffering, there is the discernment of feeling during the occurrence of aversion.
"It is not accomplished" means that through the power of non-fault, the foundation of mindfulness regarding feelings is accomplished. "Of the divine abiding" refers to the four jhānas.

The noble abiding is the attainment of fruition. Since one who does not investigate due to delusion forms attachments even toward all conditioned phenomena belonging to the category of the neutral, it should be understood that for one who is undeluded, such attachment is absent.
This is because [the foundation of mindfulness regarding feelings] is the immediate antidote to the view of suffering.
Through non-hatred (*adosa*), which is the opposite of hatred (*dosa*), there is the vision of suffering.

In the commentary on the collection of courses of action (*kammappatha-rāsi*), it should be understood that one does not injure or destroy oneself or another with regard to happiness and so forth. This is by way of the courses of action (*kammappatha*) due to their being the courses of action and sharing the same nature.
Commentary on the Pairs Beginning with Tranquility (*passaddhi*):

"Distress" (*daratha*) means agitation; it is a designation for the defilements such as restlessness (*uddhacca*) which are conditions for suffering and mental grief, or for the four aggregates. Defilements dominated by restlessness are "restlessness-and-other-defilements"; [the first of these is] restlessness.

Or, taking that as the beginning, it includes all defilements. "Like the purification of gold" means that just as the purification of gold is fit for use in various types of ornaments, so too this [purification] is fit for use in performing beneficial deeds.
*Sampajañña* is knowing equally or all around by way of its modes. [It applies] to the forward steps and so forth for the purpose of worshipping a cetiya, etc.

Discernment of purpose (*sātthaka-sampajañña*) is the discerning of what is beneficial and what is not. Discernment of suitability (*sappāya-sampajañña*) is the mindfulness that discerns whether visible forms and other objects are suitable or unsuitable for one’s purpose.
Discernment of resort (*gocara-sampajañña*) is the non-abandonment of the meditation subject while walking through the village or other areas where one goes for alms.

Discernment of non-delusion (*asammoha-sampajañña*) is the investigation of walking and other activities by way of the elements and so forth. [This applies] to those devoted to the cultivation of all meditation subjects.
These two qualities are always beneficial to all practitioners, because they remove obstacles and increase development.
As it is said: "Two qualities are very helpful: mindfulness and clear comprehension. They are called *yuganaddhā* (yoked together) because they proceed equally as mutual causes for one another;
that is the meaning. Furthermore: "Moreover, friends, a bhikkhu [practices] serenity and insight..."
For in the Sutta it is said that "one develops the yoke-union" (*yuganaddha*), by which their state of being yoked together is expressed.

Because these two factors, when joined together, are free from both laxity (*līna*) and agitation (*uddhacca*) among all wholesome states, it is said "for the purpose of yoking energy and concentration" (*vīriya-samādhi-yojana-atthāya*); the meaning is "for the purpose of expressing the term 'yoke' (*yoga*). [End of] Commentary on the Miscellaneous Factors (*Yevāpanaka-vaṇṇanā*).
"By the absence of form" means by the absence of being affected (ruppana). "Dhammas" has the meaning of those things that are apprehended as having their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

"The preliminary stage of loving-kindness" means the preliminary stage of loving-kindness that has reached absorption; the meaning is that preparatory loving-kindness (parikamma-mettā) exists in this consciousness.

"By way of abstinence" means not fulfilling [the precepts] through the occurrence of speech, but rather by means of the application of abstinence. "Unfailing factors" means factors that are not contradicted.
Discernment and resolution regarding an object, in whatever manner they occur; for one who does not resolve cannot engage in acts such as killing or in acts such as giving.

It is like a child crawling here and there, who has no discernment as to whether he will or will not act.

For even though they do not have that [object] as their objective support, when they proceed equally, there is "equanimity toward the object" (*tatramajjhattatā*) due to their state of neutrality.

"Of the bases such as bodily misconduct" refers to killing living beings and so forth.

Whether it be a collection of terms, a division of terms, or that very term itself, if it is not stated, it is said to be "omitted."

Regarding the word "pūrita" (filled): thinking that there is no connection whatsoever between what has already been stated and what is being stated now—just as there is none between various unrelated utterances of the word "man"—he says, "a discourse lacking continuity.

Thinking that because it is stated intermittently, the phenomena are not presented in their proper sequence, he says, "out of order. [The phrase] "the mass with contact as the fifth" is stated by way of its commonality to all mental states (*cittuppāda*).

And it is stated by way of inclusion within the four aggregates and their respective conditions. However, since among the aforementioned "heaps" (rāsi) there is not even the function of forming a single heap, desire and the rest are stated as "included" (yevāpanaka).

Because it has been done. “Contemplation” (*upanijjhāna*) is the act of reflecting and thinking after having approached the object. “In the sense of a means” (*hetvaṭṭhena*) means in the sense of an instrument, not in the sense of a root.

The eightfold path that was traversed and practiced during the prior stage—which is asynchronous (*nānākkhaṇika*)—is called the “path as it has been traversed” when it arises simultaneously with the supramundane moment.

By eliding the latter member of the compound, "existence in the realm of form" (*rūpabhava*) is called simply "form" (*rūpa*). Although the jhāna is not itself the path, the mention of the "path" is for the purpose of precluding other paths;

"Wholesome giving" (*kusalaṃ dānaṃ*) should be understood as non-greed (*alobha*).
Alternatively, volition (*cetanā*) is the giving; setting that aside, the other two [factors] are said to be associated with volition. They are "possible."
The meaning is that it is appropriate to call it "the path" (magga) by including it under the term "meditative absorption" (jhāna) because of its nature as a path.
"Conviction" (okappanā) means faith. Why is this meaning—"it generates and increases"—stated here when it has been seen elsewhere to have that very same meaning without a prefix?
It is stated in order to clarify that this meaning is indeed seen elsewhere even without a prefix.
“Furthermore, Udāyī”—thus the sutta is cited. For certain noble ones, other jhānas accomplished through the noble path are indeed of the very nature of meditation;
thus, by cultivating them as well, the determination of the occasion (samaya-vavatthāna) is achieved.
It is called "escape" (nissaraṇa) because by means of it, or in it, they escape or go forth. What escapes? Sensual desires (kāmā). Of those...
The meaning is "the abandoning that is the escape from sensual pleasures. For in this way, the genitive case in "of sensual pleasures" (*kāmānaṃ*) is appropriate when it refers to the agent.

As for the phrase "even by means of sense-objects," the meaning "secluded even from sense-objects" is also appropriate; thus, the particle *pi* has the sense of adding another compatible meaning, not the sense of adding the defilement-sensualities.
Why? Because in this context, the defilement-sensualities [are already covered] by the second clause.

Because seclusion has been stated [in the preceding verse]. Although the term "unwholesome" (akusala) may refer to the defilements of sensual desire (kilesakāma), it nevertheless includes all unwholesome states;

however, since seclusion from the defilements of sensual desire is stated in every respect, he says: "Because of the statement of seclusion from the defilements of sensual desire by means of the second [verse].
Even the cause for attaining the strands of sensual pleasure involves impure practice such as the taking of life; therefore, purity of practice is achieved through seclusion from that.

It has been analyzed. "The nourishing of the underlying tendency by means of purifying the defilement of craving" refers to the nourishing of the latent bias through the cleansing of that specific corruption.

"And of others as well" refers to views, conceit, and so forth, as well as contact and the rest. "The factors of the higher jhānas" (uparijjhānaṅgāni) refers to the factors of jhāna mentioned further on;
the mention of the hindrances opposed to them is for the purpose of showing their state as the counteragents to their respective opposites.

By the expression "seclusion from ill-will" (*vyāpāda-viveka*), the seclusion by suppression (*vikkhambhana-viveka*) of hatred—which has as its object the various bases for resentment such as "he has done me harm"—is stated;

and by the expression "seclusion from sloth, torpor, and so forth," which are dominated by delusion, the seclusion by suppression of delusion—which has as its object the divisions of suffering and the like, as well as the past limit and so forth—is stated through the manner of concealing them. And this [first jhāna] is that which suppresses sensual lust, ill-will, and their associated states such as sloth and torpor.
Because it has the nature of being the opposite of all unwholesome states, and because all wholesome states have that same nature,
even though the abandoning of all unwholesome states occurs through that nature, it is specifically the suppression of sensual desire and so forth; therefore, since it shares that nature,
he says that "seclusion by suppression" is stated without distinction for the hindrances, the unwholesome roots, and so on.

When thought has attained stability through its specific function, the term "access" (*appanā*)—according to the usage of the Aṭṭhakathās—is applied to the concentration of the first jhāna by virtue of its stability, which causes the removal of opposing factors; it is also applied to similar concentrations such as those of the second jhāna and beyond, which are devoid of thought.
Thus, "the application of access to thought" is stated. Otherwise, if thought itself were the access, there would be no association of that [access] with it [thought].

The meaning... [etc. ...should be seen as follows: because by showing that one possessing *vitakka* and *vicāra* possesses the *jhāna*, it is stated that the *jhāna* itself has the state of being with *vitakka* and *vicāra*.
Regarding the phrase "born of seclusion, accompanied by rapture and pleasure" (*vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ*): in the first sense, "born of seclusion" refers to the *jhāna*.

And from the words "rapture and pleasure," there is the suffix *-a* (the *a*-kāra) which expresses the sense of "possessing" (*atthi*) or "being in this" (*asmiṃ vā*), qualifying the specific quality of rapture and pleasure. In the second sense, it refers to rapture and pleasure themselves.

“Born of seclusion” (*vivekajaṃ*). The compound *vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ* is a compound in the sense of a different referent (*aññapadattha-samāsa*), and the suffix of the personal pronoun (*paccattaniddesa*) has been elided;
or, when there is elision, the reading is “*vivekajapītisukhan*” — this is the distinction. “By way of sequential enumeration” (*gaṇanānupubbatāyā*):

the meaning is that it is called “first” by virtue of its sequential enumeration, or simply because it possesses the mere quality of sequential enumeration. By means of abandoning distortions such as permanence and so forth...
The path penetrates the characteristics such as impermanence by way of non-delusion; thus, it is "contemplation of the characteristics. Nibbāna is of a nature not subject to confusion;
because its characteristic is non-perverted and because it does not become otherwise, it is the "characteristic of suchness" (*tathalakkhaṇa*).
Commentary on the Discussion of the Second Jhāna.

161–2. Regarding the phrase "with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā*): by this it is shown that the attainment of the second jhāna occurs through the transcending of those very applied and sustained thoughts by which the first jhāna is characterized as gross;
it does not mean the transcending of contact and so forth, which are not gross by their own nature.

This same method applies to the phrases "and with the fading away of rapture" (*pītiyā ca virāgā*), and so on. Therefore, these are statements concerning the transcending of applied and sustained thought, rapture, and pleasure.

The statement regarding the surmounting of applied and sustained thought is said to be an indicator of that [second jhāna] because it is a part of those [statements] which indicate the attainment of the second jhāna and so forth by means of the surmounting of increasingly gross factors.

Alternatively, since the very statement of the subsiding of applied and sustained thought indicates the attainment of the second jhāna through the surmounting of those [factors], the statements such as "with the fading away of rapture" and so on likewise indicate the attainment of the third jhāna and so forth through the surmounting of rapture and the rest; thus, its status as an indicator of that is stated.
"Like blue cloth because of its connection with the color blue"—the intention is that cloth is blue because of its connection with blue.

When that serenity (*sampasādana*) by which the jhāna is connected is shown, then by the very use of a coordinate designation (*samānādhikaraṇa-niddesa*) stating "jhāna of serenity," it is correctly understood that the application of that term [serenity] to the jhāna occurs because of that connection;
thus there is no contradiction. How is it [explained] regarding "singleness" (*ekodibhāva*)? In singleness...
Since it is stated in the passage, “the jhāna of singleness,” by means of a grammatical construction of apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the fact that jhāna increases singleness is already expressed;
therefore, one need not extract this term “singleness” (*ekodibhāva*) and provide a separate definition for it.
Thus, it is logical that the word *ekodibhāva* itself, just like the word *sampasādana*, functions to denote both concentration (*samādhi*) and jhāna.
"Appita" means they have been led to destruction.

Since the absence of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) has already been indicated by the very expression "the subsiding of applied and sustained thought"—which indicates the cause for the one-pointedness of mind through internal confidence as a means for attaining the second jhāna and so forth, and which indicates the cause for the state of being without applied and sustained thought—what further purpose is served by the explicit statement "without applied thought and without sustained thought"?
It is not [redundant], because it was not previously fully illuminated.
For by the statement regarding the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought, the non-occurrence of applied thought and sustained thought is not being asserted.
Rather, the "subsiding" of applied thought and sustained thought refers to the abandoning of craving for them.

Just as there is the occurrence of formations in those paths where craving for formations has been abandoned, and in the fruits [of the path] where craving has been abandoned, so too here [in the second jhāna], there is the occurrence of applied thought and sustained thought in one whose craving for them has been suppressed.
Since the association of the second jhāna with applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) might not have been excluded by the preceding [description],

it was stated as "without applied thought, without sustained thought" both to exclude them and to show that their subsiding consists precisely in the transcending of the desire to advert and so forth.
Commentary on the Third Jhāna.
163. "Pure nature" means the nature of one whose taints are destroyed; it is the state of being free from defilement. Regarding the phrase "the sign of equanimity":
here, energy that is neutral (*majjhatta*) and free from falling into the sides of lethargy or agitation is called "equanimity.

That very energy, because it serves as the sign for the kind of energy that must be exercised by taking that [neutral] aspect as its object, is the "sign of equanimity. This is for the sake of attaining the first jhāna.

Knowledge regarding the equanimity of formations through the reflective stabilization of the perception of the base of nothingness for the sake of attaining the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—this [knowledge] arises by way of the eight attainments.
Knowledge regarding arising, occurrence, the sign, accumulation, rebirth-linking, and destination for the sake of attaining the stream-entry path... [etc.]

[He contemplates] arising, rebirth, birth, and aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. [He contemplates] arising, occurrence, and accumulation for the sake of attaining the fruit of stream-entry...

[and so on] ...up to despair. [He contemplates] arising, occurrence, and accumulation for the sake of attaining the path of arahantship... [and so on] ...up to despair. [He contemplates] arising, occurrence, and accumulation for the sake of attaining the fruit of arahantship... [and so on] ...for the sake of attaining the dwelling in emptiness... [and so on] ...for the sake of attaining the dwelling in the signless.
“Wisdom as reflective composure is knowledge of equanimity regarding formations” (paṭisaṅkhāsantiṭṭhanā paññā saṅkhārupekkhāsu ñāṇaṃ)—these ten [types of knowledge] arise by way of insight.

“Whatever exists, whatever has come to be” refers to the five aggregates; these are abandoned by the knowledge of desire for deliverance. Just as when investigating the characteristic of the beautiful in the three things seen that possess beauty, so too, when investigating the characteristic of formations in the three characteristics that have been seen as they truly are.

One attains equanimity (*upekkhā*). "Having the flavor of effortlessness" means that even toward that sublime pleasure, there is no leaning forward, because its function is to counteract [preference].
It is said that the one possessing the jhāna experiences mental pleasure through the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and physical pleasure through the production of matter caused by physical pleasure.
This is because of being touched and pervaded. For just as in the case of one whose body is touched by water...
When such tangibles as wind, which are not overly adverse, touch the body, pleasure arises; likewise it is for one whose body is touched by these [other factors].
Commentary on the Fourth Jhāna (165):

"With non-manifest appearance" means that, unlike pleasure and pain, they do not have a manifest mode of appearance; rather, like the path of a deer on a flat rock, they appear in a non-manifest mode that must be inferred from them.
The commentary on the Fourfold Method is finished.
Commentary on the Fivefold Method: 167.
"Of whichever element of phenomena" refers to the knowledge of omniscience. For by that [knowledge], one discerns the differentiation of the modes of phenomena.

"Having understood [the disposition], he establishes [the practitioner] in a teaching suited to that. And here, in the fivefold system, the second jhāna is analyzed by being treated as belonging to the category of the second jhāna in the fourfold system:

"In which... he develops the path; he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is without applied thought, with sustained thought only, born of concentration, and accompanied by rapture and happiness. Why? Because it has the state of a fruit of the abode of beings who possess a unity of body and diversity of perception.

Because it has the same fruit as the second jhāna and because it is born from the concentration of the first jhāna, the first jhāna itself is indeed "secluded from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states.
Since those [sensual pleasures and unwholesome states] are absent here, one cannot say "quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states," nor can one say "born of seclusion.
Furthermore, in the Suttanta teachings, according to the fivefold method, the second and third jhānas...

They partake of the second jhāna alone because of the subsiding of applied thought (*vitakka*), the subsiding of sustained thought (*vicāra*), and because of being without applied thought and without sustained thought.
[End of] Commentary on the Fourfold Set of Ways (Paṭipadācatukka), §§176–180.
The "access" (*upacāra*) to each respective jhāna is so called because of the subsiding of the hindrances, applied thought, sustained thought, attachment, and so forth.
The concentration pertaining to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-samādhi*) is stable. "Conformity with that" (*tadanudhammatā*) means being in accordance with that;

they say this is "wrong mindfulness" (*micchāsati*), consisting either of the gratification of that [concentration] or of the aggregates associated with that gratification. It is also appropriate to call it "mindfulness that avoids this or that while not free from attachment.
Having done so, the alternative formulation "by way of mindfulness or by way of attachment" was made. Also, by way of its arrival...

And the statement "the modes of progress do indeed exist" was said with reference to the fact that sometimes the second and subsequent modes of progress take on the characteristics of the first mode of progress.
For the word *api* indicates non-universality;
and precisely because of this non-universality, in the Pāḷi each jhāna is associated separately with four modes of progress, four objects, and sixteen aspects.
Otherwise, nine jhānas would have to be applied to each individual path and so forth.
Commentary on the Tetrad of Objects (181):
"Not well-mastered" means not brought under control by the five kinds of mastery.
Commentary on the Mixture of Objects and Methods (Ārammaṇapaṭipadāmissakavaṇṇanā) 186. "Below" means prior to the sixteen times.

By the statement, "those who are said to produce jhāna," it is meant that for those trainees (*sekkhā*) who have performed the preliminary work and have produced jhāna by means of the path (*magga*) itself, their jhānas—because they are bound to the path—are included within the "pure ninefold" (*suddhikanavaka*).
They should be understood thus: for they do not actually produce [the jhāna].

This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the kasiṇas. (203) By the statement regarding their being the basis for cessation, their being the basis for the formless attainments is also shown. "Quick vision" means the state of having swift direct knowledge and the state of being swiftly proficient.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Bases of Mastery (Abhibhāyatana): 204.
"And another" means that it does not consist solely of what is termed the bases of totality (kasiṇāyatana), but also occurs as what is termed the bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana).
Thus, although the bases of mastery are in fact bases of totality, there exists a state of being a base of mastery distinct from their state of being bases of totality.
This shows the variety of the signs of meditation that overcome the signs of the *kasiṇas*.

In this context, "it overcomes" (*abhibhavati*) means it is "overcoming" (*abhibhu*), which refers either to the preliminary work (*parikamma*) or to knowledge (*ñāṇa*). That which has this overcoming as its sphere (*āyatana*) is an "overcoming-sphere" (*abhibhāyatana*), namely, the *jhāna*.

Alternatively, that which has as its sphere the object to be overcome—designated here as the "sphere" (*āyatana*)—is an "overcoming-sphere," namely, the *jhāna*. This is because of the overcoming of the object.

And because that base (*āyatana*) and the sphere (*āyatana*) are the foundation for specific types of bliss, and because they consist of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*), the jhāna together with its associated factors is called a "base of mastery" (*abhibhāyatana*).

Due to its connection with the Path, for one who has emerged from attainment at that time, there is a mental application (*ābhoga*) by way of preliminary development; this refers to the mode of mastery that occurred during the moment of the jhāna.
It should be understood that it is "said" because it proceeds by way of inclusion. However, in the *Āgamas*, there are these [passages]:

"One percipient of forms internally sees forms externally, limited, beautiful or ugly; [or] immeasurable, beautiful or ugly. One not percipient of forms internally... [as before] ...limited, beautiful or ugly; [or] immeasurable, beautiful or ugly. Of these—
Because they have come down [in the texts], it is stated in the commentaries on the Āgamas:
"Even though there is attention (*ābhoga*) to color, these bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) are taught only by way of the limited (*paritta*) and the immeasurable (*appamāṇa*).
For being limited or immeasurable is the cause of mastery, whether or not there is attention to color. And therein, those [bases] devoid of attention to color—
All the limited perceptions (*parittāni*) together are called "fair and ugly colors" (*suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni*); likewise, they should be understood as "immeasurable" (*appamāṇāni*).
For there is this figurative method (*pariyāyo*): having overcome those limited perceptions, if they are at times applied by way of color, one overcomes the fair and ugly colors.
But here, because it is a teaching given without such figurative methods, they are devoid of application to color.
They are taught both separately and together. For there is indeed a distinction in the manner of mastery in both cases.
And therein, because the teaching is given by way of synonyms (*pariyāya*), there is also a synonymic application of "mastery" (*abhibhavana*) to the liberations (*vimokkha*);
thus, the first two bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) are stated as "perceiving forms internally," while the second liberation is [included] within the third and fourth bases of mastery.
The third liberation is included among the bases of mastery because it functions as a mastery;

however, here, because the teaching is given in its definitive sense (nippariyāya), the bases of mastery are explained separately from the liberations in order to show them without confusion. Furthermore, all the functions of the liberations have been stated in the teaching on the liberations; this, then—

It is understood that a formal distinction has been made because, among the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*), the two where one "perceives forms internally" (*ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī*) are not mentioned as bases of mastery,
and because phrases such as "possessing form, he sees forms" (*rūpī rūpāni passati*) are expressions common to the functions of all the liberations (*vimokkha*).
Furthermore, the statement "because internal forms are not to be mastered" is found nowhere else in the sense of "he sees forms internally."
This is the statement of the reason for what was said everywhere—that "one sees external forms.

By this, it is shown that whatever has another cause is stated with that specific cause; however, as for the mention here of the internal state of being "percipient of the formless" (arūpasaññitā) due to the elegance of the teaching (*desanāvilāsa*), one should not seek any other reason for that. [This refers to] the invincibility of internal forms.
And because external forms are not clearly manifest [to them], as they are to others, the elegance of the teaching should be understood by way of the aforementioned classification.
If it is argued that the bases of mastery over blue and so forth need not be mentioned because they are already established by the phrase "beautiful and ugly," we say no;

for the reason for mastery is precisely the overcoming of the state of being blue and so forth in those who have previously cultivated their practice toward blue and so forth. For it is not the case that their mastery depends on the purity or impurity of color or its limited extent.
Either its immeasurability is the cause of mastery, or rather it is simply the state of being blue and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the liberations (*vimokkha*).

248. "Possessing form" (*rūpī*): by means of that form included within one's own continuity (*sasantati-pariyāpanna*) with which he is endowed, there is a specific form that serves as the cause for a particular jhāna.
That very specific form by which one might be called "possessing form" should be understood as the sign of the form included within one's own continuity;

it establishes the state of possessing form in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), just like the jhāna itself. The teaching on the kasiṇas [is given] precisely because of the kasiṇa-nature of the jhānas.
Because [the Buddha] was the expounder of the Abhidhamma, whereas in the Suttas he was the expounder of objects, it is said, "by way of the Abhidhamma.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Liberations is finished.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Divine Abidings begins.

251. Equanimity regarding ignorance (*aññāṇupekkhā*) is simply ignorance itself, devoid of both joy and grief. It belongs to one who has not conquered the floods (*anodhijina*), because he has not conquered the floods of the defilements by means of the paths that conquer the floods.
It belongs to one who has not conquered the resultant [states] (*avipākajina*), because he has not conquered the resultant states that arise beyond the seventh existence.

"By way of being free from taint" means by way of being non-reactive (*nippaṭighabhāvena*). Because there is no sign of even a single being as a counterpart, there is the apprehension of a delimitation.
It should be understood that because the apprehension of a "being" occurring by way of conventional truth (*sammutisacca*) does not constitute an apprehension of limited form and so forth,

it is stated that even loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the other [immeasurables]— which have a single being as their object— are of "immeasurable range" (*appamāṇagocara*) when they reach absorption (*appanā*), since they are characterized by the absence of misapprehension regarding the concept of a being.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Divine Abodes is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Foulness: 263.
It is "distended" because it has become swollen. It is "bluish-black" (*vinīla*) because it is a mixture of various colors, being broken down by white and red [discharges].
Or "blue" and "bluish-black" refers to that which has undergone a change from its former color. "Saṅghāṭa" is the state of the limbs being well-bound together.

"Weakness of the object" is the inability to fix the mind upon it due to its being an opposing factor. The similes of the flower-scatterer, the emetic, and the purgative should be applied respectively to the seeing of benefits in oneself, and to the removal of the hindrances and the diseases. This is because of their commonality with the mental application to the repulsive.
The apprehension of the meditation on the repulsive by means of the unattractive things such as hair, etc., and the meditation on the appearance of a charnel ground:
for that too arises solely through the application of attention to what is repulsive; thus they are "of the type of a charnel ground" or "having the appearance of a charnel ground.
The commentary on the discourse on the unattractive is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of wholesome states pertaining to the fine-material sphere is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of wholesome states pertaining to the immaterial sphere: 265.
"In every way" means thus, by all means—such as the perception of the sign of form, the taking up of a staff, the occurrence of fear, and so forth—with respect to forms and the signs of forms.

This is by way of seeing the defects in the jhānas that have those [lower levels] as their object, or by means of abandoning attachment to form and so forth, and the lack of desire to advert to them. "Dispassion" (*virāga*) refers to revulsion.

By such expressions as "imperturbable volitional formations," imperturbability (*āneñjatā*) is stated, and by such passages as "These, Cunda, are peaceful liberations in the Noble One’s discipline," peaceful liberation (*santavimokkhatā*) is also stated. This is by way of developing the antidote to the perception of defects.
Because perceptions of resistance (*paṭighasaññā*) have been thoroughly abandoned, one does not emerge from the formless attainments even by a great sound.
However, because they have not been thoroughly abandoned, there may be emergence from all the fine-material attainments;
yet, since even the first jhāna cannot endure even a slight sound, it is said that for one who has attained it, sound is a thorn.
In the absence of the development of the formless attainments (*ārūppabhāvanā*),

the surmounting and disappearance of perceptions of form and perceptions of resistance— which are liable to arise after death— is described as the induction of the state of non-arising for those [perceptions] until the occurrence of their own fruition.
As for the perceptions of diversity (*nānattasaññā*), however, those that do not arise in that particular existence do not arise simply because there is no occasion for them.

It is not because they are excluded by the development of the formless attainments (*ārūpyabhāvanā*). And because they are not excluded, some do arise. Therefore, it is said that there is no attention (*amanasikāra*), no adverting (*anāvajjana*), and no reviewing (*apaccavekkhaṇa*) toward them;
or rather, it is the non-performance and non-entry of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgamanas*) in the interval of the impulsion (*javana*).
And by that, through the surmounting of forms which are the causes for the attention to perceptions of diversity, there is the concentration (*samādhi*).

It shows the state of stability. For it is precisely because there is no transcendence of form that, among the form-sphere attainments, there is no mention of "non-attention to perceptions of diversity" for one [of them]. What is the advantage?

It is said that no advantage is seen in a perception that occurs in space, which is devoid of all basis for enjoyment. This refers to the statement beginning with "the transcendence of perceptions of form," etc.
This is an explanation of the benefits; it is not for the sake of [the meditation object] itself.

"In other instances" refers to the suttas. For there, even when a limited kasiṇa is removed, because only the seclusion from form is grasped and the delimitation is not grasped, its infinite pervasion is taught.
But here, although infinite pervasion is present, it is by way of the removal of the kasiṇa.
The intention is that it was not stated as "infinite space" for the purpose of showing its limited infinitude.
Here, the meaning is conveyed solely by the specific jhāna that defines the occasion, and not by the actual practice;

thus, it is not mentioned. The consciousness of the first immaterial state is described as "infinite" because it must be brought to mind in the very mode of pervading itself. The state of being opened up is "opened up-ness" (ugghāṭima).

267. "Nothingness" (*akiñcana*) refers to the complete elimination [of perception] by not grasping any aspect whatsoever of consciousness. 268. "By which" refers to the residual perception of formations (*saṅkhārāvasesa-saññā*).

By the phrase "I shall advert," etc., he shows the absence of the occurrence of adverting and so forth that are inclined toward that [residual perception], but not the occurrence of the cultivation of adverting for the purpose of transcending it.
"Neither perception" (*nāsaññā*) means the state of being without perception.
The meaning is: "And it exists for these. Contemplation of groups (*kalāpasammasana*) occurs by way of grasping a collection [of phenomena].
Insight into phenomena one by one (*anupadadhammavipassanā*) occurs by way of grasping individual phenomena such as contact and so forth.
It is the third [stage] because it transcends the consciousness that operates upon space. For, by transcending that, there is the manifestation of that very [insight].
For if it were the consciousness itself that was being eliminated in the second immaterial attainment, then that [consciousness] would be what is transcended, not its object;
nor is it logical to transcend the elimination of an object after having seen a fault in the object. Furthermore, in the Pāḷi it is said:
“Having mindfully entered the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness and emerged from it, he eliminates that very same consciousness,” but it is not said: “that very same... [the object].

“he develops the base of infinite consciousness,” or “he develops that very same [base]. However, in the passage, “having attained the base of infinite consciousness [with the thought] ‘consciousness is infinite,’” two things are mentioned: the object, which is consciousness, and the base of infinite consciousness itself.
Whichever of these two it may be, or from whichever one he has emerged, by that very term as indicated in the *Paṭṭhāna*, the word “that” (taṃ) [is used].
When the connection [of the term "consciousness"] has been established, the word "consciousness" is used for the purpose of excluding the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*).
Therefore, it is stated that there is a transcendence of the non-existence of the very consciousness of the first immaterial attainment. "Dependent on that" means supported by that.

Just as one might stand in an open space outside—detached from and separated from that which was attached to a pavilion—so too, when the consciousness attached to space is removed in its state of seclusion, that is the standing place of the third immaterial attainment.
The commentary on the discussion of wholesome states of the formless sphere is finished. [End of] the commentary on wholesome states of the three planes. 269.
These, first of all, are the five methods dominated by desire; thus, at the end of the method dominated by desire, the preceding methods [are concluded].
That was stated with reference to the occurrence [of the method] directed toward that specific sequence; however, this particular arrangement does not follow the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
For in the canonical text, after explaining the "pure method" (*suddhikanaya*) and so forth, the methods such as those "predominated by energy" (*vīriyādhipateyya*) are not mentioned.

In the *Mahāpakaraṇa*, the "triad of inferiority" (*hīnattika*) is analyzed through seven great sections (*mahāvāra*) variegated by methods such as the "direct order" (*anuloma*) and others. And therein, those which constitute a portion of the Middle Dhamma...
Having established that these are the twenty mundane great methods (*mahānaya*), it is said, "They are analyzed therein"; this is not because these methods appear there in this specific order.
Thus, having shown the place where they are analyzed, now, at this point which concludes the discussion on the wholesome states of the three planes:
The passage beginning with “In this place, however,” was stated for the purpose of showing the eighteen doors of action (*kammadvāra*).
Alternatively, by excluding the inferior and the sublime, it demonstrates that these wholesome methods of the three planes are included within the intermediate category;

thus, the classification of these wholesome methods of the three planes is made according to the triad of the inferior. The connection for the passage beginning with “In this place, however,” is exactly as previously stated. Regarding the triad of the inferior:

Among the middle group, those that have a ripening result (*savipāka*) and proceed by way of giving and so forth based solely on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa-nissita*) should be classified as inferior.

Those that proceed by way of giving and so forth based on the turning away from the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭa-nissita*) should be classified as superior. Those without a ripening result (*avipāka*) should be classified as middling.
Because they lack a ripening result, having set aside the middle group among them, the other two consist of nine [types] that are exclusively based on the cycle of existence.
There are eighteen doors of action (*kammadvāra*): nine that serve as the supporting conditions for the process of turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), and [the other] nine.

They are called "doors of action" because they are both actions and doors by virtue of being the causes for their respective fruits. Alternatively, it is said that in various instances, the consciousnesses themselves are the doors of action;

or else, the doors are the body and so forth. Furthermore, there are eighteen types of Khattiyas who are incapable, beginning with those who are "low-low" (*hīnahīna*) and the rest of the ninefold set.
The nine types of beings, such as those who are capable (*bhabba*) and those who are extremely refined (*paṇītapaṇīta*), should be understood according to their respective kamma.

In this same way, the brahmins and so forth, as well as the gods, are to be correlated. The forty-eight clans and lineages (*gottacaraṇa*) are subdivisions of those very same [groups], such as the khattiyas and others.

The state of mind being the sovereign over the mind, as stated thus: “A wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense-sphere has arisen... [pe] ...having the mind as its sovereign,” [is to be understood].
Since the word "citta" functions as a conventional designation for the collection of mind and mental factors (*cittacetasika*),
it is said that [the term] "is stated by way of the associated states.
The commentary on the wholesome states of the three planes is concluded.
Commentary on the Supramundane Wholesome (Lokuttarakusala) 277.
“He crosses over the world” (*lokaṃ tarati*): by this, he speaks of the practice that transcends the world. “He goes beyond” (*uttarati*):

by this, he refers to the fruit—the reaching of the world’s end and establishment in the fruit. By the words “having transcended,” etc., he refers to Nibbāna. For “having transcended” (*samatikkamma*) means having emerged from it.
"Having overcome" means having become dissociated. Each of these three meanings should be applied to each of the factors beginning with the path;

or rather, it is intended here specifically in relation to the path itself. "Momentary in a single moment of consciousness" is said with reference to the non-arising of the same path on two occasions.
One increases wisdom by means of that wisdom which accomplishes the non-transgression of phenomena against one another, and so forth. "It leads out" means...
Where it should have been said “leading out” (*niyyānīya*), the vowel *ī* has been shortened and the letter *y* changed to *k*, thus it is stated as “leading out” (*niyyānika*).
That by which one goes out is “going out” (*niyyāna*); that which is itself going out is “leading out,” just like the word *venayika*.
Here, where it should have been said “leading to what is to be led” (*neyyānika*), it is stated without changing the vowel *ī* to *e*.
The aggregate of mind and mental factors is said to "bear fruit"; it serves as the support for those associated phenomena that constitute its own constituent parts.
Alternatively, "fruit" refers to the knowledge of fruition (*phala-ñāṇa*), or else to the factors such as right view and so forth.
"In the supramundane state" means in the state of having transcended the world (*loka*). By this, he includes both the fruits and Nibbāna. Among these, that which exists as the fruit—

It is called a "plane" (*bhūmi*). Or, just as the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and others produced by karma are called "planes" because they serve as the support for those who possess them, so too the fruit produced by the Path is called a "plane" because it serves as the support for the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*), since he must enter into it from time to time;
for this very reason, the Noble Ones remain for a longer duration. By way of the seclusion of total eradication (*samucchedaviveka*):

Herein, the absolute severance of those [states] leading to the states of misery (apāya) should be understood as the severance of darkness by a flash of lightning, as well as the severance of the others.
Even mundane jhāna does not succeed for a worldling or for a noble one who has not performed the preliminary service without the practice;
however, because it succeeds through the path alone for a noble one who has performed the service, it is like wholesome [kamma] in relation to its results.
Likewise, because it lacks the similarity to the Noble Path (ariyamagga) due to its being fully kindled, and because it does not have that as its result,

it cannot be said that the path of practice (paṭipadā) of that jhāna is the same as the path of practice of the Path; therefore, while the teaching was given there by way of the modes of practice (paṭipadā) out of respect for them,
the "pure" teaching (suddhika-desanā) was also given for the purpose of including the aforementioned jhānas.
Furthermore, because it cannot be accomplished by anyone without the practice, the phrase beginning with "difficult practice" (*dukkhapaṭipada*) was stated in order to show it as being weighty.
"Any occasion whatsoever" refers to any among the occasions of suppression, such as once, twice, thrice, four times, many times, and so forth.
The occasions of suppression occurring once or twice are easy.

The commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariyas) maintained that there is only the painful practice (dukkhā paṭipadā), and that beyond that, no pleasant practice exists; thus they accepted the "three times of suppression" as being exclusively the painful practice. Since that has been so stated, there is nothing further to be said regarding the subsequent "four times of suppression" and so forth.
Having delimited form and formless phenomena by way of their characteristics (lakkhaṇa) and other attributes...

"Grasping" (gahaṇa) is the discernment of the material and the immaterial; "definition of name-and-form" (nāmarūpavavatthāpana) is the determination that this is merely name-and-form, and that there is no other such thing as a "being" (satta) or the like.

Since the manifestation of the Path might be sluggish for one who has grasped the material and immaterial, and because the tasks such as the definition of name-and-form might be accomplished with difficulty, it should not be said that the "state of having a painful progress" (dukkhapatipadā) is due solely to the difficulty of grasping the material and immaterial.

Why? Because even though it is easily accomplished due to the weakness of the defilements that oppose the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth, the manifestation of the path is slow because of the weakness of the faculties associated with the insight that has been thus accomplished.
"Having grasped the material and immaterial" means having grasped them without difficulty; for if they were grasped with difficulty, it would simply have to be stated [as such].

There is none. The same applies to the remaining cases as well. Regarding this section, they accepted it as "the painful practice" because, at the conclusion of the comprehension of groups (*kalāpasammasana*), while the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*) was proceeding, the defilements of insight (*vipassanupakkilesa*) that had arisen were suppressed three times;

thus, due to the difficulty involved, they accepted this stage of the practice as "painful," since this is the limit of the practice. Even though this [stage] itself is not difficult, it is so because of the difficulty of the preceding stages.
It should be understood that "the state of difficult practice" is not prohibited because it has been explained according to the method already stated.
Alternatively, he says "this turn" with reference to the aforementioned entire process of discerning form and the formless, etc., which occurs three times by way of successive stages of suppression.
However, for one who experiences no difficulty in any respect, the practice should be understood as easy.
Right speech, having the nature of embracing, is the opposite of harsh and non-embracing states such as lying, which have the function of deceiving and so forth.
Because of its lubricating quality, it embraces the associated mental states as well as the person who hears the well-spoken words conditioned by right speech.
It arouses the bodily activity that is to be performed, and itself constitutes the arising and the coordination [of that activity].
It is said that abstinence, which is designated as right action (*sammākammanta*), is also of the nature of origination (*samuṭṭhāna*).
Alternatively, "origination" refers to the lifting up of associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*), just as there is the lifting of a burden by bodily activity;

or it refers to the purification (*suddhi*) and cleansing (*vodāna*) of a living being or of associated states; or it refers specifically to the livelihood (*ājīva*), namely the functioning of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
283. "Dependent on the path" means that because it has the essential nature of the ultimate path, it is dependent on the whole by way of being a constituent part of the path;

this is the meaning. 285. "Establishment" is by way of the defilements (*kilesa*), and "accumulation" is by way of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*). Alternatively, establishment is by way of craving (*taṇhā*), and accumulation is by way of views (*diṭṭhi*).

This should be construed as follows: "Bodhi" refers to this collection of phenomena (*dhamma-sāmaggī*) which is so called. [The examples given are] the components of an army, the parts of a chariot, and so forth.
