By the word *viyāti*, he shows that through this designation of persons (*puggalapaññatti*), there is the state of being a designation for what does not exist.
Since the word *aṅga* also has the sense of "cause," they are called *bojjhaṅgā* because they lead to the awakening to the Four Noble Truths. They are called *bodhiyo* because they awaken;

since they are the very limbs of awakening, it is said: "They are called *bojjhaṅgā* because they awaken after [the truth]. This refers to the causes such as insight (*vipassanā*) and the things to be awakened to.
Because they awaken correctly (*sammā*) by facing toward (*paṭimukhaṃ*) the truths in accordance with them through direct perception (*paccakkhabhāvena*),
and because they do so without error (*aviparītatāya*), the terms "awakening after" (*anubujjhanti*) and so forth are used with prefixes that illuminate these specific nuances of meaning.
For the word *bodhi* generally encompasses all forms of awakening (*bujjhana*) associated with their respective distinctions.
299. "Crossed over" means having crossed over lust and the other [defilements]. What indeed does one do while following after misconduct? 301.

"Constant practice" (*dhuvapaṭisevana*) refers to the habitual cultivation of requisites produced by such acts as killing living beings and so forth. "Performing its own function" (*sakiccako*) means possessing its own distinct function.
"It does not exist" rejects the existence of any other separate entity. [The factors involved are] the practice of requisites, whispering [of spells], and the engagement in postures (*iriyāpatha*).
The three bases for hypocrisy are produced by evil desire. 343.
Insight leading to emergence is equanimity regarding formations together with its conformity; seeing it as empty, it is called "emptiness" (*suññatā*);
seeing it as suffering because it withers the longing of craving, it is called "the wishless" (*appaṇihita*). It stands in the place of that which is to be arrived at.
Having stood at the position of the path of arrival for the purpose of attaining the path, it receives the name "emptiness" and "wishless.
Once the name has been obtained from the standpoint of arrival, the names derived from its qualities and its object are necessarily established;

however, the fact that the name is established from the standpoint of arrival in all cases does not mean that it is established through its qualities and object alone. Therefore, because it is the cause for the establishment of the complete set of names, [the names] are established by way of its qualities and object.

Although all [three] possess the application of the three names, it is stated here that the name is obtained from the "coming" (āgamana) alone according to the non-figurative teaching—because it establishes the definition—and not from the other two. 350.

"Signless insight" (animittavipassanā) refers to the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). "In sign-bearing phenomena" (nimittadhammesu) means by way of the density of aggregates and so forth.

And because of the delimitation of their respective functions, [the five aggregates] possess objects of grasping among the aggregates. "The signless liberation" refers to the contemplation of impermanence.

How, then, is the application of the simile here to be understood? For there is no absence of the signless state in the signless liberation—which is predominant by way of the faculty of faith—any more than there is an absence of the predominance characterized as the Path in desire and consciousness; nor is there [an absence] in those things that do not have the Path as their predominance.

Just as there is an absence of giving the name "path-master" [to those factors], so too it can be said that there is an absence of giving the name "signless" to the signless, because of the absence of "signlessness" in the signless liberation (*animittavimokkha*).
Furthermore, the term *maggādhipatino* is appropriate in the sense that "those for whom the path is the master";
however, in that context, there is an absence of the state of being path-masters in the desire and consciousness associated with them. But here, the path is the signless.

Regarding the phrase "of this": the meaning that "this is the signless of the path" is not possible; therefore, it is not by means of that non-path that the path's state of being signless is untenable.
Or rather, what is intended here as the commonality? It is the absence of the name "path" for those factors that are not path-factors.
Just as, even though they possess predominance, desire and consciousness do not receive the name "path" because they are not path-predominants, nor does the path [receive its name] from them.

Because it is not a factor of the path, and likewise because faith possesses the quality of "coming" (āgamana), the name "path" is applied to it in a figurative sense (*animitta*) as its "signless" aspect;

yet, the path does not [itself] become signless through that [faith], because faith is not a factor of the path. In this way, it is shown that even for insight into the signless (*animittavipassanā*), the state of being signless does not exist in an absolute sense (*nippariyāyena*).
If it is objected: "But here, jhāna is spoken of by the names 'emptiness' (suññatā) and so forth, not as the Path (magga)," we reply:

No, because jhāna receives the names 'emptiness' and so forth due to its association with the Path. They say that according to the method of the Suttanta, even in the Abhidhamma, a name is obtained based on the qualities and the objects [of the jhāna].
Therefore, the statement "but they do not obtain [the name]" is rejected. For what reason? Because in the Abhidhamma, one does not disregard the intrinsic nature (sarasa).

The intention is that the acquisition of a name is indeed contrary [to the actual nature of things]. For the acquisition of a name based on objects possessing qualities is dominated by their own inherent essence (*sarasappadhāna*).

And if the acquisition of a name were governed solely by that essence, there would be no definitive determination (*vavatthāna*) that all paths possess the nature of emptiness (*suññatā*) and so forth.

Therefore, even though in the Abhidhamma there is an acquisition of names through two ways, that which establishes the definitive determination of the name has been taken from the perspective of what is contrary [to the essence].
He said that the paths of emptiness (*suññatā*) and the signless (*appaṇihita*) do not receive their names by means of [factors] possessing qualities as objects (*saguṇārammaṇa*).

Alternatively, "but they do not receive them" means they do not receive them by means of [factors] possessing qualities as objects independently of others. Why? Because in the Abhidhamma, names are obtained through [factors] accompanied by their own intrinsic essences (*sarasa*) together with their opposites (*paccanīka*);
for it is only when independent of the opposite which provides the definition (*vavatthānakara*) that the intrinsic essence alone [is considered].
In the Abhidhamma, there is no such thing as a "nameless cause" because that would result in a lack of definition.

Therefore, the paths—which are the insight and its conformity that serve as the antidotes to the underlying tendency toward self-attachment—receive the designation "with name" even when there is another name present, because their own nature is accompanied by an opposing factor.
However, the insight of the signless path is not the antidote to the sign itself, because it itself grasps signs and does not prevent the grasping of signs.
The path that conforms to that [signless state] is not the antidote to the sign. If it were, it would also have to be the antidote to insight directed toward the sign.
Therefore, although it exists as a flavor, it is not included in the Abhidhamma under the name "signless" because there is no opposing factor to define it as such.
However, the path conforming to the contemplation of impermanence is included only within the "pure modes of progress."

It should be seen. And for that very reason, this method was stated. "In this way" means: having cited what he will say—namely, "For one emerging from [the contemplation of] impermanence, the path becomes signless"—the meaning is that the signless path was elucidated by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā in this manner.

Regarding the question "What is the object of the emergence...": when one emerges from [the contemplations of] impermanence and so forth, the path leading to emergence has the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) as its object.

He asks, thinking that if there were formations (*saṅkhāra*), there could be no emergence from them, and that the penetration of the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-paṭivedha*) would occur while formations are the object.

He says, "having formations as its object," because even the characteristics are penetrated by the knowledge proceeding toward formations through the words "impermanent," etc., since it grasps those formations in their specific modes. They have formations as their object precisely in the sense intended by what was stated above.
Showing that it was stated as "having the characteristics as its object," he said, "What is called a characteristic," and so forth.
For a characteristic taken separately—namely impermanence, suffering, and non-self—is a mere conceptual construct (*paññatti-gatika*); it does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
Precisely because it does not exist, it is a state that cannot be defined by categories such as "limited" (*paritta*) and so on. Therefore, regarding that which is to be grasped separately...
Because the characteristic does not exist in an ultimate sense, one observes the characteristics only by observing formations according to their own nature as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self";
thus it is said: "But he who observes the three characteristics as 'impermanent, suffering, and non-self'...
And because it is only formations that are seen through such terms as "impermanent," etc., therefore they are like a corpse tied around one's neck.
They are to be relinquished as if they were [unwholesome].
Explanation of the Miscellaneous Discussion on Supramundane Wholesomeness.

"Therein" (*tattha*) means in supramundane jhāna. "And internally" (*ajjhattañca*): by this half-verse, he enumerates fivefold the plane of insight (*vipassanā-bhūmi*) upon which one must focus and from which one must emerge.
Regarding "seven or eight factors," etc., the elision of the word "factors" (*aṅgāni*) after "seven or eight" (*sattaṭṭha*) should be understood as resulting from the omission of the word "etc.
(*ādi*). "The sign" (*nimitta*): that from which emergence occurs; those [states] occurring as signs are indicated by the very term "sign."
It points out that the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*) alone determines the specific factors of the Noble Path, such as the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*). Why?

Because in the case of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations arising from various second-jhāna bases and so forth, there is an absence of the desire not to attain further factors that transcend those base-jhānas and an absence of the cultivation of dispassion (*virāga-bhāvanā*);
whereas for the other [knowledge], these are present. Or rather, even in their respective explanations... [and so on].
It should be understood that insight (vipassanā) alone determines [the jhāna level of the path]. Why?

Because even in the first Elder’s theory, paths based on the first jhāna without a foundation (apādaka) are themselves of the first jhāna due to the determination of insight; and the others are of their respective jhānas due to the determination of both the foundational jhāna and insight.
Thus, in the remaining theories as well, the determination of insight should be applied according to what is possible.

"In miscellaneous formations" (*pakiṇṇakasaṅkhāra*) means other formations than the foundational jhāna. By this, he shows that once the formations of the foundational jhāna have been comprehended, there is nothing further to be said.

"There too" (*tatrāpi*) refers even to the second Elder’s position. The state of being associated with each respective jhāna occurs through the specific determination of the insight (*vipassanā*) that comprehends those respective formations.

For in that case as well, the insight—by way of the cultivation of fading away (*virāga*) or non-fading away from each respective [jhāna]—is accompanied by joy (*somanassa*) or accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*).

And having offered [the sacrifice], one establishes the determination for the path through the factors of jhāna; thus, the determination of insight (vipassanā-niyama) should be understood in the manner already described.

"That" refers to the cultivation resembling each respective jhāna. Furthermore, this matter—such as the fruit of a once-returner (sakadāgāmiphala) and so forth—cannot be accomplished by mere aspiration alone without the support of the foundational jhāna (pādakajjhāna), the jhāna of comprehension (sammasitajjhāna), or the proximate cause (upanissaya);
nor can it be accomplished by mere intention (saṅkappa) alone without the proximate cause.
It should be illustrated by the "Exhortation to Nanda," which demonstrates non-attainment.

For in that discourse, while the Blessed One speaks of the fulfillment of intention even for a stream-enterer, he shows that whoever possesses the necessary proximate cause (upanissaya), it is their own underlying disposition (ajjhāsaya) that determines [the result], and not anything else;
thus, through each respective proximate cause, there is the fulfillment of intention, but beyond that, even if the intention exists, there is no attainment.

This meaning is thus illustrated. Likewise here too, for whichever path belonging to the second jhāna or beyond possesses the aforementioned decisive support (upanissaya), its specific inclination (ajjhāsaya) alone is the determiner;
it does not belong to another, because that [inclination] would not arise even if such a support were present.
However, according to this view, when the decisive support for the foundational or contemplative jhānas is present, the inclination occurs with absolute certainty.

It is said that "aspiration determines [the result] because of its presence or absence," since a specific intention arises only when there is the presence of the corresponding decisive support for that particular fruit.
However, the statement "in which there is no foundational jhāna" refers to mundane jhānas—excluding those based on the fourth jhāna—that serve as foundations.
Furthermore, the attainment of absorption occurs through five factors when there is an absence of the decisive support for transcending the gross factors.
Because it does not exist without [joy], he says, "the path is accompanied by joy.

By the phrase "the path accompanied by equanimity," he shows that although it is identical in being a fourth-jhāna attainment, it is not a state where residual formations remain for one capable of uprooting the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
And these various doctrines do not contradict one another, depending on whether the intention is toward a fifth-jhāna attainment or a first-jhāna attainment, and so forth.
And the intention is that [the determination] is possible. Furthermore, the underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) is purposeful;

otherwise, since the restriction would already be established by the jhānas based on the preliminary concentration (*pādaka-sammasita-jjhāna*), the disposition being called the "determiner" (*niyāmaka*) would be rendered useless.

However, here in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, having extracted only the purpose—which is exclusively what is termed insight (*vipassanā*)—in the context of the determination, [it says]: "Among their doctrines, this... and so forth.
By saying, "It is insight alone that determines [the path]," it is shown that in all these doctrines, it is insight alone that determines [the result].
For it is shown that the establishment of each respective doctrine occurs only when accompanied by insight, and not otherwise.
"It quivers" means it is unable to become a condition for the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) consciousness. If, in the fifth moment of consciousness...

It is said that the impulsion (javana) has "fallen" (*patita*). How then can the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) and the Path (*magga*) arise immediately after it at the very moment the impulsion has fallen?
This is because there is no state of "falling" for a previously unarisen subsequent impulsion.

For it is that same impulsion, when occurring many times, that may be said to have "fallen"; however, the change-of-lineage arises toward a different object and is thus a previously unarisen impulsion.

Likewise, the path [is distinguished] by way of its different planes. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the seventh impulsion-consciousness, being powerful, possesses both the state of being experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*) and the state of being an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*)?

In this regard, the intended meaning might be as follows: because the final impulsion-consciousness is well-conditioned by way of being the immediately preceding condition (*anantarapaccaya*) for the stream of result (*vipākasantāna*) which arises with the rebirth-linking as its immediately preceding condition, that seventh impulsion-consciousness..."
"It is both to-be-experienced-in-the-next-birth (upapajjavedanīya) and immediate (ānantarika), but it is not as powerful as the javana-intention that has not yet fallen away.
Furthermore, "it would follow after that conformity" means that if the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) has formations as its object, then that too is indeed conformity;
thus, like the previous conformity, it would follow after another conformity, and not the Path—therefore, it is precisely the emergence from the Path.
And it would not exist because of the non-attainment of a condition suitable for adverting toward an object similar to itself.

It is "acquired by the plane" (*bhūmiladdhā*) because the defilements that lie latent within the five aggregates of clinging by virtue of their state of being unabandoned have acquired this plane through them.
And it is "the bridge of the round" (*vaṭṭasetū*) because they encircle and bind the round; furthermore, its function is precisely the eradication of those [defilements].

The crushing of the mass of greed and so forth is what is meant. "That" refers to the process of existence (*pavatta*). It is stated that it is "a single existence" because for a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) who is reborn in that very same place multiple times, it is reckoned as one existence by way of not returning to the lower realms.

"Of this matter," however, refers to the emergence from the process of existence consisting of appropriated aggregates as previously described. From the seventh existence among the states of deprivation (*apāya*),...

The destruction of the condition for the volitional consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*) which yields its result both upward [in the higher realms] and in a happy destination should be understood as the cessation of that volitional consciousness through the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*).

"In two existences" means: in the case of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*) who has not yet cultivated the path of non-returning, it refers to those two existences that would arise within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*). "It wavers"—by this, its very nature of wavering is indicated.
It shows the absence of non-shaking, not the state of being immovable; therefore, having shown the lack of shaking, he said "of the Tathāgata" and so forth in order to show shaking again.
Or alternatively, some might see all four paths as having an identical mode of proceeding and thus grasp them as being immovable by nature;
in order to prevent such a grasping, it is said "it shakes," not for the purpose of definitively establishing that it shakes.

It is appropriate to see both [aspects]. Alternatively, even if for some the four paths have an identical mode of practice (*paṭipadā*), nevertheless, because the mode of practice is accomplished by way of the defilements and the faculties, it is of a shifting nature according to those [factors];
thus it is said "it wavers," and not "it does not waver."
The commentary on the miscellaneous discussion of supramundane wholesomeness is finished.
357. Commentary on the First Path and the Twenty Great Methods:

He for whom the aspiration "I shall develop the path" has arisen in the prior stage develops the path. Thus, in all cases, the specific development of each [factor] should be understood by way of the distinction in one's aspiration.

358. Regarding the passage beginning with "the predominance of desire" (*chandādhipateyya*), how can there be a state of predominance for desire and its co-nascent factors such as energy (*viriya*) among those phenomena occurring within a single moment of consciousness? It is by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).

For when wholesome [action] succeeds for one who possesses desire, thinking, "I shall bring it to fruition," and wholesome [action] has indeed succeeded for that person—[then desire is the predominant factor].
The desire co-arising with that [volition] is distinguished by its prior decisive support (*upanissaya*); it brings the co-arising phenomena under its own control.
When it proceeds, they proceed; when it ceases, they cease; and they possess a strength corresponding to it, like the king’s men. The same applies to energy (*vīriya*) and the others.
As for the remaining phenomena, although there may be the presence of their proceeding in some instances in the manner already described...
Because it lacks that specific nature, it should be understood that there is no state of predominance.
[End of] the commentary on the second path. 361.
By shortening the vowel *ā* to *a*, the "faculty of final knowledge" (*aññindriya*) is stated; furthermore, the vowel *ā* signifies the limit of phenomena (*dhammamariyāda*).
Commentary on the Third and Fourth Paths (Tatiyacatutthamaggavaṇṇanā) 362.
The intention is that the path-factors are not fulfilled because right view does not perform its function. For a "path" (magga) is so called because it goes by killing;
however, there is nothing for this [right view] to kill. As for conceit, its mode of occurrence is similar to that of views, occurring as "I am."
It is a standing point for views. He says this with reference to its long-standing persistence, as if it were the duration of light.
For a simile is employed through a partial commonality that is intended [by the speaker]. "In ash" means in the ash-dust of wood and so forth.

"Having rubbed together" means having moistened. "Chanda" means craving (*taṇhā*). "Underlying tendencies" (*anusaya*) refers to the underlying tendency of craving and the underlying tendency of conceit (*māna*). And in this sutta, [it refers to] that which has not been eradicated.
It should be understood that the statement "one abandons the defilements by means of one another" is introduced here as a demonstration of the eradication of unabandoned factors such as conceit—
just like the removal of an odor— and not because it was stated according to the aforementioned method of illustration.
When the mind is proceeding without interruption, the blameworthy and blameless mental factors (cetasika) that cause its defilement and purification arise.
Because its constituent parts are like limbs, it is said, "by way of the mental factors" (*cittanga-vasena*).
The commentary on the supramundane wholesome states is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the wholesome is finished.
The Section on the Enumeration of Phenomena in the Unwholesome Category:
Commentary on the First Discourse on Consciousness.
365. Having followed the method stated for the wholesome states, he says "by the method stated" because they are to be understood according to their respective suitability.
"Because there is nothing to be gone to" means because there is nothing to be awakened to. "The mere going by view" means the mere movement or the mere grasping of a view.
Unwise attention (ayoniso-manasikāra) is mentioned separately because it is both the proximate cause and the absolute cause [of views]. "Restraint through mindfulness" (sati-saṃvara).

Here, "endurance" should be understood as the patient acceptance of being touched by cold and other such conditions. "Restraint through abandonment" refers to the restraint of energy (*vīriya-saṃvara*).

"Seeing gratification" is the view of gratification (*assāda-diṭṭhi*). Delusion (*moha*) manifests as the state of wrong practice, either by way of its fruit or its manifestation; or it is the mode of apprehending the nature of what is opposed to right practice.
Even though all greed exists in the form of covetousness (*abhijjhā*), [it is distinguished here].

In order to show the characteristics and so forth of covetousness (*abhijjhā*)—which is associated with specific qualities, has reached the level of a course of action (*kamma-patha*), and arises here [in this world]—he said:
“It is toward the prosperity of others,” and so on. *Abhirati* is the delight of craving that precedes one’s own act of dedication.
*Anupaparikkhā* is delusion (*moha*). For, by way of delusion or by way of wrong view, there is an adherence (*adhimokkha*) accompanied by approval toward what is not a factual basis.
"It arises" means: in a mind devoid of shame (*ahirika*) and so forth—that is, a mind lacking protection.

By the phrase "due to being devoid of mindfulness and being the opposite of mindfulness," he shows that unwholesome aggregates (*akusala-khandhā*) which are devoid of mindfulness and are the opposites of mindfulness are themselves "wrong mindfulness" (*micchā-sati*).

Furthermore, these should be understood as associated with sharp perception (*paṭu-saññā*) during the occurrence of resentment (*upanāha*) and so forth, or when observing things done long ago and the like.
The state of being with *sadaratha* and so forth is stated without distinction due to association with the defilements (*kilesa*).

This is because certain factors such as sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*), which are the direct opposites of lightness (*lahutā*) and the rest, are absent here. "Non-quiescence" (*avūpasama*) refers to the presence of what is not settled. "Functioning as non-abiding" (*anavaṭṭhāna-rasa*) means the activity of movement.
In the phrase "non-quiescence of the mind" (*cetaso avūpasame*), the locative case is used for the purpose to be accomplished; it refers to the object that serves as the condition for non-quiescence.
Or it is called "non-quiescence.
The commentary on the section concerning the enumeration of dhammas is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the section of the exposition (niddesa).

377. Unshakability regarding co-arisen states (sahajātadhamma) should not be understood as being like unshakability regarding laziness, because [laziness] is its opposite; rather, stability through the exertion toward various evil actions is what constitutes unshakability in that context. 381.

"The distorted flickering of views" refers to the very views themselves that proceed in such and such ways by way of eternalism and so forth. "They float away" means they drift about like [foam] at a landing place. "From perversion" means from the inversion of the objective basis (vatthu).

390. Because it serves as the basis for the inversion of perception and so forth—namely, the grasping of what is unreal, such as a "natural self" (*pakati-atta*) and the like, by way of concealing its true nature, and the distorted grasping of impermanence and other characteristics as permanent and so on—it is said: "It awakens to what is non-existent and to what is not-self.

399. Although... [the passage] "...arises in one who is misapprehending" shows that there is no distinction from the preceding consciousness. *Thina* (sloth) is the state of being congealed through the absence of exertion and the absence of despondency.
Commentary on the Third Consciousness (Tatiyacittavaṇṇanā) 400.
Herein, "the five factors that are not-failing" (*apaṇṇakaṅgāni*) together with conceit (*māna*) should be understood as factors that do not fail to arise and are capable of arising.
Because conceit is indeterminate, it is not included among the fixed factors (*niyatayevāpanakā*). For in the *Paṭṭhāna*, it is said: "Fetter..."
Regarding the statement, “Dependent on a state, a fettering state arises by way of the root condition,” here, with reference to the tenfold conjunction demonstrated as follows:
“There are four instances of conjunction with sensual lust, three instances with aversion, and [one each] with conceit, doubt, and lust for existence—these three are the fetters of a once-returner;
thus there is a tenfold conjunction by means of these fetters,” [the text mentions] the fetter of sensual lust.

Having stated, "In dependence on the fetter of conceit, there is the fetter of ignorance," and having stated, "In dependence on the fetter of sensual lust, there is the fetter of ignorance," and also, "In dependence on the fetter of conceit,
there is the fetter of lust for existence and the fetter of ignorance," the fact that conceit is indeterminate is clarified by these formulations; likewise...
Also in the pair of defilements (*kilesaduka*). And here it will be said: "The binding of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) is tenfold; likewise, the defilements (*kilesa*) are tenfold.
It has the function of grasping by way of uplifting alone, not by way of exertion for the accomplishment of various tasks as does energy (*vīriya*).
Even in the case of inferiority, grasping by not lowering oneself should be understood as "grasping" (*sampaggaha*).
Commentary on the Fourth Consciousness: 402.
Being distracted for the sake of maintaining [the object] and generating effort, they are described as "possessing effort for the sake of maintenance.
Commentary on the Ninth Consciousness.
413. Its function is to spread because it originates from undesirable visible forms and because its own mode of manifestation is one of spreading.
Bile (dosa) should be regarded as like putrid urine mixed with poison, since it is undesirable in its application and its result.

Regarding expressions of function such as "having a disagreeable taste," one should understand that by the negation of a particular quality, the function of its respective opposite is implied. Its course is bitter.
Biting remorse (*kaṭukañcukatā*)—such as regarding one’s own excellence, one’s dwelling place, and so forth—should be viewed as a form of slavery due to its dependence on others.
For just as a slave is dependent on others when in a state of servitude, so too is one possessed of remorse.

Indeed, such a person is unable to proceed according to their own nature in what is wholesome. Alternatively, it is because of the dependence on grieving over what has been done and left undone, whether unwholesome or wholesome.
On account of both of these, one possesses remorse (*kukkucca*); thus, it is like a state of servitude. 418.
"Contrary aspect" (*viruddhākāra*) means the aspect or contrary nature of a contrary person or mind.
By this, he shows that "opposition" (*virodha*) is the act of opposing. "Speech" (*vacana*) should be regarded as a mere illustration; indeed, all [of it]...
For it is said that an action being performed by such a person is not well-planted or well-generated.

Some explain the meaning of the word *ropa* (planting) in this very sense. That [explanation] is not authoritative; for it was stated with the intention that, since anger lacks such a mode of occurrence by its own nature, its fullness might otherwise arise through some other cause.
**Commentary on the Eleventh Consciousness** 422.
"Free from doubt" (*vigata-cikicchā*) is said because it is difficult to cure, not because there is an absolute absence of doubt; this explains that meaning.
424. Because there is no certainty and because the mind does not settle, it is described as "merely the persistence of occurrence," since it is merely a condition for the process of mental activity.
425. Due to its inability to reach a single mode [of consciousness], it recedes from what is present before it because of its own slowness. 429.
Restlessness (uddhacca) remains fixed upon the very mode grasped by itself and wanders about; thus, it is a flickering within a single object alone.
As for doubt (*vicikicchā*), although it arises in relation to only one object among form and so forth, nevertheless, as it arises in the form "Is it thus?
Is it this?", it looks toward another mode of apprehension—thinking "Could it not be so?
Could it be something else?"—and thus there is a wavering across multiple objects.

“‘In this same way, this should be understood’—having thus shown the miscellaneous points mentioned regarding these two types of consciousness, he says ‘In all [twelve] as well’ etc., in order to show them in the twelve.

Since, even among the wholesome [states], only the co-nascent predominance (sahajātādhipati) was cited without citing the objective predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), it might follow that here too only that [co-nascent predominance] should be cited; therefore [he says]: ‘Co-nascent predominance...’”

"Even though it is obtainable, it was not extracted," this was said because the predominance of the object (*ārammaṇādhipati*) is not obtainable. For that [predominance of the object] is indeed obtainable in the eight types of greed-accompanied consciousness.
As for "the rest as well," there is no other co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*) apart from the predominance of investigation (*vīmaṃsādhipati*) that could be extracted;
thus, there is nothing at all to be said regarding the predominance of the object. Regarding "any state whatsoever," this refers to desire (*chanda*) and so forth.

There is also one [condition] that is co-nascent (*sahajāta*). First, regarding the triad of wholesome states (*kusalattika*), it should be understood that [this condition] is prohibited in the *Paṭṭhāna* because not a single question—such as "dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises conditioned by the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*), but not by the root condition (*hetupaccaya*)"—is raised in the sections beginning with the "Dependent" (*paṭicca*) chapter. For otherwise, [if it were not prohibited], there would be the following [undesired consequence]:
"Dependent on an unwholesome state, an unwholesome state arises conditioned by the predominance condition, but not by the root condition."
By virtue of this, it could be said that they are "single.

"Because of the absence of what is to be abandoned by seeing" means because of the non-existence of that which is to be abandoned by seeing, or because of the absence [of such things] among those things to be abandoned by seeing.
By this, since they do not draw forth rebirth-linking, there is no arrival there among those things to be abandoned by seeing.
By means of "non-arrival," he establishes the non-attracting of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Furthermore, in order to establish "non-arrival" through "non-attracting," he says, "Among those...

and so forth. Rebirth-linking would occur right here [in this very life]. And if that were the case, it would be abandonable by vision (*dassanena pahātabba*), because that which leads to the states of deprivation (*apāya*) is abandonable by vision. Yet this [rebirth-linking] cannot be abandonable by vision.
Therefore, the intention is that it is not included in the analysis of what is to be abandoned by vision (*dassanena pahātabba-vibhaṅga*).
How, then, is this known—that there is "non-arrival among those things to be abandoned by vision because it does not draw in rebirth-linking"?
It is because it has been stated that only those things to be abandoned by vision function as a kamma-condition at different moments. For [kamma] is of two kinds: ...
“Unwholesome states are to be abandoned by vision and to be abandoned by cultivation.
In this context, the status of volition to be abandoned by cultivation as a kamma-condition occurring at different moments is not stated; it is stated only for the others. [It is said:
“A state to be abandoned by cultivation is not a condition, by way of kamma-condition, for a state that is neither to be abandoned by vision nor to be abandoned by cultivation.”
For here, only the co-nascent is analyzed, not those belonging to different moments. Likewise, in the negative section as well:
"A state to be abandoned by development is a condition, by way of object-condition, for a state not to be abandoned either by seeing or by development...
[etc. ...by way of co-nascent condition... [etc. ...by way of decisive support condition... [etc. ...it is a condition by way of post-nascence condition."
Only this much was stated; it was not stated that "it is a condition by way of kamma-condition. And in the other case, it was so stated.

Furthermore, since volition accompanied by restlessness is mentioned only among those things to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there would be no asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*).
If there were such a thing, then the state of being an asynchronous kamma-condition would have been stated for the volition to be abandoned by cultivation, but it was not.

Therefore, if they were associated with restlessness (*uddhacca*) and existed as asynchronous kamma-conditions (*nānākkhaṇika-kammapaccaya*), they would have to be mentioned among those things to be abandoned by vision (*dassanena pahātabba*);
since that is not the case, they are not mentioned. The intended meaning here is that they are "not included" (*anāgata*) therein because they do not draw forth rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

Furthermore, by the non-mention of asynchronous kamma-conditions, the state of being a process-result (*pavatti-vipāka*) for those things to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāya pahātabba*) is excluded.
For it is impossible to deny that even for a result occurring in the course of existence (pavatti), there is the conditionality of asynchronous (nānākkhaṇika) kamma. And it has been said:
"A state associated with pleasant feeling is a condition, by way of kamma-condition, for a state associated with painful feeling, [when they are] asynchronous," and so forth.
If there is no giving of a result for those things to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā), how...
Are those states subject to ripening (*vipākadhammadhamma*)? Because they possess a nature that is capable of ripening, like the consciousnesses of direct knowledge (*abhiññācitta*) and so forth.
As for what was said: "At whatever time an unwholesome state of consciousness has arisen, accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness...

[therein] there is non-distraction; knowledge regarding these states is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), and knowledge regarding their ripening is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*)."
This too might have been said with reference specifically to those [states] that are struck by result (vipākāraha). However, this point must be thoroughly investigated;
for there is room for discussion here. For the word "result" (*vipāka*) does not denote what is struck by result in the same way that the term "dhamma of result" (*vipākadhamma*) does.
The commentary on the unwholesome section is concluded.
Regarding the section on the indeterminate (abyākatapada), [it is said]:

"In order to show them by way of classification, beginning with 'the indeterminate resultant' and so forth, the passage starting with 'Which phenomena are indeterminate? is commenced. 431. Among those, [the text begins] with "the indeterminate resultant" and so on.
By this, there is a connection. Regarding the phrase "of that too," the connection is with the statement: "It was said at the beginning... desiring to illustrate its arising...
Because it has been accumulated (*upacittattā*), it has increased in such a way that it turns toward its own result (*vipāka*) by displacing the result of another.
Because the conditions for form and so forth are common to other consciousnesses, [the result] is distinguished by what is not common.
By means of the physical basis (*vatthu*), the names "eye-consciousness" and "ear-consciousness" are designated.

This is because the sharpness or dullness of consciousness corresponds to the sharpness or dullness of the eye and other faculties, and because these faculties serve as specific conditions for those consciousnesses. Furthermore, it is "consciousness dependent on the eye" because it is supported by the eye and because it cognizes visible form; thus, its characteristic is "consciousness dependent on the eye and cognizing visible form."
Eye-consciousness. Therein, by the expression "dependent on the eye," it excludes any other consciousness that has visible form as its object.
By the expression "cognizing visible form," it precludes contact and the other mental factors that depend upon the eye.
And by the terms "eye" and "visible form," it clarifies the act of cognizing in terms of both its support and its object. Its function is the grasping of the mere object, which is visible form.
It has the taste of the object consisting of mere form. Regarding the phrase "by way of jhāna factors":

this is stated here by applying the designation of those [factors] to things similar to them, because equanimity, pleasure, pain, and one-pointedness—which exist in all consciousnesses except for the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness—are jhāna factors.
For there can be no status as a jhāna factor in the absence of being a condition for jhāna. Indeed, it is said: "The jhāna factors are associated with jhāna... and so forth.
“Material phenomena are a condition for [mental] phenomena by way of the jhāna-condition. However, the status of these as a jhāna-condition has been rejected. As it is said:
“Dependent on an indeterminate state, an indeterminate state arises, but not by way of the jhāna-condition.

Dependent on one aggregate accompanied by the fivefold sense-consciousness, three aggregates [arise],” and so forth. Even in the absence of the jhāna-condition, there is the stability of feeling and consciousness.
The description of the second group is given because such states consist of equanimity and so forth, and because there is no other category for those that have become thus.

436. "Pure by nature" means that, since they are not themselves opposed to dark qualities (*kaṇhadhamma*), they have acquired a pure state by virtue of being based on the heart-basis which is serene and naturally pure; this is the intended meaning. And this...

The method [of reasoning] does not apply to the fourfold existence (catuvokāra); therefore, in that case, there would be no brightness of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) or of the unwholesome consciousness emerging from it.
Consequently, the cause for its brightness must be stated there. Or rather, this is the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of consciousness:

that it is bright. 439. Regarding the word "also" (api) in the phrase "this also," the particle refers back to what was previously stated as being accompanied by mere persistence (ṭhitimatta), namely, that which is associated with doubt (vicikicchā).
It is said: "By way of nature" means by way of non-transgression. That too is a specific distinction.
"Having struck the sensitive body, it rebounds against the great elements that are the conditions for sensitivity"—the meaning is that it rebounds after having entered the sensory range (*āpātha*).

And just as when it is said, "arisen with reference to form," there is no temporal sequence of priority and posteriority between the object and its arising, so too here in the case of striking and rebounding.

It should be understood thus. The simile is stated for the purpose of showing the collision of both [elements], not for the purpose of showing the priority or posteriority of the supported and the support. And here, "external" is merely an illustration;

for even an internal object becomes an object [of consciousness]. Alternatively, that which is other than the bases of the consciousness-element is called "external. This is the resonance resulting from the impact.

It becomes powerful; therefore, when there is contact with desirable or undesirable tangibles, the conditions for pleasure and pain—namely, the strengthening of the elements and the disturbance of the elements—persist for a long time.

If it is argued that because other consciousnesses possess both intrinsic emptiness and existence, they attain the state of mind-element (*manodhātu*), we say no, because of the presence of specific distinctions.

For visual consciousness and the others are dependent upon the eye and so forth, and their nature consists in the occurrence of seeing and the rest with respect to the respective objects of the eye and so forth.

Furthermore, there is a distinction. As for mental consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*), because it has no other support and is preceded by the mind, and because it lacks the state of being the door of exit and the gateway for consciousness that depends on another [physical] basis—due to its lack of such a condition—it possesses a function of discerning with particular excellence;
this is the distinction. Devoid of that specific quality, the element consisting of mere mind is called the "mind-element" (*manodhātu*); thus, the mind-element itself is said to be threefold.
It is not distinguished [from consciousness]. Therefore, in this context, the word *eva* in the term *manodhātu* (mind-element) should be understood as having the sense of "only" (*mattasaddattha*).
For it serves the purpose of excluding other distinctions, as in the case of the term *viññāṇa* (consciousness).

Furthermore, because it functions as the gateway for the exit and entry of the mind-door, the mind-element should be seen as lacking the specific quality of discernment; for that very reason, it is not called "mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*).
For that consciousness does not proceed from the mind as a condition for the mind, nor does it proceed from the mind while being a condition for the mind;
rather, it is a condition for seeing and so forth, and it proceeds by means of them, preceding and following them.
It is not called "right intention" because, unlike the great resultant [states], it lacks the quality of being a producer. For therein, from the three-rooted...
Even when arising with two roots, it is similar to right intention and so forth by virtue of having a cause. Regarding the phrase "in the stream of the fivefold sense-consciousness":

just as one who is reciting a familiar text does not notice certain passages of the recitation that have fallen into the stream of the recitation, so too there is no such thing as non-observation for the Tathāgata; yet, this is not the case within the stream of the fivefold sense-consciousness.
The absence of jhāna factors is the reason for their not being mentioned here.
If [the subsequent description] were included within that same category, then the two mental consciousness elements following this would not be included in that category.

Therefore, because they lack the condition of the path—due to being rootless like the fivefold sense-consciousness—even though initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra) exist, they are not considered jhāna factors.
Because they are weak and, like the fivefold sense-consciousnesses, do not admit of calculation, they are included within the stream of the fivefold sense-consciousnesses.
For this very reason, even in the case of the three rootless functional [consciousnesses], the jhāna factors and the powers are not mentioned in the Section on Compendium (Saṅgaha-vāra);
however, in the Paṭṭhāna, the status of these weak factors such as initial application (vitakka) and so forth as jhāna-conditions is stated merely by virtue of their function as jhāna-conditions.

469. Since the investigating consciousness (santīraṇa), arising after having obtained the proximity condition (anantarapaccaya) with the same basis as the preceding mind-element (manodhātu), is stronger than that mind-element, it experiences the flavor of the object according to its nature. Thus, regarding a desirable object, it is accompanied by joy;
regarding a desirable-neutral object, it is accompanied by equanimity, because of its superior experience. Therefore: "In this case, regarding a desirable object..."

Thus it was said, beginning with “...only. However, although determining (voṭṭhabbana) is powerful, because it turns away the flow of resultants and makes the mind dissimilar [to them], it lacks the experience [of feeling] like a resultant due to its engagement in a different function of attention;
therefore, in all cases, it is accompanied by equanimity alone. The same applies to the five-door adverting consciousness and the mind-door adverting consciousness.
Because it is unprecedented by way of its function.
The commentary on the rootless wholesome resultant [consciousness] is finished.
The commentary on the eight great resultant consciousnesses.

498. Regarding the passage beginning "Non-greed is an indeterminate root," and so forth: first, with respect to the wholesome side, since it is stated in the descriptions of non-greed and non-hatred that "whatever at that time is non-greed, non-covetousness...
[etc. ...non-greed is a wholesome root," and "whatever at that time is non-hatred, non-malice...
[etc. ...non-hatred is a wholesome root," here too, in their respective descriptions, it is said: "Non-greed is an indeterminate root" and "Non-hatred..."
The statement "the root of the indeterminate" would be appropriate [in that context]. However, in the explanations of the faculty of wisdom and so forth, it is stated there as well:
"The jewel of wisdom is non-delusion, the investigation of phenomena, and right view"; it is not stated there that "non-delusion is a wholesome root.
Therefore, here too, the reading "non-delusion is a root of the indeterminate" should not exist. Just as in the case of non-greed and non-hatred...
It should be understood that this was stated for the purpose of showing that non-delusion (*amoha*) is also an indeterminate root (*abyākata-mūla*).
"Not producing intimation" means it prevents the doors of bodily and verbal action. "Having the nature of not being subject to ripening" means it also prevents the door of mental action;
for the doors of action are said to belong to those things that are subject to ripening. Likewise, "not occurring" refers to its absence as a meritorious deed such as giving and so forth.
"From non-arising. By this, he excludes only those [kamma] that are bases for the performance of merit.
"By strong conditions" means by conditions such as the object (ārammaṇa) etc., which are produced without application (payoga).

For when a kamma has been accumulated by any kind of consciousness among the *asaṅkhārika* (unprompted) and so forth, it arises without prompting—that is, without application—when the kamma, the sign of the kamma, or the sign of the destination presents itself.

Rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), when arising, is either unprompted (asaṅkhārika) or prompted (sasaṅkhārika), depending on whether it is presented by kamma and so forth with or without effort and application.
The life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and death-moment (cuti) are exactly like rebirth-linking.

The registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) should also be understood as being either unprompted or prompted, just like wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses. To examine among these which are strong and which are weak:
Regarding this, he said: “Therein, all the omniscient Bodhisattvas,” and so forth. As for the phrase “it transforms according to time”:

it means that during a period when there is an abundance of karma conducive to a short lifespan, it transforms by way of the conditions consisting of the semen and blood produced from a continuum accompanied by such karma, as well as by way of the conditions of irregular heat, food, and so forth, generated by the irregular revolutions of the moon and sun based upon those [conditions].
*Commentary on the Discussion of the Extraction of Ripening (Vipāka)*
In order to show what kind of result there is, in what place it ripens, and how much, the discussion on the extraction of the results (*vipākuddhāra*) is commenced.
"Right here" means when the kamma has been accumulated by a single volition (*cetanā*). By way of a double-rooted rebirth-linking, there is also a twelvefold path and a twelvefold type;
by way of a rootless rebirth-linking, there is also an eightfold rootless [path]. [This applies] to both the unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) and the prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*).
Not desiring a confusion between resultant states that are prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) and those that are unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*), the second elder said, "twelve," and so forth.
For in the case of the former, the state of being prompted or unprompted is due to its condition (*paccaya*), whereas for the others, it is due to the kamma.
Not desiring even a two-rooted (*duhetuka*) state from a three-rooted (*tihetuka*) one, the third elder said, "ten," and so forth.
In this section on the exclusion of results (*vipākuddhāra*), they took up the Sāketa Question for the purpose of determining the linking of rebirth (*paṭisandhi*) by way of kamma.

They took up the exposition of the "predominance" (*ussada*) in order to show how, through kamma, there arises the characteristic of the predominance of various specific qualities or defects in the result.
The exposition of the causes (*hetu*) is stated here according to the intention of the First Elder. Regarding the distinctions found in the doctrines of the Second Elder and others:

I shall explain this in each respective place. Because knowledge serves as the antidote to the causes of misfortune such as being born blind or deaf, even though it is extremely weak when accompanied by only three roots (*tihetuka*), it can still draw along a rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) that would otherwise be drawn by two roots (*duhetuka*);

therefore, he said, "It is not rootless. As for the passage in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* concerning the rootless rebirth due to misfortunes such as being born blind or deaf within the happy realms (*sugati*):

Having excluded [the other types], it is stated: "In what eight causes does rebirth conditioned by the attainment of a fortunate plane (gatisampatti) and associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta) occur?

By this, it is demonstrated that a rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) associated with knowledge does not occur through kamma dissociated from knowledge. Otherwise, [it would have been said] "of seven causes..."

“Rebirth occurs conditioned by this”—this too should be stated. For it is said: “In the attainment of a happy destination, for which eight roots associated with knowledge does rebirth occur as a condition?
At the moment of impulsion of wholesome kamma, three wholesome roots are co-nascent conditions for the volition born at that moment. Therefore, it is said: ‘Also conditioned by wholesome roots...’”
Regarding formations (*saṅkhārā*): at the moment of craving, two unwholesome roots act as conascence conditions for the volition born at that moment.

Therefore it is said: "Formations also have unwholesome roots as their condition. At the moment of rebirth-linking, three indeterminate roots act as conascence conditions for the volition born at that moment.
Therefore it is said: "Consciousness also has mind-and-body as its condition."
“With consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form”—this was answered in the case of rebirth associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*).
Thus, while rebirth dissociated from knowledge and rebirth associated with knowledge both exist, [it is asked]:

"In the attainment of a fortunate destination (*gatisampatti*), for which seven causes associated with knowledge does rebirth arise as a condition? At the moment of the impulsion (*javana*) of wholesome kamma..."
Having stated, "Two roots are wholesome," one might think that the answer can be given elsewhere in the same manner as previously explained.

However, just as rebirth-linking associated with knowledge does not occur because of the non-statement of "the conditions for the seven roots in association with knowledge"—thereby implying it is absent from what is dissociated from knowledge—so too [one might argue] regarding the attainment of a happy destiny: "In the dissociated from knowledge, there are six roots..."

Having stated only, "Rebirth occurs conditioned by [the roots]," because he did not say, "conditioned by the seven roots," it follows that rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) does not occur even when dissociated from knowledge, since it is associated with knowledge.
For here too, it is not impossible to apply three or two roots at the moments of kamma-intention and to apply two at the moment of rebirth-linking. However, for this Elder...
This may be the intended meaning: “The reading given here is stated with an omission by way of showing the result that corresponds to the kamma.
If it is argued that this would entail that the reading is also incomplete in the case of the statement, “For the eight roots associated with knowledge,” we say no;
because weak kamma with two roots is incapable of giving a result associated with knowledge. [This applies] to that which possesses three roots.
However, just as there is no impairment of capacity in the ripening of a rootless [consciousness], there is likewise none in the ripening of a two-rooted one.
The statement that "feeling is to be exchanged for the object" refers to investigation (santīraṇa) and registration (tadārammaṇa).

For, due to the absence of the capacity to grasp distinctions, eye-consciousness and the others are accompanied by equanimity alone toward objects that are desirable, undesirable, or neutral; and so too is body-consciousness.
"Accompanied by pleasure alone due to a specific kind of resistance.
To show the occurrence of fruition (vipāka) at that time—possessing distinctions and occurring during that specific interval as the object-condition for all the impulsion moments—it is said:

"Of one who has entered [into] restraint or non-restraint...," because at other times there is no occurrence of fruition such as the fivefold sense-consciousness, which is complete [only in those states]. "Like a crab... etc.
Regarding the phrase "crossing over the life-continuum" (*bhavaṅgotaraṇa*):

by this he shows that it is like crossing a river by an improper path, such as the tracks of crabs, without first entering the irrigation channel (*mātikā*) which serves as the route for entering the river after filling the field;

so too, when the "object-identical" consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*), which serves as the route for entering the life-continuum, has not arisen, there is a crossing over the life-continuum without the proper path.
Among these three "vain" (mogha) sections, the second should be understood after investigation.

For if, in the section on dependence (*paṭicca-vāra*) and others within the "conformable" (*anuloma*) triad of feeling, it were stated that "due to the condition of repetition (*āsevana-paccaya*), two are not in the path" and "due to the condition of the path (*magga-paccaya*), two are not in repetition," then that vain section would also be applicable.
However, if even the "determining consciousness" (*voṭṭhapana*) were to be a condition of repetition, [then that section would indeed apply].

It may be so for both the wholesome and the unwholesome. For there is no state that, having acquired the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*), is not called a "condition by way of repetition" (*āsevanapaccaya*).
However, the status of the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) as a condition by way of repetition for wholesome and unwholesome states has not been stated [in the Paṭṭhāna].
It is said: "Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises, but not by way of repetition. Dependent on an unwholesome..."
It is indeed excluded by the statement: "Dhamma... [etc.

...is not a condition by way of repetition-condition (*āsevanapaccaya*). Even if it were argued that "this was stated with reference to feelings of a different kind," even so, just as it is said, "Adverting is a condition for wholesome aggregates and unwholesome aggregates by way of proximity-condition (*anantarapaccaya*)," so too should it be stated that "it is a condition by way of repetition-condition."

If it is argued that "the distinction of genus (*jātibheda*) has not been stated," one must reply: "Just as for the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) state—which differs in level (*bhūmi*)—there is the status of being an object-condition (*āsevanapaccaya*) for the fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) states and so forth, so too it would exist for that which differs in genus. And according to the principle of non-difference in genus, just as it is stated:

"Adverting (*āvajjanā*) is a condition by way of proximity-condition (*anantarapaccaya*) for the aggregates accompanied by roots (*sahetuka*)," so too [should it be stated] by way of the object-condition (*āsevanapaccaya*).

It might have been stated as "condition," but it was not. Therefore, even in the triad of feeling, when the enumeration is determined by the abbreviated calculation—namely, "one [case] for the repetition condition, not in the path;

one [case] for the path condition, not in the repetition"—the second futile section, described in the aforementioned manner, must be examined, since the state of being a repetition condition does not apply to the act of determining (voṭṭhabbana).

Adverting (āvaṭṭanā), however, is so called because it turns toward the stream of resultant continuity; and attention (manasikāra) is so called because it performs the function of impulsion (javana), which is dissimilar to that [adverting].

Having established this, it is not stated in the *Paṭṭhāna* that "adverting is a condition for wholesome aggregates by way of proximity-condition" and so forth, but rather simply that "adverting... is the case. Therefore, from adverting...
If [a state] is unable to become the object-prenascence for four or five impulsion moments, it cannot serve as a condition for the adverting to visible forms and so forth;
this is its intrinsic nature. Thus, it would be appropriate to present this as the second "futile section" regarding the non-completion of the impulsion process.
However, since this too has not been mentioned in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it should be thoroughly investigated. [This refers to] the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
Because it is the state of being a follower of the javana, it is said: "The life-continuum has that as its object. And in the *Paṭṭhāna*, it is stated:

"A life-continuum with root-cause is a condition for a life-continuum without root-cause by way of proximity-condition," and "A life-continuum without root-cause is a condition for a life-continuum with root-cause by way of proximity-condition.
[This applies] to wholesome and unwholesome [javana], which have only pleasant and painful fruition.

Resultant consciousness does not differentiate between the desirable and the undesirable; however, impulsion (javana) differentiates between the desirable and the undesirable by way of attachment, detachment, and so forth.
Therefore, it is said: "It is impulsion alone that experiences the flavor of the object.
To show how there is an occurrence in the form of adverting and so on despite the absence of a [permanent] agent, [the text describes] the fivefold...
They took it as the "niyāma" (fixed law). And *niyāma* is simply the specific nature, function, condition, and state of phenomena.
"Giving a corresponding fruit" means the giving of a fruit suited to each respective [cause]. "Giving a corresponding result" (*sadisavipākadāna*) has the same meaning as "giving a suitable result.
The singular designation "this object" (*idaṃ vatthu*) is made because it serves as the basis for a single verse. "A region of the world" (*jagatippadeso*).
There is also another world-region besides those already mentioned. For evil that is obstructed by time, destiny, physical basis, or effort would not ripen;

it is not obstructed by location. The fixed order (*niyāma*) of phenomena such as the basis for omniscient knowledge, rebirth-linking, and so forth, and its state of being the cause for the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world-system, is the "fixed order of phenomena" (*dhammaniyāma*).
This is what is intended here. By this, he shows the meaning that the status of adverting and so forth occurs by way of this fixed order, and not by way of a creator.

"In this place" refers to the section on the sixteen types of resultant consciousness. The simile of the water-wheel (*nāḷiyanta*) regarding the twelve [types of consciousness] is not stated with reference to their performing functions simultaneously at a single door upon a single object;
rather, it is stated merely in terms of each of the twelve performing its own respective function at a single door.
Immediately after a functional consciousness similar to that which produces a rootless rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*),...
Showing the object of that [consciousness] which is rootless, he said: “But for any one of the four double-rooted wholesome javanas... it becomes established.

However, in the case of one with a rootless rebirth-linking, when a triple-rooted javana has occurred, the arising of a rootless object-attaining consciousness (tadārammaṇa) by means of the kamma that provides the rebirth-linking is not prohibited. The same applies to one with a double-rooted rebirth-linking.
Immediately after a three-rooted consciousness, a two-rooted consciousness with that same object (*tadārammaṇa*) should be understood as not prohibited.
Furthermore, this exposition of resultants is based on kamma that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) with a full complement of results; it is merely an illustration of its primary mode.
Thus, sixteen resultant consciousnesses and so forth for a single three-rooted kamma during the course of existence (*pavatti*) should be applied according to the method already stated.
Therefore, when a single or multiple object of registration (*tadārammaṇa*) occurs through any given action,
it becomes distinguished by the distinction of the conditions known as "impulsions" (*javana*), which are the specific causes for those [beings] to whom that object is a continuous succession;
thus, this determination of the object of registration is stated by way of the impulsion, not by way of what is produced by various distinct actions.
And having established it thus, in the *Paṭṭhāna* [it is said]: “One contemplates the associated aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

When the wholesome or unwholesome [states] have ceased, a rootless resultant arises by way of being its object. This refers to the rootless resultant with that as its object immediately following knowledge. And:

“When the wholesome or unwholesome [states] have ceased, a root-possessing resultant arises by way of being its object”; this refers to the root-possessing resultant immediately following the unwholesome.

It was stated that [the result] has a cause and that same object; nor is it a negation of that [result] on the grounds that "it was not shown by this Elder. However, as for the statement, "But that which [arises] with javana...
and so forth, this was said with reference to wholesome [kamma], because it is held that there is no result similar to an unwholesome one, just as there is none to a wholesome one.
But this is said with reference to the determination of the "prompted" (sasankhārika) and "unprompted" (asankhārika) types.
When that has been stated, it is not the case that even for unwholesome [kamma] this is not applicable.

"This is impossible" (aṭṭhānametaṃ) is said with reference to the absence of either wise or unwise turning over (*āvaṭṭana*), or wise or unwise defining (*vavatthāpana*), by way of such [mental] determination.

"Prohibited" (*paṭisiddha*) is said by taking the mere non-speaking itself to be the prohibition. By kamma produced through craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), there is no ripening consisting in the experience of the sublime or supramundane realms.

"There is not" means that the absence of an object-referent (*tad-ārammaṇa*) should be understood there. When an object has come into range, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), being inclined toward it, produces the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*);

thus, adverting arises because of its inclination toward the object. However, since the life-continuum is always already inclined toward its own object, even though it serves as a condition for a consciousness directed toward another object, [that other consciousness] would arise without adverting were it not for the absence of that [life-continuum's inclination].
It arises simply because of being inclined toward its own object. "Habitual" (*ciṇṇatta*) means that it has frequently arisen previously even without an act of adverting (*āvajjana*).

"Active manifestation" (*samudācāratta*) means that it has frequently arisen previously when an object has come into the range of perception and also regarding the object of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Alternatively, "habitual" refers to the state of having been practiced by a person; "active manifestation" refers to the state of occurring frequently by itself. Regarding cessation...
The statement "the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the proximity condition" is said with reference to the immediate attainment of cessation following it;
it does not mean that the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception functions as a proximity condition for cessation in the same way that the immaterial aggregates do.

Furthermore, there is no arising of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception without some preliminary work (parikamma); its "adverting" is simply the adverting of that preliminary work itself.
This [state] must also be blameworthy, just like any other;

however, the intended meaning here should be understood as follows: the uniformity observed in the state of being an immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*) for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*)—and not for cessation (*nirodha*)—is seen elsewhere in the sense of being a preparatory stage for a different purpose and for the sake of its arising; yet, that [uniformity] belongs to it [the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception].

It is an immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*), and thus it arises. In this way, even though there is no arising of an adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) as previously described, the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) arises without adverting when there is a state of inclination toward sounds and so forth. And having established this, it was said: "The noble path-consciousness and the fruition-consciousnesses immediately following the path.
For if this were intended with reference to the absence of an adverting consciousness that takes Nibbāna as its object, [then the statement would not hold].
It might be said that the expositions on the lineage (gotrabhū) states serve as illustrations, since by means of them the faultlessness of these [states] is established.

Furthermore, at the time of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), because of the statement: "The conformity [consciousness]—whether having a limited object or a sublime object—is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of the proximity condition (anantarapaccaya)," they are shown to be "immediately following the path" due to being devoid of an adverting consciousness (āvajjana) with a common object.
If it were as stated, "the fruition-minds," then the minds of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) would not need to be excluded.

However, although the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) and purification (*vodāna*) moments have neither been practiced nor manifested with respect to Nibbāna, they have indeed been practiced and manifested with respect to other objects.
Furthermore, because the fruition-attainment minds exist subsequent to the path-process (*maggavīthi*) for the purpose of preparing for that [Nibbāna], they are included.

It has not been performed; nor has the consciousness of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), which follows in immediate succession (*anulomānantara*), been practiced or brought into active manifestation. Furthermore, because there is no preliminary preparation for that purpose—as there is in the case of the path immediately following the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*)—the phrase "for one emerging from cessation" is used as an illustration.
As for the statement "it does not arise without an object," this was posed as a question because this [consciousness] lacks the status of having a sublime object (*mahaggatārammaṇa*).
This was stated for the purpose of determining the object.

"Therein" means in the discussion on resultant [consciousness]. The illustration of the simile of the man blind from birth and the cripple is for the purpose of showing that resultant consciousness does not arise without its support.

"The grasping of the object" refers to the grasping of their respective objects by the eye and the other [senses], which constitutes the resultant consciousness such as eye-consciousness and so forth.

This was stated for the purpose of showing [the function]. And because it serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the eye and so forth, and because it serves the purpose of seeing and so forth for that very resultant consciousness, it is said:

"as a decisive support in its actual sense. "Only the heart-basis" means that whereas previous moments of consciousness are supported by the heart-basis and follow upon the sensitive matter of the bases while having other objects, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is not like that.
What is meant is that this [consciousness] proceeds depending solely on the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), devoid of any other physical basis or object.
Even here, the intended meaning of the phrase "having the material heart as its base" should be understood as being accompanied by another base.
For consciousness has the sensitive matter (*pasādarūpa*) as its base, just as a monkey climbs a rope; and its functions such as going and so forth are like those performed by the rope.

"The remaining consciousnesses follow that [moment]" means that it is shown that the impact on the sensitive matter (pasāda) and the movement of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occur simultaneously, like the movements of a monkey when a string is pulled;
thus it is also shown by the phrase "one by one... arrives.
"The time when the life-continuum is turned back" refers to the time when the door-guardians, such as eye-consciousness and the rest, [are active] for the one who is like a foot-massager.

The state of being an immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) for adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*), which is similar to the taking up of a perception (*saññā-dāna*), is stated as such because it is considered to be the "revolving of the life-continuum" (*bhavaṅgāvaṭṭana*).

The performance of functions such as receiving (*sampaṭicchana*) by the resultant mind-element (*vipāka-manodhātu*) and so forth, is stated by way of their commonality (*sāmañña*)—namely, merely grasping firmly, merely cognizing a broad square shape, merely cognizing the state of a coin, and merely bringing about the presentation of the object to kamma.
It does not mean that there is an absence of firm grasping and so forth in those [subsequent moments], nor that the seeing of the coin is identical to the state of receiving and the rest.
It should be understood as "intended.
The phrase "this is white" should be understood as an illustration that, by virtue of the commonality of seeing a white form, visual consciousness alone accomplishes the function of seeing.
In the same way, this should be applied to the ear-door and so forth, by way of hearing and the rest. By way of heating...

One who has the habit of eating molasses or whose purpose is molasses is a "golika. The phrase "by way of decisive support" (*upanissaya*) is not spoken with reference to the condition of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
Rather, that which does not exist when another is absent is what is intended here by the term "decisive support.

The expression "dependent on light" is also spoken with reference to its presence when light exists, not to the causal relation of decisive support. [The term] "situated on a slow path" (*mandatthamagata*)...
It occurs by itself without becoming a condition for a volitional (nāma-kiriyā) consciousness.
Regarding the observation of a fault in both the unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) and prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) [kamma], it means that a result cannot arise from a kamma of a nature contrary to its own;
thus, there is no arising of a prompted result from unprompted kamma, nor an unprompted result from prompted kamma.

"Having seen the fault. However, for those [mental states] that are rootless (*ahetuka*) and whose functions consist merely in the initial impact upon visible forms and so forth, there is no state of being "prompted" (*asaṅkhārika*), because their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is not opposed to the "prompted" (*sasaṅkhārika*).
Nor is there a state of being "unprompted" (*sasaṅkhārika*), because their intrinsic nature is not opposed to the "unprompted.

Since they are not in conflict with either, it is admitted that they arise by way of both. "The determination of consciousness" (*cittaniyāma*) refers to the determination of the object-representation (*tadārammaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "five from the functional," and so forth, it is stated that the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) arises immediately after a functional impulsion (*kiriyajavana*).
However, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, it is stated: "When the wholesome or unwholesome has ceased, the resultant arises as registration";

thus, registration is said to follow immediately only after those states that have the nature of producing a result (*vipākadhammadhamma*). And in the Wholesome Triplet, it says: "Whether trainees or worldlings, [they take] the wholesome as impermanent," and so forth.
Having mentioned only wholesome and unwholesome javanas, the "registration" (tadārammaṇa) is stated immediately following them;
it is not stated after the indeterminate (abyākata), nor is any instance found anywhere where registration is stated to follow a functional (kiriya) javana.
Furthermore, there is no reason for its omission if it were actually present; therefore, this doctrine of the Elder must be examined. For the javana is indeed expansive (vipphārika).
