It is appropriate to say that the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) follows [the process] like a river current following a boat; however, it is not the case that for one possessing the sixfold equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā), the functional impulsion (kiriyajavana) of peaceful conduct follows like a river current following a leaf-boat.

Regarding the statement "the lumped-together impulsion (piṇḍajavana) impels," this is because wholesome, unwholesome, and functional impulsions have been spoken of collectively; thus they are so described.

The impulsions (*javana*) are spoken of as if they were condensed; or rather, having been shown by being condensed within a single object of registration (*tadārammaṇa*), they are spoken of as having impelled.

Furthermore, when speaking of this "condensed impulsion" (*piṇḍajavana*), one takes only the four unwholesome [impulsions] accompanied by equanimity, and thus twelve impulsions accompanied by equanimity are spoken of as if they were condensed. However, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, it says: "Wholesome..."
Because it is said: “One relishes and delights in it; with that as its object, lust arises; wrong view, doubt, restlessness, and grief arise.
When the unwholesome has ceased, the resultant [consciousness] arises as registration (tadārammaṇa) of that.
Therefore, the other two types [of consciousness], which are accompanied by doubt and restlessness and occur with a desirable object, also [function as registration] in the wholesome resultant.
[The moments] should be grouped together. However, immediately following those, there must be a rootless resultant [consciousness] with that same object;
and since that has already been included by way of its function as investigation, there is nothing new to be included.
Furthermore, because rootless [consciousnesses] do not admit of being grouped together—this is the intended meaning—it is not grouped here.
Regarding the phrase "but here at the end of a three-rooted javana," this is said by the first Elder to show that in this second position,
a three-rooted registration (tadārammaṇa) is appropriate at the conclusion of a three-rooted javana because it is of the same nature as the javana, and because no other [registration] is obtainable.
This refers to the rootless registration mentioned immediately after an unwholesome [javana], and the rooted registration mentioned immediately after a wholesome [javana].

For one who asserts that [consciousness] arises immediately after an unwholesome state, there is no visible reason why a three-rooted (*tihetuka*) rebirth-linking-producing kamma—which even when producing a two-rooted or rootless (*duhetuka-ahetuka*) result—should not produce it immediately after a three-rooted javana.

Thus, it should be understood as being "logically consistent" (*yutta*) even though it was not explicitly stated; this is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Alternatively, according to whichever of those various Theravāda positions...
The prescription of "with effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*) and "without effort" (*asaṅkhāra*), and so forth, was stated with a specific intention;

it should be understood as being appropriate according to that very intention, and not mixed with another intention by means of another intention—this is the meaning. "Exactly like the cause" means exactly like the generative kamma-cause.
"It will become clear in the *Mahāpakaraṇa*" means that the method of arising, which is evident in the textual tradition (*pāḷi*) found in the *Mahāpakaraṇa*, will be made manifest.
He speaks with the intention that "it will be.
The commentary on the discussion of the wholesome-resultant of the sense-sphere is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the discussion of the resultant of the fine-material and immaterial spheres.
499. "Without obstacle" means being devoid of conditions for decline. "Distinguished by way of the path, etc. refers to the distinction in the path and the object.
For instance, when one who has produced a jhāna that is difficult of practice and slow in direct knowledge enters it again and again, that jhāna remains of that same mode of practice.
When this [jhāna] is not lost, its result, as it arises, is of that same mode of practice.

"It is worthy to become [such]. However, the state of being dominated by desire (*chanda*) and so forth occurs at that moment through the status of desire and the rest as dominant conditions (*adhipati-paccaya*), not by way of their arrival. For indeed, a single jhāna possesses different dominant factors at different moments.
For it is precisely the fourth jhāna that is cultivated in the form of the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).
Therefore, the predominance of desire and so forth is not stated with respect to the arrival of the result [of kamma].
The commentary on the discussion of the fine-material-sphere and immaterial-sphere resultant [kamma] is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion of the supramundane resultant [kamma].
505. Just as it accumulates a circle [of suffering], so too mundane karma conditioned by craving and the like is said to be "accumulated.
However, since supramundane [karma] does not function in this way, it is not described in that manner. "By way of pure arrival" means:
unmixed with those factors that give the name "signless" or "wishless"—namely, the objects possessing qualities—and which illustrate the emptiness of the fruit even while they exist.

The meaning is as follows. By way of arrival, having stood in the position of the path’s arrival—which possesses the names "emptiness" (suññatā) and "wishless" (appaṇihita)—the giving of the three names to its own fruit has been applied;
however, for the other [path], it should likewise be applied in the same manner. For this is merely a demonstration of the method.

But by way of objects possessing qualities, even for the path that follows immediately after the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), which possesses the three names, in the position of its arrival—
It is not excluded that, having stood [in the attainment], there is the giving of the three names to one's own fruit.

Furthermore, if the attainment of the functional fruit were to acquire a name by way of proceeding toward insight (vipassanā), then—just as with the path—it would lack the acquisition of the name "signless" (animitta).

However, just as with the fruition attainment immediately following the path, the attainment of the functional fruit also possesses the distinctions of the jhānas and the modes of progress (paṭipadā).
Thus, when the name "emptiness" (suññatā) and so forth are acquired, it also acquires the name "signless" (animitta).

The phrase "not having subsided" (avūpasanta) is stated with reference to the state of being an immediate condition (anantarapaccaya) for such very same faith... pe ...and wisdom, because it is not interrupted by anything else.
By this, zeal (chanda) and the others are also dominant factors (adhipati) that produce their own subsequent, similar instances of zeal and so forth.
This explains the meaning that [the factors] arise only when [the path] has become the dominant influence.

555. Since the fruit of the path—which consists of right view and the rest, which cuts off the defilements, and whose intrinsic nature is deliverance—must likewise have the nature of deliverance characterized by the subsiding of the defilements, it is therefore said of the fruit as well: "It is a path factor; it is included in the path."

Thus it was said. And having established this, the eightfold and fivefold paths are extracted in the *Maggavibhaṅga* and in the section on the fruits; likewise are the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgā*).
"With reference to the path" means he spoke thus with reference to the meaning that [the enlightenment factors] are called "paths" because they resemble the path.
The commentary on the discussion of supramundane fruition is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Unwholesome Resultants (Akusalavipākakathāvaṇṇanā): 556.

Just as there is no distinction in investigation (santīraṇa) regarding desirable, desirable-neutral, or undesirable-neutral objects, so too there is no such distinction regarding undesirable, undesirable-neutral, or desirable-neutral objects. However, it is stated in two ways—intense and weak—with reference only to undesirable objects.
The commentary on the discussion of unwholesome resultants is concluded.
Commentary on the Mind-element (Manodhātu) as Functional-Indeterminate (Kiriyā-byākata): 566.
"Wind-flower" (vātapuppha) means a vain flower; it does not bear fruit even when the tree is uncut, being merely the flower of a cut tree.
But it might bear fruit even when its root has not been cut. Thus, for one whose roots of existence have been severed, that which continues to arise without bearing fruit is like a windflower;
however, for the other, what continues to arise is like a flower on a tree whose trunk has been cut down, for that would indeed bear fruit as long as the root of existence has not been severed.
568. Regarding the commentary on the mind-element of functional mental consciousness (*kiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu*):
"Craving for gain has been abandoned"—this shows a previous occurrence that served as a condition for this consciousness.
However, this consciousness is devoid of investigative wisdom; it arises only for one who produces mere mental joy (*somanassa*). Thus...

This should also be understood in the case of making offerings at shrines (cetiyas) and so forth. The phrase "performing the duties" (vattaṃ karonto) is said with reference to the activity of the mind-door consciousness regarding the object of touch for one performing those duties.

Alternatively, it refers to the very occurrence [of consciousness] occurring within the five doors themselves, which serves as the cause for the reflection that abandons the craving of greediness toward what is obtained through the five doors.
In various places it is stated, “By means of this consciousness, one becomes joyful”; thus he said, “In this way, it is first obtained in the five sense-doors.

Having spoken of unimpeded knowledge regarding the past and so forth, [he says] that because of such statements as, “For the Blessed Buddha endowed with these three qualities, all bodily action conforms to knowledge,” “this arises for the Blessed One.”
The aforementioned statement must be examined. Because a rootless consciousness lacks roots, it has no firm foundation;
thus, its status as a "power" (bala) is incomplete. Therefore, in the section on enumeration, it is not stated that "there is the power of concentration" or "there is the power of energy.

For this very reason, in the section on inclusion, the jhāna factors are also not mentioned for rootless states. For the same reason, in this case as well, regarding these two types of rootless consciousness—
The powers are not included within the [five] faculties. However, because energy is present, it is stronger than the remaining rootless factors;

and because here there is a state of mere strength in concentration and energy—just as there is a state of being merely a condition for the jhānas in the case of applied thought and so on—it was therefore established in the section of the exposition by stating "the power of concentration" and "the power of energy. But because...
The intention is that because it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, right concentration and wrong concentration, as well as right effort and wrong effort, are not mentioned [in that context].
This being so, this [distinction] would also not have to be stated regarding the great functional consciousnesses (*mahākiriyacitta*); yet it is stated.
Therefore, whether right or wrong, they do not attain the status of being conditions for the Path because they lack the nature of leading out (*niyyānika*).
It should be understood that the "winds of concentration" (*samādhivāyāma*) are not mentioned here in this manner.

The knowledges of the superiority and inferiority of the faculties (*indriyaparopariyatta*), of the underlying tendencies and dispositions (*āsayānusaya*), and the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇa*)— which arise immediately after this— as well as the knowledges of the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*),
the Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), have the preliminary exercises (*parikamma*) that arose immediately prior to this as their immediate antecedents.

Because these [consciousnesses] proceed only toward the object that has been adverted to, it is said: "The six... seize. It is called "great" (mahā) because, due to its vast range, it is like a great elephant;
thus, it is a "great elephant" (mahāgaja). This concludes the commentary on the functional consciousnesses of the fine-material and immaterial spheres.
577. Now, the construction should be made thus: "those actions which have arisen are to be understood. "Individual existence" (*attabhāva*) refers to the five aggregates.
The commentary on the Section on the Arising of Consciousness is finished.
2. The Section on Matter (*Rūpakaṇḍa*).
Commentary on the Summary:
Now, the indeterminate (abyākata) matter must be analyzed; however, it is not possible to analyze it by establishing a temporal limit (samaya-vavatthāna).
For it is impossible to establish a temporal limit for matter based on the arising of consciousness, because there exists matter that is not produced by consciousness (acitta-samuṭṭhāna).
Furthermore, because mind-originated matter arises from many different moments of consciousness,

and because some consciousnesses that originate matter do not do so in every instance, there is no fixed determination [of time]; and because material phenomena— excluding the two types of intimation—
are not co-existent with consciousness, it is not logical to define the duration of sublime and measureless states by the attainment and abiding therein.
Because, unlike the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), there is no state of "having entered and abiding" with respect to material phenomena;

nor is it logical for them to consist of derived matter (*upādārūpa*), since derived matter does not function as co-nascent or other such conditions [for itself]; nor is it logical for them to consist of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), because some primary elements proceed without certain derived matters, and because they exist at different times—for it is not the case that "at whatever time... [the primary elements and their derivatives are simultaneous].

It cannot be said that "at the time when the earth element has arisen, at that same moment the eye-base exists," because the eye-base does not exist simultaneously with the earth that serves as its support (the ear, etc.
or with the earth produced by consciousness and other factors. The same should be applied to the ear-base and the others.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that at that moment the intimation (viññatti) or the accumulation (upacaya) and so forth exist, since these are not co-existent with the primary elements (mahābhūta).
At one time, many thousands of material groups arise and persist; unlike immaterial phenomena, there is no coexistence of two material groups within a single moment.

Since the cessation of one group and the arising of another occur simultaneously while that very group is still functioning, it is impossible to define the indeterminate nature of matter by means of temporal delimitation in any way whatsoever.

However, since it is not possible to analyze [the indeterminate] by way of its intrinsic nature (sabhāva) through methods such as the "single" (ekaka) or the "cause" (hetu), in order to analyze it in that manner,
[the author] first shows in the Cittuppādakaṇḍa that there exists an indeterminate (abyākata) which has not yet been analyzed.

Because it would be illogical to provide a conclusion after indicating only a portion [of the definition] without defining the indeterminate by its very intrinsic nature through a formal determination of its status (samayavavatthāna), [the author proceeds as follows].
Gathering together all that has been analyzed and all that has not been analyzed, he said: "Which phenomena are indeterminate? The wholesome...

[and so on] ...and the unconditioned element. These phenomena are indeterminate. For when that which is to be analyzed has been shown as yet unanalyzed, it is appropriate to perform the analysis once the desire to know has been aroused. However, in this context, the indeterminate [phenomena] consisting of fruition and functional states are not [included here], because they have already been analyzed.
It should be analyzed; and the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) is not to be analyzed because it lacks differentiation.

As for that which is to be analyzed here because it possesses differentiation and is not yet analyzed, the author, while analyzing it, said: "In this context, what is all form? and so forth. This is the construction of the text (*pāḷi-yojanā*) here.

Regarding the phrase "having shown the method" (*nayaṃ dassetvā*): here, the act of grasping [the preceding] itself is the showing of the method. That is understood by applying it to the resultant states (*vipāka*).

"Released among the functional-indeterminate" (*kiriyābyākata*): it is "released" because it is stated by taking [the category of] the functional-indeterminate—which is to be described as belonging to the sense-sphere and so forth—and having applied [the term] "sense-sphere" and so on to that. "The twenty-five material phenomena":

these are the ten bases mentioned in the Canon and the fifteen subtle material phenomena; or, alternatively, they are so called by treating the processes of accumulation (*upacaya*) and continuity (*santati*) as one.
And the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). "Ninety-six" refers to: the seven decads beginning with the eye-decad; the three [groups] beginning with those produced by temperature (*utusamuṭṭhāna*);

the two octads produced by temperature and mind; and the two sounds. Material phenomena that occur as groups (*kalāpa*) are called "material components" (*rūpakoṭṭhāsa*) because they possess the nature of being components of material groups.
"Components" (*koṭṭhāsa*) means parts or members. Alternatively, "component" (*koṭṭha*) means the body.
The hair and so forth on his shoulders are "sections" (koṭṭhāsa); likewise, other parts are also called "sections" because they are like sections. Nibbāna is taken without limitation;
it is taken without limitation as something divided by way of being described as the destruction of lust with remainder, the destruction of lust without remainder, the unconditioned, and so forth.
For in actual meaning, there is only one unconditioned element.
584. "All" means the entire Cakkavāḷa. "Circular" means having a circular shape;
the meaning is that its circumference is three million six hundred and forty thousand yojanas.
And here, what is round is called "circular. "Four nahutas" means forty thousand.
*Nagavhayā* means they are so called because they are named after the word *naga*; the meaning is that they have the name "mountain.
They appeared as large as three *gāvutas* and more, due to the bodies of the devas, dānavas, and others.

Herein, this is the etymological derivation: they are *bhūtāni* (beings), meaning born or produced; being large, they are *mahābhūtāni* (great beings). This is by way of showing many wonders and by way of showing many extraordinary qualities.

And because he is a great being (mahābhūta) like a master illusionist, he is called "the Great Being" (Mahābhūta). Alternatively, yakkhas and others are called "great beings" (mahābhūta) because they are great by way of their very birth;

this term *mahābhūta* should be understood as a conventional designation applied to them. Furthermore, earth and the other elements are "great beings" (mahābhūta) because they are like [those] great beings.
Since the word *bhūta* possesses both genders, it has been rendered here in the neuter. Regarding the phrase "due to the great protection": here...
Explaining the meaning of the words, he said: "Beings that are great, or beings with a great retinue.
In this context, regarding the latter sense, by eliding the word *parihāra* (retinue) from the second member of the compound in the first phrase, they are called "great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*).
"Accimato" means of fire. "One hundred thousand koṭis" means one [unit consisting of] a hundred thousand koṭis. "Cakkavāḷa" refers to all of that.
They speak of it as one by way of its being the field for the command. It dissolves by means of alkaline water. "It is scattered" means it falls apart.

Showing the transformation in the clung-to (upādinnaka) aggregates, he said, "it becomes rigid," and so forth. The word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "by a wood-mouthed [serpent]" has the sense of a simile;
just as one bitten by a wood-mouthed serpent becomes rigid, so too [does one become rigid] through the disturbance of the earth element.
That body becomes like a woodpecker’s mouth; the meaning is that it becomes as rigid as the mouth of a woodpecker when it has entered [into a tree].
Alternatively, the word *vā* (or) has the sense of the word *eva* (only). And this should be understood by supplying the phrase “by the disturbance of the earth element” from what follows.
In this context, the meaning is: “Even though the body is bitten by a woodpecker, it becomes rigid only through the disturbance of the earth element.”
“Because it exists, that body is never dissociated from the earth element; it is as if it has entered the mouth of a wooden saw.

Alternatively, the word *vā* has the sense of indefiniteness. In this case, the meaning is as follows: “A body bitten by a wooden-mouthed [creature] may or may not become rigid depending on the presence of mantras or medicines;
however, due to the disturbance of the earth element, that [body] which lacks such mantras or medicines [does become rigid].”
“The body becomes as rigid as a log placed in a fire. “Putrid” means decomposed.
“The great mutations have arisen” means that the great mutations have come into being, or else it means they are present.
And here, by eliding the word *vikāra* (mutation) from the latter member of the compound in the first phrase, they are called “the great elements” (*mahābhūtāni*).
Although earth and the other elements are well-known to the whole world, when they are grasped according to their true nature by abandoning perversion, they cannot be grasped without great effort;
thus, even though they are well-known, they are called "great" because their nature is difficult to discern.
For one who stands taking those which are easily discerned as "not great" fails to grasp them correctly.

Having seen them, one understands: "Oh, these are great! Regarding the term *upādāya*, because it signifies a subsequent occurrence or activity as understood by this [term], it is called "derived matter" (*pavattarūpa*).
For in this way, by the word *upādāya*, its state of being dependently originated is expressed.
Alternatively, that which is taken up (*upādāyati*) or relied upon (*nissayati*) is *upādāya*; matter that is itself *upādāya* is *upādāyarūpa*.
This is a designation for material form that is absolutely dependent on something else and lacks any other support.

However, in order to show that this [designation] does not apply to a "being" (satta), nor to feeling and so forth—since it exists even in their absence—the text says, "of the four great elements," and so on.
For material forms that serve as supports do possess the status of being a master (sāmibhāva).
Commentary on the Compendium of the Threefold Matter (Tividharūpasaṅgaha):
585. Among the miscellaneous dyads (pakiṇṇakaduka), there is none other than the internal dyad (ajjhattikaduka) that proceeds by way of triplets in conjunction with all the dyads;
furthermore, the dyad of intimation (viññattiduka) does not proceed [in this manner]. Thus, it is the first among those dyads that are conjoined with all [the others].
Having taken only the internal dyad (ajjhattika-duka) and combined it with all the remaining dyads, the triads (tika) have been stated.

For by this method, the application of triads resulting from the combination of other dyads with one another can also be understood. Commentary on the Compendium of the Fourfold and Other Matter (Catubbidhādi-rūpa-saṅgaha-vaṇṇanā).

586. Among the tetrads (*catukka*), because the two types of intimation (*viññatti*) arise exclusively from consciousness, the "consciousness-originated" dyad (*cittasamuṭṭhānaduka*) shares the same course as the "two intimations" dyad (*viññattiduka*) and so forth.
Thus, although a tetrad could be obtained by joining it with the "derived" dyad (*upādāduka*), it was not mentioned.

Likewise, [tetrads] obtainable by joining the "visible" dyad (*sanidassanaduka*) and so forth with that [consciousness-originated dyad] and with the "gross" and "distant" dyads (*oḷārikaduka*, *dūraduka*) were also not mentioned.

Since the Blessed One—who knows the individual essences, functions, and the modes by which phenomena are to be understood exactly as they are—did not himself effect the connection between these [terms] and others, or between those [others] and these, what need is there for further investigation into the reason?
It must certainly be understood that such a connection was not to be made, precisely because it was not made by the Blessed One. As for the other miscellaneous dyads (*pakiṇṇaka-duka*), however...
These are suitable to be combined with other miscellaneous dyads, and they have indeed been so combined.

However, in the Vatthu-duka and others, by excluding the dyads such as those having ear-contact as their object, and instead using other available dyads such as those having external bases as their objects, four tetrads are obtained for the combination of the *upādinnaka*-duka and the *upādinnupādāniya*-duka;
and for the *cittasamuṭṭhāna*-duka, [four tetrads are obtained] by using all available dyads such as those having external bases as their objects.
However, it should be understood that by combining the remaining factors with those others and all the bases, starting from the "heavy" (*vatthuduka*), they are not obtained.
The commentary on the enumeration is finished.
Analysis of Matter (*Rūpavibhatti*).
594. The exposition (*niddesa*) is precisely the demonstration of the absence of differentiation for that which lacks differentiation, because it effects a definitive determination.
Therefore, by means of the word "only" (*eva*), which serves to restrict the absence of differentiation through the statement "all form is not only the cause," etc., he provides the exposition.
"Root-cause" (*hetu-hetu*) means the fundamental cause; or alternatively, "cause-condition-cause" (*hetu-paccaya-hetu*) has this same meaning.

The statement "the great elements (*mahābhūtā*) are causes" conveys the very same sense as "the great elements are conditions. Because the words *hetu* and *paccaya* have the same meaning, a condition is itself a cause, thus it is called a "condition-cause.
Furthermore, that which is the cause of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) is precisely what is called its "establishing cause" (*paññāpanā-hetu*).
Because of its absence, there is an absence [of the result]. Regarding the statement, "The ripening of past, future, and present undertakings of kamma according to their basis and cause":
although other conditions exist here, wholesome and unwholesome states are supreme and primary because they determine desirable and undesirable ripening;
they produce desirable and undesirable objects through the accomplishment of destinations, acquisitions, status, and success or failure in application.
Just as karma is called a "cause" because it is the primary factor, with this same intention the objects of karma are called "supreme causes.
And he will say: "Destiny, the physical basis, time, and effort are the conditions for fruition; karma is the cause.
However, here, since the object is supreme just like karma, it too deserves the designation "cause"; thus it is called a "supreme cause."
Regarding "formations" (*saṅkhārānaṃ*): ignorance is called the "cause" because it is the common condition for meritorious formations and the others.
"Pervades" (*pharati*) means it goes to and reaches [them]. "Negative exposition" (*paṭikkhepaniddeso*) is stated here by way of the negation of what has appeared in the matrix (*mātikā*).

However, in this context, the fact that matter is not included under the category of "cause" and so forth in the matrix is stated because of its own specific nature; and its "determination" is due to its having no other nature.
In this context, within the pair of terms "material" (rūpī) and "immaterial" (arūpī), only the term "material" is stated as "matter" (rūpa).

By this, the synonymy of the terms "material" and "matter" is established, because only that which possesses the characteristic of being affected (ruppana-lakkhaṇa) has the status of being material matter. The phrase "arisen and cognizable by the six consciousnesses" demonstrates the specific nature of matter as distinct from the immaterial; for the immaterial, when arisen, is not cognizable by the six consciousnesses.
"Just as form is cognizable": by this, it is established that form which has arisen is cognizable by the six consciousnesses, and not what is non-form;
thus, having excluded the non-form, this defines the specific nature (sabhāva) as belonging to form alone, rather than form being defined by this nature.
For there is past and future form which, though arisen, does not possess the nature of being cognizable by the six consciousnesses. It is precisely this...

Furthermore, by the word *eva*, he restricts the rule (*niyama*): "The rule as stated exists in material form (*rūpa*) indeed; it is not as if it were non-existent, as it is in the immaterial (*arūpa*).
Alternatively, "all material form" refers to the primary and derived elements (*bhūta-upādāya-rūpa*) without specifying temporal distinctions;
it is called "all. That "all" has a nature perceivable in the same way as the immaterial, and the term "arisen" (*uppanna*) is used to exclude the past and the future.
By this he qualifies it; the meaning is that all that arisen material form is indeed cognizable by the six consciousnesses. [Objection:
But does this not result in the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) also being cognizable by ear-consciousness and the others? [Reply:
It does not so result, because one has grasped all material form collectively as a single unity by way of showing its uniform characteristic, [and thus] as something distinct from the non-material.
This is because it shows that the intrinsic nature of what is cognizable by the six consciousnesses [is present].

However, if there were this restriction—that only present matter is cognizable by the six consciousnesses—then in the phrase "all matter," this restriction regarding the state of being cognizable would not have been stated;
instead, the restriction of the single-characteristic of all matter as being "present" would not have been shown.

In the Pāḷi, the word "only" (*eva*) is used in the phrase "to be understood by consciousness alone" (*viññeyyameva*), not in the sense of "only what has arisen" (*uppannameva*). Therefore, since there is no necessity that only what has arisen must be cognizable by the mind, what is the use of its being included within the range of hearing?
Consequently, the meaning should be construed according to the method already stated.
"Of what kind? means how it is established by its qualities. Knowledge itself is the basis of knowledge. It is a grouping of things belonging to the same class.
"Grouping by way of common genus" (*sajātisaṅgaha*) means a grouping with those of the same genus. "Place of birth" (*sañjāti*) refers to that wherein things are born;
"grouping by way of place of birth" (*sañjātisaṅgaha*) means a grouping according to the category of their origin.

Right mindfulness and the other factors, which arise in the locus of concentration through mutual assistance and non-separation, are grouped within the aggregate of concentration. And where [there is] one who possesses mindfulness and the other aids...

The performance of its own function by concentration is the state of concentration within that thought-moment. And because right intention possesses the state of absorption, its function is similar to penetration;
thus, view and intention are included in the aggregate of wisdom by virtue of this common function of penetration.
The commentary on the singlefold exposition of the analysis of material form is finished.
The Exposition of the Twofold [Treatise]: Explanation of the Discourse on the Analysis of Grasping (Upādābhājanīyakathāvaṇṇanā). 596.

The vision of the assembly of beings with little dust in their eyes and so forth is the Buddha-eye; among the six unique knowledges, it is the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties in others (indriyaparopariyattañāṇa).

It is to be seen. The vision of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*). Knowledge and vision occurring in such modes as "Suffering is to be fully understood;
it has been fully understood" is the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*); like the previous two, that too belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
The vision of the Dhamma of the Four Truths is the eye of Dhamma (*dhammacakkhu*). The material continuities arising from the four causes, which serve as supports, [are the objects of this eye].

“Requisites” (sambhārā). “With requisites” means together with the requisites, that which possesses the requisites. “Origin” (sambhava) refers specifically to the water element as that which has originated from its origin.
“Shape” (saṇṭhāna) refers specifically to the sense-sphere of visible form (vaṇṇāyatana) as it exists in shapes such as circular and so forth.

However, these are mentioned separately because both the water element and the sense-sphere of visible form—whether existing in that state or not existing in that state—are present in the aforementioned mass of flesh.

For the "flesh-mass" consists of fourteen constituent parts (*sambhāra*). Regarding its dependence on three elements (*dhātu*), this should be applied to the statement that it arises together with those [parts] dependent on the four elements.
Alternatively, because the water element and the sphere of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*) lack the specific configuration of the flesh-mass, they are mentioned separately;

thus, there is no contradiction in its dependence on the four elements. When one perceives that flesh-mass by way of white and so forth, one does not perceive the sensitive eye-organ (*pasādacakkhu*).
Desiring to state specific qualities such as its extension and so forth, he repeats what was already said:
"There is earth," and so on. By the phrase "in the place where the bodily configuration arises," he rejects the remaining black circle (*kaṇhamaṇḍala*).
It stands pervading the seven layers of the eye like oil, having received assistance from the four elements that serve as its own support.

It persists, being protected and surrounded by its own dependent factors such as vitality (*āyu*) and beauty (*vaṇṇa*), and being supported by the temperature, consciousness, and nutriment that originate the threefold continuity of material form.
Furthermore, by the expression "the dispersal of the seven layers of the eyelid," he shows that the eye consists of many aggregates (*kalāpa*).
As for the phrase "in measure, the size of a louse's head," it is said because it functions in a location the size of a louse's head.
"Contemplates forms" (*rūpāni manupassati*): the letter *ma* serves as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhikara*). Alternatively, *manu* means a mortal (*macca*).

It is "gathered together" by those things that act as supports. "By way of method" (*pariyāyena*): it is appropriate to say that the clarity of four [elements] belongs to one or two of them, just like the wealth of those who possess equal property;
it is by this method. The body is simply the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). "Impact" (*nighaṃsa*) is simply the striking against [resistance].

*Paṭighaṭṭanānighaṃso*: The resonance (*nighaṃso*) born from the striking together (*paṭighaṭṭanā*). Or, the resonance produced from the "striking together" which consists in the eye-consciousness attaining the state of being a support by way of being directed toward visible forms (*rūpa*); thus it is *paṭighaṭṭanānighaṃso*.
The phrase "if it should come into the range" is a statement of hypothesis concerning the causal activity, while "one would see" refers to the resultant activity.

Having made that assumption, there is speech based on that assumption. And here, it should be understood that because of the multiplicity of causal functions, even though they are not explicitly stated, they are nevertheless implied.
By the phrase "or for seeing," the eye is included as that which does not undergo the state of being a support for visual consciousness at any of the three times.
The meaning of "the leader in seeing" (dassanapariṇāyaka) is the state of being a guide in the act of seeing.
For just as a lord, saying "Do this and that," directs and employs his men in their respective tasks,

so too this [eye] is called "the eye" because it directs those phenomena— such as visual contact— in their task of seeing, as if commanding them by virtue of being their support. For it "sees" (*cakkhati*), and thus it is the "eye" (*cakkhu*) in the sense already described.
The meaning is that it instructs and guides by means of a method. Alternatively, it is called *cakkhu* because it sees (*cakkhati*), instructs, or makes manifest forms that are even or uneven.
It is a "place of birth" (*sañjāti*) because things are born therein. What is born there? Contact and the other [mental factors]. Likewise, it is a "convergence" (*samosaraṇa*).
It exercises the function of a lord (*indaṭṭha*) by way of the occurrence of its own states—such as visual contact—in their respective degrees of intensity or dullness.
"Causes [it] to be made": even that which is grasped as permanent, stable, and a self, is so called in the sense of breaking up and falling away.
"The instrument of engagement" (*vaḷañjana*): it is so called because contact and the other factors enter through its door;

it is used in the sense of the engagement of those factors belonging to that door. 597. The term "alternative" (*vikappa*) has the meaning of a conceptual supposition, as previously stated. "While being struck": while proceeding toward a specific state of facing the sensitive matter (*pasāda*).

599. By the very statement that eye-contact and the others arise contingent upon visible form (*rūpa*), it is implied that other [mental states] associated with those [faculties] also arise contingent upon visible form.
And by the intention of stating their arising through that specific condition—namely, how visible form serves as their condition—he said, "By this," and so forth.
In that context, for those [states] which have the sensitive eye-faculty as their basis...

By the expression "of contact and so forth," it should be understood that the arising of the mind-element and its associates—which resemble it by virtue of having that same object as their support—is shown to occur through the relation of pre-existence (*purejāta-paccaya*). However, in order to show where there is a distinction, he says:

"of those included within the cognitive series of the eye-door javana," and so on. For these [states] consist in the relishing and delighting of one who proceeds by making material form the object of esteem (*garuṃ katvā*).

Those [mental states] associated with it arise by way of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), object-strong-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya), and so forth; others arise by way of object-prenascence (ārammaṇapurejāta) alone.
Thus, the word "taking as an object" (ārabbha) indicates not only the state of being an object-condition but also the state of being other conditions;
whereas the term "object" (ārammaṇa) indicates only the state of being an object-condition. This is the distinction between them.
600. "Hears" means he hears by way of being the support for ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa*).

Since the activity known through the tongue is "tasting," he says "in the sense of tasting" (*sāyanaṭṭhena*). The body (*kāya*) is the coming together (*āya*) of base things—namely, contact and so forth associated with suffering—or it is the coming together of the suffering of pain (*dukkhadukkha*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*).
Because the body-base (*kāyāyatana*) pervades [the sense-fields], there is also the presence of the body-sensitivity (*kāyapasāda*) within the eye-sensitivity (*cakkhupasāda*).
[The opponent objects: "Since it exists, because it permeates the eye-sensitivity (*cakkhupasāda*), it would not be non-pervasive; yet it is said [to be non-pervasive].

Therefore, the manifestation of the tangible (*phoṭṭhabba*) by the eye-sensitivity and the manifestation of visible form (*rūpa*) by the body-sensitivity (*kāyapasāda*) follow as a consequence. Thus, he charges [the theory] with a confusion of characteristics (*lakkhaṇasammissatā*). [The author replies:
Because the eye and the body have different bases and belong to different groups (*kalāpa*), [this does not apply], for there is no [manifestation] of one [sensitivity] in the place of another.

He said: This was stated to show that even for those things that possess visible form, taste, and so forth, and share a common basis, there is an absence in one another due to their not attaining each other's nature;
how much more so, then, for those with dissimilar bases?

And because it is both susceptible to the impact of physical form (*rūpa*) and a clarity of the primary elements (*bhūta*), it is called "the clarity of the primary elements susceptible to the impact of physical form. Such is its characteristic.
The eye. "Impact with visible forms" (*rūpābhighāto*) means either impact upon visible forms or impact by visible forms. This is the second method stated for all cases:

sensual craving and form-craving—which serve as the cause for the karma that produces a personal existence (*attabhāva*) with either complete or incomplete sense bases—deserve the designation "desire to see" and so forth, because they constitute the longing for existence within those respective sense bases.
In this context, the karma that has the desire to see as its cause is their "origination" (*samuṭṭhāna*).

The eye has as its source kamma originating from the desire to see; it has the characteristic of being clarity in such primary elements (bhūta), or it is the clarity of such primary elements [originating] from the desire to see... [and so on] ...clarity. Such is the characteristic of the eye.
Its function is to attract a person or consciousness toward visible forms.
"‘The body of all’—what is the distinction here? Is it not the case that the sensitive matter (pasāda) of the elements, such as heat and the rest, belongs to all [beings] alike? True, this is so;
however, this statement "of all" indicates the meaning of "those who are equal," because it is spoken in order to preclude the state of having a partial excess for one who follows along.
Regarding the phrase "of heat and the rest," it refers to the heat comprised by the lamp.

The meaning is that, as is appropriate in both the former and latter arguments, because they are sustained by the respective qualities of those elements— by light in the case of air, by sound in the case of earth, by the odor of earth in the case of water, and by the taste of what is called saliva (phlegm) in the case of water—
they must be assisted for the apprehension of visible form and so forth. This is said "to show the predominance of visible form and the rest," as in the case of luster in fire and sound in air.

The proponent of the first view stated that "visible form and the others are their qualities" because one observes the earth’s fragrance—such as its sweet scent—and its sweet taste, which are distinguished from the earth itself when it is being perceived by its own nature. To this, he gave the reply beginning with, "We would wish...
By this same method, the refutation of the second proponent's position is also established.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the passage beginning with "But they might say" was spoken in order to refute and restrain the third doctrine of Kaṇāda, who asserts that the eye and other sense organs are composed of fire, space, earth, water, and air, each possessing its own specific qualities such as form and so forth.
Furthermore, although a fragrance is perceived in the flow [of water], it is distinct from the cotton [fibers] because the water is conjoined with the earth.
If it is argued that there is no attainment of a superior state by the scent of cotton, we say no, because it is not overwhelmed.
While earth joined with water is overwhelmed by the water, the cotton-earth is not; therefore, it must possess a superior scent.
Furthermore, since fire joined with hot water is perceived as great, its color must also be like its touch.
If it were to be apprehended as luminous, then the color of cold water—which is not connected with fire—would have to lose its color due to the presence of the color of hot water.
Therefore, because of the absence of both [of these], the status of visible form and so forth as specific qualities of fire and so forth is negated.
By that negation, this reason—"because of being sustained by the qualities of fire and so forth, namely, visible form and the rest"—is established.

“Reversed. Thus, he said, “Therefore, one should abandon this,” and so forth, to show that through such a succession, the absence of both [subject and object] becomes the cause for abandoning the conceptualization of distinctions.
Furthermore, the illustration of visible form, taste, and so on was stated to demonstrate that even within a single aggregate, visible form, taste, and the rest are dissimilar;
how much more so, then, in the case of different aggregates, such as the eye and other sense bases, even in the absence of any distinction in their primary elements (bhūta)?

If there is no specific difference in the primary elements (*bhūta*), what then is the cause for the specific differences in the eye and so forth? To show this, he said, "That which [is] mutual," and so on.

It should be understood that even a single kamma, when produced through the aspiration for an existence possessing the five sense bases, is described as both "not common to one another" and "a specific kamma" because it is the cause for the specific differences of the eye and so forth. For it is not by that specific [kamma] alone...
It is a condition for the eye; by that same [condition], it becomes one for the ear, because it has attained the state of being another faculty.

By the statement, "At the moment of rebirth-linking, a single sublime volition is a condition for kamma-produced matter through the condition of kamma," it is understood that at the moment of rebirth-linking, a single volition is the kamma-condition for all kamma-produced matter existing at that time. [This is not so] in the case of various volitions...
For then, when there is the arising of the faculties, it would follow that the *kaṭattārūpa* (matter produced by past karma) brought about by both limited and sublime karma would be attained;
yet, a single rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is not produced by multiple karmas. Thus, it is established that the arising of multiple faculties occurs through a single karma.
That which has a non-adherent support is "anallīnanissaya"; this refers to the object consisting of visible form and sound. [This applies] to odors and tastes.

The nose and tongue sense-bases adhere to their respective supports; thus, they are "adhered to by way of support. Tangible objects (phoṭṭhabba) themselves adhere to the body-support because they consist of the three primary elements (bhūtattaya).
The intention is that only that which is "attained" (sampatta)—meaning it produces resistance through impact and friction—is [considered] "near.
Sound, however, comes via the succession of elements like the wind and adheres to the support of the ear.
It is said that when one proceeds to define [the sound] by approaching it and striking the ear, one proceeds to the definition slowly.
But if this were so, the sound-base produced by consciousness would never be an object-condition for ear-consciousness;
for it is not possible for the arising of something produced by consciousness to occur externally.
Regarding the statement, "It is heard after a long time": why was this said? Is it not the case that sounds such as those of a washerman are heard after a long time by those standing at a distance?
No; because there is a distinction in the apprehension of sounds according to how clearly they manifest for those who are distant or near.

For just as there is non-apprehension and apprehension of specific features in the sound of speech according to how clearly it manifests for those who are distant or near, so too is it with the sounds of washermen and others.

In the case of a nearby sound, from the beginning until the end, as it gradually becomes manifest, and in the case of a distant sound, when its occurrence becomes manifest either at the end or in the middle by way of a mass, there arises—specifically after the process of the ear-consciousness and the subsequent cognitive series that grasp the determination—the conceit:
"I heard it quickly" or "I heard it after a long time. Yet, that sound, wherever it arose...
That sound, being dependent [on the bell], enters the range of the ear at the very moment it exists.

However, a sound situated at a distance should be understood as a condition for the arising of an echo elsewhere or for the movement of a vessel and so forth, just as a magnet is a condition for the movement of iron.
Or, just as the primary elements (bhūta) that follow the striking of a bell serve as the support for the resonance.

Since the primary elements (bhūtas) that have arisen by way of production—beginning with those whose nature is impact and following those produced by impact up to the ear-sensitivity—are themselves of the nature of impact, the sound dependent upon them is said to undergo gradual discernment after having been impacted through the succession of elements by virtue of its support.
[If one were to ask] "From which direction is it? it would not be known. Why? Because the sound is apprehended only in the location of the ear.

"One whose underlying intention (*ajjhāsayo*) is uneven is called ‘one of uneven intention’ (*visamajjhāsayo*). Even though the eye itself is devoid of intention, it is described as ‘of uneven intention’ because it inclines toward what is uneven.
Alternatively, the eye of a person possessing vision is described as ‘of uneven intention’ by way of that person’s own underlying intention."
Because it proceeds precisely through the cavity of the ear-hole and because it is the cause for grasping the object, it is said that "it forms its inclination right there.

Regarding the hearing of sound by means of the ear's status as the support for ear-consciousness, one who explains the meaning according to the intention of the *Aṭṭhakathā* says, "inside a cave," and so forth; whereas one who speaks according to his own intention [states otherwise].
Saying, "What is the significance of this natural law? and so forth, they spoke.

"That which has wind as its supporting condition for its fragrance as its object" means *vātūpanissayagandhagocaraṃ*. Herein, wind is the supporting condition (*upanissaya*) for the apprehension of fragrance;
however, by way of that designation, the fragrance itself is called "having wind as its supporting condition. Alternatively, it is simply the wind [that is meant].
The decisive support (*upanissaya*) is the wind-decisive-support (*vātūpanissaya*). Of what? Of olfactory consciousness.
That which exists for this [consciousness] as another concomitant condition (*sahakārī-paccaya*) is the wind-decisive-support; thus, odor is the condition.
Water, too, exists as another concomitant condition, such as saliva and so forth. Likewise, earth. For, of the tangible object (*phoṭṭhabba*) to be grasped—

The earth element, which serves as the support for the body when it is being pressed, and which serves as the basis for those elements that are the supports for the body when it is being pressed by a tangible object, is always the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the apprehension of the tangible.

However, in the apprehension of a tangible object without pressing, the earth element that serves as the basis for the body-base (*kāyāyatana*) should be understood as its decisive support; and its status as a decisive support is indeed appropriate at all times.
The expression “five-colored” is for the purpose of showing the diversity of the threads that serve as their basis. “Five-colored” means of five kinds.
The phrase “absolutely” is stated for the purpose of excluding those other material phenomena within the group (kalāpa) that cannot be separated by compression at all times;
for it is not the case that those [other phenomena] are absolutely inseparable, since they belong to different groups.
616. "Appearance of color" (*vaṇṇanibhā*) refers specifically to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*);
with reference to that alone, the neuter designation "visible" (*sanidassana*) is employed.

Therefore, because blue and so forth—which are non-figurative forms—cannot be known by touching, whereas length and so forth can be known by touching, the sense-sphere of visible form is not "long" in a non-figurative sense. "Depending on this or that" means...
"Depending on a collection of primary elements (bhūtasamudāya) arranged in the form of long and so forth.

"Situated in such and such a way" means that the sense-sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana), which is a collection of colors situated in the arrangement of long and so forth, is spoken of by the conventional designations of "long" and so on.

"Mutually delimited" means that because one does not exist within the other, they are distinguished from each other. "The distinction between the object (visaya) and the field of activity (gocara)" refers to the fact that the eye-consciousness has no other purpose [than that] and that it mostly operates with respect to that [object].
620. And because sounds such as those of drums (*bheri*) are sounds of musical instruments, he says "the remainder that has been mentioned.

By the term "non-human beings" (*amanussa*), it is not only other living beings besides humans that are included, but also things such as wooden objects; this is the intended meaning when he says "all the rest as well.
Even so, although [these] have not been included in the Canon (*pāḷi*) by way of describing specific bases (*vatthuvisesa*), they should be described in that manner, or else—
The intention is that it is called "pana" (food). 624.
*Vissagandha* means an unpleasant odor of flesh and so forth. *Lambilam* means sweet-sour. 632.
*Sañjānanam* is that by which one perceives; it is a characteristic mark (*upalakkhaṇa*). By its respective conditions, such as karma, consciousness, and so on...
Even though the female sex-signs (*itthiliṅga*) and so forth arise together with the faculties within the body, they arise having assumed their respective forms;
therefore, they are said to "arise dependent upon the female faculty.

Furthermore, its status as a faculty is stated because of its predominance (*adhipati-bhāva*) specifically over the female sex-signs and so forth, [and] because of the material conditions for the forms of the female sex-signs and so forth within the continuum (*santāna*) that is conjoined with the faculties.
This is because [the female sex faculty] does not produce anything other [than itself], and because those material phenomena are its conditions.

Furthermore, since even within the "group of existence" (bhāvadasaka), the female sex faculty is neither the producer, nor the sustainer, nor the supporter of material phenomena, nor of any other constituent material phenomena;
therefore, like the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) and like nutriment (āhāra), it [sustains] all the other material phenomena.

Nor is it stated that there is a faculty-condition or a non-disappearance-condition for the material qualities of other groups [of atoms]. This same method applies to the masculinity-faculty (*purisindriya*) as well.

Regarding the material qualities in the form of gender-marks (*liṅga*) and so forth, because the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is cognizable by the eye-consciousness, the cognizability of the gender-marks and so forth by the eye-consciousness is stated.
633. It should be understood that the statement "both... are established through the wholesome" refers to a happy destination (*sugati*); for in an unhappy destination (*duggati*), [it is not so].

If rebirth-linking occurs only through unwholesome [kamma], then the state arising at that time would also have to be unwholesome, just as it is in the case of rebirth-linking; for it would follow that it is so even during the course of existence (pavatta).

However, since these two do not occur together within a single continuum—according to the statement, "When the female faculty arises in one, does the male faculty arise in him? No"—therefore, this applies even to a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka).
It is stated that there is only one faculty.

To demonstrate the occurrence of the conventional designation "body" within bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) exclusively, the *Sādhaka-sutta*—which states, "Restraint by means of the body is good"—is cited.
Movement is the manifestation and communication of a state; it is also called "stiffening," due to the predominance of the air element (*vāyodhātu*).
The meaning of *viññatti* (intimation) is the mode of stiffening of the primary elements (*bhūta*).
For just as in the case of upward-moving winds and so forth, when a group of elements has an excess of wind, there occurs therein the state of intimation of the primary elements.

For this very reason, intimation is described in terms of the function of the air element (*vāyodhātu*) as "stiffening the body and making it rigid. And for that same reason, [it is said] regarding the air element:

It is appropriate to say that "shape is bodily intimation," and likewise, "vocal intimation is from the earth element" because it is a modification of the primary elements (bhūta) dominated by the earth element.
Alternatively, "speech as a specific differentiation" refers to [names such as] *Tissa* or *Phussa*, which are specific differentiations.

Or else, speech is "vocal differentiation" when it is embraced by the verbal formations of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and—due to not yet having been brought into the range of hearing—is undifferentiated, or is being led toward that state [of being heard].
It is said. "They support the postures" means they support the postures as they occur.
For while the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) flows on uninterruptedly, the limbs sag as if they have sunk down;
but this does not happen when the wakefulness-consciousnesses mentioned as "thirty-two and twenty-six" are occurring. When those [consciousnesses] are occurring, however—

The limbs [of the body] proceed precisely as postures in their natural course, remaining well-supported. This is stated specifically regarding the death-consciousness of those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*):

"At the moment of arising of the final consciousness of those belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), or of that consciousness immediately after which the final consciousness of the sense-sphere will arise, or in the case of those in the final existence (*pacchimabhavika*) in the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) or the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*)."

Furthermore, from the statement: "And for those who, having been reborn in the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere, will attain final Nibbāna there, at the moment of their death, verbal formation will cease, but bodily formation will not cease," it is understood that the death-consciousness of others as well does not produce matter.
For [this is so] because of the mind that produces matter...
Because of the absence of connection with the descent into the womb and so forth, there is no production of bodily formations;
nor is it logical to say, "Having passed away, his mind-originated [form] continues," nor is there any scriptural passage stating, "The death-consciousness produces material form. 637.
*Na kassati* means it does not undergo distress. *Gataṃ* means understood. *Asamphuṭṭhaṃ catūhi mahābhūtehi* means untouched by the four great elements.
In whatever aggregate there is a delimitation of the primary elements (*bhūta*), that [delimitation] is untouched by those very [elements].

For even though there exists a state of contact between the primary elements of one aggregate and the primary elements of another aggregate, space is the limit of form, defined as the distinctness of each respective element;
thus, whatever the delimitation of those [elements] may be, it remains untouched by them. Otherwise, there would be no such state of being delimited for those primary elements.
Because they have attained a state of pervasiveness. For non-pervasiveness is indeed non-contact.

Since the mutual inseparability of lightness and the other [qualities] makes their diversity difficult to discern, he says "even though this is so," and so forth, in order to demonstrate their respective diversities through their specific variations and predominant forms.
And the aforementioned conditions [give rise to] each respective variation.
They are stated as such because they function as specific conditions; however, without distinction, all are conditions for all.
641. Accumulation from the beginning is *ācaya*; it is initial arising. Subsequent accumulation is *upacaya*. Continuity is *santati*.
In that context, although *ācaya* was not mentioned in the summary list, it is understood by the term *upacaya* itself; thus, "that which is the repeated accumulation of the sense bases..."
He said, "It is the accumulation (*upacaya*) of material form for those things that are being produced.

However, since the prefix *upa-* in the canonical text (*pāḷi*) has both the sense of "first" and the sense of "above," this meaning is understood: "Accumulation (*ādicaya*) is accumulation; accumulation above is continuity (*santati*).
For otherwise, it would follow that the first arising, which is designated as "accumulation" (*ācaya*), would not have been mentioned.
Thus, what is stated by the description beginning with “the accumulation of the bases”? Accumulation is stated by means of the “base.

For accumulation, increase, and continuity are indeed called “accumulation” insofar as they constitute the state of being produced; thus, because accumulation and so forth are manifested through the bases, accumulation is stated by means of them.
By the very mention of the accumulation and so forth of the bases, it follows that the bases are of the nature of accumulation and are subject to arising.

The bases (āyatana) are described as being characterized by accumulation (ācaya). For arising (uppāda) is the characteristic, not a "material form" (rūpa-rūpa). With this very intention, he said: "Only the base is described.
For when one describes accumulation as the characteristic, it follows that the bases, which possess that characteristic, are what are described.
Even so, what has been described? By means of the bases of accumulation—that is, by means of the bases that consist of accumulation—it is accumulation itself that has been described.

The intention [of the author] is this: by speaking of the *āyatana* itself, rather than merely stating "accumulation" (*ācaya*) in both the summary (*uddesa*) and the exposition (*niddesa*), he lists "accumulation" (*upacaya*) and "continuity" (*santati*).
By means of analyzing these through the discussion of accumulation via the *āyatana*, what has been stated?
The word "accumulation" (*ācaya*) refers to "growth" (*upacaya*), and "growth" refers to "continuity. Explaining each of these two in their respective order, he says: "arising" (*nibbatti*).
"‘Growth’ has been explained," he said. Since accumulation and continuity are identical in meaning, they are both "accumulation" (ācaya);

thus, by way of defining and analyzing that [term], the diversity of the modes of production and growth is stated through the explanation of accumulation via the sense bases (āyatana), and so forth—this is the meaning.
To clarify this very point, he said, "For in meaning," and so on. And because both of these are synonyms for the materiality of birth (jātirūpa) itself, [they refer to it].

Therefore, the meaning is that among the specific characteristics of the materiality of birth, such as accumulation and so forth, and its modes of occurrence and so forth, "accumulation" (upacaya) should be understood as having the characteristic of accumulation and so on, while "continuity" (santati) should be understood as having the characteristic of occurrence and so on. 643.
"Exposition of the natural state" (pakatiniddesa) means an exposition according to the natural mode of the ripening of the fruit; it is the very fruit that is to be reached by aging.
Or rather, it is nature (*pakati*). And it is not merely the brokenness and so forth that constitute aging;

rather, from the time of the *kalala* onwards, as the subsequent material phenomena arise at the moment of reaching decay for the preceding material phenomena, they arise in accordance with the ripened forms, becoming increasingly transformed.
Thus, at the time of the full ripening of the material form through gradual transformation, those things whose intrinsic nature is brokenness and so forth arise.

These [characteristics] are said to be "the path gone by" (*gatamagga*) due to aging, because they have arisen in mature material phenomena—designated as the "path gone by" through maturation—just as grass and trees on paths to water and so forth are broken down;
yet they are not aging itself. Uninterrupted aging (*avīcijarā*) is that whose succession of aging is imperceptible.
Its function is to lead toward death.
644. "Having reached that" means having reached its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva), which consists of decay and destruction; thus, form wastes away, fades, and breaks apart.
Just as one who has been beaten and cast down becomes weak, dependent on others, and prone to lying down, so too is one overcome by old age;
thus, old age is like being beaten.

645. "By way of what is to be done" means by way of its functional nature. Its subtlety is stated because it lacks the state of hardness—unlike stones that have been gnawed by hyenas or spat upon by jackals—and because it lacks toxicity—unlike snakes or scorpions.

"The characteristic of nutritive essence" (ojā-lakkhaṇa): here, *ojā* is a specific quality dependent on the primary elements, which follows throughout every limb and member, acting as the essence of the nutrient fluid (*rasa*) and providing support and strength.
The commentary on the discourse concerning what is subject to clinging is finished.
Commentary on the discourse concerning what is not subject to clinging (646):
"It does not cling at all" means it does not rely [on anything] at all; rather, the meaning is that it both relies [on something] and is relied upon [by something].
647. "But the former," however, refers to the earth element, water element, fire element, and air element as stated in the first section of the fivefold compendium.

Alternatively, the intention is that among the earth element and so forth mentioned in the exposition of the tangible base (*phoṭṭhabbāyatana*), it is the water element that was mentioned in the preceding section;
or else, because the aforementioned tangible base is past, it is considered "former," while [the water element] is "latter" because it is future.

And it should be understood that the water element was mentioned previously. "Life" refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "Heat" refers to the fire born of karma (*kammaja-tejo*). "Whatever element... [etc.
"...does not arise simultaneously" means that when multiple earth elements have entered the range of the senses at one moment, they do not arise together within each of those respective instances;
the same applies to heat and air elements. This is said when multiple objects have come together.

By way of its being directed toward itself and by way of the excellence of the clarity of the object, its first arising is shown in one particular instance; however, its arising elsewhere certainly exists as well.
He asks, "But how does the transition of consciousness from one object to another occur? in order to understand the means by which that transition takes place.
651. In the case of iron balls and the like, the earth element would disperse if it were not bound by a corresponding water element;
therefore, it is said that "the water element binds them and makes them firm.

For just as a suitable amount of water binds particles of dust and forms them into a lump of clay that can be set down, so too, in the case of iron balls and the like, [it occurs] through appropriate conditions.
It should be understood that the water element (*āpodhātu*), arising right there, holds [the body] together by binding it in that manner.
It is said that "it becomes a support without touching" because the water element lacks the quality of tangibility (*phoṭṭhabba*); likewise, it is said that "it binds without even touching.
For there is no mutual dependence among the tangible elements (*phoṭṭhabbadhātu*) by way of their being tangible objects, as is the case here.
In this way, the intention should be understood as follows: there is [contact] between the tangible and the tangible element.
For among the primary elements (bhūta) that exist inseparably (avinibbhoga), mutual dependence and mutual conditionality cannot be denied;
nor is it appropriate to distinguish between contact and non-contact among those that have become one through inseparable co-nascence (sahajāta). "It does not burn having become hot" means...
This rejects the very nature of fire and does not admit coldness;

by rejecting the nature of fire itself, coldness is also rejected. For fire itself is cold, since it is seen to ripen cold things during times such as snowfall, and because cold and heat are mutually opposed, no distinct element called "cold" exists alongside heat.

It is logical. However, the non-occurrence of cold within a mass of heat, and the non-occurrence of heat within a mass of cold, is logical because they are two distinct types of fire that are mutually opposed.
"Alteration of state" refers to the softness of hard substances such as sugar and the like, or the hardness of liquids such as juice and the like;
it also refers to the arising of the earth element and so forth in states of deficiency or excess due to specific conditions. "Alteration of characteristic" [is as follows:]...

The abandonment of characteristics such as hardness and so forth does not occur in these [elements]; rather, there is only a change of state (*bhāvaññathatta*) consisting in their being inferior or superior—this is the meaning.
(652) "Only of those that are unclung-to, etc. means they are included among the descriptions and mentions of those that are exclusively unclung-to, exclusively mind-originated, and so forth.
Or, by the phrase "or whatever else," the previous points, such as the absence of the state of non-self-agency (*akammassakatatta*), are also included.

It illuminates this point. For since those [terms]—such as "not clung-to" (*anupādinnā*) and "not produced by karma" (*akammaja*)—have the same meaning as "not made by one's own karma" (*adinakammassakatattā*) and so forth, they would have to be stated by the other term as well if they were not already stated by one;

or conversely, if they were to be stated, they should be stated [by both]. Therefore, because they must be understood as referring exclusively to things that are "not produced by karma" and so on, it should be seen that they are not included among those things that are "not exclusive" (*anekanta*).

666. … It is exclusively [unconditioned] … it is discernible because of their being subject to change; however, the intention is that since it is unproduced, its arising cannot be predicated by anyone.
The commentary on the Exposition of Pairs is finished.
The commentary on the Exposition of Fours.
"Of the last term" means of the term "cognized. For all material form is indeed cognized;
since it cannot be divided [into separate categories], there is nothing seen, heard, or sensed other than what is cognized. Therefore, without even posing the question, the answer was given.
The intention is that it is impossible to ask, "Which material form is seen? as something distinct from the cognized. Just as...
When two [categories] have been mentioned, the question "Which is that form which is derived (*upādā*)? was asked with reference to its difference from what is not derived;

likewise, when the four beginning with the seen (*diṭṭha*) have been mentioned, one might ask "Which is that form which is seen? with reference to its difference from the three beginning with the heard (*suta*).
That such [a distinction] does not exist is why it was not asked; the same applies to the heard and the others. This is because of the specific inclusion of seeing and so forth.
Furthermore, because there exists something else known through seeing and so forth, it is described as a tetrad.
969. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pentad:
"Attained the state of fire" means that by its very nature it has reached the state of fire. Even though it was stated by another...
Here, "guidance" should be understood as the act of gathering together and providing direction for those who ought to be gathered.
This should also be applied to each of the four terms beginning with "the known. The method regarding the existence of divisions within the tangible is found in the *Aṭṭhaka*.
Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discussion.
975. By the statement "there are no hindrances," the abandoning of even the hindrance of torpor (*middha*) is expressed;
yet it cannot be said that matter (*rūpa*) is to be abandoned, nor that the Sage lacks physical illness, given his statement: "My back aches;
I shall stretch it. "Conscious sound" refers to sounds such as the voice produced by consciousness.

It is said with the intention that these [characteristics] do not possess intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*) of their own; rather, they are merely the states of the material phenomenon (*rūpa*). For "aging" is the process of maturing of a material phenomenon as it matures, and "impermanence" is its exhaustion as it exhausts;
these are simply the states of the material phenomenon itself, not things possessing independent natures.

Likewise, "birth" is the arising of what is being born, and that too is merely the state of the material phenomenon, not something possessing an independent nature. Thus, "not, however, in the ultimate sense... [is stated].
It is said: "Birth gives rise [to aging-and-death].
That which has those as its condition is "conditioned by that" (*tappaccayā*). The state of being conditioned by that is "the state of being conditioned by that" (*tappaccayabhāvo*).

The conventional expression (*vohāra*) that proceeds by way of that state of being conditioned by that is "the conventional expression of the state of being conditioned by that" (*tappaccayabhāvavohāro*); it obtains that. [This occurs] at the moment of the phenomenon (*dhamma-kkhaṇa*) that has been produced.
The intended meaning is "at the moment when the phenomena are being produced. For it is not the case that those phenomena do not arise at that time;
rather, since birth (*jāti*) is rightly defined as the very state of arising, it is logical that its origination from karma and other factors, as well as its production thereof, should occur.
However, at that time, those phenomena do not age or perish; therefore, their states of aging and dissolution are not originated by consciousness and the other [causes].

The phrase "and those produced from that" refers to what is worthy [of being so called]. If it is argued: "Even so, the word *upādinnā* (clung-to) expresses being taken up by the associated karma, not being produced;
therefore, the state of being clung-to (*upādinnatā*) should be predicated of the various types of karmic results (*pākabhedā*) that are clung-to," we say no.

This is because the word *ādinna* (taken up) denotes production. For that which is produced by the associated [karma] is "clung-to" (*upādinna*); thus, both the moment of the power of the conditions and the production itself [are denoted].
This conventional expression proceeds only by way of grasping; since that [grasping] is absent at that time, aging-and-death does not proceed.
Because conditioned phenomena possess aging-and-death, when their arising occurs, aging-and-death exists, and when it does not, it does not exist.
For what has not been born does not ripen or break up; therefore, with reference to its dependence on birth, it is said: "Aging-and-death is dependently arisen."

"Dependent on a basis for their existence" means that because birth and the other [characteristics] consist merely in the state of being born, ripening, and decaying in those things that are being born, ripening, and decaying, it is said that birth and the others have an existence dependent on a basis such as "being born.

If this is so, then since birth and the others—which possess the intrinsic nature of arising and so forth—belong to the derived matter of the eye-base and the rest, they would be dependent upon that [matter]. Thus, regarding those things dependent on the primary elements (*bhūta*):

If it is argued that, just as there is a state of being derived (*upādāyabhāva*) for those characteristics, so too there would result a state of being derived-for-a-derived (*upādāyupādāyabhāva*) for those things dependent upon derived matter;
[we reply: no, because the state of being bound to the primary elements (*bhūtapaṭibaddhabhāva*) is not excluded from the characteristics of derived matter that are bound to the primary elements.
Furthermore, because the arising and so forth of the material phenomena included within a single group (*kalāpa*) occur simultaneously, [there is no such fault] in the case of a single group.
Since origination and the other [characteristics] each occur individually, just as the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*)— which sustains each individual group (*kalāpa*)—
is called "derived form" (*upādāyarūpa*), so too birth and the others, whose intrinsic nature consists in the origination and so forth of the groups,
are likewise called "derived forms. In this same way, the forms of change and delimitation should also be applied.
