The temperature-originated [matter] that is connected with action-originated [matter] acquires distinctions such as being beautiful or ugly, well-formed or ill-formed, and so forth, due to the specific nature of the action;

therefore, it is called the "action-condition. External temperature-originated matter that serves as the cause for experiencing the result of action is "temperature-originated by way of the action-condition.
It is either a condition that assists action or a condition that acts as an assistant to action.

The condition of kamma is *kamma-paccaya*. That very temperature is the "kamma-condition-temperature" (*kamma-paccayautu*). The analytical meaning of the term *kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhāna* is: "that which has this as its source (*samuṭṭhāna*) by way of the kamma-condition-temperature.
When any temperature—whether cold or hot—has arisen, from that the pure octad (*suddhaṭṭhaka*) arises;
that temperature is its source. For the second pure octad, which is dependent upon what is temperature-originated (*utusamuṭṭhānika*), that same [temperature] is likewise [the source].

The first [type of] temperature is a condition. However, the third pure octad is described as "temperature-conditioned and temperature-originated" according to the method previously stated, because it is produced by temperature acting as an auxiliary to preceding temperature. Thus, this preceding temperature impels three successions;
thereafter, upon the encounter with another temperature, it impels another triad of successions, and from that, by another...

The occurrence [of the example] should be understood as follows. This should be understood according to whether the contact with that [temperature] occurs shortly or after a long time, depending on the smallness or greatness of the cold and heat;

it is not illustrated by means of the three continuities (*santati*) of what is not clung-to (*anupādinnaka*), but rather should be seen through another mode by way of the primary temperature that originates the cloud. To show this, [it says]: "originated by temperature..."
He said, “...named Valāhaka,” and so forth. The non-actualization (*aparinipphannatā*) is stated because the various forms possess the nature of undergoing transformation and so on.

For the intention is that they are called “form” (*rūpatā*) precisely because they consist of the transformation of form and the like. Furthermore, it is precisely because they consist of the transformation of form and the like that their actualization (*parinipphannatā*) is stated;
this is for the purpose of precluding the state of being unconditioned (*asaṅkhatabhāva*), [showing] that they exist when form exists and do not exist when it does not.
The commentary on the Section on Similes is finished.
3. The Section on the Schedule:
Commentary on the Exposition of the Triads.

985. "Of all" refers to all those [phenomena] divided by way of the arising of consciousness and by way of the unconditioned (asaṅkhata). This has been explained in detail according to the method of word-commentary for contact and so forth, as well as for the eye and so forth.
However, therein, because there is no division of the unconditioned, the word-commentary should be understood as applying only to the unconditioned elements (dhātu).

But as for the miscellaneous factors (yevāpanaka), subtle derived matter (upādāyarūpa), and that which lacks the characteristics of sensory alteration, delimitation, and the state of supporting material form—
It should be understood that no exposition was given here for the heart-base because it is not required for exposition due to its having been already extracted;
for there is no "teacher’s fist" regarding the teachings of the Tathāgata. "Having set aside" means having left behind the detailed exposition;
the meaning is "having removed," or alternatively, "having included within the detailed exposition. The meaning of the verse has already been stated in the introduction (nidāna).
The meaning of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) is the state of being a condition by way of its roots. It is called "source" (*pabhava*) because things originate from it;

that same term is further specified as "producer" (*janaka*). It is called "origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*) because things arise from it; its qualification is "that which brings about production" (*nibbattaka*).
Alternatively, all these are synonymous terms. Why was it said "by way of their function"? Is it not because the wholesome roots possess the nature of a cause?

"By way of the phenomenon (dhamma)"—is it appropriate [to say this]? This is true; however, with reference to the fact that it is shown by way of the common root-meaning (*mūlaṭṭha*) of the three, namely non-greed and so forth, it is stated "by way of the purpose (attha). By this it is understood that "phenomenon" (*dhamma*) refers to the state (*bhāva*), while "purpose" (*attha*) refers to the function of the phenomenon (*dhammakicca*).
This is because of such statements as: "Non-greed is the cause for the arising of kamma," and so on.
"Arising from those" (*taṃsamuṭṭhāna*) means that those roots of skillfulness (*kusalamūla*) are its source of arising.

Furthermore, since it has arisen from them, he said, "arisen from non-greed and so forth. Alternatively, the sense that "those associated with the roots of skillfulness are its source of arising" is also possible.
Here, however, excluding volition (*cetanā*), the others are called "associated with that" in their capacity as the source of arising.

They should be explained as follows. Therein, by means of the roots, one exhausts the wholesome states from the perspective of their condition; by means of the aggregates, from the perspective of their intrinsic nature;
and by means of kamma, from the perspective of their function of producing another [existence]. Furthermore, by means of the roots, he shows the cause for the blamelessness of wholesome states;

by means of the aggregates, the blameless intrinsic nature produced through association with those [roots]; and by means of kamma, the state of having a pleasant result. Or alternatively, by means of the roots, [he shows it] through the perfection of the primary cause (*nidāna*).
It is "good in the beginning" by way of the excellence of intrinsic nature through the aggregates; "good in the middle" by way of the excellence of rebirth through kamma;
and "good in the end" by way of the excellence of finality. 986.
Why is it said that "there is no unwholesome state above that"? Is it not the case that delusion accompanied by doubt and restlessness [is unwholesome]?

"Does it exist? Yes, it does. However, since that [state] cannot exist without being associated with those [other states], when those associated states are grasped, delusion (*moha*) is thereby grasped as well;
thus, it is said "there is nothing beyond this," because it is absent elsewhere. That which exists in one is "one-pointed" (*ekaṭṭha*);
that which is one-pointed by way of co-nascence is "co-nascent one-pointed" (*sahajekaṭṭha*). That which is to be abandoned is "abandonment" (*pahāna*), by way of its nature as abandonment.
"Existing together" (ekaṭṭha) means "existing together in abandonment" (pahānekaṭṭha). For when two things are to be abandoned together, they exist together in a single person;

this is because, whether one is cut off and the other is not, or both are cut off or both are not, they are mutually inseparable by virtue of the fact that the cutting off of one entails the cutting off of the other.
987. “Three characteristics” refers to impermanence, suffering, and non-self. “The three designations” refers to the designation of names, the designation of kasiṇas, and the designation of beings.

It should be understood that when things such as monasteries or beds are expressed in conventional usage without abandoning the ultimate sense, they are included under the category of the “designation of beings” by way of the inclusion of the “designation of beings.
And these [categories], beginning with the characteristics, are like the “intimation” and so forth mentioned in the two preceding sections.
They were not mentioned because they are not intrinsic natures (*sabhāva-dhamma*), nor were they said to be unobtainable.
For it is not appropriate to say that any intrinsic nature is not included within the triad of the wholesome (*kusala-ttika*). 988.

Regarding "the plane of pleasure" (*sukha-bhūmi*): even the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and other planes are applicable here. For the plane of the sense-sphere and so forth, when accompanied by pleasure, is the "plane of pleasure."

Regarding the phrase "the planes such as the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara)," since it is the phenomena themselves that are called "sense-sphere" and so forth, the meaning is understood to be "in the arising of consciousness belonging to the sense-sphere and other planes.
Having established this, after stating "on the plane of pleasure," the words "in the sense-sphere" and so forth were spoken for the purpose of showing its subdivisions.
Furthermore, in the Abhidhamma, the term *bhūmi* (plane) is conventionally used for the sense-sphere and the others; thus, [it refers to] "the four..."

In such passages as "skilled in the planes" (*bhūmīsu kusalo*), there is no mention of other planes. "From the text" (*pāḷito*) means by way of elucidating the meaning of the words in such statements as "results are the ripenings of the distinguished [kamma]";

and "from the sense" (*atthato*) means by way of elucidating the meaning of what was spoken in such passages as "this is a designation for immaterial phenomena that have reached the state of having ripened. [This applies] to the triplets and couplets through the delimitation of names and so forth.
Either by way of the vision of their definition according to the text, or by way of the meaning through making that meaning known.
991. "Sāliphalam" refers to cooked rice (*sālipāka*). 994. Regarding the statement "our uncle, the Elder":

even for clinging that has a person as its object, the condition is only the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), not the supramundane ones; how much more so, then, for clinging that has the aggregates [in general] as its object? Therefore he said, "they are not included."

998. Just as they cannot be grasped by means of clinging and are thus non-clinging (*anupādāniya*), so too, because they cannot be grasped by means of defilements and are thus undefiled (*asaṃkilesika*), he said:

"Asaṃ... [etc. ...the same method applies. 1006. A self grasped by means of views does not exist. However, those things which are the objects of perversion (*vipallāsa*) do exist; they are simply the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
Therefore, that in which there is the grasping of the distorted modes such as permanence where none exists is precisely what is designated as the pentad of aggregates of clinging.

The body (*kāya*). In this context, it is specifically stated as "the existing body" in order to show that aspects such as permanence are non-existent therein, and to show that its intrinsic nature, such as being subject to deformation (*ruppana*), does indeed exist.
However, supramundane states are never grasped in a non-existent aspect; therefore, they do not require this qualification.
The view regarding the existing body, or the view existing in the body, is the "personality-belief" (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*). By means of a self...
The meaning is that because the form grasped does not exist, it is itself merely a memory; it is not the self or what belongs to the self that was grasped by it.
This latter meaning is stated on the grounds that it is possible, but the former alone is primary. For in the second case, the basis for the view remains unspecified.
Indeed, when "body" is used to refer to the pentad of aggregates, there is no exclusion of the supramundane.

For the word "body" (kāya) is certainly applicable even in the supramundane context; indeed, in such cases as "tranquillity of body" (kāyapassaddhi), the word "body" refers to the supramundane aggregates.
"By virtue" means by virtue that is not a cause for purification. "Accepted undertaking" (gahitasamādāna) refers precisely to the arising of a misconception;
for it is called "acceptance" (samādāna) because by means of it one accepts dog-like conduct and other such practices.
In this context, *sīla* (virtue) should be understood as that which is not to be transgressed, and *vata* (vow) as that which must be constantly practiced out of devotion.
"While staying right here" means while staying in this very Indasāla Cave. *Uggaha* (learning) is the act of committing [the words] to memory.
*Paripucchā* (inquiry) is the questioning of the meaning. *Vinicchaya* (decision) is the making of a determination by means of admonition and resolution together with those who are skilled.

The analysis [is as follows]: they are *puthujjana* because they have not destroyed (*avihatattā*) the many various types of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), or because they are produced by those [beliefs].
Alternatively, the word *jana* expresses the very state of being undestroyed. Regarding the phrase "those who look toward the faces of various teachers," the etymological meaning is:
"those for whom there are various people" are *puthujjana*. Regarding the phrase "various... not emerged," [the word *jana*] means "to be produced."
They are called *janā* because beings (*jana*) are born (*jāyanti*) therein; thus they are destinies (*gati*). Those who have various (*puthu*) births (*jana*) are *puthujjanā*.

Or, those from which further births arise are *janā*, namely volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth. Because these [formations] exist manifoldly (*puthu*) in them, they are *puthujjanā*. Alternatively, the word *jana* should be understood in the sense of volitional formation and so forth.
The "torments" (*santāpa*) are the fires of passion (*rāgaggi*) and so forth. Or, all defilements (*kilesa*) without exception are "fevers" (*pariḷāha*).

Regarding the phrase "among the various five strands of sensual pleasure" (*puthu pañcasu kāmaguṇesu*): here, one who is born is called a "person" (*jano*), such as [one characterized by] "lust, greed," and so forth.

Those for whom there is a diverse person are "worldlings" (*puthujjana*). Alternatively, those people who are born among the diverse [objects] and are attached—thus the word *jana* should be understood as having the meaning of lust and so forth.
"Obstructed" (*palibuddhā*) means bound or afflicted. By the term "unlearned" (*assutavā*), blindness is expressed; therefore he said, "the blind worldling is mentioned."
"Bring her"—this is *avaḍḍhi*. In all cases, the formation of words should be understood according to the characteristics of etymology (*nirutti*).

The Paccekabuddhas know what was done over many hundreds of thousands of eons and make it manifest; they perform assistance through the generation of mindfulness, the acceptance of material gifts, and so forth, and likewise they perform their duties with care for one who is suffering. [The same applies to] the Sammasambuddha.
Furthermore, he recognizes and makes manifest the assistance rendered even during incalculable and immeasurable eons, as well as the decisive support (upanissaya) for the paths and fruits;
and like a lion, he delivers the teaching of the Dhamma everywhere with full diligence and speed.

"The state of the Noble Ones" (ariyabhāva) refers to those qualities of the path and fruit through association with which one is called "Noble"; these are the states that make one noble. The factors that produce the state of a Noble One...

The "seeing of impermanence and so forth" refers to the contemplation of impermanence and the other characteristics; alternatively, it refers to impermanence and the rest as they are being clearly seen (*vipassiyamānā*).
"Streams" (*sotāni*) refers to the streams of craving, views, defilements, misconduct, and ignorance.

Having stated, "I declare the restraint of the streams," the subsequent statement, "by wisdom these are closed up," makes it known that the restraint of the streams is their closing up—that is, the knowledge of complete eradication (*samuccheda-ñāṇa*).

"Patience" (*khanti*) means endurance; it consists of the aggregates (*khandha*) that function in such a manner. Some say it is wisdom (*paññā*), or else it is simply non-hatred (*adosa*). "Of bodily misconduct, etc.

refers to the misconduct of body and speech known as immorality (*dussīlya*), to negligence known as forgetfulness (*muṭṭhassacca*), and to covetousness, dejection, evil, impatience, ignorance, and laziness.
"Non-equanimity" is the failure to turn away from conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*); it is a state of attachment.
The meaning is as follows: regarding the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhiti*), the "contrary state" refers to the grasping at eternalism or annihilationism, or the delusion that conceals it.
Regarding *nibbāna*, the "contrary state" refers to delight in the conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*), or the delusion that conceals *nibbāna*.
"Grasping at the sign of formations" refers to that defilement which, because it has not been abandoned, prevents insight from relinquishing the sign of formations.
It should be seen. The construction should be understood as follows:

"That which is abandonment by way of absolute non-occurrence due to the cultivation of the four noble paths, occurring through either the transcendence of or the relinquishing of the grasping after the signs of formations.
But by what means is there this abandonment? It is understood that it occurs precisely by means of the noble paths themselves, because of their cultivation.
By the expression "non-arising. Regarding the phrase "belonging to the side of origination" (*samudayapakkhika*):

here, since all four paths constitute the clear realization of the Four Truths, they are "belonging to the side of origination" because they are to be abandoned together with each respective origination that is to be abandoned by them, because they share the nature of origination, and because it is stated in the *Saccavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Truths) that all defilements have the state of being origination.
Views and so forth are what are spoken of. *Vinaya* means the leading away (*nayana*) or the removal (*apayāpana*) of the body, speech, and mind from their improper functioning;
or it is the leading away (*vināsanayana*) of bodily misconduct and so forth; or it is the leading away (*vinayana*) that consists in straightening them by severing their crooked functioning.

*Esesa* means "this is that very same thing," the sense being that it is not different in meaning. *Tajjāta* means "of that same nature" in terms of its essential meaning. *Sappurisa* (a true person).
The meaning is: the nature of the noble ones (ariya-sabhāva), and the state of being a noble, true person (sappurisa-bhāva).

"Non-dual" (advaya) means devoid of duality; it is like one who, having grasped the color itself as "the flame," perceives the oneness of those two as if seeing the flame as "only the color," or like one who, having conjectured a self as "form" according to their reasoning, or having seen form as "self" according to their view.
Having grasped these, one should see them as a unity.

And here, although there is no actual occurrence of the thought "form is self," the apprehension of a self in form proceeds just like the apprehension of color in a painting. Furthermore, the similes are stated solely to demonstrate the apprehension of non-otherness and so forth;
they do not intend to show that the self exists in the same way that color and so on exist, nor that color and so on are non-existent in the same way that the self is non-existent.
“Sarīranipphattiya” means by the completion of the body. “Vicikicchā” is so called because one who is unable to reach a decision and is searching [for it] suffers.
“The state of these conditions” (idappaccayatā) refers specifically to the intrinsic nature of birth and so forth, or to the capacity of birth and so forth to produce aging, death, and the rest.
Since that [capacity] does not exist apart from birth and the rest, it is a designation for those very things; thus it is called “conditionality” (paccayatā).
1009. Here, future defilements are called "defilements associated with that" (*tadekaṭṭhā kilesā*); in order to demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “And of this text...
is commenced. By way of being co-existent and associated with that (*sahajekaṭṭhavasena*), it is understood from the sense that [it refers] to the view arisen therein.
“Associated with those” (*taṃsampayutto*) is also logically understood to mean “associated with those fetters which are defilements.”
Or alternatively, it is called "arising from that" (*taṃsamuṭṭhāna*) because those fetters and defilements are its source.
Furthermore, since there is the presence of both associated and arisen states even among defilements that are themselves free from fetters, the connection is made specifically with the defilements.
(1011) "As in the case of the fetters, etc. means as in the case of the aforementioned fetters, the defilements that share a single function with them, and so forth. "By those" refers to...

By means of the paths of seeing and development. Having established that volitional consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*) is wholesome or unwholesome, while name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is resultant, he said:
"The abandoning of even the wholesome and so forth is permitted. 1013.
"And the causes" refers to the meaning of the compound word *pahātabbahetuka* by way of a partial expression of the compound.

It says this. And here, according to the former method, the restriction is understood as follows: "These states have roots to be abandoned by vision"—meaning these alone have roots to be abandoned by vision, and none other than these—rather than [the restriction] that "these alone have roots to be abandoned by vision.
Therefore, the state of having roots to be abandoned by vision for these [states] is not fixed, because delusion accompanied by doubt is rootless (*ahetuka*).

The first method explains the meaning by way of exposition. Therefore, having set aside those [states] to be abandoned by vision through the Dhamma according to the first method, the second method is stated in order to set them aside according to their meaning. 1029.

Or, the supernormal powers and so forth are "lofty" (mahaggata). Those associated with the knowledge of others' minds, the recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the future are "lofty" because they have immeasurable objects.
1035. *Ānantarika* (immediate) refers to those [deeds] which are connected with the immediate [state], whose purpose is the immediate fruit, or whose nature it is to produce the immediate fruit.
Furthermore, because their fruit cannot be obstructed by opposing factors, they are free from obstacles;
thus it is said, "they yield fruit without obstacle. Alternatively, the word formation is established through etymology as *anantarāyāni* (without obstacle) being *ānantarikāni*.
They are to be understood. By the word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "even in one," it is shown that there is no such thing as [an obstruction] even when many [defilements] are accumulated.

Furthermore, these [defilements] do not possess mutual obstructiveness because they lack opposition; and their lack of opposition is due to their having the same fruit and because they provide mutual support.
[For example, the view] beginning with: "There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings."

The doctrine of causelessness (*ahetukavāda*). The doctrine of non-action (*akiriyavāda*) consists of such statements as: “For one who acts or causes to act, who cuts or causes to cut... [and so forth]... for one who acts, no evil is committed.
The doctrine of nihilism (*natthikavāda*) consists of such statements as: “There is no gift,” and so forth.
Among these, the first doctrine denies the cause of bondage and liberation; the second, action (*kamma*); and the third, its result (*vipāka*). This is their distinction.
"Taṃ hi" (that indeed) refers to the rootless, etc., fixed wrong view, but not that which has not yet reached the state of being fixed.
"In the sense of a condition" should be understood as the state of being a condition distinguished by association, namely, what is termed the path-condition.
And here, the exclusion of the path-factors is intended to show the path-rooted [consciousness] which is devoid of the state of being a path-condition.
Therefore, he defines [the factors] as being rooted in the path without confusion. However, if someone were to say:

"Even though each individual factor is associated with those [mental states] that are rooted in the path, this expression 'excluding the path-factors' is still appropriate," then—just as in the third method—it would not be necessary to say "excluding" here either; yet it has been so stated. Therefore...
The meaning should be understood according to the method already stated. For this method is intended to show the distinction between those path-factors that are associated and those that are not.
The intention is that the remaining path-factors have been set aside previously. For it was established in the preceding method that contact and the other factors also have the Path as their cause.
When right view has been established in the second method, the state of being accompanied by roots (sahetuka-bhāva) is shown in the third method. How is it shown?

For one possessing the Noble Path, instead of saying, "Non-greed and non-hatred—these states are the causes of the path," it separately shows non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion as the causes of the path, stating: "These states—non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—are the causes of the path; that which is associated with them... [and so on].

Because the consciousness aggregate (*viññāṇakkhandha*) is shown separately among those things having the Path as their cause, would it not follow that the state of having the Path as its cause is not shown for Right View (*sammādiṭṭhi*), which was stated as "non-delusion (*amoha*) among those having the Path as their cause"? No, it is not not shown.
For just as, after showing the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), [the text] states separately: "Greed, hatred, and delusion associated with them—these factors have causes to be abandoned by seeing."
Having determined the causes to be abandoned by the statement, "And the defilements associated with them," it is shown that greed,
hatred, and delusion— being mutually co-nascent, mutually associated, and constituting the aggregate of formations— are causes to be abandoned by vision; likewise here,

although it is concluded that "these states, beginning with non-greed, are the causes of the Path," they are [included] because they constitute the aggregate of formations that are mutually associated.
It is established that by the expression "the aggregate of volitional formations associated with that [path]," it is shown that they are "rooted in the path";
likewise, for right view, which is also called non-delusion, there is the demonstration of its state of being rooted in the path.

However, if one were to say that in the second method the path is both the path and the root, then the state of being rooted in the path would have to be expressed by a different, unique way of speaking for something other than that.
Having shown that, the third method may be intended for the purpose of demonstrating that right view possesses the state of being caused by the Path through its association with those [factors].
One might say: "In one possessing the Noble Path, non-greed and non-hatred—these states are causes of the Path," and so forth.
However, since the status of being a cause of the Path is possible for those factors by means of this other common synonym, namely "causes of the Path" (*maggahetu*), [the third method is employed].
Having shown that all these are "path-roots" (*maggahetu*), the third method is intended to demonstrate that those associated with them, as well as others, possess the state of being path-rooted;
therefore, "non-delusion" (*amoha*) is also mentioned therein, for it is not the case that it is not a path-root.

Furthermore, since these three methods are set forth according to specific distinctions of meaning, they should be understood as "formal presentations by way of meaning" (*atthato nikkhepā*). Alternatively, [they may be understood] by their own nature (*sarūpena*).
The phrase "from the Dhamma" refers to the laying down [of the factors], and "by way of the meaning, the meaning"—thus this construction is also possible.
In that regard, the second and third methods constitute the laying down from the Dhamma by way of showing the cause and the possessor of the cause according to their own form.

The first method, however, is the laying down by way of the meaning, because it does not show them in that way [as cause and effect] and because it leads to the understanding of the state of cause and possessor of the cause among those factors associated with the path-limbs.

1040. When the mind proceeds toward a state of being inclined, leaning, and tending toward a particular intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*), that [nature] should be understood as its objective predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*).
One who reviews after having known by means of the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*) is called "one reviewing by means of that.

"In this case too" refers either to this very statement in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) or to this section in the *Paṭṭhāna*, where, setting aside the Path and so forth, [the relationship] of others...
By the very fact that the state of being a predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*) was not mentioned in the text of the refutation, this is the meaning: "having set aside one's own path and fruit.
In the phrase "predominance of investigation" (*vīmaṃsādhipateyya*), concomitant predominance (*sahajātādhipati*) is indicated by way of the primary predominance;
this is merely an illustration of the method, and thus other similar types of concomitant path-predominance are also indicated.
Therefore, it should also be connected as "having energy as its predominant factor. For this too has indeed been stated in terms of its meaning.

1041. One's own nature is one's personal identity (*attabhāva*). The result of karma that has gained an opportunity arises after the passing of a thousand eons for beings with a lifespan of many thousands of eons;
or else, having gained an opportunity even after the passing of a thousand eons—
"Whatever will come to be, that too has already found its opportunity"—this is said with reference to one's own kamma-result (vipāka).

"There is no such thing as 'not being'" means the intention is that there is nothing called "un-arisen. Since they are included among those things subject to arising, it is said by the phrase "phenomena subject to arising" (uppādino dhammā);
thus he says, "Phenomena subject to arising are called 'born' (jāta). "Self" (attā) is defined as the formless (arūpa).

He spoke of the formless life-continuum (*arūpabhavaṅga*). For in that context, the conventional expression "self" occurs in the sense of being composed of the perception of the base of infinite space and so forth. But if, as you say, [the life-span]...
[etc. ...were to give all its result (*vipāka*), then—on the grounds that it gives a result even when no opportunity has been obtained—it would also have to give a result that has already matured.
Consequently, there would have to be the result of only a single karma, and thus no room for any other karma.
It would not exist because it would be purposeless; there would be no occasion for its arising, or for the yielding of fruit once arisen.

Alternatively, if it were to yield its result without having gained an opportunity—even when devoid of other conditions—it would follow that it yields its result even in the absence of other conditions such as ignorance and craving.

Thus, there would be no room for another karma leading to diminution (*apacayagāmika-kamma*) which dispels other conditions like ignorance and craving, and which brings about the exhaustion of karma. This would remain true even if the Path (*magga*) had been developed.
The meaning is that there would be no capacity for karma to ripen if it were devoid of other conditions such as ignorance (*avijjā*).
Alternatively, because there would always have to be the occurrence of a result (*vipāka*), there would be no opportunity for the occurrence of anything other than a result.

"That, however" refers to the accumulated karma. This, moreover, [is said] regarding both that which has a fixed result and that which has an unfixed result, provided it has obtained an opportunity through the result of the former.
It should be understood that [the text] has begun in order to show that "it produces a result" (vipākam uppādeti).

The eight attainments (samāpatti) are called "certain results" (dhuvavipāka) because they invariably ripen as a result, since their intrinsic nature (sabhāva) has not been abandoned due to the absence of powerful [counteractive factors] and the absence of the cultivation of the supreme path (aggamagga).
When "accumulated karma" (āyūhitakamma) is being discussed, why is "unarisen" (anuppanna) mentioned? Because whatever will be accumulated, that too [is included therein].
Because of the existence of the occurrence of sound produced by effort.
1050. Regarding the term *upādinnā*: here the meaning is not "taken by one who has approached" (*upetena ādinnā*); rather, the prefix *upa-* is merely a prepositional adjunct (*upasagga*).
Therefore, [it means] having grasping as its object, or by means of graspings; and others [say it is] without misinterpretation: "I cultivated the path, my..."

They are called "clung-to" (upādinnā) precisely because they have been taken up by such grasping as "the path has arisen," and so forth. Alternatively, it should be understood that by the term *upādinnā* (clung-to), only those phenomena that are not the path or its fruits are expressed, while by the other terms [such as *anupādinnā*], the path and fruit phenomena are meant.
The commentary on the exposition of the triads is concluded.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Tenfold Setting Forth (Dukanikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā) 1062. "By way of loving-kindness" (*mettāyana-vasena*) means by way of the pervasion of loving-kindness (*mettā-pharaṇa*).

It should be understood that although it ought to be said "by way of loving-kindness" (*mettāyana-vasena*), it is stated with a long vowel. Loving-kindness (*mettā*) or the act of being kind (*medana*) is "loving-kindness-making" (*mettāyana*); and that occurs by way of affection (*sineha*). "It sympathizes" (*anudayati*)...

Where "anudātā" should have been said, it is stated as "anuddā" by the addition of the letter *da*. "Anuddāyanākāra" means the mode of protecting (*anurakkhaṇākāra*), for protection is indeed *dāyanā*.
"Anuddāyitassa" means of one who has protected. For one who hears [the teaching] such as "Birth, too, is suffering," there is hearing;
for one who comprehends it through impermanence and so forth, there is comprehension; and for one who destroys delusion regarding this by means of the Path, [there is penetration].
Knowledge regarding suffering operates at four times: at the time of penetration, at the time of reviewing after having penetrated, and so forth.
1065. *Cittassa saṃrañjanaṃ* is the mind’s delight; *cittassa sārāgo* is the mind’s passion. They “devour” (*gijjhanti*) means they long for. They “cling” (*sañjanti*) means they bind.
“In the sense of clinging” (*lagganaṭṭhena*) means in the sense of enveloping, or in the sense of hanging on. “To that very becoming” (*tassa tasseva bhavassa*)...

It draws along [the kamma-formations] by way of being the condition for rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) for the purpose of producing resultant and kamma-produced matter (vipākakaṭattārūpa) reckoned as the existence of sense-sphere desire (kāmabhava) and so forth.
His consciousness runs on and is reborn in another becoming.
The "abiding in the agitation of craving" is simply the occurrence of craving itself, in the form of the eighty-nine types of mental wandering through craving (taṇhāvicarita) and so forth.
“Moist” (*saritāni*) means moistened by way of lust (*rāga*). “Lubricated” (*siniddhāni*) means made slippery by way of the joy (*pīti*) associated with that [lust].
“Spread out” (*visatā*) means expanded. It is “diffused” (*visaṭā*) by way of pervading the phenomena of the three planes, such as visible forms and so forth.

This is stated by changing the *ta*-sound of the previous word into a *ṭa*-sound. “Vast” (*visālā*) means extensive. “It penetrates” (*visakkati*) means it creeps along or it endures. One who is lustful...
For even when struck by a foot that serves as a basis for passion, one endures it. They say that "osakkana" (retreating), "vipphandana" (quivering), or "visakkanā" (counteracting) [refer to this].
It is deceptive because it grasps the impermanent and so forth as permanent and so forth.
"Visaṃharati" means that by seeing the advantages in sensual pleasures in various ways, one withdraws the mind from its engagement directed toward renunciation through those various modes.
It contracts. Or, "poison" (*visa*) refers to suffering; the meaning is that it carries or bears that [suffering].
It is "rooted in poison" (*visamūlā*) because it is the cause of the karma that produces suffering; or, it is "rooted in poison" because poison—namely, suffering—is its root.

It is "fructifying as poison" (*visaphalā*) because its fruit is poison—namely, suffering—due to being the origin of suffering. Through craving, there is only the enjoyment of suffering, such as form and so forth.
"Not from the deathless" means that it is called "the consumption of poison. In all instances, the derivation of the words should be understood according to their etymological analysis (*nirukti*).

However, in order to show the primary meaning herein, it is further stated: "Or else, by its poisonous nature," and so forth. "This state and another state" refers to the states consisting of human existence, divine existence, and so on.
“By way of aspiration” means by way of fixing the mind upon form and so forth. Other relatives are indeed bound by craving alone, yet they are not [always] bound;
craving, however, is constantly present, and thus it is called a “separate relative.
“From eating” means from pervading and from consuming. He shows both of these by the phrase “from overwhelming,” and so on. “By way of longing” means...
"By way of wishing": in the manner of seeing no difference between the act of wishing and that which has been wished for.
"The mind is obsessed" means the mind is stolen away. "A snare of Māra" means lust is a snare of Māra because it is seized by Māra.
(1066) "Arising with respect to formations, it does not constitute a breach of the path of action"—by this, he shows that anger arising with respect to sentient beings is an improper occasion.
It is understood that it "does. For even when anger arises with the thought: "He has not acted for my benefit, he does not act for my benefit, he will not act for my benefit;
he has not acted for the benefit of one dear and pleasing to me, he does not act for his benefit, he will not act for his benefit;

he has not acted for the harm of one not dear or pleasing to me, he does not act for his harm, he will not act for his harm"—this anger is called "groundless anger" because it has arisen without a [valid] basis.
It is appropriate for it to be thus. "Harboring ill-will" (*āghātento*) means killing.
It is stated that the fault of tautology (*punarutta-dosa*) is avoided because the words *dosa* (fault/ill-will) and *paṭivirodha* (opposition) have each occurred twice.

Alternatively, "opposition" (*paṭivirodho*) was stated previously for the purpose of qualifying resentment (*paṭigha*), while "fault" (*doso*) was stated for the purpose of qualifying malice (*padosa*) and so forth, and [the latter] for the purpose of qualifying the act of hating (*dussanā*) and so forth.
Later, because it is stated as "defect" (*dosa*) and as "contrariety" (*paṭivirodha*) for the purpose of specifying a particular kind of opposition, there is no fault of tautology.
In the summary list (*mātikuddesa*), which indicates the mere existence of phenomena whose specific limits are not determined, the summary is made using the plural number without a specific limit;
therefore, he asks using the plural itself: "Which phenomena are without conditions? (*katame dhammā appaccayā*).
For the enumeration and the questioning are carried out with reference to one who does not know the phenomena by way of their intrinsic nature, their classification, and so forth.
Therefore, they were enumerated and questioned without having been previously classified.

The plural number was used for the conclusion—even after pointing out that single [unconditioned element]—in order to demonstrate that there is nothing beyond this unconditioned element; thus, the conclusion was made in the plural before the detailed exposition.
This refers to the period beginning from when [the Buddha] first understood those capable of being enlightened.
1101. However, one should construe the passage as: "What is there that does not exist? What has he not spoken?

This very absence of restriction—that is, the absence of a fixed definition—is expressed by the phrase "this alone is cognizable by the mind. In the Canon, it is stated that what is cognizable by eye-consciousness and so forth is precisely what is cognizable by the eye and so forth.
Regarding the statement "is said," since it must be understood that what is cognizable by mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) is indeed cognizable by the mind, the commentary states:

"But by what [is it cognized]? and so forth. As for the phrase "cognizable by some and not cognizable by others," this should be applied by distinguishing the sense-sphere mind-consciousness (*kāmāvacara-manoviññāṇa*) according to its objects and other factors; for, by means of a sense-sphere mind-consciousness having fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and other objects, [the latter are not cognizable].
Furthermore, sense-sphere phenomena are not cognizable by consciousness associated with lust for form and so forth, but they are cognizable by the other [types of consciousness].

In this way, the non-cognizability and cognizability of certain sense-sphere objects—such as sounds and others—by means of visible-form objects and so forth should be applied accordingly, as well as according to the distinction of the doors [of sense].
Alternatively, investigation accompanied by joy takes only a desirable object.

The other [object] cannot be cognized by that [consciousness]. Thus, in all cases—whether they be wholesome resultant states accompanied by equanimity or unwholesome resultant states—the appropriate application should be made accordingly.
It should be understood that the fine-material-sphere states and so forth cannot be cognized by sense-sphere resultants and the like;
however, some of them can be cognized by immaterial-sphere states, as this follows from the context. Because they cannot be cognized by Nibbāna, it is said: "they cannot be cognized by some."
This was said with reference merely to the possible occurrence of that term’s meaning, not because Nibbāna is a state of mental consciousness that follows after [the senses].

(1102) "Lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure" is stated by way of the most prominent [type of lust]. It would be appropriate to say that, setting aside the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), all greed is the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*).
Lust accompanied by the view of eternalism is called the "taint of existence" because it is associated with the view of existence (*bhavaditthi*).
This is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. However, as for the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), it is stated in the *Pāḷi* that "it arises only in those dissociated from views.

That lust (*rāga*) is also fit to be the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*). Furthermore, the taints of sensual desire and the rest, which serve as the causes for suffering pertaining to the present life and the future life, are also stated to be twofold.

1103. Furthermore, in the exposition of the "outflow of sensual desires" (*kāmāsava*), the phrase "in sensual desires" (*kāmesu*) can be understood to mean "in the sensual objects (*vatthukāma*) belonging to the three planes of existence, which serve as the objective bases for sensual lust, lust for views, and so forth.
For even though that craving (*taṇhā*) arises therein, it does not receive the name of "sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) and the rest.
While the desire characterized by the wish to act (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) arises even in regard to the unwholesome, the desire for the Dhamma (*dhammacchanda*) does not.

1105. Another [view] grasps the soul (*jīva*) even though it functions only within the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*); yet, it does not settle upon form (*rūpa*), nor... nor upon consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
By treating it as something other than those, one grasps the soul; thus, there is the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).

For one who grasps a certain self, such as Brahmā and so forth, as "it exists" in terms of permanence, and another as "it does not exist" in terms of impermanence, [the view arises]: "It both exists..."

“Nor does it exist” is the view of partial eternalism (*ekaccasassatadiṭṭhi*). When asked “Does it exist? he says “Neither,” and when asked “Does it not exist? he says “No,” thus rejecting everything;

this is the view of endless equivocation (*amarāvikkhepadiṭṭhi*). The meaning is that it is an “endless” (*amara*) view because it is uninterrupted, or it is a view of equivocation resembling a “deathless fish” (*amaramaccha*).

Since it is stated that lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇika-rāga*) is the "outflow of sensuality" (*kāmāsava*), one rejects the status of the outflow of sensuality for the lust found among Brahmās in their celestial palaces (*vimāna*) and so forth,
as well as for the lust of views (*diṭṭhirāga*). However, if there exists greed (*lobha*) distinct from both the outflow of sensuality and the outflow of existence (*bhavāsava*),
then when it arises in states dissociated from wrong views (*diṭṭhigata-vippayutta*), the outflow of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) associated with it is said to be "dissociated from the outflows."
Just as in the case of [states] associated with displeasure, doubt, or restlessness, it should also be stated that this [delusion] is dissociated from the taints (*āsava*):
"In the four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by greed but dissociated from views, the delusion that arises may be associated with the taints, or it may be dissociated from the taints.
[And it is said: "The taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) arises in eight types of consciousness-arising accompanied by greed."

Because of the statement, "Dependent on the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) arise the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava)," it cannot be said that lust accompanied by views is not the taint of sensual desire.
Furthermore, since it is appropriate to bring them up even according to the sequence of the defilements (kilesa), the mention of the taints is made for the purpose of showing what is to be abandoned;
thus, when they are brought forward in relation to their abandonment, those defilements which are themselves to be abandoned are also included.
The meaning is that it is appropriate to bring forward even the paths for those who abandon [defilements] according to the order of enumeration. 1121.
Regarding the "first analysis of conceit" (*paṭhamakamānabhājanīya*), this refers to the exposition of the conceit "I am superior" (*seyyohamasmi*). For therein it says:
"A certain person, on account of birth, or clan, or lineage, or beauty of complexion, or wealth, or Vedic learning..."
"Whether by means of a field of work, a craft, a branch of knowledge, learning, ingenuity, or some other basis, one generates conceit;

such conceit, such imagining... [as before] ...such desire for a banner of the mind"—this explains the meaning of "conceit of superiority" as it occurs toward those who are superior, equal, or inferior, without specifically referring to a particular individual.
Having intended this, he said: "It is stated that 'one conceit arises in three types of persons.
This should be understood as an illustration showing that this was not stated only in the first *mānabhājaniya*, but was stated likewise in the second and third *mānabhājaniyas* as well.
Alternatively, the term "in the first *mānabhājaniya*" refers to the classification of all three conceits spoken of without depending on specific individuals.
He said: For the "second distribution of conceits" refers to the nine conceits—beginning with "the conceit 'I am superior'"—which are spoken of by referring to a person as their locus;
whereas the "third" [distribution] refers to the mass of conceits spoken of without referring to a person as their locus.
Furthermore, in the aforementioned second distribution of conceits, for each one...
The phrase "it is said that three types of conceit arise for each" is stated here in order to show the similarity with the commentary on the meaning given there;
thus, the expression "in the first *mānabhājanīya*" is used. The intention is that since that same conceit has come down here, the meaning explained there is appropriate here as well.
"By way of producing conceit" means by way of performing the functions [of conceit] such as "I am superior," and so forth. "Successively" (aparāpare).

"Dependent upon" (*upādāya*) is said with reference to this meaning: that the successive [states of] conceit arise, reaching upward by way of being the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for each preceding one.
It is specified as "by the mind" (*citte-na*) because the mind characterized by the desire for leadership (*ketukamyatā*) attains a state of loftiness.

(1126) "Slandering" (*khiyyana*) is the manifestation of an intolerant disposition. "Honoring" (*mānana*) means worship of such a kind as "acting kindly toward others through the mind. "By way of acting out of envy" means by way of the function of being unable to endure gains and so forth.

1127. The phrase "noble disciples" (*ariyasāvaka*) is intended to show the absence of stinginess regarding the dhamma of realization, [implying]: "The noble disciples alone possess realization, and they do not withhold it [out of stinginess].
"Text" (*gantha*) refers to the Pāḷi; "discourse-path" (*kathāmaga*) refers to the composition of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).

"Another dhamma" (*dhammantara*) refers to [the act of] dividing wholesome and other dhammas [from one another] and, out of one's own greed, [claiming] that which was spoken by the Tathāgata [to be something else], such as unwholesome dhammas and so forth.
"Or, while speaking the words of a non-Buddhist (titthiya), he will reveal himself. "Having revealed himself" means having proclaimed oneself to be otherwise than one actually is.
"But whoever" refers to a non-Buddhist or a householder who, unwilling to see the flawed nature of his own doctrine, acts out of ignorance or dogmatic adherence.
"One who does not wish to share" is *veviccho*; the state of such a person is *vevicchaṃ*. "Lacking respect" means being devoid of respect for giving due to stinginess (*macchariya*).
"Taking with a ladle" refers to taking food with a ladle; it is called "taking with a ladle" because it is like taking with a ladle.
For just as taking with a ladle does not allow one to share the aforementioned food, so too does stinginess [prevent sharing] regarding dwellings and other things.

Or, "that by which one grasps" is *gāha*; a ladle itself is a grasp, thus it is a "ladle-grasp. Just as a ladle with its handle bent does not pour out [the contents], so too is stinginess (*macchariya*).
That which is grasped by being withheld is "not given," and the state of that is "non-giving-ness," which is stinginess. It functions by way of the thought:
"Let my dwelling place and so forth be mine alone, whether shared with others or not."
The characteristic of grasping for one’s own excellence should be connected with the characteristic of concealing one’s own excellence by way of acting [with the thought], “May it not go to another.

As for what was said, “desiring to take what belongs to another,” that should be understood as stated to show the state of being a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for stinginess, which is greed for the property of others.
For if that were merely a demonstration of the occurrence of stinginess, [it would not serve to distinguish it from other forms of greed].
And it might be said that it has the characteristic of grasping the prosperity of others.

(1140) One should investigate the existence of greed as a "not-outflow" (*noāsava*), considering the distinction between covetousness and sensual lust—namely, that they may function as two outflows or as a single outflow, yet covetousness itself does not possess the status of being a non-outflow. For there are no phenomena that are both an outflow and a non-outflow.
“An outflowing state is a condition, by way of root-condition, for an outflowing state and for a non-outflowing state”—this is the seventh and ninth question.

And in the enumeration, it is stated as “seven in the case of root,” not “nine. However, if greed associated with wrong view were present as a non-outflowing [state], then the answers to the seventh and ninth questions would also be applicable, and the enumeration [would likewise differ].

“It may be said that there are nine [factors] by way of cause. This is because, while greed dissociated from views (*diṭṭhivippayutta*) is a non-outflow (*noāsava*), the fault already shown previously applies.

1159. In the exposition of the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchandanīvaraṇa*): “In sensual pleasures” (*kāmesu*) means in all objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) belonging to the three planes and associated with outflows (*sāsava*).
For all greed is the hindrance of sensual desire. For this very reason, its arising in the formless realm (*ārūpa*) was stated: “The hindrance...”
Dependent on a state, a hindrance-state arises, but not by way of the pre-existence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*).

In the formless realm, dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire, there arise the hindrances of restlessness and ignorance. In the formless realm, dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire, there arise the hindrances of sloth-and-torpor, restlessness, and ignorance.
1162. *Iriyāpathika-citta* (posture-consciousness) refers to the forty-eight types of consciousness that support the bodily postures.
Among these, the consciousness accompanied by strong stiffness and torpor is described as "unable to maintain the posture. *Olīyati* means it hangs down or slackens. 1163.
*Onayhati* means it covers or overspreads; this occurs by way of preventing the movement [of the mind] toward various objects and by way of preventing its expansion.
Or, it is the confinement within. "Of some" refers to trees such as the *sirīsa* and others. They might exist by means of the material body (*rūpakāya*) alone;
the intention is that, by that [means], there would be the attainment of the state of form for the experience of pleasure and the realization of Nibbāna.

Therefore, because the expression "of the body" establishes its nature as form. For the statement "the mental body does not sleep well" refers to the material body having reached a state of heaviness due to forms originated by sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*).
The "sinking" of the limbs and so forth is stated with reference to falling asleep, not to the continuity of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) devoid of a conscious state of wakefulness.
"Because it is its fruit" means that, by way of metaphorical designation (*phalūpacāra*), sleep is shown to be like a faculty;
thus, just as in the description of the faculties, the gender and so forth are mentioned, so too in the description of torpor (*middha*), "sleeping" and so on are mentioned—this is the meaning.
Since there is no contraction within the material body (rūpakāya), it is understood that [contraction] is spoken of in relation to the mental body (nāmakāya).
The "enveloping" (onāha) and "surrounding" (pariyonāha) are also mentioned in connection with that. Furthermore, the material body has no state of being expanded or unexpanded by its own nature;
rather, in the case of the mental body, when the mental body is expanded, it is light, and when it is unexpanded, it is heavy—thus, by way of its unexpanded state.

Since the state of enveloping and so forth belongs only to the group of mental factors (*nāmakāya*), enveloping and the rest are understood as belonging to the group of mental factors. Therefore he said: “For form is not the enveloping of the group of mental factors...

[etc]... it does not exist. For just as the state of being an obstruction belongs only to the group of mental factors, so too the state of enveloping and the rest belongs only to the group of mental factors.
The other [person], not understanding this intention and seeing the enveloping and so forth of forms by means of forms such as clouds and the like, asks: “Is it not...”

And so he said, beginning with the words “cā” and so forth. If it were thus—if the quality of obstructing matter were established, while it were not so for the immaterial—then since obstruction is seen in the case of matter, such as in the building of dams and the like, it would follow that there could be no obstruction of the immaterial either.

It is appropriate that intoxicating liquor and fermented spirits constitute a defilement, given that they are unwholesome; [this applies] to the addiction to intoxicating liquor... and to the pursuit of occasions for negligence.

And although it is logical that [the use of liquor] weakens wisdom because it is unwholesome, nevertheless, having acknowledged the other’s intention, he said, "No, because it is a description of conditions," showing that the state of being a defilement and the state of weakening wisdom regarding *surā* and *meraya* are spoken of by way of the result (*phalavohāra*), since they are the conditions for both defilements and for the weakening of wisdom. "In this very same way... [he said].

Just as gold—when defiled by the five impurities such as iron, copper, tin, and lead—is neither soft, nor workable, nor radiant, but is brittle and does not properly fit for its intended use; even so [is it with the mind].
"By way of the exposition of conditions" means by way of the exposition of the state of being a condition for the defilements and for the weakening of wisdom.

The meaning is: "because of the description of the fruit in relation to the condition. The intention is that the defilement itself has already been described in the descriptions of the secondary defilements (*upakkilesa*).

When it is shown as associated with an obstruction (*nīvaraṇa-sampayutta*) precisely because it is an obstruction, this undertaking is not for the purpose of demonstrating its state of being an obstruction;

rather, it is for the purpose of demonstrating its association with obstructions in those cases where its status as an obstruction is already established, according to the principle of "as far as obtainable" (*yathālābha-vasena*).
Furthermore, the statement that [the hindrance] is dissociated is not tenable.

For just as the two [states]—standing and walking—are mentioned in relation to oysters, shells, and so forth according to their availability, there is no such statement regarding the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor (thīnamiddhanīvaraṇa) saying it is "associated or dissociated," which would allow for such a possibility according to its occurrence. This is because it is stated that [the hindrance] cannot arise from the mind.
The meaning of the statement beginning with “because it has been abandoned” (*cattattā*) is that, at the moment of jhāna, mental sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) cannot possibly exist;
or alternatively, the meaning is that by the statement beginning with “because it has been abandoned,” the impossibility [of their presence] is expressed and made manifest.
By the passage “But as for sensual desires... well-seen,” he speaks of the abandoning of ignorance regarding the danger of sensual desires and so forth. That [ignorance] therein—
"Abandoning" (*pahāna*): regarding that [state] as "abandoning" with respect to form (*rūpa*), it is called "that" (*taṃ*) by way of referring to the act of abandoning;
or, the meaning is "the removal of that. By this, he demonstrates precisely that form is not to be abandoned.

However, no other mode is stated here than that found in such passages as "having abandoned six things," where the non-abandonment of torpor (*middha*) is shown. It is not as... [as stated]—thus, "six things" (*cha dhammā*).

The meaning is this: while the five hindrances (*pañca nīvaraṇāni*) are described as "to be abandoned" (*pahātabba*) precisely because they are things that must be abandoned, form (*rūpa*) is not described as "to be abandoned" simply because it is something that must be abandoned.
And with the phrase "and by other suttas," he says "for thus... and so forth in order to show those suttas that were mentioned. [He speaks of] the occurrence of the wholesome (*kusalappavatti*).

They obstruct, thus they are obstructions (*āvaraṇa*). They shut off, thus they are hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). They overwhelm and ascend upon the mind, thus they are mental obsessions (*cetaso ajjhāruha*).
The functions of obstructing and so forth are appropriate only for the formless; likewise is the function of causing blindness and so forth.

In this regard, among the four terms, each subsequent one has the meaning of the preceding one. The suffering of saṃsāra is affliction; because it produces that [affliction], it belongs to the side of affliction (*vighātapakkhika*).
The obsession of the mind arises from improper attention and constitutes a mass of unwholesomeness; since this occurs only in the formless (arūpa) state, torpor itself is formless. 1166.
Someone may feel remorse after eating an improper meal, such as a meal in a group, thinking it was proper but later realizing it was not;
and someone else may feel remorse after performing blameless acts, such as visiting monks or worshipping a shrine, thinking they were blameworthy when they were not.
One who lacks faith becomes remorseful. "Basis" (*vatthu*) means the root. "Of such a kind" (*evarūpa*) means of such a sort by way of that root; this is the meaning.

Regarding the term "state of remorse" (*kukkuccapada*), its meaning is exactly as stated among the *yevāpanaka* (miscellaneous) terms: "that which is done badly is *kukata*; the state of that is [remorse].
The "mode of being remorseful" (*kukkuccāyanākāra*) refers to the mode of producing remorse, the mode of performing remorse, or the mode of going toward remorse.
By this, remorse (*kukkucca*) is shown by way of its functional nature. Vinaya-remorse is simply the arising of a mental state that occurs as, "Is it allowable? Is it not allowable?
It should be understood that restlessness (*uddhacca*) and remorse are mentioned together because they share the common function of agitating the mind.

It should be understood that the abandonment of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) by means of the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmi-magga*) is stated here according to the most extreme case of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
For if greed were not an hindrance, then it would have been stated that "a state which is not an hindrance is a condition for a state that is an hindrance by way of the root-condition," and so forth;
yet this was not stated. Furthermore, in the enumeration, it is said "four in the case of the root-condition," not "nine.
Therefore, it is logical that all greed is the hindrance of sensual desire, and its abandonment by the path of Arahantship is appropriately described.
1219. "And desire" refers to both the defilement of desire (*kilesakāma*) and [the desire for views].
"A later view takes up an earlier view" means that one grasps the earlier view as "eternal" and thus takes it up;
or rather, a later view arising in the very same manner as the earlier view strengthens that earlier view and is said to take it up. "The cow-vows, ox-vows, and so forth" refers to such [practices].
He spoke of views. "From adherence" means from the state of adhering, or from the act of adhering.
"Merely a doctrine of self" means that because of the non-existence of a self, this is merely a verbal expression, namely "self. "They cling" means they grasp firmly. How? As "self.
For the meaning is that those who adhere [to it] as "self" grasp the mere expression with firmness. Thus, it is merely a doctrine of self.
It is said, "they cling. Or, by the phrase "mere doctrine of self," he refers to the mere basis for speech.
For they cling to the mere basis for speech as "self," because the actual object does not exist.
(1221) "Given" refers to a gift; since that has no fruit, he rejects it, saying that what is called a "gift" is not truly a gift, just like [the concept of] form.
A great sacrifice (*mahāyāga*) is a sacrifice similar to the Mahāvijita sacrifice. Invoking by calling out is *āhuna*, which is giving.
The act of hospitality toward guests (*pāhuna*) is *pāhuna*. Giving for the sake of auspiciousness during marriages and other ceremonies is an auspicious rite (*maṅgalakiriyā*).
Because one standing in the next world perceives this world as "non-existent," the next world is so called; and because it looks beyond (*paraṃ avekkhitvā*), it is [the next world].

The meaning should be understood as follows: because this world is not to be gone to nor come from—since there is no coming here from the other world and one is simply annihilated right there—one who stands in the other world with their mind grasps this world as "non-existent.
For this view does not belong only to one who has been reborn in the other world. In the phrase "standing in this world," the same [explanation] applies here as well.
This is the method. Or rather, this is the meaning here: "There is no such thing as a 'place of wandering' called this world or the other world, because there is no actual wandering;
for [beings] are simply cut off right there, in each respective place. *Upapāta* is the falling into a subsequent existence from a previous existence;
those whose nature (*sīla*) is this are *opapātika*. Furthermore, they are those who are about to pass away and those who are about to be reborn.

Having said this, he stated: "One grasps [the view] that there are no beings who pass away or are reborn. "The practice in conformity" (*anulomappaṭipadā*) refers to the practice of virtue and so forth that is conducive to *nibbāna*.

By the phrase "grasped without exception," it is indicated that—unlike in the group of defilements (*āsava-gocchaka*) where passion for Brahmās and the wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*) and so forth is not included, nor in the group of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa-gocchaka*) where sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is not [fully eliminated] by the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*)—[here all such passions are included].
By the statement "through the vision of what is to be abandoned," its limited scope was stated; that [limitation] is now excluded.
By the expression "by the path of Arahantship," it should be understood that abandonability by all four paths is intended.
For it is not the case that delusion and the rest, which were not attenuated by the preceding paths, are abandoned by the path of Arahantship alone.

1287. *Nirati-atthena* means by way of being devoid of joy (*pīti*), or by way of being devoid of strong attachment (*nikanti*). For they do not take delight in painful feeling (*dukkhā vedanā*). By the prefix *ava-*, two meanings of the word *ava* are stated:

the sense of plunging into (*avagāha*) and the sense of downward (*adho*). 1301. That which is accompanied by doubt (*vicikicchā*) has conflict (*raṇa*) due to delusion (*moha*); it has conflict through association with greed (*rāga*) connected to views (*diṭṭhi*) in the sense of being something to be abandoned.

That which is accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca*) [has conflict] through what is termed greed for the fine-material realm (*rūpa-rāga*) and greed for the immaterial realm (*arūpa-rāga*). However, in the *Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta*, it says: "That which is pleasant due to the linking of sensual desires..."
Because of such statements as, "The pursuit of pleasure is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial;

this state is accompanied by suffering, harmful, distressing, and feverish, and is a wrong practice. Therefore, this state is 'fraught with peril' (saraṇo)," it is precisely the state of being a wrong practice—which consists in the nature of suffering, harm, distress, and fever that result from its fruit—that is called "fraught with peril."
"It is known" means that by these [two], the fact that all unwholesome states have been eradicated is established.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Pairs in the Suttas (Suttantikadukanikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā), §1303:

"Because it has been separated" means because it has been made distinct and revealed. "He exhausts without leaving a remainder" means that just as a diamond exhausts the place where it has fallen without leaving a remainder, by not allowing it to manifest again.
1311. *Tappatīti* means he feels remorse (*vippaṭisārī*) or grieves (*anusocati*).
1313. By the word *ahaṃ* following the word *iti*, that meaning which is understood through the word *ahaṃ* acting as a cause is what is "discussed" (*saṃkathīyati*) or "uttered" (*udīrīyati*);

this is the meaning. For otherwise, if the meaning of the word were being expressed by a statement that was itself being spoken, it would result in the fallacy of infinite regress (*saṅkhā*), and so forth.

It may be that [the term] is a designation for all wholesome and other phenomena. They say that "being" (*bhāva*) is a synonym for "sentient being" (*satta*), or it is a designation for the "element" (*dhātu*).

Having thus far shown the designation of a sentient being by the word "given" (*datto*), he says "bed," etc., in order to show another type of designation, namely, the designation of the "appropriated" (*upādāpa-ññatti*).
By saying "I," which is a designation for what has come into existence, both the speaker and the listener—

It is understood through the state of clarifying the meaning by means of a previously grasped perception (*saññā*). For as long as that [perception] is not known, there can be no cognition of its meaning;
thus it is specifically called an "appellation" (*adhivacana*) because "it is known" (*ñāyati*), which is the conventional designation (*samaññā*).
Or else, it is an appellation because it is known, conventionally designated, and made manifest by way of grasping this meaning as "I am," through the function of perception.
“Paññāpīyati” means it is designated as “I”; the meaning is that it is established in this way.
“Voharīyati” means it is spoken of. “Uddheyyaṃ” means that which is to be extracted. “Api nāmasahassato” means even by many thousands of names;
the meaning is “even by thousands of names. A name that has the nature of arising spontaneously is called an “opapātika-nāma” (spontaneously arisen name).
It is called *kamma* because it is performed (*karīyati*). That which is merely a name is *nāmakamma*. Likewise for *nāmadheyya*.
For the words *karaṇa* (instrument) and *ṭhapana* (placing) also possess the sense of *kamma*. Now, if they have the sense of instrument:

by means of this, a purpose is performed and established—that is, one is designated as having such-and-such a name—therefore both the instrument and the placing are called "name" (*nāma*). Alternatively, if they have the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*): the instrument is merely the act of making known.
And it is said: "the settling. "Name and expression" (*nāmanirutti*) means "name and phoneme" (*nāmabyañjana*); thus, it is simply called "name.
For it is not the mere manifestation of the meaning designated as "earth" that expresses or manifests the name "earth"; rather, it is the name itself that expresses or manifests [it].
Therefore, in order to exclude the possibility that what is non-name might possess the nature of an expression or a phoneme, it is stated: "name and expression, name and phoneme."

Thus it has been said. The method here is the same as for the phrase "a mere verbal expression. In this context, however, "concept" (*paññatti*) is mentioned because it is that which is to be made known by the four terms—“reckoning” (*saṅkhā*), “convention” (*samaññā*), “description” (*paññatti*), and “usage” (*vohāra*)—whereas the others are mentioned because they are the means by which it is made known.
Furthermore, among those, the former is a "derived concept" (*upādā-paññatti*) devoid of the functions of arising and passing away, established through worldly convention; the latter—

The teachers say: "It is a designation by name (nāmapaññatti), by which the previous designations—such as visible form and so forth—are made known by means of a mental-door consciousness-series that has grasped the previously established convention immediately following the stream of ear-door consciousness.
However, since this is the meaning of this passage and its commentary, as for what was stated in the *Mātikā*—"merely a word..."—[it refers to this].
“[The term] ‘designation’ (adhivacana) refers to that which occurs by way of making a reference; ‘language’ (nirutti) refers to expressions spoken with a cause [of arising];
and ‘concept’ (paññatti) refers to that which makes known in a specific manner. If this were so, there would be a contradiction.

For there is no occurrence by way of making a reference that consists of mere words for that which is devoid of the functions of arising and falling away, since occurrence exists only for that which possesses arising and the rest.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as a name being spoken after having extracted it from its release from both word and word-meaning and having established it with its cause;
nor is there the making known of a word-meaning whose intrinsic nature has not been extracted in this or that manner.
Moreover, the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—that "this designation (*paññatti*) is of two kinds according to the manner already described"—is not seen [in the text]. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*...

However, only six types of designations have been mentioned, beginning with the designation of what exists (*vijjamāna-paññatti*). Among these: (1) the designation of what exists is, for example, "form" (*rūpa*) or "feeling" (*vedanā*);

(2) the designation of what does not exist is, for example, "woman" (*itthī*) or "man" (*puriso*); (3) the designation of what does not exist by means of what exists is, for example, "one possessing the three knowledges" (*tevijjo*) or "one possessing the six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiñño*);
(4) the designation of what exists by means of what does not exist is, for example, "the sound of a woman" (*itthisaddo*) or "the sound of a man" (*purisasaddo*).
“Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness,” and so forth, are designations of the existent by means of the existent.
“A kshatriya youth, a brahmin youth,” and so forth, are designations of the non-existent by means of the non-existent.

And it cannot be understood here that the two kinds of designation mentioned above have been stated; for a designation of the existent is a conceptualization... [etc. ...an expression regarding what is existent.

The designation of the non-existent, such as "conditioned phenomena" (*saṅkhā*) and so forth, is a "designation of the non-existent. The "others" are those conditioned phenomena and so forth that function as the qualifiers and the qualified of those very [non-existent things].

By the term "designation of the non-existent," there is the "derived designation" (*upādāpaññatti*), which is that which is to be designated; and there is the "name-designation" (*nāmapaññatti*), which is the means of designating it.
If it is argued that while some [terms] are stated [as names], others are merely designations (*paññatti*) as previously described—this is not so, because it is unproven.
For it is unproven that this meaning was stated by this commentary when there exists a direct, primary meaning already followed in the Canon (*pāḷi*).

Furthermore, if [it were so], then the various types such as the seven chariot-paths, the earth-kasiṇa, direction, time, the kasiṇa of smoke, the kasiṇa of light, the space derived from the removal of the kasiṇa, the space-kasiṇa, the sphere of nothingness, and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), etc., [would also have to be considered mere designations].
Dependent designation (*upādāpaññatti*) is non-existent designation (*avijjamānapaññatti*); since its non-existence is stated by that very expression, it cannot be said to exist.

And just as beings and so forth—which do not exist because they are merely to be designated—are of the nature of non-existent designations, so too it follows that material form and so forth—which do exist because they are to be designated—would be of the nature of existent designations. Therefore...
The statement "all phenomena are designations" (*sabbe dhammā paññatti*) should be understood as a description of designated phenomena that is not distinct from the paths of designation. Furthermore,
even if the description of "number" (*saṅkha*) and so forth is for the purpose of showing the distinction between that which is to be designated and the act of designating, nevertheless,
according to such passages as "one phenomenon is contained within all phenomena, and all phenomena are contained within one phenomenon," [it refers to] those things to be designated.

Since the state of being a path of description (*paññatti-paṭha-bhāva*) has already been shown, and since the paths of description for those things to be described are expressed by the very word "description" (*paññatti*), the term "path of description" (*paññatti-patha-pada*) need not be stated.

Nor can it be said that the exposition of "number" (*saṅkhyā*) and so forth is for the purpose of showing the distinction between the thing to be described and the act of describing, because the words "number" and so forth have the same meaning [as "description"]. For it has been said: "Even by death..."
In the passage, "What a person conceives of as 'I am' is abandoned," it says: "'Person' is a designation (*saṅkhā*), a common appellation (*samaññā*)... [and so on]... a mere expression (*abhilāpo*).
Likewise, in the passage, "'Māgaṇḍiya' is the name, the designation, the common appellation of that brahmin," and so forth.

Apart from the grasping of a conventional sign such as "this one is named so-and-so" and the grasping of verbal expressions such as "form is Tissa," there is no other thing established with its own intrinsic nature (*asiddhasabhāva*).
