The capacity to designate meaning is possible, yet there is also the incapacity to do so for those [words].

For if it were the case that they were incapable of designating meaning without a designation, and also incapable of being designated by a designation, then another designation would have to be stated for that [designation], and for that one as well;
thus, there would be an infinite regress (*anavatthāna*). Consequently, there would be no comprehension of meaning, nor even the grasping of the convention (*saṅketa*).
Regarding the conventional designation (*saṅketa*) as a mode of description, one might think, "This is the meaning of this statement," or "This word is the indicator of this meaning.

However, when the conventional designation is grasped merely for the arising of a recognition (*saññā*), there is no purpose in imagining a word as something separate from its meaning. [As it is said:
"The discourse of the Buddha, the Blessed One, strikes against the worldly ear," and "Do you recollect..."
“Ānanda, you have never before heard such a name as ‘Janavasabha’,” and by statements such as,
“I am Koṇḍañña, O Blessed One,” the fact that names are expressed through designation is established. Therefore,
the meaning should be understood after investigating it so that it is not in contradiction with the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā.
If suchness and the rest are not non-existent designations, what then is a non-existent designation? This matter has been explained:
"The conceptualization... [and] the verbal expression of non-existent things such as 'a being' (satta) and so forth is a non-existent designation.
And because beings and the rest are non-existent, their existence cannot be asserted; yet those who might say, "Because they are non-existent like form (rūpa) and the rest..."
"Non-existence was stated, not because of a state of non-being. This argument has already been refuted by the discussion on "being and non-being.
Furthermore, it is not the case that because form is not feeling, it is therefore called "non-existent.

Likewise, if beings and so forth exist, they cannot be said to be "non-existent" simply because form and so forth are not present. However, in regard to those forms and so forth, or the eye and so forth—
And as those [phenomena] proceed in such and such ways, diverse perceptions arise, such as "a being," "a woman," "a chariot," or "a jar," along with corresponding designations.
Apart from those [constituents] such as visible form and the eye, there exists no referent for the designations "being," "chariot," and so forth, which is grasped by those perceptions;
therefore, the expressions "being," "chariot," and so on, are called "designations of what does not exist."
And these are not called "false" because they function by way of worldly convention (*lokasamaññā*). For that very reason, those expressions are called "conventional truth" (*sammutisacca*).
Although that expressed meaning itself does not exist, it receives the designation and usage of a "conceptualization" (*paññattivohāra*) on account of the expression that does exist;
and it is called "conventional truth" because it functions as the expressed meaning of a word according to the perception as it has been grasped.

It is understood from the discussion stating, "Conventional knowledge (sammutiñāṇa) has only the [four] truths as its object, not anything else," and from the statement, "The earth-kasina and so forth, as well as robes and so forth,
are conventional truth (sammutisacca)," that this was said with precisely that intention. For, when form and the other aggregates are occurring in a continuum, the grasping of a "being" and so forth—
which occurs by way of apprehending them as a unity without letting go of those [aggregates]— is what constitutes eye-consciousness and the rest.

Just as one perceives and designates a "being," a "chariot," and so forth—which do not exist and are not found among those aggregates such as form and so on, nor in the eye and so on—it is therefore said that this [designation] cannot be described as having a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*) and so forth.
Likewise, based on the continuum of the aggregate-mass which is grasped as a unity, there occurs the perception and designation: "a person who is a good friend" or "a person who is a bad friend."
For one who cultivates that which has become the basis for the perception of a "person" (puggala), there arises both wholesome and unwholesome states;
thus it is said: "The person is also a condition by way of the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya).

However, since there is no such entity as a "person," just as the earth element is perceived after the water element and so forth have been mentally excluded, it is not so with form and the other [aggregates].
Having analyzed the aggregates, a person is not apprehended. And the view of a person has been refuted by the discourse on the person.
And it was said to the bhikkhunī Vajirā:
"Whom do you conceive as a 'being,' Māra? Is this a speculative view of yours?"
“This is merely a heap of pure formations; herein no being is found.
To show the occurrence of the designation “being,” she spoke thus:
“Just as from a collection of parts, the word ‘chariot’ arises;”
"Thus, while the aggregates exist, there is the conventional designation 'a being.
If a person (*puggala*) does not exist, how can the apprehension of a person have an object?

It is because it apprehends an object even though that object does not exist. For even that which does not exist may be apprehended—whether it be a conceptual construction or a conventional worldly notion—as if it were existing.
It is called "having an object" (*sārammaṇatā*) because it arises only by apprehending an object that has become its intrinsic nature (*sabhāvabhūta*).

For the expression "having an object" merely indicates that consciousness and mental factors do not function without an object; it does not indicate whether the object apprehended by them exists or does not exist.
This [statement] negates the existence of anything apart from the conditioned (*saṅkhata*) and the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).
The determination for those who follow in every respect. (1316) “In the sense of making its own name”:
the meaning is that it has the intrinsic nature of making its own name independently, without depending on anything else.
For when one makes the name of another, that naming depends upon that other; therefore, it is called "making a name" with reference to something else.

The nature of being named does not exist [in the name itself]. Therefore, it does not follow that the status of being a name belongs to the great multitude of people, to relatives, to qualities, or to those who perform the act of naming.
Furthermore, for that which has its name conferred by others, the nature of being named does not exist;

thus, the status of being a name is simply non-existent. However, because feeling and the other aggregates are established by their own intrinsic nature, the names "feeling" and so forth [do apply to them].

The state of being "name" (nāmatā) is stated by way of its nature as a designation. By the illustration of earth and so forth, he demonstrates precisely the establishment of the intrinsic nature of name, not a commonality of the state of being name;
however, because the word "name" is conventionally established for immaterial phenomena alone and not for earth and so forth, those [material things] do not possess the state of being name.
Furthermore, it is already stated in the *Mātikā* that earth and so forth do not incur the status of being name.
For there is no occurrence of non-material phenomena (arūpadhamma) in the form of a composite mass that could be designated by another name after abandoning the names "feeling" (vedanā) and so forth,
in the same way that material phenomena (rūpadhamma) such as hair and so on occur under the names "hair" and so forth after abandoning the names "earth" (pathavī) and so forth.

Alternatively, material phenomena consist of the eye and so forth, and visible forms and so forth, because of their relationship as the manifestor and the manifested, [which would not exist] without a name.

The immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhammā*) are not manifest in that way; therefore, because they are grasped as dependent upon name (*nāma*), like the contact of designation (*adhivacana-samphassa*), they are called "name.
Furthermore, the contact of resistance (*paṭigha-samphassa*) is also called "name" because, unlike the eye and so forth, it is not manifest without name.
Alternatively, this is included because of its immateriality and its similarity to other names, or because of its similarity to other types of contact. This is also the meaning of the word.

For here, in the case of the statement "it is called *rūpa* because it manifests (*rūpayati*), and it is called *nāma* because it bends (*nāmayati*"), a sequence of prior and subsequent [explanations] is possible.
"It manifests" means that even without a name, it makes itself known; "it bends" means that, because it would otherwise remain unmanifest, it makes for itself a name which makes it known.
Regarding "by way of the object-predominance condition": although matter does indeed possess the state of being an object-predominance condition, [the following applies].
It is called "name" (*nāma*) because it is a condition by way of its own specific nature, preeminent like Nibbāna which is the ultimate consolation; thus, Nibbāna itself is stated to be "name.

(1318) "For the purpose of showing the manifestation of the root of the round" means that the manifestation of the root of the round for sentient beings consists of ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*); such is the meaning. In this context, "manifestation" (*samudācāra*) refers to that which manifests; [it is] the very root of the round.

"Manifestation" refers to the manifestation of the root of the round (*vaṭṭamūla*); since the occurrence of the roots of the round is shown by the vision of those very roots, the meaning is also that it is for the purpose of showing the manifestation of the roots of the round.
And in each case, the expression "self and world" is stated by taking into account the specific modes of grasping as "self" and "world."
Or, it is said "both self and world" with reference to one who, having grasped a single aggregate as self, perceives another [aggregate] as the world that serves his enjoyment;
or with reference to one who, having grasped his own self as "self," perceives the self of another as "the world.
"That will be" means that the pentad of aggregates grasped in both those ways will come to be.
The meaning is: "settled" and "clinging. 1332.
That which is to be trained in together is *sahadhamma*; that which exists therein is *sahadhammika*.
Because the word *dovacassa* occurs in the sense of the object (kamma), the suffix *-āya* has been added without changing its meaning, and thus it is stated as "*dovacassāya*."
In this sense, he said, "the action of one who is difficult to speak to. Alternatively, *dovacassāyaṃ* is the going (*ayaṃ*) or proceeding of one who is difficult to speak to (*dovacassa*).
It is the speaking in opposition to what is spoken, the grasping of a contradiction. *Garuvāso* is dwelling with respect for those who are venerable because of their virtues.
*Sajeṭṭhakavāso* is dwelling among elders—those to whom one must give assent—on account of birth and so forth. Or, the venerable ones are those toward whom one ought to feel dread (*ottappitabbā*).

The elders are to be respected. Since that volition by which one is ill-spoken of deserves to be called "ill-spoken-ness" (*dovacassatā*), he said, "It is simply the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandho*).

(1333) A name joined with the prefix *du-* is a "bad name" (*dunnāma*). With the intention that "following" (*anusikkhana*) means attending upon even when not approaching, he said, "'Bhajanā' means approaching. "In every way" means both openly and in private, through body, speech, and mind.

1336. *Vinaya* refers to what is stated in the *Vibhaṅga* and the *Khandhaka*. Because one does not incur an offense either before or after the transgression of the basis (*vatthu*), it delimits the offense together with that basis.
Therefore he said: “Together with the basis... this is called skill in regard to offenses.

“Together with the formal act (*kammavācā*)” means by means of the formal act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*), the covering over as if with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*), or the formal act [of confession], [thinking] “I...”
And by such statements as, "Venerable sir, I have fallen into such-and-such an offense," one indeed delimits both the emergence from the offense and the formal act (*kammavācā*) simultaneously.
Alternatively, the "basis" (*vatthu*) is the cause of the offense, while the "formal act" is the cause of the emergence;
thus, it is said "together with the basis, together with the formal act" in the sense of knowing the result along with its cause.

1338. This same meaning is stated here as being "together with the preliminary work" (*parikamma*). "By means of the wisdom of emergence" (*vuṭṭhānakapaññāya*) means by means of the preliminary-work wisdom that serves as the cause for emergence.

1340. All wisdom regarding the objective sphere of the elements (*dhātu*) is skill in the elements (*dhātukusalatā*); the intention is that "skill in attention" (*manasikārakusalatā*) is a portion of that.

With this intention, the wisdom consisting in knowing the learning and attention is stated even in the first phrase. Alternatively, in the first phrase, it refers to the dhamma-text of the elements (*dhātupāḷi*) that has been mastered through recitation.
“Attention” (*manasikāra*) is said to be the act of attending (*manasikaraṇa*).

In that context, wisdom that consists of learning—the wisdom of grasping, the wisdom of attending, the wisdom of hearing the meaning of the *Dhātupāḷi*, and the wisdom of retaining it both in its wording and its meaning—knowing the delimitation by way of nature as “this is called the eye-element,” and so forth, and knowing the delimitation by way of number as “there are exactly eighteen,” is what is referred to by the term beginning with “wisdom of learning. In the latter phrase...
That fivefold wisdom is "learning" (uggaha). Furthermore, the attention directed toward impermanence and so forth that proceeds from it is called "attention to learning" (uggahamanasikāra).
Knowing that [attention] is simply its occurrence; or, knowing the learning as it occurs—just as it has occurred—such knowing is "knowing learning.
Attention, too, is the knowing that "it should be applied in this way" and "it has been applied in this way."
The arising of attention (*manasikāra*). Both of these are called "skill in attention.

For since even the learning (*uggaha*) is appropriately termed "attention" due to its association with attention, it is fitting to say that everything—both that which is to be attended to and the means of attending—is "attention.
And skill therein is "proficiency in attention" (*manasikārakusalatā*).
1342. Or, in all three cases... it is said that "it is suitable," and thus its status as learning by heart (*uggaha*) and so forth is stated. Insight (*paññā*) is comprehension (*sammasana*);
when associated with the Path, it accomplishes the function of comprehending impermanence and so forth by abandoning the perception of permanence and so forth.
Attention (*manasikāra*) associated with comprehension likewise accomplishes the function of attending to impermanence and so forth when associated with the Path. Therefore he said:

"Right attention is a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. By this, however, he shows that "skill in dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppādakusalatā*) is the knowledge of how ignorance and the other factors function as conditions for the arising of formations and so forth, such that "by means of this condition, this comes to be.

(1344) Mango seeds and the like are mentioned for the purpose of illustrating unclung-to (*anupādinnaka*) phenomena. [The mention of] ear-consciousness and so forth is because they are of a different class and unsuitable [for that illustration].
The eye-faculties and so forth, which do not produce [their respective consciousnesses], are called "dissimilar conditions" (*visabhāgapaccaya*);

and the ear-consciousness and so forth, which do not arise from them, are called "phenomena arisen from dissimilar conditions. Alternatively, a condition for an eye-consciousness that is dissimilar to the ear-consciousness is a "dissimilar condition";
[thus, it refers to] that which has arisen by means of a condition—the ear-base—which is dissimilar to the eye-base.
[It is] arisen from dissimilar conditions. 1346.

Regarding the exposition of *ajjava* (straightforwardness): since it is stated that *ajjava*, *ajjavatā*, *ujutā*, and *ujukatā* are synonymous, [the author] provides the term "humbleness of mind" (*nīcacittatā*) in the exposition of *maddava* (gentleness) to distinguish it from the expositions of straightforwardness and pliancy found in the expositions of *ajjava* and *maddava*. Therein:
Regarding the phrase “humility is gentleness,” the repetition of the word “gentleness” is for the purpose of qualifying humility.
For while self-depreciation (*omāna*) is indeed a form of humility, it is not gentleness.
[The monks] dwell having taken upon themselves and bearing the misdeeds and harsh words of others by not creating opposition.
“Serenity of mind” (*cittassa samathanatā*) means that non-ill-will is the mind’s own state of being (*sako mano-bhāvo*).

Alternatively, taking the continuity of consciousness (*citta-pabandha*) as a unity, it speaks of its serenity through the mind accompanied by joy (*pīti-sahagata-manas*) arising within it. Or, “one who is glad-minded” (*attamano puggalo*);

the state of such a person is “glad-mindedness” (*attamanatā*). To prevent the view of a self (*puggala-diṭṭhi*), it is stated as “of the mind” (*cittassa*), since that [glad-mindedness] does not belong to a [substantial] being.

1349. It should be understood that one acts even with the mind by failing to perform what ought to be done through body and speech, and by consenting to what ought not to be consented to; or alternatively, this is stated by way of the breach of the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) and so forth.
1350. Regarding "egg-like growths" (*aṇḍakāni*): they refer to masses of resin or *ahicchattaka* fungi that have arisen on trees with sap-filled wounds.
However, the term refers to the lumps of powder or knots that arise like eggs on a tree of soft wood when it has been heated.
Or they should be understood as "eggs. It should be seen as harsh, entering as if rubbing against the ear like a lotus stalk.
"Anger-adjacent" (*kodhasāmantā*) means those produced by anger and acting as its attendants.

"Polished speech" (*porī*): *porī* refers to a woman who has grown up in the city; speech that is delicate and soft like her is called "polished" (*porī*). "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to what was stated as "it is spoken."

The construction "kiriyāya" (by action) is also possible, or alternatively, "vācāya" (by speech). By the phrase "saṇhavācatā" (gentleness of speech), etc., he shows the volition that brings forth that speech.
1351. That which is a breach by way of gain of material goods is called a "breach" by way of gain of material goods. There are only two.
The word *hi* refers to the flaws that arise through the acquisition of material goods (*āmisa*) and the Dhamma as previously described.

"By way of a direction suitable for travel" means by way of a direction appropriate to the path of travel. "Standing on the side of conciliation" means one should say, "I am performing conciliation," and not out of a desire for gain, honor, and so forth;
this is the meaning. That which must necessarily be done is a duty (*kicca*); the other is a task (*karaṇīya*).
Emergence from an offense other than through formal rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) is called "emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*). 1352.
"Discourse with requisites" (*sasambhārakathā*) means a discourse on seeing accompanied by its causes; or, it is a discourse on seeing together with its requisites.
Having stated, "For which lack of restraint of the eye-faculty," he further says, "of that eye-faculty..."
It is said, "for the purpose of closing with the door of mindfulness," and not for the sake of non-restraint.

This should be understood as having been stated by taking into account that the "coveting and so forth" shown to be the cause of the non-restraint of the eye-faculty is demonstrated as the causal activity of one whose eye-faculty is unrestrained; for the phrase *yatvādhikaraṇaṃ* refers to whichever eye-faculty [is involved].
The meaning is "for what reason. For whom is it for what reason? For one who is unrestrained. And what is unrestrained?

That which is characterized by that through which, on account of the unrestraint of the eye-faculty, [defilements] flow in; [the phrase] "for the restraint of that" is the construction of the meaning.

However, as for the statement "at the moment of impulsion, there is immorality," and so forth, since all of this has already been stated right here, it need not be said again in the section on the six [faculties].
This should be applied to the doors as appropriate. For there is no immorality—consisting of bodily or verbal misconduct—in the five doors.

Just as when there is no restraint at a city gate, the houses and other structures connected to it become unrestrained, so too, when there is no restraint in the impulsion (javana), the doors and other factors connected to it become unrestrained; thus, [the same applies] regarding the restraint of others.
This demonstrates only the commonality with others in terms of being restricted, not the commonality between what precedes and follows, nor the commonality between the internal and external.
Alternatively, when the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and so forth act as doors, the javana that arises again is treated as if it were external;

thus, it is described as being like the gate of a city, while the other [the preceding state] is like the interior of the city’s gate. Or, when non-restraint has arisen in the javana, thereafter, for the door, the life-continuum, and so forth—

It should be understood that by entering through the "impulsion" (javana), which is like a city gate because it functions as the cause for falling into non-restraint (asaṃvara), there is the plundering of the "door," the "life-continuum" (bhavaṅga), and so forth, by the thieves of immorality and the like, resulting in the destruction of the "merchandise" of wholesome states (kusala). 1353.

"Purposefulness" (idamatthikatā) is the state of having a need for this nutriment in the sense of overcoming [craving]. "Lack of contentment" (asantuṭṭhi) is the lack of satisfaction regarding the consumption of nutriment.
The meaning is: discontent occurring at the moment of consuming food, which is a longing for delicacies and the like.

Herein, it should be understood that these two factors—discontent (*asantuṭṭhitā*), which is greed (*lobha*), and lack of moderation and lack of reflection (*amattaññutā* and *appaṭisaṅkhā*), which are delusion (*moha*)—constitute "lack of moderation in eating" (*bhojane amattaññutā*).
Pride-intoxication (*mānamada*) is that which occurs through such thoughts as "I am superior," and so forth, based on the capacity to indulge in unwholesome qualities (*asaddhamma*).
Pride that has arisen, or lust itself, is the "intoxication of man.
Food mixed with sugar, ghee, milk, and so forth, cooked until thick, is "lump-food" (*piṇḍarasa-bhojana*); or it is food such as meat broth, cooked until thick. "Little" means a small amount.
"For stability" means for the purpose of stability. And when eating for that purpose, one eats because one thinks, "I shall maintain the body."
Therefore, it is said: "for the purpose of setting aside. The phrase "arising due to the condition of not eating" is a qualification of hunger (*khudā*);
its purpose is to show that [hunger] is that whose non-occurrence must be brought about by eating. "The entire dispensation" includes both the Dhamma of the scriptures and all wholesome states.
[This refers to] feeling arising due to the condition of not eating, and feeling not arising due to the condition of eating.
What is the distinction between these two? The former consists of feelings characterized by hunger that have arisen in their usual course;

for they arise in one who does not eat, increasing further as time goes on. The latter, however, consists of feelings characterized by hunger—such as the burning sensation in the limbs or piercing pains—that do not arise in their usual course.
For these, having been previously unarisen due to the condition of eating, will not arise at all. [The third type] has violence as its characteristic cause.
There is a distinction regarding the harming of sentient beings.
"Maintenance" (*yātrā*) is said to mean "sustenance" (*yāpanā*); since it was also stated previously as "for the sake of sustenance," what is the difference here?
Previously, it was explained as "for the sake of sustaining the life-faculty" (*jīvitindriya-yāpanatthāya*), but here, however, it refers to the non-interruption of the four postures (*iriyāpatha*).
"Subsistence" and "maintenance"—this is the distinction here. Acceptance without knowing the measure of the donor, the gift to be given, and oneself;
or acceptance for the purpose of squandering what has been given in faith; or that by which one would incur an offense—this is unrighteous acceptance (*adhammika-paṭiggahaṇa*).
Use without reflection is unrighteous use (*adhammena paribhoga*). Regarding that which is blameless and beyond reproach...
By means of consumption, one makes oneself blameworthy and subject to reproach regarding the requisite.

The meaning is that, knowing one’s own natural strength, digestive power, and so forth, thinking “I shall be free from blame,” one consumes food in a measure that is appropriate, with the thought, “In this way, I shall be beyond reproach.
A pleasant abiding in the postures is a comfortable dwelling. For it is said that after consuming this much, the postures proceed comfortably... [as before] ...thus they are called "postures."
Eating and drinking, which are the causes for the occurrence of happiness, are described as if they were accomplished by those postures because they are grasped as being instrumental to them.
They write, "One should drink water without having eaten," but the reading is actually "having eaten.
Furthermore, it is stated again by way of permitting only a small amount—
“If that which is allowable covers it, this robe serves its purpose;
it is sufficient for dwelling in comfort.
For one sitting cross-legged, the rain does not fall upon the knees.”
“It is sufficient for dwelling in comfort,” he said.
“The benefit of food” refers to the fact that food endowed with the eight aforementioned factors is not to be censured.
"And the benefit is dwelling in happiness" is the meaning. "Knowing the proper measure" means knowing by way of the suitability and the faultless quantity of food. 1356.

One whose mindfulness (*sati*) has perished because it has reached destruction, and who has lost it because it is overcome by opposing factors, is one whose mindfulness is perished and lost (*naṭṭhamuṭṭhassati*); the state of being such is "the condition of having perished and lost mindfulness" (*naṭṭhamuṭṭhassatitā*).

1368. "Attained to purity" refers to the virtue of the path and its fruition (*maggaphala-sīla*). "Supramundane states" refers specifically to supramundane states such as mindfulness (*sati*) and so forth. However, since there is no perfection of virtue belonging to the fine-material or immaterial spheres, this should be construed according to what is possible.
1373. "Possessed of wealth" means having the requisites of wealth. "Conformity with the four truths" means conformity to the penetration of the four truths;
for by the term "of the truths," penetration is expressed in relation to those things to be penetrated, namely, the penetration of the four truths.
Or it is said that [the path] is the conformity to the Four Truths, which must be penetrated by means of the supporting condition (*upanissaya*). 1378.

When someone says, "Make my house your primary responsibility and enter for alms," what is being given is called *dhurabhatta* (a meal of primary responsibility). Alternatively, *dhurabhatta* is a meal given after one has personally taken charge as the primary provider, having first instructed others regarding the regular meal (*niccabhatta*) and so forth.
1379. "Paṭivāseti" means he turns back, or he causes [them] to recede.

1380. “The aggregates formerly inhabited” (*pubbe nivutthakkhandhā*) refers to the aggregates included within the continuity (*santati*) of previous births. “Connected with the aggregates” (*khandhapaṭibaddha*) refers to such things as clothing, ornaments, vehicles, villages, and countries. “At the time of destruction” (*khayasamaye*) refers to the moment of the Path (*maggakkhaṇa*). 1381.
“In the sense of resolute confidence” (*adhimuccanaṭṭhena*) means in the sense of proceeding according to one’s pleasure, characterized by an unrestrained leaping forward (*pakkhandana*).

1382. “The end of what is exhausted” (*khīṇanta*) means the limit, the conclusion, the state of completion of what is exhausted; or else, it is the initial stage of what is exhausted. This same method applies to [the terms] “the end of what has ceased” (*niruddhanta*) and so forth.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Twofold Pairs is finished.
The commentary on the Section on the Exposition is finished.
4. The Section on the Commentaries.

Commentary on the Extraction of the Meaning of the Triplets (Tika-atthuddhāravaṇṇanā) 1384. "The path of method" refers to the progression through the methods such as the Suttanta-bhājaniya and so forth, as well as the progression through the methods such as the *anuloma* (conformity) and others.
For even that brings about ease once the meanings have been determined here. "The extraction of questions" refers to [the extraction] for each of the forty-nine [triplets].
The extraction of those [terms] found within each of the nine questions, and the setting down of the numerical counts found therein, is the method of enumeration (*gaṇanācāra*).
"Extraction of the meaning" (*atthuddhāra*) refers to the extraction [of the sense] that "these specific mental arisings and so forth are the meanings such as wholesome and so on.
"Each pillar" (*kaṇṇikaṃ kaṇṇikaṃ*) refers to the phenomena analyzed and classified in the sections on the arising of consciousness (*cittuppādakaṇḍa*) and matter (*rūpakaṇḍa*).
The meaning is: "having joined together by way of groups (rāsi-rāsi), such as 'the wholesome in the four planes' and 'the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness-arising,'" and so forth.

*Ghaṭa* and *gocchaka* are indeed synonyms for *kaṇṇika*. Here, however, the singular designation "the wholesome in the four planes" is used because the wholesome contact and other factors belonging to the four planes attain a state of oneness in their quality of being wholesome. [This applies] to the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* and the *Rūpakaṇḍa*.
This exposition of the meaning (atthuddhāradesanā) is undertaken by way of the phenomena (dhamma) cognized through the arising of consciousness in the four planes and so forth;
therein, the meaning is that those wholesome states analyzed within the four planes, up to "the cognized," are "wholesome phenomena" (kusalā dhammā).

Even though the detailed expansion of the triad of the wholesome was previously cognized, nevertheless, therein the phenomena were [treated] according to occasion and according to their intrinsic nature as contact and so forth.
And although [the categories] have been analyzed, divided, and understood, they were not brought together under a single characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*);

therefore, setting aside the distinctions of occasion (*samaya*) and so forth mentioned there, this exposition of the triad of the wholesome (*kusalattika*) is here again analyzed for the purpose of awakening by bringing together all those things divided by various distinctions under a single characteristic, such as the wholesome.
And herein, having provided the exposition of the wholesome in the singular number,

The reason for using the plural number in the conclusion has already been stated. If there is a convergence into unity among wholesome states (*dhamma*), why was the question not also formulated in the singular?

Because in the enumeration (*uddesa*), the word "wholesome" functions as a qualifier of "states," and because those states qualified by it were what was questioned, and because their specific numerical distinction had not yet been determined. [This is explained] in the exposition (*niddesa*).

However, it is appropriate to speak of it as a unity by bringing together the expression "wholesome in the four planes," since this shows the wholesome distinguished by its detailed classification across the four planes. For here, the term "wholesome" (kusala) is the primary factor;

and it functions by taking up a unity based on the wholesome aspect itself, which remains established in its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva) regardless of what is to be distinguished, rather than by way of division.

1385. Regarding the phrase "twelve unwholesome types of consciousness": here too, the first unwholesome type of consciousness is stated by treating it as a unity in its nature as a consciousness associated with wrong view accompanied by joy, without yet specifying its divisions such as those based on occasion, contact, and so forth.
In this manner, up to the twelfth, they are called "the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness. Thus, within the four planes...

In the cases of "resultant" (*vipāka*) and so forth, the application should be made accordingly. Regarding the term *cittuppāda*: here, that in which something arises is called an "arising" (*uppāda*).
What arises? Consciousness (*citta*). Thus, the meaning is possible by way of characterizing the whole through its part, as in "the arising of consciousness is *cittuppāda*.
For when this is the case, it is established that *cittuppāda* is the aggregate of consciousness and mental factors (*cetasika*). Thus it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).

However, the term "consciousness" (*citta*) is employed in the phrase "consciousness itself is the arising, thus 'arising of consciousness' (*cittuppādo*)" for the purpose of excluding anything else that might arise;
the term "arising" (*uppāda*) is employed for the purpose of excluding the state of consciousness not arising.

Alternatively, in the "Section on the Arising of Consciousness" (*Cittuppādakaṇḍa*), because the fact that consciousness arises—as in "consciousness has arisen"—is well-known, it is stated that "consciousness itself is the arising."
It should be understood that the mention of "arising" (uppāda) is made because there exists a state of mind that has not yet arisen and must be brought about.

Furthermore, this meaning should be seen as stated by taking the description to be primarily focused on the mind (*cittappadhāna*), as in the case of such expressions as "the two fivefold consciousnesses" (*dvepañcaviññāṇāni*). 1420.

Regarding the phrase "in the six doors": here, there is nothing at all to be said concerning the five doors; even in the mind-door (*manodvāra*), it is only a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*) [that is relevant].
The javana is followed by the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) known as "registration" (tadārammaṇa). For that [registration] is the result of limited (paritta) kamma;
and since a result is the experiencing of desirable or undesirable objects, and a result conforms to its kamma, the result of limited kamma is the experiencing of only a limited object.
Therefore, all registration is "limited-object."
It has been said. If it is argued that, in this case, even the sublime result (mahaggata-vipāka) would necessarily involve the experience of the sublime [object], we say no.
This is because the result must correspond to the karma which is dominated by concentration (samādhi), has reached absorption (appanā), and has perception as its primary object.
Therefore, while concentration consists in the experience of bliss, it should be understood that it too has the object of the karma as its own object, precisely in accordance with that karma.
And precisely because it conforms to the kamma, even a sublime javana does not follow upon an object that is limited (paritta).

For that very reason, sense-sphere resultant consciousness—which constitutes rebirth-linking and so forth—takes only a limited object, such as the sign of the kamma (kamma-nimitta), and not a sublime or immeasurable one.
This is because it has been stated: "A state with a sublime object [does not arise] for one whose object is limited..."
"An immeasurable object dhamma is a condition for a limited object dhamma by way of kamma-condition," yet there is no fruition (vipāka) that is sublime or immeasurable which has a limited object;

and here, it is stated that all sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) fruitions have only limited objects. Therefore, in accordance with the nature of the kamma, even that which has a sublime or immeasurable object— [...is a condition for a limited object dhamma by way of kamma-condition.]
If limited kamma gives rebirth-linking, it gives only that which has the sign of the kamma-process or the destination as its object.

It should be understood that even the resultant [consciousness] occurring in the course of existence takes only limited objects such as visible forms and so forth. Furthermore, laughter occurring in those whose taints are destroyed—though dissociated from mindfulness by way of residual habituation—occurs only with respect to limited things, not with respect to others; for in the absence of defilements, there is no presence of conditions for such laughter.

Therefore, its having a limited object was stated. The lack of zeal in giving and so forth by those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) should be understood only in the sense of not performing [the act] with earnestness, and not in the sense of unwholesome states such as laziness;
for they are supreme persons whose every exertion has subsided. And their lack of earnestness should be understood as being simply free from striving.
The statement "of those that are too familiar" indicates the object of a review that is devoid of attention and dissociated from knowledge; it does not restrict the object to that [review] alone.
For even for one associated with knowledge, the status of being an object is indeed even more thoroughly established in the case of things that are too familiar.
Just as when reciting a text that is very familiar, one does not notice it even after two or three passages have been reached.

Because it has been recited by one possessing mindfulness dissociated from knowledge, the same process occurs even in the case of well-mastered jhānas; thus he said, "of those that are exceedingly well-mastered," and so forth.
By the phrase "the designation of the kasiṇa-signs, etc.," he refers to all previously mentioned designations based on derived phenomena (upādāpaññatti).
Regarding this, the teachers say that it is an existing object, unlike [material] form and so on, which does not exist [independently]. This is conventional truth (sammutisacca).

However, when the kasiṇa-signs and so forth are being spoken of, they are said to be "conceptualized by way of verbal expression" (*vacanavohārena paññatti*) merely because they are the basis for words.
For it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā that its conceptualization is an "unreal conceptualization" (*avijjamāna-paññatti*), and thus its non-existence is established.
Nevertheless, by means of a perception (*saññā*) that functions as if that which is non-existent were existent, [the Buddha] spoke of the "limited" (*paritta*) and so forth. "This..."
It cannot be said that "the name is the object," because even though it occurs by depending upon those very phenomena, it does not stand within the phenomena themselves.
Therefore, it is stated that it "should not be said" to have a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*) and so forth, together with its associated factors.
However, this statement "its object should not be said" refers to the fact that the objective field of perception (*saññāvisaya*), in the form as it is grasped, is "not to be defined."

In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated that they have an object which cannot be specified by forming a *aññapadattha-samāsa* (possessive compound) as "those whose object is not to be designated" (*navattabbārammaṇā*)—referring to fifty-five types of consciousness-moments (*cittuppāda*) by way of the fifty-four consciousness-moments and material form (*rūpa*). "Kevalaṃ" means without the act of clinging (*parāmasana*).

"By way of going to what is undesirable" (*aniṭṭhaṅgata-vasena*) means by way of proceeding toward what is undesired; or, a consciousness-moment that has gone to a double-edged uncertainty (*dveḷha*) regarding what is undesired.
"Proceeding in an undesirable manner" refers to its occurrence in that specific mode; thus it is called "proceeding by way of an undesirable state.

Distraction (*vikkhepa*) is the scattering of the mind among various objects. Non-stability is the lack of tranquility. Having understood the term "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*) as referring to the purification of the change-of-lineage, he says "at the time of the change-of-lineage."

"Having 'the basis for all' as the fourth": here, the word *sabbattha* (all) should be understood in the sense of "belonging to all. Alternatively, that which is the foundational cause (*pādaka*) for all [meditations] such as insight (*vipassanā*) is "the basis for all";
this is a designation for the fruit by way of its objective domain (*visaya*). "Having the space-kasina as the fourth" refers to having the delimiting-space-kasina as the fourth.
For that belongs to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), not the other [the infinite-space-kasina]. Furthermore, from the perspective of proficiency (*kusala*), there are twelve kinds.

By the phrase "also by way of functional," the twenty-fourfold classification is stated. Since it also serves as a basis for the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), the wholesome and the functional are combined together and described as having a universal basis; thus, he says it is "accompanied by risk" because functional jhāna has a limited basis.
"He absorbs it into the exalted consciousness" refers to what is stated in the sequence beginning with, "When his mind is thus concentrated..."

It is stated that, having grasped the manifest mind of the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhānacitta*) by means of the preliminary stages (*parikamma*), one merges the mental body (*rūpakāya*) into the mind with the resolve-mind (*adhiṭṭhānacitta*).
As for the statement "the mind of the foundational jhāna merges into the mental body," this too refers to the aforementioned mind of the foundational jhāna being made the object;
thus, the continuum of consciousness (*cittasantāna*) merges into the mental body, following along with it.

"It is said that having performed [the preliminary], one resolves": this refers to what has been stated. Furthermore, these two types of resolution bring about both invisibility of the body and visibility of the body.

It should be understood that by means of the preparation consisting in the desire to go, and because the perception associated with that [desire] possesses the qualities of the perception of ease and lightness, it also accomplishes the act of going.
"The mind of a stream-enterer" should be understood as the individual path and fruition consciousness of a stream-enterer.

For it has been stated that [the Blessed One] knows the minds of Māra and others; why then would one who possesses the knowledge of penetration into others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*) not know a consciousness associated with the taints (*sāsavacitta*)?
Buddhas have cut off the crossroads; they have severed the cycle of saṃsāra. "Also by means of reviewing the path, fruition, and Nibbāna."

In this context, it should be understood that the reviewing of the path and its fruits occurs once the path and fruits have been known through the knowledge of recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*), and the reviewing of Nibbāna occurs once the immeasurable states (*appamāṇadhamma*) having Nibbāna as their object have been known;
thus, the reviewings of the path and so forth establish the fact that the knowledge of recollection of past lives has an immeasurable object. "The aggregates are immeasurable..."
For it is stated that "the knowledge of recollection of past lives is a condition for [the path] by way of object-condition," but not that it is Nibbāna.
Therefore, even when the function of reviewing the path and fruit is said to be performed by the knowledge of recollection of past lives, one cannot say that it involves reviewing Nibbāna;
yet in the Aṭṭhakathā, it is seen that its having Nibbāna as its object is indeed permitted.

"Will be reborn in the sense-sphere realm" (*kāmāvacara*) refers to the knowledge of the aggregates that will arise [there]. "Will attain final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna" (*parinibbāyissati*) means it is possible to understand this as: "He will attain final nibbāna by means of the paths and fruits which have nibbāna as their object and which constitute the complete extinguishing of the defilements.

(1429) "Because of not being co-nascent" (*asahajātattā*) means because of not being associated (*asampayuttattā*). For there is no state of co-nascence between immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) and other immaterial phenomena.
"Because of association, there is another [consciousness]"—this refers to what was stated as "at the time when other phenomena are the object.

However, even at the time when the Path is the object, one should apply the principle that it cannot be designated as having the Path as its dominant influence (*adhipati*) if it does not treat the Path with reverence.
Regarding "niyogato," he said "by necessity" (*niyamena*) with reference to this meaning; or alternatively, *niyogā* means those things which possess necessity.

The meaning is "fixed. For it is stated in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* (Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness) that among the types of consciousness explained there, none has exclusively the future as its object.
Furthermore, it is said that in the course of existence (*pavatti*), [consciousness] takes either kamma or the sign of kamma (*kammanimitta*) as its object and thus has the past as its object;

however, regarding the state of having the present as its object when taking the sign of kamma as its object during the course of existence, this is explained in the commentary to the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga*.
He will explain this. Therefore, it should be understood that this was said with reference to the sign of past kamma that has entered the range of the mind-door during death at the mind-door.

In the case of death with a hundred objects remaining, when the rebirth-linking occurs in relation to a sign of destiny while five consciousness-moments still remain of the life-span, there are four bhavaṅga moments with present objects; and in the other case, six.
With this in mind, he said: "And thereafter, at the time of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

For when death occurs with that same object while the impulsion (javana) has not yet arisen regarding the object that is the sign of the destination—just as in the case of a being belonging to the fine-material or immaterial realms who is reborn in the sense-sphere realm—then the six life-continuum moments subsequent to the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) have present objects.
In the case of [mental states] associated with wrong view (*diṭṭhi*), the tasting (*assādana*) and so forth should be understood as being accompanied by misapprehension (*saparāmāsa*).

Regarding the preliminary stage of those impulsive moments (*javana*) that take concepts (*paṇṇatti*) or Nibbāna as their object, he demonstrates the method by way of those [impulsions] for which, during their preliminary stage, it is absolutely impossible for the adverting consciousness (*āvajjanā*) to have past objects and so forth as its objective field.
This applies even to the preliminary stage of impulsive moments that take Nibbāna as their object.
It should not be said that it is so; yet it is not exclusively so, because in the sequences of the paths and fruits, its object is not Nibbāna. [Objection:
"These are fragrances"—surely present fragrances are being grasped here; how then can there be future-objectivity in this case? [Reply:
Because it proceeds with the thought, "May they not wither for two hundred and eighteen years," it is directed toward the future, thinking, "May they not wither."
For the intention is that the mind proceeds by grasping a scent that has not yet arrived.

When one transforms the body by means of the mind, the resolving consciousness (*adhiṭṭhānacitta*) has a present object, because it takes as its object the very body that exists at that moment and has become manifest.
Likewise, [it functions] by way of producing long, short, small, large, blue, and so forth in one’s own body, or by way of another miracle.
It should be applied to the instrument (karaṇe). Regarding the phrase "in this interval, one or two series of moments (santativāra) are to be understood":

the meaning is that the series of material phenomena (rūpa-santati) and the series of immaterial phenomena (arūpa-santati) occurring within this interval are what are called "one or two series of moments.

Alternatively, they are called "one or two series of moments" because they are produced from causes such as the primary elements (utu), which are extremely subtle in nature. Both of these constitute the present; that is, they belong to the present by way of duration (addhā-paccuppanna).
The meaning is that both of these occur. “Is carried away” means it is dragged along by the delighting in craving and views.

Regarding the phrase “some say,” they refer to the residents of Abhayagiri; however, since they do not accept a moment of stability for consciousness, it would be incorrect for them to say, “or one penetrates at the moment of stability.
Likewise, those who [hold that] for oneself and another, supernormal power occurs at a single moment...
For those who say, "The mind that is currently occurring arises," their statement that "it penetrates [the object] at the moment of its duration or at the moment of its dissolution" is inconsistent.
For it is not the case that what is arising during those two moments can be said to arise in the same single moment as the consciousness of another.
Furthermore, that which is arising during the moments of duration and dissolution has only a partial aspect of the present object.
It falls under the category of having a partial object that has passed away.

And as for what was said—"when one adverts to the mind of a multitude by way of a mass, thinking 'I shall know another's mind'"—in this case, since the multitude consists of many individuals other than oneself, it should be stated that the occurrence of adverting is with the thought, "I shall know the minds of others. Furthermore, the term "of another" refers to the multitude.
Even if such a meaning were possible, it would still be inappropriate for that person alone to penetrate [the truth] by adverting to a "heap of minds" (cittarāsi).
For adverting to a heap is not the same as adverting to a single part. Therefore, one should not say, "When the minds of the great multitude were adverted to," and so forth.
As for what they say—that "the consciousness of the possessor of psychic power and that of another arise simultaneously"—the intended meaning here might be this:

one who has attained knowledge of the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa), desiring to know another's mind, enters the foundational jhāna, emerges from it, and without making a distinction as to whether it is past and so forth, [knows] by way of the commonality of consciousness: "I know this person's mind."
Having performed the preliminary work (parikamma) and again entered the basic absorption (pādakajjhāna), and having emerged from it, he adverts to the mind by means of the general method alone;

then, immediately after three or four preliminary acts, he penetrates and discerns another's mind with the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariyañāṇa), just as one sees a form with the divine eye.
Beyond that, however, there is the defining of states such as "with lust" and so forth by means of sense-sphere consciousnesses.
It is like the determination of blue and so forth.

Therein, when a being whose heart-base has been seen by the divine eye becomes present, the adverting consciousness—adverting by way of the commonality of mind—takes that existing, present mind as its object and adverts to the mind. And the preliminary applications [take] each respective existing mind.
Having made the object by means of the commonality of mind itself, they proceed as preliminary exercises for knowing the mind.
However, the knowledge of penetration into others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*), while penetrating and discerning the existing mind, arises in the very same moment as that [mind].
In this regard, because they grasp the continuity of the stream of consciousness as a single unit, the acts of adverting and so forth proceed as if they were the mind itself.

And that very mind which has been discerned by the knowledge of penetration into others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) is the same; therefore, because they arise with an identical mode of appearance, there is no diversity of objects for the adverting consciousness and the impulsion consciousnesses in any instance other than the path and fruit moments, which are undesirable [to the practitioner].

Thus it is established that the preparation (parikamma), having a present object, serves as the condition of repetition (āsevanapaccaya) for the knowledge of penetration into others' minds, which also has a present object.

Thus, the triad of the past is likewise undifferentiated. Otherwise, if "present" were stated here as referring to both the present of continuity (*santati-paccuppanna*) and the present of duration (*addhā-paccuppanna*), it would follow that the past and the future also possess the status of being "present.

If that were the case, one would have to state such things as: "A present phenomenon is a condition for a present phenomenon by way of the proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*)," and so forth; but this is not [the case].
And that has been stated: "A past state is a condition for a present state by way of proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*);
preceding past aggregates are [conditions] for succeeding present aggregates...

up to: 'adaptation is a condition for change-of-lineage'. From such statements, it follows that [the term 'proximate'] refers only to the immediate past within the context of the present as duration (*addhā*) and continuity (*santati*).

The four aggregates are known as "past," yet nowhere in the Canon is it stated that the term "present" occurring in the Abhidhamma mātikā refers to either the present as duration (*addhā*) or the present as continuity (*santati*).

Therefore, by means of those [terms], the fact that the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) has a present object is explained through the arising of consciousness in a single moment for both the possessor of psychic power and the other person.
But when one makes the mental application (ābhoga), thinking, “I know that which this person’s consciousness has proceeded;

I shall know that which will be,” and then performs such acts as entering the foundational jhāna, then both the preliminary work of adverting and the knowledge of others’ minds have only past and future objects as their domain, because the distinction is made by the act of adverting itself.
However, those who say: "One possessing psychic power (*iddhimā*), desiring to know another's mind, adverts (*āvajjeti*).
The act of adverting ceases together with that very object, which is present at the moment of adverting. Then there arise four or five impulsion moments (*javana*);

of these, the last is the psychic power consciousness (*iddhicitta*), while the rest are sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) consciousnesses. For all of them, that very same [other person's] ceased mind is the object."
Based on this statement— "It exists, and yet those [consciousnesses] do not have different objects because they have present objects by way of duration"—
it follows that even though advertence (*āvajjana*) and impulsion (*javana*) have present and past objects respectively, there is no difference in their object; likewise,
when one adverts to consciousness-moments occurring one, two, four, or five moments in the future, the advertence and impulsion possess their respective objects as appropriate.
They argue that even though the future, present, and past serve as objects, there is no lack of diversity of objects;

therefore, when four or five mind-moments in the future have been adverted to, the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), which takes the present moment as its object, is established immediately after the preliminary work (parikamma) whose object was the future.
To them, [the following objection is raised]: "A state with a future object [cannot be the condition] for a state with a present object..."

Because these questions—“A state with a present object is a condition, by way of repetition-condition, for a state with a past object; and a state with a present object is a condition, by way of repetition-condition, for a state with a past object”—have not been raised, and because it is stated in the enumeration that “there are three [condition-types] in repetition,” this [point] is not established.
For there is no wholesome functional or sublime state that is without repetition.
Furthermore, the status of this doctrine as a support for the statement that advertence (*āvajjana*) and impulsion (*javana*) have objects that are present-for-a-moment and ceased is not established;
for it was with reference to the fact that advertence lacks the apprehension of the future— since no distinction is made between what has occurred and what will occur—
and because of that absence, the impulsions likewise lack the apprehension of the present, that [the doctrine] was stated.

Because it has been so stated. For at that time, adverting occurs with reference precisely to the consciousness that has become manifest immediately after the vibration of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

Furthermore, if the knowing consciousness were also to have the present as its object, there would be the fault of the two consciousnesses—adverting and knowing—occupying the same place simultaneously;

and it is not desired that there be adverting to a portion of a single mass [of objects] or adverting to whatever happens to be encountered. Therefore, in an undesirable situation, [there would be no room for] adverting and impulsion (*javana*).

And having rejected as incorrect the statement that "the mind present at the moment (khaṇapaccuppanna) becomes the object of the knowledge of penetration into others' minds" because it would entail the fault of having multiple objects,

one should instead observe the absence of multiple objects by way of the fact that the advertence and the impulsion have the present of the duration and continuity (addhāsantatipaccuppanna) as their object,
precisely because they do not incur the aforementioned faults during that time. Thus, the state of being currently occurring for the advertence and the impulsion—
If it were said that "the state of having a ceased object" is what was stated, even that statement would not be accepted by the former proponent.

For if that were the case, then—as in the instances such as "adverting is wholesome"—since the condition of immediate antecedence (*anantara-paccaya*) would be established for something included within another term, one would have to say:
"Adverting with a present object is a condition, by way of immediate antecedent condition, for aggregates with past objects. Yet, this has not been stated.
But why has the fact that knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) has the present as its object (*paccuppannārammaṇatā*) been investigated in this way?

Is it not stated in the analyses (*vibhaṅga*) of these [dependent origination factors]—namely, "a past state is a condition for a present state; a future state is a condition for a present state by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*)"—that "past aggregates are a condition for the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (*iddhividhañāṇa*), for the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*), and for the knowledge of recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*)"?
“Future aggregates are related to the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*),

the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*), and to adverting (*āvajjanā*) by way of object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*); and in the triad of arisen [states],

“unarisen aggregates and arising aggregates are related to the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of future states, and to adverting by way of object condition.”

Having included the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) with the statement, "Adverting is related to [the mind] by way of object-condition," it is stated in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the formula "a present phenomenon is related to a present [phenomenon]" that "present aggregates are related to the knowledge of supernormal powers (*iddhividhañāṇa*) and to adverting by way of object-condition";
and in the "Arising Triplet" (*uppannatika*), it is stated that "arisen aggregates are related to the knowledge of supernormal powers..."

Since only this much is stated—“Adverting is a condition for [the consciousness] by way of object-condition”—it is understood that “knowledge of others’ minds does not operate with respect to a present consciousness.
For if it were to so operate, then, as with the preceding cases, the inclusion of “knowledge of others’ minds” would have had to be made for the others as well.
This is true; however, it has been abbreviated by way of showing the method, which is to be understood.
It is understood from the Pāḷi: “A state with a past object is a condition, by way of object-condition, for a state with a present object;
a state with a future object is [a condition] for a state with a present object; a state with a present object is [a condition] for a state with a present object.

For in the commentaries (*vibhaṅga*) on these, it is said: “By means of the knowledge of penetration of minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*), [one knows] the mind of one possessing a present mind that has a past object...”
[He] knows. Present aggregates with past objects are a condition, by way of object-condition, for the adverting of the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa).
[Thinking: "By the knowledge of others' minds, one knows the mind of one possessing a present mind with a future object...
[and so on] ...by the knowledge of others' minds, one knows the mind of one possessing a present mind with a present object. Present objects..."

“Present aggregates are a condition for the advertence of the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariyañāṇa) by way of object-condition”—thus it is stated that the knowledge of penetration of minds occurs with a present object.
It should be understood that this investigation was undertaken for that very reason.

“Of those” (*tesaṃ*) means “of those two knowledges”; this is the genitive case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). “Wholesome aggregates” (*kusalā khandhā*) refers to the [supernormal] powers of the knowledge of supernormal feats (*iddhividha*), the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa*), and the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsa*).

This is a description using the plural number; it does not depend on the knowledge of penetration of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) or the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their deeds (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*).

If it is argued that this does not prove that those [states] have the four aggregates as their object, we say no. For elsewhere it is stated: "Aggregates without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitakkavicāramattā khandhā*), as well as sustained thought itself, are related to the knowledge of penetration of others' minds, the knowledge of recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*), and the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*) by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*)," and: "Aggregates with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakkasavicārā*)..."

Because it is stated that "the aggregates and applied thought are a condition for the knowledge of penetration into others' minds, the knowledge of recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of future states, by way of object-condition," the plural designation is used even when referring to the knowledge of penetration into others' minds; this is because the meaning [of the plural] is thus established.

Likewise, regarding the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their deeds (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*), [it is said]: "The aggregates devoid of applied thought but possessing sustained thought..."

Is it not the case that, because [the phrase] "and investigation" (*vicāro*) and so forth is not mentioned in such passages, the state of having the four aggregates as its object is not established? No; for there is another reason for its non-mention there.
For by the knowledge of the destination according to karma (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*), the four aggregates associated with karma are grasped with karma as the primary factor.

Just as the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*)—by virtue of its preliminary work—grasps the distinction between [states] with applied thought and so forth, and the distinction between those with lust and so forth, [so too does this knowledge].
One analyzes the mind, yet one does not analyze it with such differentiation; rather, one analyzes the aggregate as a whole by way of its function.

Therefore, in the context of making such a distinction—as in the passage beginning, "the aggregates without applied thought but with sustained thought, and sustained thought itself"—this was not stated;

it was not because the four aggregates are not the object [of that knowledge]. This, then, is the reason for its non-mention. Some [hold] that even there, regarding the knowledge of recollection of past lives...
They indeed recite [the text] thus: “...of the knowledge of the destination according to karma and of the knowledge of the future.

For that [knowledge] is not incapable of making manifest the classification of karma according to its divisions into wholesome and unwholesome, nor into those with applied thought and so forth. Indeed, the manifestation of the state of misconduct and good conduct is itself the manifestation of the specific association with greed and so forth, or non-greed and so forth.
1435. Regarding the phrase "by way of the absence of a personal internal state":

because it is a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*), if it were not a personal internal state by any definition whatsoever, it is described as "exclusively external" precisely because of its entirely external character. It is not because it is a non-existent phenomenon (*asabhāva-dhamma*) that it is external;
for, unlike the *kasiṇa* and so forth, there is no possibility of even a mere personal internal state existing in what is non-existent. This is because it is a non-existent phenomenon.
The intention is that since there is no such thing as an internal state consisting of the kasiṇas and so forth, it was not mentioned in the "Internal Triplet" (ajjhattattika).
The connection is that all of that—the sphere of nothingness and so on—is stated in the "Object-of-Past-Object Triplet" (atītārammaṇattika) as "having an indeterminable object" (navattabbārammaṇa).
And here, the meaning of "stated" (vutta) is that it has been made manifest by these reasons: because it is permitted and because of the verbal expression.
Now, the *tanti* (the canonical text) draws in that base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*)—which was stated as "this is the base of nothingness"—by means of the word "that" (*taṃ*).

As for the meaning stated here: even though the base of nothingness is mentioned here [in this context], it is said with reference to its having a single object together with that [base] within the triad of past objects;
for it is stated that wholesome states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*), etc., have an indeterminable object (*navattabbārammaṇatā*).

"Others do not accept that [explanation], on the grounds that 'here too it is intended to show that those [objects] have the status of being objects that cannot be so designated; thus, when that is stated, they too are already stated, and for that reason they are not mentioned separately. For there is no such figurative statement (lesavacana) in the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa*.
If there were, then in the triad concerning limited objects (*parittārammaṇa*), as to which of the [mental states] having a common object possess limited objects and so forth..."
And "inexpressibility" has already been stated. Furthermore, in the triad concerning past objects, having stated only one among them, nothing else should be said.

Likewise, in the triad of feelings, regarding those with identical feelings for whom association with pleasant feeling has been stated, having stated only one in the description of joy within the triad of jhāna factors, nothing else should be said. The same applies to the descriptions of equanimity-associated states and so forth.

It should be applied. However, because the extraction of the meaning has already been performed in the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa* without the inclusion of "stain" (*lesa*), just as with the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), when there is the state of being "not-to-be-stated" (*navattabba*) within the triad of internal objects for sense-sphere wholesome states and so forth, those too should have been stated as "not-to-be-stated";
yet they were not. Therefore, even though non-existence is common [to all], it is by means of that specific mode of occurrence of non-existence which results in an undesirable state...

The base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), while occurring, cannot be said to be "arisen"; because that occurrence does not exist, those [bases] were not stated to be "indeterminate" (*navattabba*).
For the kasiṇas and so forth are produced solely by a specific mode of grasping and do not exist by way of intrinsic nature;
thus, it was stated that their objects are "external" by virtue of being grasped externally. However, the base of nothingness is not [defined] by way of external grasping.
It is said that it cannot be stated [that omniscient knowledge] does not arise in the manner of internal apprehension, nor that it arises as internal apprehension.
However, the mode of apprehension by which the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) arises is not the same mode by which omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) arises.

If it were to arise in that same way, it too would become merely the base of nothingness. For just as [it is impossible for the objects and specific modes of arising of the defilements (*kilesa*)...]*
The omniscient knowledge that knows everything does not grasp it in the same way as those [beings] grasp it, because even that [knowledge] would fall into the state of being defiled;

likewise, knowing the mode of occurrence of the base of nothingness according to its true nature, it does not grasp that base of nothingness as one would grasp it [as an object], so how much less so anything else?
Therefore, it was not stated that the wholesome states of the sense-sphere are "not to be described" [in this context].
This is the determination of those teachers who do not accept that there exists a single entity called "separation," which constitutes the objective domain of the base of nothingness.
However, since a resultant [state] does not become an object for anyone, the resultant base of infinite space [is excluded] from among the resultant and other bases of infinite consciousness.
The meaning is that it is not the object of anything; likewise, the base of nothingness is not the object of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

For instance, in the *Vipākattika* (Treatise on Ripening), among the questions based on the roots of "states subject to ripening," "states not subject to ripening," and "states neither subject nor not subject to ripening," it says:

"Wholesome consciousness of the base of infinite space is a condition, by way of object-condition, for wholesome consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness; wholesome consciousness of the base of nothingness..."
It is said: "The wholesome [state] of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition, by way of object-condition, for its own resultant and functional [states];

likewise, the functional state of the base of infinite space is for the functional state of the base of infinite consciousness; and the functional state of the base of nothingness is for the functional state of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
However, this is not the case regarding those states rooted in resultant phenomena, such as the resultants of the base of infinite space and the base of nothingness.

It is stated: “The [resultant] of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for wholesome and functional [states] by way of object-condition.

This means that once one has emerged from a resultant state, there is no possibility of mental directing; the sense is that there is no directing of the mind after having made a resultant state its object. For indeed, once a resultant state has been made the object, there is no directing.
"His own aggregates, etc. means that by taking the immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandha) as "aggregates," the word "etc. includes matter (rūpa). Or, when referring to what is internal, the word "etc.
includes the designation (paññatti) of "self. This same method applies to the inclusion of the aggregates and so forth belonging to others.
Furthermore, by including the designation, he refers to the designations based on the non-faculties such as the kasiṇa-meditations and so on. By the word "etc."...

Or rather, in the context of grasping designations, I shall explain everything regarding "derived designation" (*upādāyapaññatti*). Among [the objects of] karma and so forth, it should be understood that karma is internal, the sign of karma is both internal and external, and the sign of destiny (*gatinimitta*) is external.
However, for one being reborn as a worm within one's own body, even the sign of destiny could be internal. This was the case for Mallikā when she was giving the rice-porridge.
The Blessed One manifested a smile on account of the king’s attainment of the position of chief queen, the attainment of Arahatship by the minister Santati while seated upon the neck of an elephant,
and the realization of Pratyekabodhi by the flower-garland maker Sumana as he was making an offering with a handful of flowers.
In this triad, they are said to find no place because they did not find a place in the dyads of limited object and past object;
however, here they are not "not-to-be-stated," meaning that they do find a single object among the internal and so forth.
For these five [jhānas] have the kasiṇa as their object due to the four kasiṇas—namely, the universal-footed, space, light, and the fourth kasiṇa—and the fourth divine abiding (brahmavihāra).
Because they have concepts as their object, and because the fourth [meditation on] breathing has the sign as its object, they are "external objects. Regarding the phrase "of one's own body and mind":
this means "of one's own body and mind"; there is no purpose [in mentioning them separately], therefore the meaning is that it is not an internal object.

Regarding the phrase "or of matter not bound to the faculties," here the words "or of the three kinds of concepts" should also be brought in by means of the word "or" (*vā*); this is an indication of the method.
Or rather, it should be viewed thus: "At such a time, there is an external object.
The commentary on the extraction of the meaning of the triplets is finished.
The commentary on the extraction of the meaning of the dyads.
1473. "Pride... [etc. ...arises in one way"—this is stated by way of showing the unmentioned modes.

Otherwise, since pride arises together with the fetters of sensual lust and ignorance, it would have to be said that it arises in two ways. This same method applies to the craving for existence and so forth. Likewise, regarding the phrase "doubt...":
here, the meaning of "thus" (*tathā*) is "in one way" (*ekadhā*).

1511. "In those associated with volitional formations" (*sasaṅkhārikesu*) should be understood merely as a demonstration of the occasion for the arising of the hindrance of sensual desire together with the other three hindrances;
it is not for the purpose of demonstrating that it necessarily arises there along with them, because dullness-and-drowsiness (*thinamiddha*) is not fixed [in its occurrence].
"By way of the lower limit": since restlessness arises in all unwholesome states, there are two [types of consciousness] accompanied by restlessness.
The meaning is that in other cases, when there is an absence of sloth-and-torpor (thīna-middha) and worry (kukkucca), three [hindrances] arise at the very least; thus it is said, "two or three.

However, regarding the simultaneous arising of as many as possible, since the possibility exists for them to be both hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and associated with hindrances (*nīvaraṇa-sampayutta*), the word "two" was stated in order to show their minimum occurrence. From that...
The word "three" is stated in order to show that this meaning also occurs in the case of their simultaneous arising (*sahuppatti*).
The expression "two or three" is an indefinite designation meaning either two or three; thus, it is understood that there may even be four or five.
Furthermore, where there is simultaneous arising, there are both hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and those associated with hindrances (*nīvaraṇa-sampayutta*); such is the characteristic of this [state].
"This is the demonstration" means that where four or five [mental factors] arise, there this point is established.
And having done so, it is said "two or three" in the section on the defilements (*kilesagocchaka*).

For by way of demonstrating their characteristics, both the defilements and those associated with defilements are mentioned; it is not by way of demonstrating the actual occurrence of all those that are possible.
