If restlessness arises in all unwholesome states, why is it said that "the hindrance of restlessness arises in a mental state associated with restlessness"?
It is for the purpose of showing the specific object of restlessness when it is devoid of the other hindrances among the five hindrances mentioned in the Suttanta.
However, the sixth hindrance [restlessness] is [treated] in the Abhidhamma as distinct from the others...
Regarding "accompanied by": for that consciousness which is free from the other hindrances, there is no specific object whatsoever.

Because there is no possibility of its arising without those factors accompanied by it, and because there is no occurrence of a mental state characterized by such [hindrances], there is indeed no specific object;
therefore, it is said that "it arises in all unwholesome states. However, as for the mental state accompanied by restlessness...
The specific object of restlessness, characterized by its tendency to follow after other mental states (sesadhammā), is what is meant here.

Therefore, although restlessness arising in all unwholesome states could be taken generally as the "hindrance of restlessness" (uddhaccanīvaraṇa), he said, "it arises in consciousness-moments accompanied by restlessness," in order to manifest it through its own specific object. And thus:

It should be understood that this exposition was made in order to define the five hindrances— those accompanied by greed and mental distress, and those accompanied by agitation, doubt, and restlessness— with respect to specific objects, and then to reveal the sixth [hindrance] as their pervasive factor. However,
some take the term "accompanied by agitation" in its general sense to include all forms of agitation under the heading of "agitation," and [proceed] with that...
They say, "in the consciousness-arising accompanied by that [restlessness]," but this meaning is not highly regarded because,
unlike the twelfth consciousness-arising, all unwholesome consciousness-arisings are not characterized by restlessness. Furthermore, if they were characterized, then—
as in the case of the phrase "in the eight greed-accompanied [consciousnesses]" and so on— it would have to be stated as "in twelve" in order to exclude other consciousness-arisings.

...because it ought to be stated as "in those accompanied by restlessness. However, since restlessness is not specifically distinguished [as a separate factor] among all unwholesome states—just as the hindrance of ignorance (avijjā-nīvaraṇa) is not—it might be said that this [hindrance of restlessness] also "arises in all unwholesome states. Yet it was not so stated;
therefore, the meaning should be understood according to the method already explained. And because the hindrance of restlessness, like the hindrance of ignorance, exists in all unwholesome states...
Therefore, in the *Nikkhepakanda*, it is stated: "The hindrance of sensual desire is both a hindrance and associated with the hindrance of restlessness," and so forth.
Consequently, one must seek the intended meaning [of this passage] without assuming that the hindrance of restlessness arises in the very same moment of consciousness as [the other hindrances].
In the *Kilesagocchaka* (Cluster of Defilements), the ten bases of defilement beginning with greed (*lobha*) are presented here in the Abhidhamma in this very sequence.

Therefore, since there is no specific object for the defilement of restlessness (*uddhacca*)—which is mentioned here alone when it is excluded from the other defilements mentioned alongside it—it is not explained by way of a specific object;
rather, it is stated: "Restlessness, shamelessness (*ahirika*), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*) are present in all unwholesome states."
It is said: "it arises. Regarding the description of the defilements and the defiled state:

since the term "defiled state" does not have the same meaning as the term "associated with defilements," but rather indicates being scorched and afflicted by impurity alone, therefore, instead of providing a description identical to the description of "associated with defilements," it is stated: "those very defilements are both defilements and defiled."

1577. Regarding the phrase "two or three defilements" (*dve tayo kilesā*): some say that here the expression "two or three" is used by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhi*) based on the context mentioned in the *Hetu-gocchaka* and other sections.

If it were spoken by way of conventional usage without regard for the actual meaning, then in the *Gantha-gocchaka* one would have to say, "where two or three ties (*ganthā*) arise together. And as for what they say: "Where... [the text continues].
"The word *ekato* (together) is meaningful in the context of the group of defilements (*kilesagocchaka*) because it is possible for two or three [defilements] to arise together with others;
however, it is not so in the context of the group of causes (*hetugocchaka*) and so forth, since the intended meaning can be understood even without it.

This too is incorrect, because even in the context of the group of causes and so forth, the word *ekato* serves the purpose of excluding the inclusion of both the causes themselves and those associated with the causes when there is a diverse arising. Therefore...
And having avoided the application of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*) and etymological interpretation (*anvatthakathā*), the meaning should be understood according to the very method already stated.

By the passage beginning "Lobha [arises] in six ways," etc., it should be understood that by showing the simultaneous arising of greed, aversion, and delusion with others, their simultaneous arising with greed and the rest is also shown. The remainder is of plain meaning.
The explanation of the section on the commentary is finished.
Four thousand and three hundred more—
these are the words in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* that illuminate the meaning of the verses.
Requested with due respect by one named Dhammamitta,
this commentary on the hidden meaning of the words was composed by Ānanda, known by the name Subuddhi.
Thus ends the *Līnatthapadavaṇṇanā* to the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
The Sub-commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī is completed.
